News.title: Brits to bask in 38C highs tomorrow in 5th UK heatwave – as Burnham calls first Cobra meeting amid extreme heat warning
News.content:
BRITS are expected to bask in 38C heat tomorrow during the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer.

Andy Burnham will chair his first Cobra meeting in response to the extreme heat, which has caused widespread wildfires and plunged many parts of the country into drought.



The Prime Minister will meet with ministers, officials, and agencies today as temperatures continue to rise, with the Met Office issuing rare amber “extreme heat” warnings for tomorrow.

Today, Brits are expected to enjoy dry and sunny weather – perfect conditions for the total eclipse this evening.



In the northwest there will be some isolated outbreaks of rain and partly cloudy, but generally warm temperatures.

Thursday could see temperatures rise to a balmy 38C with very hot conditions expected across much of England and Wales and potentially some evening showers in the northeast.



Rare amber “extreme heat” warnings are in place for London and parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday.

Met Office chief forecaster Chris Bulmer said: “While the peak heat will be more short-lived than recent heatwaves, temperatures widely into the mid-30s Celsius on Thursday brings the potential for impacts for some, which is why a Met Office warning has been issued.



“High pressure is now becoming dominant and temperatures will build day by day.

“Southerly and south-easterly winds will also tap into the hot conditions over Europe which helps develop this further notable heat in what has been a hot and dry summer so far for many in the south of the UK.”

The Government has urged the public to pay attention to UK Health Security Agency heat health alerts, and advised people should drink plenty of fluids and check in on family, friends and neighbours who may be at high risk.



Nearly three quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, after a record dry July and very dry start to August has combined with high temperatures to put pressure on water resources.

Southern Water has applied for a rare non-domestic drought order which would ban businesses from non-essential water use, including cleaning cars and filling swimming pools, saying an “exceptional” lack of rain has threatened supplies in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.

It warned that 165,000 people in the Southampton West supply area could face restricted supplies, with Environment Secretary Angela Eagle to decide on the application, which would be the first such ban since May 2006.

These hot conditions have led to the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June.

Ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), Home Office, and Department for Health will attend, and the Environment Agency will also be present.



A No.10 spokesperson said: “The Prime Minister will chair a meeting of COBR – the government emergency committee – this afternoon on the UK’s ongoing response to extreme heat, wildfires and drought.

“We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units.

“We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment.”

This comes as Steve Wright, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union (FBU), warned the UK faces a national emergency “right now” with fires across the country.

Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August alone, while July was the busiest month on record for wildfires with 458 incidents, the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) said.



Steve told Times Radio: “In many parts of the country, firefighters do not have the new modern equipment to deal with these.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They do not have the new modern personal protective equipment, the lightweight fire kit that we wear, the right helmets, lightweight helmets, breathable uniforms to make sure they’re better protected, their health is protected when they’re out dealing with these incidents for hours and hours on end.”

The Government said it had announced £97 million in new funding to upgrade national firefighting capabilities, including off-road vehicles and specialist equipment.

News.title: ‘I have lots of threats you don’t know about’, Trump says as he confirms secret jet switch to throw off Iran’s assassins
News.content:
DONALD Trump has confirmed he secretly switched jets as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month to throw off Iran’s assassins.

The US president was smuggled off Air Force One by a Turkish airport catering truck to board a different military jet in Ankara after multiple suspected threats.



On Tuesday night, Trump said: “I go by the Secret Service and the military.

“They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane. I just have to do what they say.”



Trump’s security team had reportedly been briefed on two potential dangerous situations which prompted the secret jet switch on July 8.

One saw a person armed with a shoulder-fired missile had been spotted near the Nato summit, US intelligence sources told The New York Times.



And a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane had also been detected, officials told CBS News.

Trump didn’t confirm the two threats but he told reporters aboard Air Force One: “I guess there was a threat out there.

“I have a lot of threats that you don’t know about.”

Trump previously said he was Iran’s “number one target” during the summit in Ankara.



The high-stakes switch raised questions about whether the journalists and White House staff left on the decoy plane were in danger.

But Trump revealed the aircraft he flew on was “at greater risk”.

“I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for”, he said.



As well as the missile threat in Ankara, Iranian operatives reportedly knew where the US president was staying in the city, including the floor of the building.

Ahead of the extraordinary mission, the public were told Trump would fly on an older version of Air Force One.

On social media Trump claimed he was taking the legacy 747 back “for old time’s sake”.

But the US president actually used a third plane, Air Force C-32A.

Footage from the Ankara airport shows a catering truck with a raised box bed with its dock raised on the far side of Air Force One as Trump boarded the plane.



As the press boarded moments later, the truck drove virtually unnoticed to the nearby C-32A jet which carried Trump to the UK.

Those aboard Air Force One were instructed to keep their window shades closed at the request of the Secret Service.

The stealthy relocation came after a night of heavy US strikes on Iran.



Both flights landed at RAF Mildenhall and Trump appeared before TV cameras and descended the decoy plane’s stairs.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

White House communications director Steven Cheung said: “The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff.

“As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ by man near UK city centre in early hours as cops release CCTV
News.content:
HORROR ATTACK Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ by man near UK city centre in early hours as cops release CCTV

A WOMAN was allegedly sexually assaulted in the early hours as police release images of a man they are looking for.

The man reportedly approached the victim and led her to a secluded area just before 4am in Hyson Green, Nottinghamshire.

He then left the area and walked down Alfreton towards Nottingham city centre.

Police have urged anyone with information to make themselves known.





A spokesperson for Nottinghamshire Police said: “Police have released an image of a man they are looking to trace following a sexual assault in Hyson Green.

“The incident happened on Saturday 4 July near Alfreton Road just before 4am.

“The victim was approached by a man, unknown to her, before she was led into a secluded area.

“He then left the scene, walking down Alfreton Road in the direction of the city centre.

“Detectives have carried out extensive CCTV inquiries, forensics, and taken witness statements, but so far no one has been arrested in connection with this incident.

“They are now releasing an image of a man that could help them with their investigation and are calling on the public’s help to identify him.”

Detective Sergeant Jacqueline Sharpe, who is leading the investigation, said: “We have carried out multiple lines of inquiry since the incident was reported to us.

“As part of our investigation we would like to trace a man who could help us further our inquiries and are calling on the public’s help.



“Do you know the man in the image? Are you the man in the image? Please get in touch with us as soon as possible.”

News.title: Human skeletons unearthed during redevelopment of busy roundabout in UK city centre
News.content:
GRIM FIND Human skeletons unearthed during redevelopment of busy roundabout in UK city centre

ELEVEN human skeletons have been unearthed during a roundabout redevelopment.

The skeletons were discovered during the redevelopment of the Queensgate roundabout in the centre of Peterborough.

The remains have been removed and will be reburied in Church of England burial grounds elsewhere in the city.

Police were called to the roundabout following reports of one skeleton before a further 10 were found.





The force have confirmed they were not treating the site as a crime scene.

The remains are part of a cemetery from the Georgian and Victorian era which was cleared when subways were built in the 1970s.

The grim discovery was made as part of the as work to remove two of the underpasses for the new Peterborough Station Quarter redevelopment.

The new City Link aims to create a more direct route for cyclists and pedestrians from Peterborough Railway Station to the city centre.

News.title: M54 closed after lorry carrying 70 tonnes of hay catches fire in middle of lane – sparking long commuter delays
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

LORRY INFERNO M54 closed after lorry carrying 70 tonnes of hay catches fire in middle of lane – sparking long commuter delays

THE M54 has closed after a lorry carrying 70 tonnes hay burst into flames in the middle of the motorway causing rush hour chaos.

The westbound carriageway was closed between junction three for Albrighton and junction four for Telford after lorry caught fire last night.



Smoke was sent billowing into the sky as six fire engines were deployed just before 6.30pm.

The flames have since been extinguished but the road remains closed this morning while recovery and clean-up crews are on the scene.



National Highways said road resurfacing may need to take place and urged drivers to follow the diversion routes.

A spokesperson said: “The M54 in Staffordshire/Shropshire is closed westbound between J3 (Albrighton) and J4 (Telford) due to an HGV fire.



“The carriageway was closed shortly after 7pm on 11th August due to a lorry transporting hay which caught fire.

“Shropshire Fire and Resue services are in attendance.

“National Highways Traffic Officers are also in attendance assisting with traffic management.”

News.title: Five 17-year-old boys dead after their car plunged off cliff with driver and front passenger ejected from vehicle
News.content:
HORROR SMASH Five 17-year-old boys dead after their car plunged off cliff with driver and front passenger ejected from vehicle

FIVE teenage boys have died after their car plunged off a cliff in a horror crash, with two of the youngsters thrown from the vehicle.

The group of 17-year-old friends were all pronounced dead after emergency crews discovered the wreckage on a steep hillside in Colorado on Sunday morning.



Cops said the car had driven off the edge of a cliff in Grand Junction, around 245 miles from Denver, late on Saturday evening.

First responders rushed to the scene at around 7.45am the following day and found the vehicle on the hillside, according to the Grand Junction Police Department.





All five boys, who lived in Grand Junction, were pronounced dead at the scene.

The Mesa County Coroner’s Office said three of the teens had been wearing seatbelts, including the driver and front-seat passenger.

The other two were not wearing seatbelts and were ejected from the vehicle during the crash, officials said.

Investigators are now looking at whether speed played a role in the tragedy.



It remains unclear which of the teenagers was driving.

Authorities have not officially named the victims because they were under 18, but devastated relatives and friends have identified them online as Braden Taylor, Tristan Tucker, Titus Gould, William Simms and Tyler Martinez.

Heartbreaking tributes have since poured in for the five friends.

Tucker was remembered as being “full of life, potential, and a free spirit” on a GoFundMe page launched following his death.

He had reportedly been preparing to start his senior year of high school and was about to get his driver’s license.



Simms’ sister Emily confirmed her younger brother had also died alongside his friends.

“My sweet sweet baby brother and his best friends left this world too soon,” she wrote on Facebook.



Emily also launched a fundraiser to support her grieving family.

“Our family is heartbroken and trying to process a loss we still cannot fathom. We were all very close, and losing him so suddenly has turned our world upside down,” she wrote.

A Meal Train fundraiser has meanwhile been set up to support Gould’s family.

His mom, Larissa Gould, has not publicly spoken about her son’s death but changed her Facebook profile picture on Monday morning to a photo of herself with him.

Friends and loved ones flooded the comments with messages of support and condolences.



Taylor’s grandfather Calvin Wilken also confirmed the 17-year-old was among those killed.

“Very sad news our youngest grandson Braden 17 died in a car rollover down 5 ledges of a very steep drop off over looking the railroad tracks and the Gunnison River,” Wilken wrote alongside a picture of his grandson.

“He was a passenger with 4 of his buddies, all deceased. Just a few blocks from their old house on the ridge top housing development above.”

Martinez’s grandmother Debbie Gallegos Martinez also shared her heartbreak after learning her grandson had died.

“With a heavy heart and tears rolling down my cheek my grandson was one of this [sic] boys,” she wrote on Facebook.



Another relative, Angela Chris Martinez, pleaded for prayers for all five families.

“Please keep our family in your prayers and prayers for the families that lost your boys, this is devastating and heartbreaking,” she said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Martinez’s mom, Aimee Huffman, has also shared pictures of herself with her late son in the days since the tragedy.

The Grand Junction Police Department said its investigation into the fatal crash remains ongoing.

News.title: Children among 18 killed and at least 32 injured after truck rolled over in deadly crash in Egypt
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRUCK SMASH HORROR Children among 18 killed and at least 32 injured after truck rolled over in deadly crash in Egypt

AT LEAST 18 people, many of them children, were killed after two pick up trucks collided in Egypt.

Another 30 were injured after the trucks carrying workers crashed and flipped over in the Al-Dawawis area of Ismailia on Tuesday.



A major emergency response was launched with 30 ambulances and police cars deployed to the scene.

The wounded and dead were transported to a nearby hospital.



“Most of the dead are children 13 and 14 years old,” a medical source at the hospital told AFP.

The youngest victim was 10 years old.

Victims’ families gathered outside Al Qasasin Specialized Hospital as they waited to receive the bodies of their loved ones.

Jomana Waleed, a 16-year-old survivor of the crash, revealed her sister’s heart-breaking last words as she stood outside the hospital.



She told AFP: “She said I want to see mama.

“And then she stopped breathing, she was dead.”

Security forces are scouring the scene to determine the cause of the crash.



The truck was transporting workers from two villages in Sharqiya who were employed at a farm in Ismailia, Al Jazeera reports.

Dangerously overcrowded pick-ups are a regular mode of transport for informal workers in Egypt.

At least 1.3million minors are engaged in some form of child labour in Egypt, according to official figures.

And children under the age of 15 are the most common victims of fatal road accidents – which are on the rise across the country.

The Ministry of Labour said it would provide financial support to the families of those killed and injured.



Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi had ordered an investigation into the accident which remains ongoing.

It comes after two people were killed and 36 were left injured after a coach full of tourists smashed into a truck near Hurghada on the Red Sea coast.

Local authorities said the coach belonged to a Red Sea tourism company.

The two dead were confirmed as the coach driver and one of the passengers.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Hurghada is around 290 miles south of Cairo, Egypt’s capital.



The area is popular with tourists, who are drawn to its long, golden beaches and shimmering blue waters.

News.title: Six burning riddles that haunt Essex Boys murders 30 years on… including fate of ‘corrupt’ supergrass & hitman theory
News.content:
KNOWN as ‘the most notorious crime scene in British history’, the Essex Boys Murders have captured the imagination of amateur sleuths for three decades.

Despite two men being imprisoned for the grisly gunshot killings back in 1998, theories about the so-called ‘real killers’ and clues allegedly missed by investigators continue to swirl – and is now it’s back in the spotlight as a documentary examining the case lands on Netflix.



The bodies of Tony Tucker, 38, Patrick Tate, 37, and Craig Rolfe, 26, were discovered in 1995 inside a Land Rover down a quiet lane on a farmer’s field in Rettenden, Essex, and the trio had a troubled past.

They were small-time gangsters known for peddling ecstasy and other drugs in Essex nightclubs and allegedly had a legion of enemies.

Police insist they were lured to a quiet spot for a drug deal and slayed by shotgun-wielding assassins in what was described as a “brutal gangland execution”.



The men jailed for their murder – Michael Steele, nicknamed the ‘Angel of Death’, and Jack Whomes – were career criminals, yet protested their innocence until their release.

The constant denials led to multiple failed appeals and ultimately saw them serve a longer time behind bars.

Now further speculation has emerged after Netflix released 2023 documentary Murder of the Essex Boys: Blood and Betrayal, which is number two in the UK Top Films category and has been hailed as the “best watch ever”.

In December, the 30th anniversary of the grisly executions, The Sun revealed another fresh twist in the tale, with unearthed tapes revealing how Whomes’ brother – a long-time campaigner for his freedom – had nobbled a key witness during the trial.

While the bombshell revelation led one former Essex detective to say it was “time to draw a line” under the case, further challenges may yet lie ahead, with the Criminal Cases Review Commission currently considering an application by a team of private detectives working pro-bono.



Skeptics around the prosecution’s argument point to it mainly relying on the testimony of a so-called “supergrass”.

Snitch Darren Nicholls, who was a paid police informant, gave evidence after being arrested with 10kg of cannabis in his van and claimed to be Steele and Whomes’ getaway driver.

Questions about how reliable this evidence was, alongside other theories related to the evidence and motives for other potential suspects, have led to enduring speculation.

Having recently investigated the case during a visit to sleepy Rettendon, which still remains haunted by the notorious crime three decades on, it was clear to me that many locals still harbour doubts and frustration over what happened that fateful night.

So what are the burning riddles that have endured for 30 years – and, as exasperated residents told me, still see hundred of amateur sleuths pile into the village every year?



Who were the Essex Boys’ enemies?

Police are certain they jailed the right men for the killings – yet if theories are to be believed, there would be no shortage of would-be-murderers with motives because The Essex Boys had plenty of enemies.

Bernard O’Mahoney, who ran security at Raquel’s nightclub where the trio peddled ecstasy at the height of the 90s rave scene, told us they were “failed drug dealers, robbers and low-life bullies” who often preyed on the weak.

He claimed everyone knew they “would never make it to the old folks’ home” and it was only a matter of time before they were killed, due to a series of violent incidents they were allegedly involved in.

There was the death of Leah Betts, who passed away on her 18th birthday after taking an ecstasy pill bought from the Essex Boys.



Some theories claim the gang were killed due to someone being disgusted by their drug peddling after the teen’s death became national news and appalled people across the country.

Meanwhile Bernard said the trio’s increased drug use made them so hostile they went “on a rampage, threatening everyone they encountered”, which could have provoked an attack.

They were also said to have angered two of Essex’s “most notorious and powerful ganglords”, who warned they would “end up dead”, according to the nightclub doorman.

It’s also claimed there were heated exchanges with a former Essex Boy, who many months before the killings, shot Tate while he sat on the loo and threw a brick at him through a window. He survived that initial attack.

Was it a revenge attack?



Another theory emerged from Marie Tate, mother of victim Pat, who claimed the deaths were a revenge killing after Tucker and Rolfe killed a man over a drug debt in 1994.

She claimed the victim was Kevin Whitaker, 28, whose body was found at the side of the road with needle puncture marks in his arm. Police concluded he died from a drug overdose.

Marie claimed her son Tate told her that the duo injected Whitaker with paralysing drug ketamine, so he was “powerless but conscious”, before injecting him again with Lignocaine, which killed him.

Friends of Whitaker, she alleged, “avenged his death” by taking out the trio in Rettendon. Police did not believe the incidents were linked.

There’s also the claim from a “mid-tier” East End villain called Billy Jasper, who insisted the trio were murdered over a drug debt owed to a major South London criminal and they hired an East London firm for the hit.



The crook, arrested in 1996 for armed robbery, claimed to have been paid £5,000 to be the getaway driver for the killing and testified at Whomes and Steele’s trial.

Some believe the murders were the act of a professional assassin, rather than a plucky criminal, due to the successful head shots on a dark night with no streetlights nearby.

Was it a drug deal gone wrong?

Bernard supports the drug-deal gone wrong claim, favoured by cops, however for many years he didn’t believe Steele or Whomes were behind it.

He claimed the trio were coaxed to meet their killers on the quiet lane by someone they had “previously threatened to kill”.



On the night they died, they travelled to a farmer’s field in Rettendon for a drug plot dummy run ahead of receiving £1million cocaine set to be flown in.

But Bernard claimed the Essex Boys had a different idea, telling The Sun had no intention to play fairly.

“They planned to bash up the guy who flew in the coke, take the coke and split it three ways,” he said.

However, as it transpired the whole thing turned out to be “a baited hook” according to Bernard.

The individuals the Essex Boys were planning to steal the cocaine from was Steele and Whomes, whom they had allegedly already defrauded of money in a previous dodgy weed deal.



Bernard said Tate received a gunshot wound to the stomach, and was the last to be shot in the head, because the gunman wanted him to die slowly as a final act of revenge.

The ex-bouncer added: “He’d been the catalyst of all the trouble that had been caused and so it was deemed essential that he should watch the murder of his friends before he was executed.”

Rolfe’s brother Brian, who was also involved in crime, recalls seeing his brother had “a gun in the glove compartment and two kilos of coke” in his car, the night before the murder.

However, O’Mahoney has since reversed his position on the killings and now believes Steele and Whomes were guilty.

He changed his stance after Whomes’ brother John, who had been campaigning for the conviction to be overturned, appeared to suggest to him during production of a 2015 documentary that his brother and Steele were guilty of the murders, despite his efforts to get them freed.



Did they Essex Boys know they were being set up?

Bernard tells us in the dying weeks ahead of the Boys’ passing, things were rather turbulent.

He alleges Tate and Tucker were spending nearly £1,000-a-day on crack cocaine and were becoming increasingly volatile due to being “out of their heads all the time”.

“They were like zombies,” Bernard told us. “Smoking that shit, then going to sleep, waking up and doing it again. They transformed into psychotic bullies, who couldn’t be reasoned with.”

After the death of Leah Betts, Tate was “going off his head” due to the world’s media descending upon Raquel’s nightclub.



Additionally, Bernard says around that time there was a botched £120,000 weed deal after they discovered only a third of the stash was real.

“Everything appeared to be going wrong,” Bernard says. But he insists they still had lofty ambitions and believed the fateful cocaine drop, which claimed their lives, would make them rich beyond their wildest dreams.

Bernard is certain they had no idea they were being lured into a trap when they visited the farm in Rettendon for a ‘dummy run’ of the cargo drop off.

He adds: “They were greedy, jumping for joy, thinking they would be millionaires. They even booked an 8pm meal to celebrate.”

It’s claimed Steele met them on a Hungry Horse car park nearby and directed them to the field where they would be gunned down by Whomes.



How soon they realised it was a trap is unclear. Could they have known when Steele got out of their car to open the farmer’s field gate and they realised there was no plane waiting for them? Or, maybe it was only when Whomes emerged from the bushes with a shotgun?

Was the ‘supergrass’ reliable?

The testimony of ‘Fat Darren’ Nicholls largely was responsible for the imprisonment of Steele and Whomes.

The investigation had stalled before the petty crook and police informant’s arrest in May 1996, when he was caught with 10kg of cannabis.

Nicholls told police he was the getaway driver, and that Steele had lured the trio to the murder spot, on Workhouse Lane, and a passenger in the boys’ Land Rover.



Upon arrival, Nicholls said Whomes jumped out of the bushes, handed Steele a shotgun and the duo blasted the gang to death.

The so-called ‘supergrass’ claimed Steele boasted, while driving off, that the trio “won’t f*** with us again”.

It was claimed weeks before the murder that Tate threatened to kill Steele after he lost money when one of their drug deals went wrong.

Nicholls pleaded guilty to drug running and was given a lenient sentence, a new identity and rehoused at a secret location upon his release.

At trial, even the judge Mr Justice Hidden remarked: “You must bear in mind it was in his own interest to become a prosecution witness – he hopes to get less time to serve.”



And while in prison, an inmate held in the same secure unit as Nicholls back in 1997, claimed the supergrass admitted he lied. Three others also testified that Nicholls confessed to being untruthful.

“He said the story he was supposed to tell in court was a pack of lies,” one of the witnesses said.

The prisoner initially chose to “ignore Darren’s perjury” because he believed there were “forensics, witnesses” and other evidence that proved Steele and Whomes’ guilt.

Describing his motivation for speaking out, he said: “Now I realise Darren wasn’t the cherry on the cake – he was the cake.”

During the killers’ 2006 appeal, judges concluded that Nicholls may have received up to £15,000 as part of a book deal on the case, prior to the duo’s trial.



He had also agreed to appear in a TV documentary about the case, which is suspected may also have led to a fee.

Appeal Court judges would later say Nicholls had a “corrupt” ­relationship with his Essex police handler, throwing further doubt on his testimony.

Why maintain their innocence?

Both of the killers maintained their innocence throughout, despite being career criminals heavily involved in the drugs trade.

This was considered unusual because it meant they served the full minimum terms for their sentences – and in fact, Steele remained in prison for a further four years.



While Whomes was released in 2021, Steele was only let out on licence back in May this year – neither have spoken to the press.

Bernard told us his suspected this could be because if either of them spoke out, it could land those who testified on their behalf in trouble for committing perjury – lying in court.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson confirmed the Essex Boys’ killers was let out under “strict conditions and intensive probation supervision”.

They said he “faces an immediate return to prison if he breaks the rules”. One of those conditions is not being permitted to discuss the case with journalists.

But according to Parole Board documents, Steele still maintains that “the killing was organised by another criminal and a corrupt police officer”.



Their inability to talk about the case has poured even more fuel on the flames, triggering further waves of speculation and theories.

Now, with Steele aged 82, it seems the chance to extract any more information from him about the case is fading fast and, if sleuths are to be believed, he may well take his secrets to the grave.

News.title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
News.content:
With most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.

But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.

People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.

Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses.

And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead.

They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.

Here are some viewing methods to try instead.

News.title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief warns
News.content:
The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.

The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.

Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.

But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong".

"Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure.

"I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."

On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs signed a letter to the prime minister calling for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, such as under the early release scheme.

The letter stated: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."

The police chiefs from Scotland, England, Wales and Northern Ireland also urged Andy Burnham to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.

Probation officers help former prisoners with housing, employment and access to benefits once in the community, and help protect the public by assessing the risk of further offending.

Their workload will increase substantially when more offenders - some of whom will have been convicted of violent offences - are released months earlier than planned as part of the Sentencing Act.

According to the chief inspector, probation caseload has increased by 8% over the last two years.

Much of that is down to a separate early release scheme which was implemented in 2024 after prisons nearly reached full capacity.

That scheme has led to tens of thousands of offenders being let out sooner.

When asked what risk the additional early releases due to start in the autumn could pose to the public, Jones said "that could be a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder".

One probation officer told the BBC the upcoming releases had put him and his colleagues into "a state of panic".

"We can't cope with this - we've been saying that to anybody who will listen.

"At the minute I think it's pure panic in terms of where we're at. I don't understand how there can be this level of pressure put on us.

"The worst that can happen is that things are missed, plans aren't put into place and we don't give people the level of service they need and that leads to serious further offences.

"That leads to death under supervision."

In a statement, an MoJ spokesperson said the department had exceeded its recruitment target for last year, with 1,389 trainee probation officers starting.

The spokesperson said this is "making sure the Probation Service has the resource it needs to keep dangerous offenders under closer surveillance than ever before".

"The Sentencing Act is restoring order to a prison system left on the brink of collapse, while our record Â£700m investment in probation and community punishment is ensuring staff have the resources, powers, and technology they need to manage offenders safely in the community," the spokesperson added.

News.title: Woman assaulted by double murderer says nightmare became 'real life' when police let him attack again
News.content:
A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on to kill and attack more women.

Laura, whose surname we are not using, said she had been trying to protect other women by reporting Levy in 2018, but feels betrayed by what he was later allowed to do after being released from jail.

Levy was convicted on Friday of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins and raping another woman in London in 2025. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.

He was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the Tube in London between 2023 and 2025.

Police, prosecutors and the courts made a series of disastrous decisions that left Levy free. He attacked 14 more women before being taken off the streets, despite being a sex offender who was monitored by the Met Police.

Levy was a registered sex offender because he sexually assaulted Laura â and a separate victim - in summer 2018.

Laura says that Levy is "evil" and that his attack "completely changed my life".

But she now realises that what she would "think about, dream about, have nightmares about was actually happening - he was actually still out preying on vulnerable women".

Waiving her anonymity, she said she had been trying to protect other women by ensuring that Levy was jailed.

"I feel like when I reported it, I was doing the right thing and I thought I was doing it to protect other women.

"I feel absolutely devastated for all of those women that have been affected by him â and the families."

Laura says she feels let down by the whole criminal justice system including the Met Police, the courts and judges who bailed Levy, as well as the Crown Prosecution Service.

"They're all as guilty for allowing him to continue to do what he was doing", she says.

"They could have prevented so many women from being hurt.

"They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."

News.title: Burnham to chair Cobra meeting on extreme heat as temperatures surge again
News.content:
The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.

It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June.

A spokesperson for No 10 said this summer was proving "challenging" in the UK, particularly for "firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units".

"We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment," they said.

The hottest weather this week is expected on Thursday across the Midlands, Eastern England, London and south-east England, Yorkshire and Humber.

Temperatures could potentially reach 38C which would equal the highest temperature of the summer so far recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on 26 June.

This would be the hottest August day since 2003, when 38.5C was recorded.

It is also likely to be the fourth calendar month this year to record 35C or more, which is unprecedented.

On Monday, drought officials declared 71.3% of England in drought, meaning there are a total of 45 million people now living in a drought area, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.

Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August, and 458 in July, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.

A fire in the New Forest has been burning since Sunday, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood.

Last week, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS should be "preparing for summer pressures now in the same way we prepare for winter".

She told LBC Radio plans were in place to respond to higher numbers of people coming in to A&E.

On Tuesday, the Met Office said this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, with the mean temperature currently at 16.48C set to surpass the figure set just last year.

This is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the Cobra meeting was just a first step, and a "climate emergency" had led to hundreds of deaths and was "stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit".

He called for "concrete action" and said he looked forward to hearing how Burnham intended to "prepare for the threats to come".

News.title: Serious failings found in new military crimes unit, leaked report finds
News.content:
A leaked Ministry of Defence (MoD) report, obtained by the BBC, has highlighted serious failings in a new military command set up to investigate the most severe crimes, including rape and sexual assault.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) was launched after the death of 19-year-old Gunner Jaysley Beck. An inquest found the Army's mishandling of sexual assault and harassment complaints made by Beck contributed to her taking her own life, and exposed "systemic failings".

However, an internal review highlighted ongoing concerns with the unit and warned the military still risks failing victims.

The MoD said the findings had been accepted and significant work has been undertaken since.

The DSCC was created in 2022 to investigate serious crimes independently, outside the military's chain of command.

However, the BBC can reveal that an internal review, which was carried out between 21 August 2025 and 12 November 2025 and overseen by a former senior civilian police officer, concluded that if the DSCC was subjected to scrutiny similar to civilian police forces there would be "a significant risk of (it) being graded as inadequate".

In a statement, the MoD said the review was commissioned "to provide honest challenge, identify areas of improvement and to help ensure the highest standards for victims and witnesses".

It added that following the findings, the DSCC had carried out significant work "including further investment in victim and witness support, strengthening governance and safeguarding arrangements and accrediting investigators to nationally recognised policing standards".

The DSCC was committed to transparency, continuous improvement and ensuring victims receive the support and service they deserve, the statement continued.

News.title: Homes near pylons to get £250 a year off energy bills – first sites revealed
News.content:
UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast the UK's power infrastructure had undergone decades of "woeful underinvestment".

He said he understood the objections of those living nearby, but added the pylons were "crucial" to ensure the National Grid maintained future resilience.

"I totally accept that people might not like that, but it is critical national infrastructure and it has to be built somewhere," he said.

"Building any kind of infrastructure in these communities does cause disruption. But that doesn't mean we shouldn't build any kind of infrastructure and I'm afraid in this country, for too long, we have taken that view, and the result is that we have been held back by not having the infrastructure the country needs."

Shanks added: "Either we go through decades of not upgrading the grid and take the risk that the grid will actually fail, but we also lose the opportunity of cheaper bills, homegrown power connecting.

"We're not prepared to take that risk."

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says Britain's electricity grid was largely designed for an era when power came from coal and gas-fired power stations, and now needs major upgrades to cope with growing amounts of renewable energy.

Ministers say the lack of capacity means some wind farms are sometimes paid to switch off because there is not enough network infrastructure available to carry the electricity to homes and businesses that need it.

Greg Jackson, chief executive of the UK's biggest domestic energy supplier, Octopus Energy, said the electricity system is inefficient, brittle and expensive.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the discount scheme was a "positive first step", adding that last year the UK spent more than Â£1bn paying wind farms to turn off on windy days.

"We should just be giving that electricity more cheaply to the people and businesses who live in the areas where we're generating it," he said.

"By doing that, you'd be able to stop wasting that money and instead put the electricity to use cutting bills for those people. But crucially cutting bills for everybody else as well because it's less wasteful."

News.title: Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
News.content:
Most of the incidents in Manchester, Liverpool and Sheffield involved private e-scooters, often on public roads, pavements or footpaths, despite that being illegal.

Private e-scooters are meant only for use on private land, with the owner's permission.

Half of the children injured were aged between 10 and 13. Nearly two-thirds were boys.

Most injuries were sustained by the rider - only 5% were pedestrians that had been hit by an e-scooter - and the most common cause was falling off the e-scooter.

Around 11% were collisions with a vehicle, which was often linked to more serious injuries.

Injuries to the arms and legs were the most common, followed by head or facial injuries.

The doctors say tougher laws are urgently needed. Helmet use is not mandatory in the UK, unlike some other countries.

Some have described the private e-scooter situation in the UK as the "Wild West" with few following any rules.

The researchers told the Emergency Medicine Journal that schools, local councils, youth groups and road safety campaigns all have a role to play.

"Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy, but there must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use," they say.

To legally rent an e-scooter in the UK, which can be used on roads and cycle lanes, you must be at least 16 and hold a full or provisional driving licence, and the rental company must provide appropriate insurance. Rental e-scooters typically have a limited top speed of around 15mph.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.

"It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under 16s, and we're bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets."

News.title: Watch: British driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record
News.content:
A British driver who was the first person to break the sound barrier in a car on land has set a new speed record, this time in a hydrogen-powered vehicle.

Andy Green, a 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot, reached a speed of 406mph (654km/h) at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, the fastest a hydrogen-powered car has ever travelled.

Green's record was measured as an average of two runs in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines, with a combined 1,600 brake horsepower (bhp).

In 1997, Green drove the jet-powered ThrustSSC across Nevada's Black Rock Desert at 763mph (1,228km/h), making him the first, and still the only person, to break the sound barrier on land.

News.title: PM admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Burnham told BBC's Wake up to Money he will deliver an "accumulation of smaller things" that "combine to take the pressure down" on household budgets.

He spoke of an overhaul of train fares and "more public control" of energy, water and housing but did not give details on how he would bring this about.

Burnham has made a number of announcements to help people with the cost of living since taking office, including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to 'subscription traps'.

Asked whether the changes he had announced were not significant to people struggling, he said: "I can accept criticism that this isn't enough, because I wouldn't say it's enough.

"But I take an approach to politics where I do what I can, when I can. Just take that little bit of pressure off and address an issue that you know needs addressing.

"It's not the end of the story," he added.

The prime minister, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, said he believed "more public control of essential services" such as water, energy and housing, "would mean we could get to a more substantial answer to the cost of living crisis".

On water, he said it would not be easy to reverse the privatisation of water companies in England and Wales that took place in the 1980s.

"But very much, I'm looking at what can be done. Same with energy."

He also said that, following the return of rail operators to public ownership, he wanted to "remodel the rail fares so that we can get more public benefit for people".

It comes as the government said on Wednesday that people living within 1,600ft (500m) of new upgraded electricity pylons and substations across Britain will receive a Â£250 annual discount on their bills for a decade.

News.title: 'As long as dad hides mum's body, he should not be released'
News.content:
"We would like to be able to lay her to rest, to give her the dignity she deserves - and to finally be able to say 'this is over'."

Cat Razzell is speaking about her mother, Linda, who disappeared on her way to work in Swindon in March 2002 when Cat was just 13.

Linda was in the process of divorcing Cat's father, Glyn Razzell, who was later convicted of her murder and sentenced to life in prison.

He has never revealed what happened to Linda and no trace of her has ever been found.

For almost a quarter of a century her family have been left without answers, unable to grieve properly or even hold a funeral.

The case is now under renewed scrutiny after the Parole Board decided in April that he could be released. That decision has since been referred to the High Court, with a two-day hearing held on Monday and Tuesday.

Cat believes her father should not be released until he admits what he did and reveals where her mother's body is.

News.title: Poorest areas should not house all asylum seekers, says Burnham
News.content:
Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.

The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.

The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.

Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised.

"I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said.

"We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."

But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."

After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.

HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast on Wednesday morning, immigration minister Anna Turley said the number of hotels had gone from a peak of 400 under the Conservatives to 160 under Labour, and pledged all of them would close by 2029.

Turley said the government had already saved Â£1bn by closing hotels and opening alternative, secure sites for asylum seekers, including two former military bases, student accommodation and former industrial sites around the country.

"I think this is about fairness and we won't be asking anybody to take more than they can, and we won't be asking anyone to take more than their fair share," she said.

"What we've seen in the past is places like Blackpool, and other communities around the country where housing is perhaps cheaper and more plentiful, have had to take more than their fair share of asylum seekers," she added.

"That's put a huge burden on local communities and created real civil unrest, so we want to make sure that we're managing the system much better in a more sustained way that's reducing the impact on local communities.

"It's important that everybody plays their fair share in that, and it's about making sure that no one community is more over-pressured or overburdened than others."

Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.

In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country.

"Andy Burnham just doesn't get it," he wrote on X.

"Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."

Government statistics, external showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.

The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.

The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.

The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.

The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.

It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607).

Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.

He complained about the government's dispersal system and said Greater Manchester's public services could not continue to support "disproportionate" numbers of people compared with elsewhere in the country.

Burnham at the time said the north-west of England was hosting 25% of the national population of asylum applicants who require housing and support - with Greater Manchester housing 70% of the region's numbers.

The then-Home Secretary Sajid Javid replied by promising to work towards a fairer distribution.

News.title: Boy, four, taken to hospital after fake squishy toy explodes in his face
News.content:
A mum says she feels "guilty" for buying a fake squishy toy that exploded in her son's face, resulting in him needing hospital treatment.

Jodanna Bevan bought the toys from Shein for her children after seeing them discounted.

Hudson, four, was squeezing his when it "popped and exploded all over his face", with Jodanna describing the filling as a "thick white substance" with a sandy texture.

While his bloodshot eyes "seemed OK" after washing them, Jodanna said by the next morning they were extremely swollen and he was unable to open them, so she took Hudson to hospital.

Shein said it took the claims seriously and the product was no longer available on its platform.

Hudson needed water flushed through each eye to correct their pH balance, and Jodanna, from Bridgend, said it was "horrendous as a parent to watch him go through that".

She said Hudson's vision was damaged but he was given eye drops to fix it.

Hudson, like children across the UK, was drawn to the toys after they became a sensation on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube.

They often resemble dumplings, but children "can't see what's inside the box so they're excited to see which one they get".

News.title: Criticism as thousands of seats empty at Europeans Athletics Championships
News.content:
Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships on Monday evening.

A crowd of 13,623 watched as Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt stormed to her first senior international title, in a stadium that has a capacity of 23,000.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with some describing them as "extortionate", while BBC commentator Steve Cram commented that spectator numbers were a "little disappointing".

But Birmingham 2026 organisers said they were "delighted" with ticket sales, which have "far surpassed" their targets with "Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity".

On Monday, Category A tickets for the home straight cost Â£150 with no concessions for juniors.

For the men's 100m final on Tuesday, those same seats cost Â£110, again with no concessions - while a similar ticket for the same final in Rome two years ago was 88 euros (Â£75).

It is Britain's first time hosting the championships in their 92-year history.

News.title: Man guilty of harassing MP Stella Creasy on Tube train
News.content:
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP for Walthamstow after preventing her from leaving a Tube carriage and behaving in an "abusive and aggressive" manner.

Clifford Wilby, from east London, targeted Stella Creasy on a Victoria line train between Walthamstow Central and Finsbury Park on 15 July last year.

Westminster Magistrates' Court heard how Wilby spoke to Creasy about knife crime and her "failings as a Member of Parliament" before filming her, leading to members of the public intervening.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

Wilby and Creasy first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 as part of her role as an MP.

She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else's case.

Creasy said he had "made a series of very serious allegations", became abusive and "referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath".

The meeting was stopped because of Wilby's behaviour.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to block new betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and for many people, the high streets they grew up with are "unrecognisable".

He said the plans were "shaped" by a series of BBC News investigations which exposed organised crime on high streets, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes, vapes, cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco for up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham told the BBC that the changes would make it "easier for police to close a vape shop and have it closed for longer".

He said: "At the same time we're changing the planning regime... which should stop the proliferation of vape shops on our high streets."

The prime minister added that Operation Vulcan in Cheetham Hill, Greater Manchester, cleared the area of counterfeits and crime and "proved" what could be achieved.

"When I look at police reform across England, I will be asking for a similar approach to be taken," he said. "I want the strongest possible neighbourhood policing, with all agencies involved, to rip out criminal behaviour that is pulling places down."

Burnham said he did not accept the decline of the high street as "inevitable".

"I don't see why anywhere should have to accept they have empty shops, vape shops and the challenges that come with that."

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday that many people were frustrated at vape and gambling outlets "popping up even near schools and some of them are linked to illegal activity and crime".

News.title: Man dies after punch from security guard in Turkey bar, inquest hears
News.content:
A rugby player was punched in the head by a security guard while on holiday in Turkey and died after he returned home, an inquest has heard.

Scot James, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, had been in hospital since he suffered head and brain injuries in an alleged bar assault on 5 July.

He fell and hit his head during a "verbal exchange", Pontypridd Coroner's Court was told on Tuesday.

The 34-year-old was repatriated to the UK and died on 26 July at the Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Llantrisant, Rhondda Cynon Taf.

A provisional cause of death was given as blunt head injury.

James' family described him as a "loving father, son, grandson and partner" in tributes following his death.

Maesteg Celtic RFC said he was an "outstanding player and a great character".

Coroner Rachel Knight said a full inquest was necessary as there was reason to suspect the death may have been unnatural.

She said that as police in Turkey would potentially be investigating James' death, the next inquest hearing would be scheduled for later this year.

Knight said it may be necessary to pause inquest proceedings pending the outcome of any criminal investigation and confirmed the court would liaise with Turkish authorities.

Police in Turkey are understood to be investigating the death, with assistance from the Foreign Office.

In a statement, James' family said he "had a warm heart, a great sense of humour, and a natural ability to bring people together".

"We are heartbroken by his loss," they said.

"No words can truly express the pain we are experiencing or the void his passing has left in our lives."

Maesteg Celtic RFC said: "Everyone at the club is devastated by this news and our thoughts go out to his family and friends at this difficult time."

News.title: Box of ultrarare ‘Holy Grail’ Mario games discovered in Wisconsin
News.content:

Prominent Nintendo game collector Jason Ganos was stopped in his tracks when a pop culture shop owner in Wisconsin revealed he possessed a long-forgotten box of Super Mario cartridges sitting in storage.

According to Ganos, the haul turned out to be an exceptionally rare hoard of 97 "absolutely pristine" copies of Super Mario Brothers Duck Hunt, the popular Nintendo title launched in 1988.

It was his Holy Grail.

Following preliminary research, he discovered that the cartridges represented a previously unknown variant of the game and marked the final recorded production date for the title.

A majority of the games are set to go up for sale on Friday in an online auction that will run until 9 September.

“I still don’t quite believe that any of this is happening,” Ganos said. “I just think it’s kind of serendipitous that this happened. It’s just still very bizarre to me.”

Ganos, a hard-core fan covered in Nintendo tattoos and who has operated Nintendo Wire, a news service for Nintendo announcements and nostalgia for over 10 years, said he would not venture to guess how much the games are worth.

But when he saw the box, he immediately knew it was special.

open image in gallery This photo provided by Nintendo Wire shows a box of nearly 100 uncirculated Nintendo Entertainment System copies of Super Mario Bros. and Duck Hunt on Wednesday, June 17, 2026, rediscovered in a warehouse in Waukesha, Wis., by OneStopWonders store owner Kevin Braun and Nintendo Wire publisher Jason Ganos. (Jason Ganos/Nintendo Wire via AP) ( Jason Ganos/Nintendo Wire )

“It’s like pulling out like a Holy Grail,” Ganos said, later adding, “They’re gorgeous.”

The discovery came after the owner, Kevin Braun, of One Stop Wonders in Waukesha, outside Milwaukee, asked Ganos to help him sell some stuff, including common Nintendo games and Pokémon cards.

Braun mentioned the box of Mario cartridges that had been sitting in storage for years. He recalled buying them from a customer whose family had kept them for metal scraps but thought they were not worth much.

The cartridges of Super Mario Brothers Duck Hunt he had were made in 1993, long after the company discontinued the bundle in 1991. Braun and Ganos still aren’t sure why the copies they possess were made but assume they were either warranty replacements or part of a bundle with a box retailer that never panned out.

Knowing the potential significance of the possession, Ganos booked a flight immediately.

“I flew down to California with 97 carts in my carry-on luggage, sweating bullets going through TSA, like why do you have 97 little circuit boards in your carry-on?” Ganos recalled thinking nervously.

He anxiously made it through airport security to meet with video game experts to have the cartridges verified and graded, giving them a perceived value.

There had never been a cartridge rated a perfect 10 at Professional Sports Authenticator video games, Ganos said.

open image in gallery This photo provided by Nintendo Wire shows a box of nearly 100 uncirculated Nintendo Entertainment System copies of Super Mario Bros. and Duck Hunt on Wednesday, June 17, 2026, rediscovered in a warehouse in Waukesha, Wis., by OneStopWonders store owner Kevin Braun and Nintendo Wire publisher Jason Ganos. (Jason Ganos/Nintendo Wire via AP) ( Jason Ganos/Nintendo Wire )

Five of the 97 Ganos possessed received a perfect score.

“I think there’s going to be historic significance to the tens,” Ganos said when talking about how much the games may sell at the auction. “Like number one, it’s so many people’s childhoods, and number two, there’s never been a 10 in an NES cart before.”

Ultrarare video game cartridges, especially ones with unique production history, can be sold for six- to seven-figure prices in the collector’s market. Ganos said the 97 carts are also unique because of their perfect condition, which, much like comic books or sports cards, often sell higher.

Ganos can’t estimate the ultimate worth of the cartridges because they are incomparable to other video game collectibles he has seen before. They could be worth hundreds, thousands or tens of thousands, he said.

Ganos and Braun are only auctioning off three of the perfect 10 scored cartridges at Golden Pop’s Culture Auction beginning Friday. They are both keeping one copy with a score of a 10, and a few others rated in the higher 9’s.

The games can be played if the buyer wants. But because they are pristine, Ganos hopes to keep them that way.

“Finding uncirculated stuff for me is just like super exciting,” Ganos said. “This game was the first video game I’ve ever played. Mario Duck Hunt was just such a big part of my life growing up.”

Braun and Ganos also plan to do a charity auction after they are finished with the current one.

News.title: Fiat Panda crashes into luxury jet as plane taxis for takeoff
News.content:
A Fiat Panda crashed into a luxury plane as it was taxiing towards a runway at an airport in Italy.

Footage shows the white car, operated by Milan Linate Airport’s handling company, smashing into the business jet on Monday morning (10 August).

The vehicle cut across the aircraft’s path before ploughing into the plane’s nose.

No physical injuries were reported.

A Milan Airports spokesperson said: “Operations have been restored and flights are operating as scheduled. We apologise for any inconvenience and thank passengers for their understanding.”

An investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collision is underway.
