World.title: ANALYSIS: OsunDecides2026: Ex-governors, their remarkable feats, low moments
World.content:
Osun State was created from the old Oyo State in August 1991 by the military government of General Ibrahim Babangida. Since then, the state has been ruled by appointed military administrators and elected civilian governors, each leaving a distinct imprint on its political and developmental trajectory.

The state’s first administrator was Leo Ajiborisha, a colonel, who oversaw the establishment of some of the institutions required to run the newly created state before handing over to its first elected governor, late Isiaka Adeleke, in January 1992.

The return to civilian rule in 1999 ushered in a succession of elected administrations led by Bisi Akande, Olagunsoye Oyinlola, Rauf Aregbesola and Gboyega Oyetola. The incumbent governor, Ademola Adeleke, was elected in 2022 amidst several political controversies.

Over the past three decades, these administrations have pursued different approaches to governance. Some have been celebrated for fiscal discipline, social welfare programmes, institutional development, and infrastructure, while others have been criticised for debt accumulation, labour disputes, political infighting, electoral controversies, and allegations of financial impropriety.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This analysis examines the major achievements and low moments associated with each administration and what they reveal about the evolution of governance in Osun State, as the state prepares for another gubernatorial election on Saturday.

Leo Ajiborisha: Building the foundation

Leo Ajiborisha, a military officer, was appointed the first administrator of Osun State upon its creation in 1991.

His administration largely focused on establishing the basic institutional framework of the new state and preparing it for the transition to civilian rule.

Among the notable steps taken during his tenure was the establishment of the Osun State Civil Service Commission in September 1991. His administration also established the Osun State Broadcasting Corporation, with its radio station in Ile-Ife, which commenced operations in November 1991.

Mr Ajiborisha handed over power to Isiaka Adeleke in January 1992, marking the beginning of elected civilian administration in the new state.

Mr Ajiborisha’s tenure was brief, reflecting the transitional nature of the military administration.

He later held senior military positions, including Director of Operations at the Defence Headquarters and Principal Staff Officer to former Head of State Abdulsalami Abubakar.

Isiaka Adeleke: The first civilian governor

Isiaka Adeleke became Osun State’s first elected governor in January 1992 under the defunct Social Democratic Party (SDP).

As the pioneer civilian governor, he faced the task of consolidating the institutional structures established during the state’s formative period.

One of the notable initiatives of his administration was the establishment of the Osun State Polytechnic, Iree, which is now part of the state’s tertiary education infrastructure.

Mr Adeleke’s administration was abruptly terminated following the military takeover of November 1993, which aborted Nigeria’s Third Republic.

His tenure, therefore, lasted only about two years and did not provide sufficient time for many of his administration’s programmes to mature and manifest.

He eventually served as a two-term senator, representing Osun West from 2007 to 2011 as a PDP member. He was later reelected under the APC in 2015 but died in April 2017.

Anthony Udofia and Anthony Obi: The return to military rule

Following the 1993 military takeover, Nigeria and Osun returned to military administration.

Anthony Udofia became the second military administrator of the state under the regime of Sani Abacha, Nigeria’s late head of state. His administration focused largely on maintaining government operations and pursuing social and developmental programmes.

Mr Udofia was replaced by Anthony Obi, who served as military administrator from August 1996 to August 1998. Mr Obi’s tenure coincided with one of the most politically uncertain periods in Nigeria’s history.

Mr Obi was later redeployed to Abia State, where he remained until the return to civilian rule in May 1999.

Theophilus Bamgboye: Preparing for civilian rule

Theophilus Bamgboye became the fourth military administrator of Osun State under General Abdulsalami Abubakar’s transitional government.

His administration operated during the final phase of military rule and was primarily concerned with maintaining government institutions while preparing the state for the return to democratic governance in 1999.

Mr Bamgboye, an indigene of Omu-Aran in Kwara State, handed over to Bisi Akande, the first elected governor of Osun State under the Fourth Republic.

Bisi Akande: Fiscal discipline and difficult reforms

Mr Akande, who was elected on the platform of the Alliance for Democracy, governed the state from 1999 to 2003.

His administration was strongly associated with fiscal discipline, institutional reforms and an emphasis on reducing government waste.

Mr Akande’s government also pursued free education and healthcare initiatives, reflecting the social-democratic orientation of the Alliance for Democracy administrations that controlled all the South-west states at the time.

His administration’s attempt to rationalise and downsize the state civil service generated significant opposition from organised labour.

The reforms, which were presented as necessary, were opposed by workers and contributed to the political difficulties the governor faced in the 2003 election.

Mr Akande eventually lost the governorship to Olagunsoye Oyinlola, thus spending only one term of four years in office. He had served as the secretary to the defunct Oyo State Government and later deputy governor of the state under late Governor Bola Ige.

Olagunsoye Oyinlola: Expanding infrastructure and education

Olagunsoye Oyinlola, a retired brigadier-general and former military administrator of Lagos State, governed Osun State from 2003 to 2010 on the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP.

His administration placed considerable emphasis on infrastructure, agriculture, education, healthcare, water supply, transportation, security and job creation.

One of his most significant legacies was the establishment of Osun State University, which was designed as a multi-campus institution to expand access to university education across the state.

His administration also implemented various welfare and development programmes, particularly in rural communities.

The low moments

Mr Oyinlola became embroiled in a prolonged legal and political dispute over the 2007 governorship election.

The dispute culminated in the Court of Appeal nullifying his election victory in 2010, resulting in his removal from office and the emergence of Rauf Aregbesola.

The episode became one of the defining political controversies of his administration and further demonstrated the growing influence of electoral litigation in Nigeria’s political system. His sack by the court led to off-cycle governorship elections in Osun.

Rauf Aregbesola: Ambitious reforms amid financial crisis

Rauf Aregbesola governed Osun State from 2010 to 2018, becoming the state’s longest-serving elected governor so far.

His administration was marked by ambitious infrastructure projects, aggressive social welfare programmes and major reforms in education.

Mr Aregbesola’s supporters often point to his administration’s expansive approach to public works and social intervention as among its most enduring legacies.

Major achievements

The administration established the Osun Youth Empowerment Scheme, popularly known as O-YES, which provided employment opportunities for thousands of young people.

In education, his government introduced the “Opon Imo”(Tablet of Knowledge) digital learning initiative, which provided students with electronic educational materials. It also constructed mega schools as part of a broader attempt to transform public education infrastructure.

Another major initiative was the O-MEALS school feeding programme, which provided meals to pupils in public primary schools.

Infrastructure was also a major feature of the administration. Mr Aregbesola’s government undertook extensive road construction and rehabilitation across urban and rural communities.

His administration also promoted cultural identity, including the adoption of the title “Ogbeni” and the designation of Isese Day as a public holiday.

The low moments

The most controversial aspect of Mr Aregbesola’s tenure was the state’s worsening financial situation and the resulting impact on workers and pensioners.

Amid declining federal allocations and the state’s debt obligations, the government introduced a “modulated” salary structure under which some workers received only part of their monthly salaries. The policy generated intense opposition from labour unions and created hardship for thousands of workers.

His education reforms also generated significant controversy. The restructuring and reclassification of schools, including the merger of some historically single-sex schools, triggered protests and religious tensions, particularly over the issue of school uniforms and the use of the hijab.

The administration’s borrowing and debt accumulation also became a major political issue. Critics argued that the loans used to finance infrastructure projects created a substantial financial burden for subsequent governments.

Mr Aregbesola’s political relationship with his successor, Gboyega Oyetola, later deteriorated, contributing to divisions within the Osun chapter of the APC.

Gboyega Oyetola: Fiscal consolidation and political turbulence

Gboyega Oyetola succeeded Mr Aregbesola in 2018 after a controversial election and governed until 2022.

Political tension in Osun State peaked during the fiercely contested September 2018 poll, which was eventually declared inconclusive. This led to a controversial supplementary rerun, which escalated allegations of voter intimidation and high-stakes manoeuvring between the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) and the opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP)

During the 22 September 2018 election, early tallies showed Mr Adeleke was leading Mr Oyetola by a narrow margin of 353 votes, but INEC declared the election inconclusive because the total number of cancelled votes (over 1,000) exceeded that margin.

The PDP, Mr Adeleke’s party, and various observers criticised the inconclusive status, describing it as a “manoeuvre” by federal authorities to favour the ruling party. This prompted INEC to schedule a rerun for 27 September 2018, in seven polling units across four local government areas. The political tension between the APC and PDP became apparent, as the PDP deployed almost all its forces, including both current and former governors at the time, as well as the then Senate President, Bukola Saraki; all in an effort to influence the election outcome in their favour.

Third-place Social Democratic Party (SDP) candidate Iyiola Omisore eventually aligned with the APC ahead of the rerun, despite several attempts by the PDP to gain his support.

The rerun took place under unprecedented security deployment. PDP leaders and local monitors reported widespread harassment, heavy clampdowns, and restrictions preventing their supporters and accredited journalists/observers from accessing polling units

Mr Oyetola of the APC was ultimately declared the winner after the supplementary election, cementing a highly polarised political atmosphere that left lasting friction across the state.

The Oyetola administration inherited significant financial obligations, including salary and pension arrears, while also facing the challenge of sustaining government services amid fiscal constraints.

One of his central priorities was financial management. His administration stopped the payment of modulated salaries and restored full monthly salaries to workers.

The government also began addressing inherited pension obligations and invested in healthcare infrastructure.

Major achievements

The Oyetola administration renovated and upgraded primary healthcare centres across the state and invested in the State Specialist Hospital in Asubiaro, Osogbo.

It also constructed the Olaiya Flyover in the state capital, one of the most visible infrastructure projects of his administration.

In education, his government reversed some of the controversial reforms introduced by the Aregbesola administration, including changes to school names, uniforms, and school structures.

The administration also sought to reduce the state’s reliance on new borrowing.

The low moments

Mr Oyetola’s tenure was overshadowed by intense political rivalry within the APC, particularly his deteriorating relationship with Mr Aregbesola.

The internal division weakened the party ahead of the 2022 governorship election, which Mr Oyetola narrowly lost to Mr Adeleke of the PDP.

His convoy was also attacked during the EndSARS protests in October 2020, highlighting the volatile security environment of the period.

After leaving office, the Oyetola administration faced allegations from the succeeding government concerning the management of state resources and certain projects. Mr Oyetola, who is currently the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, and his associates rejected such allegations, describing them as politically motivated.

Ademola Adeleke: Infrastructure, welfare and political battles

Ademola Adeleke became governor in November 2022 after defeating Mr Oyetola in the governorship election.

His administration has emphasised infrastructure, workers’ welfare, healthcare and education.

The Adeleke administration has highlighted the construction and rehabilitation of roads, as well as the development of major infrastructure projects, including flyovers in Osogbo.

Workers’ welfare has also featured prominently. The government says it has cleared substantial portions of inherited salary and pension arrears while improving welfare for pensioners.

In healthcare, the administration has undertaken the rehabilitation and upgrading of primary healthcare centres, including efforts to improve power supply at health facilities.

The administration has also supported the development of the University of Ilesa and promoted initiatives to expand the state’s digital economy.

The low moments

Despite these initiatives, Governor Adeleke’s administration has faced significant political and legal controversies.

One of the biggest disputes has centred on the control of local governments following legal battles over the status of elected local government chairpersons. The controversy generated tension between the state government and opposition politicians and raised questions about compliance with court decisions.

The government also faced criticism following its decision to terminate the appointments of some workers recruited by the previous administration, particularly teachers and health workers.

Its handling of the state’s finances has similarly attracted scrutiny, with opposition politicians questioning some expenditures and projects. The administration has rejected allegations of financial impropriety and defended its spending as part of its development agenda.

Mr Adeleke’s public persona has also remained a source of political debate. His frequent public dancing, which supporters see as a sign of his accessibility and connection with ordinary citizens, has been used by critics to question the seriousness of his leadership.

The Overview

Political analysts have argued that the history of governance in Osun State reflects many of the broader challenges confronting Nigeria’s subnational governments.

The state’s early military administrators focused primarily on establishing institutions and maintaining stability. The return to democracy brought a stronger emphasis on education, healthcare, infrastructure and social welfare.

Yet the experience of successive administrations also reveals a recurring tension between ambitious development programmes and the state’s financial capacity.

Mr Akande’s fiscal reforms generated labour resistance. Mr Oyinlola’s administration was defined in part by electoral litigation, while Mr Aregbesola’s ambitious infrastructure and welfare programmes were accompanied by a severe salary crisis and concerns about debt.

Mr Oyetola attempted fiscal consolidation but struggled with internal party divisions. Mr Adeleke, the dancing governor, has pursued infrastructure and welfare programmes while facing legal disputes and political opposition. This political crisis and party fragmentation have lingered, prompting Mr Adeleke to defect to the Accord Party, where he will seek re-election on Saturday.

The political crisis/tension pattern unravelling in the state suggests that the central challenge for Osun is not merely the ability to initiate projects but the capacity to sustain them without imposing unsustainable financial obligations on future administrations.

As the state approaches another political cycle, the competing legacies of its former governors will remain important to the debate over what constitutes effective governance: infrastructure, social welfare, fiscal discipline, institutional stability or political inclusiveness.

World.title: Only 40% of births registered in Nigeria — NPC
World.content:
By Folarin Kehinde

ABUJA — The National Population Commission, NPC, has raised the alarm that only about 40 per cent of births in Nigeria are currently registered, despite more than five million children being born in the country annually.

The Commission disclosed this in Abuja during the commemoration of the 2026 Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, CRVS, Day.

Speaking at the event, Chairman of the NPC, Dr Aminu Yusuf, said the low registration coverage, particularly of births and deaths, remained a major challenge to Nigeria’s efforts to build a comprehensive and reliable national population database.

Yusuf, however, said the Commission had taken a major step towards closing the gap with the nationwide launch of a fully digital Civil Registration and Vital Statistics system on the Vital Rights Platform on July 1, 2026.

According to him, the launch marked the end of manual registration and the beginning of a new era of technology-driven civil registration in Nigeria.

He said the digital system would enable the country to securely and promptly record births, deaths, marriages and other vital events, while providing reliable data for governance, planning and sustainable development.

The NPC chairman explained that the digital platform would improve the storage and security of vital records, reduce duplication through automated verification and unique identifiers, and facilitate interoperability with health institutions, identity management agencies, planning bodies and statistical institutions.

He said: “More than five million children are born in Nigeria every year. According to the most recent Nigerian Demographic and Health Survey, only about 40 per cent of births are registered, while death registration coverage remains unacceptably low.

“These statistics underscore the urgent need to accelerate registration coverage through sustainable public awareness, stronger partnerships and increased community participation.”

Yusuf said the Commission was also decentralising registration services to bring them closer to Nigerians, particularly those living in rural and underserved communities.

He disclosed that digital registration services had already been extended to about 4,000 of the 8,809 wards across the country, with plans to achieve nationwide coverage.

The NPC chairman further revealed that more than 4,000 functional registration centres had been established across the 774 local government areas, while the Commission had commenced an expansion programme aimed at increasing the number to about 8,000 centres nationwide.

He said the expansion would reduce the distance, cost and time involved in accessing registration services and help ensure that no child or vital event was excluded because of geographical barriers.

Yusuf said the Commission had also strengthened partnerships with the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, ALGON; National Identity Management Commission, NIMC; UNICEF; and BAMFOR Technologies Limited through a partnership compact signed in January 2025.

He added that the NPC was working with the National Primary Health Care Development Agency, state governments and health institutions to integrate birth registration into routine health services, allowing children to be registered as close as possible to their point of birth.

Also speaking, UNICEF Nigeria’s Chief of Child Protection, Natalie McCauley, described birth registration as a fundamental child right and the state’s first legal recognition of a child.

McCauley said a birth certificate provided proof of identity and laid the foundation for access to healthcare, education, social protection and legal protection throughout a child’s life.

She commended Nigeria’s progress in expanding digital birth registration, noting that services were now available in more than 4,000 wards across the country, including rural, hard-to-reach and humanitarian settings.

She urged the government and stakeholders to focus on three priorities as Africa enters a new CRVS decade: integration, decentralisation and digitalisation.

According to her, civil registration systems must work seamlessly with health, identity management, social protection and education systems, while services must be brought closer to families, especially those in remote communities.

“Every registered birth strengthens child protection. Every registered child becomes more visible to the systems designed to serve and protect them,” she said.

McCauley assured that UNICEF would continue to support the Nigerian government and its partners to strengthen birth registration systems, increase awareness and ensure that no child was left behind.

World.title: 10 types of foreigners who lost their U.S. visas as 175,000 canceled
World.content:
The United States Department of State has revoked more than 175,000 visas under President Donald Trump as part of an intensified effort to identify foreign nationals who violate U.S. immigration rules, commit crimes or pose risks to public safety and national security.

According to the department, the majority of the visa revocations followed law enforcement encounters involving criminal offences. Assault, driving under the influence, theft and drug-related crimes were among the leading reasons for the cancellations.

Other cases involved reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud and embezzlement, among other offences.

The State Department said the revocations are part of its ongoing vetting process designed to ensure that visa holders comply with the conditions attached to their visas and do not pose a threat to Americans.

Here are 10 categories of foreign nationals whose visas have been revoked or who have faced deportability determinations:

1. People charged with sexual assault

The State Department revoked the visa of a foreign national charged with felony rape and sexual battery, including an alleged offence involving a mentally disabled victim.

2. People accused of kidnapping and child exploitation

Another foreign national faced charges including felony kidnapping, human trafficking and sexual exploitation of a minor.

3. People arrested for domestic violence and violent conduct

Visa revocations also involved foreign nationals arrested for offences including disorderly conduct, resisting arrest with violence, drunk driving and domestic violence.

4. Birth tourists

A U.S. embassy in North Africa revoked more than 100 visas belonging to parents accused of travelling to the United States primarily to give birth so their children could obtain U.S. citizenship.

5. People accused of child sexual offences

The department cited cases involving foreign nationals charged with offences including sodomy of a child, aggravated sexual battery and possession of child sexual abuse material.

One individual was reportedly charged with more than a dozen counts related to possession of such material.

6. Drug and dangerous-driving offenders

The State Department also cited a foreign national who was arrested while driving with heroin and a blood alcohol level more than three times the legal limit.

7. Foreign nationals accused of endorsing violence

Multiple foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk also had their visas revoked, according to the department.

The cases included individuals who made comments appearing to praise the killing or express support for violence.

8. People involved in major healthcare fraud

One foreign national accused of operating a legitimate business helping vulnerable patients access healthcare was allegedly involved in a Medicaid fraud scheme involving more than $5 million in fake services.

9. People accused of fraudulently obtaining visas

The department also cited a foreign national accused of building a company around false claims, deceiving investors and defrauding clients of millions of dollars.

According to the State Department, the individual allegedly used fabricated claims and forged letters to fraudulently obtain a U.S. visa.

10. Foreign nationals considered deportable on foreign policy grounds

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also determined that several foreign nationals are deportable on foreign policy grounds.

The cases cited by the department include a Cuban national linked to an alleged influence operation connected to Cuba’s communist regime, Iranian nationals with alleged connections to the Iranian government, a Laotian child sex offender who received a pardon from Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, and a Kuwaiti national accused of expressing a desire for violence against the U.S. president and referring to Americans as his “enemy.”

The State Department said the Trump administration will continue to identify, investigate and revoke visas belonging to foreign nationals it considers threats to Americans.

The department stressed that a U.S. visa is a privilege rather than a right and said it would continue using available measures to protect communities from people who violate the conditions of their entry or pose public safety and national security concerns.

Vanguard News

World.title: Christianity in trouble if Jingir’s comments ignored — Ayodele
World.content:
LAGOS — The Leader of INRI Evangelical Spiritual Church, Primate Elijah Ayodele, has criticised the Federal Government over its alleged silence on recent remarks attributed to Islamic cleric, Sheikh Sani Yahaya Jingir.

Ayodele said Jingir should be arrested over the remarks, warning that failure to caution religious leaders against inflammatory statements could threaten peaceful coexistence in the country.

The cleric spoke in a video posted on social media while reacting to a statement attributed to Jingir in which he reportedly said those who did not accept a Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket should leave Nigeria.

Jingir was also reported to have described Christians as “infidels” in the video circulating on social media.

Reacting, Ayodele in a video posted by Tunde Ednut, alleged that the government would have responded differently if a Christian religious leader had made a similar statement.

“If the government does not caution this, then Christianity is in trouble in Nigeria. This senseless old fool, Islamic cleric Jingir, should be in jail by now.

“If a Christian had made such a statement, they would have picked him up immediately,” Ayodele said.

He urged the Bola Tinubu administration to caution Jingir and other religious leaders against making statements capable of inflaming religious tensions.

Ayodele warned that failure to address inflammatory rhetoric could further undermine peaceful coexistence and national unity.

World.title: My husband paid the supreme price fighting for justice — Widow laments
World.content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

It was an emotional atmosphere at Umuenu Umuawulu in Awka South Local Government Area of Anambra State when a widow, Mrs Nkechi Obi, wife of the former chairman of Umuenu Quarters Assembly, Umuawulu, Mr Humphrey Obi, broke down in tears to narrate the circumstances that led to her husband’s death while pursuing justice in the community.



The people of Umuenu Quarters of Umuawulu had gathered that day to protest the alleged attempt by another village in the area to usurp their massive Agu Umaauenu land. Elderly men, women, and youths of the community who gathered in the village hall vowed not to give up their inheritance, especially when the battle had taken the life of their former chairman.



“My late husband narrated to me the history of that land, and there was peace in the community until some rich and influential people developed interest in the land. I remember that my husband used to plant rice on the said land and nobody was molesting anybody.



“Until the unfortunate incident that led to his death, most families were going there to farm. We were also harvesting palm fruits, processing them and keeping them there until we were ready to carry them to the market, and nobody was stealing them. It is therefore unfortunate that my husband became a victim of this land dispute”, Mrs Obi lamented.



Bernard Mbolu, President, Umuenu Quarters Assembly, said although Umuawulu is made up of three quarters, namely: Enugwu, Umuenu and Agbana. Umuenu quarters is facing a big challenge because the village is being denied the land its people inherited from their forefathers. According to him, litigation over the land lingered from local authority court to customary court from 1927 to 1963, and it got to the Supreme Court, which decided on the matter in 1963, which was decided in favour of Umuenu.



Mbolu said: “ The highest court in the land decided that Umuenu people are the rightful owners of the land known as Agu Udo Umuoma and Agu ofuu, which were collectively named Agu Umuenu.

“There was no other quarter contesting the ownership of the land with us until 2020.



During the litigation, the other quarter in Umuawulu was testifying in favour of Awgbu Community that they were the rightful owners of the land. When we defeated Awgbu in court, and Awgbu people wanted us to have a permanent boundary demarcation, we did and signed a Memorandum of Understanding, MoU, with them.



“Surprisingly, Enugwu Quarters that testified for Awgbu people invaded the land after they had testified for Awgbu people that it was their land.



The matter was taken to Igwe in Council, and the then PG of Umuawulu, Ozo I.K Nkala set up a 20-man committee, with Umuenu and Enugwu quarters nominating 10 members each, while the neutral quarter, Agbana, produced the chairman and the secretary.



“After hearing from the two quarters, the committee decided that the land is owned by the Umuenu people. Surprisingly, Enugwu people rejected the decision, and in 2024 when our people went there to farm in line with the court decision, they attacked our people with dangerous weapons and in the process, cut off the hand of one of our brothers, Mr Humphrey Obi, who later died following the injuries he sustained during the attack.”



He explained that there had also been attempts to resolve the matter amicably, including tabling it during the Umuawulu town hall meeting, yet our neighbours insisted on continuing with the dispute.



“On December 31 , 2024, we all went to the disputed land for inspection, and after the two quarters stated their cases, Umuawulu Community set up another committee made up of all lawyers produced by the community. Barr Azubuike Anazo was the chairman, while Barrister Emeka Orji was the secretary.



“This committee also agreed that the entire land belongs to Umuenu and urged our people to discontinue all the litigations. Surprisingly, on July 7, 2026, we received a message that the state Deputy Governor wanted all of us in his office, following a petition by Enugwu people.



“ We were told that the Deputy Governor wants to create a permanent boundary between Enugwu and Umuenu , which we are rejecting because the matter had since been decided by the highest court in the land and various committees”, Mbolu stated.



According to the chairman, “this Agu Umuenu is the only land we have, and we are rejecting the pressure being mounted on the Deputy Governor to intervene in the matter.



They have even more land than us, and we wonder why they are insisting on taking our land.

World.title: National Museum immortalises Igbo’s most influential colonial warrant chief
World.content:
By Chinedu Adonu

FOR decades after his death, the remarkable story of the very powerful and influential Igbo Paramount Chief in the present-day Enugu State, Chief Onyeama N’Eke, merely lived mainly in family memories and fading historical records. Not much is being said about this powerful Warrant Chief in the wider world.

However, recently those memories have found a permanent place for records as the National Museum of Unity, Enugu, unveiled a life-sized memorial statue and exhibition gallery dedicated to the legendary traditional ruler.



For members of the Murus Association, the descendants of Chief Onyeama’s daughters, who were instrumental to the project, the event was more than the unveiling of a monument. It was an emotional fulfilment of a four-year mission to ensure that future generations would know about the man they affectionately describe as “The Lion.”



Visitors admired an exhibition filled with rare photographs, personal artifacts and historical documents, including the motorcycle presented to Chief Onyeama during his visit to England in the 1920s.

The display also chronicled his contributions to education, Christianity, traditional governance and the growth of Enugu’s coal industry.



The exhibition, titled: “The Legend of Their Era: Chief Onyeama N’Eke,” was organised by the National Museum of Unity in collaboration with the Murus Association, the descendants of the renowned traditional ruler.



The man, Chief Onyeama N’Eke



Paramount King, Chief Onyeama N’Eke (1870s–1933) was a powerful and influential warrant chief and traditional ruler in Colonial Igbo land. Ruled in Eke, the present-day Udi Local Government Area of Enugu State, he built a vast, wealthy dynasty across the Agbaja region and became one of the most influential Igbo leaders of his era. He was well recognised by the colonial rulers, who used him to carry out some local administrative functions.



Speaking at the ceremony, Curator of the National Museum of Unity, Enugu, Mr. Aloysius Duru, said Chief Onyeama’s story deserved to be preserved because of his extraordinary impact on society.



“You cannot talk about coal mining in Enugu without mentioning Chief Onyeama N’Eke,” Duru said, recalling how the traditional ruler supplied labour to the coal mines and fearlessly defended the interests of his people during the colonial era.



He also praised the late monarch for embracing Western education, employing teachers from Sierra Leone to educate his children and introducing Catholic missionaries to his kingdom- bold decisions that transformed the lives of many in the community.



For Chief Luke Mmamel, Chairman of the Murus Association, the unveiling was deeply historic and personal.

He described the late monarch as a visionary leader who established an Appeal Court, strengthened community security, advanced Christianity and earned widespread respect for defending the interests of his people during the colonial era.



“We are immortalizing him today not only for ourselves but for generations yet unborn. His life remains a shining example of visionary leadership, courage and service,” he said.



His words reflected the pride shared by family members who funded the project to ensure that the achievements of their maternal ancestor would never be forgotten.



Enugu State Commissioner for Culture and Tourism, Dame Ugochi Madueke, who witnessed the event, described the memorial ceremony as a victory for cultural preservation and pledged to work with the family to transform the historic Onyeama Palace into a heritage and tourism destination.



“We are here not only to remember a great man but to celebrate a legacy that continues to inspire generations. The Onyeama Palace deserves recognition as a heritage and tourism destination.

“I am committed to working with the family to make that vision a reality,” she pledged.



Explaining the background of the project, a member of the Murus Association, Chief Joe Mmamel, said efforts to establish an exhibition in honour of Chief Onyeama began about four years ago.

He explained that the association secured approval from the Federal Ministry responsible for tourism after presenting the late chief’s historical achievements and national significance.



According to him, the approval led to the establishment of the exhibition hall and commissioning of a life-sized sculpture painstakingly produced by a renowned sculptor, Bonak.



He commended Duru, the curator, for his unwavering commitment to the project, describing him as an honorary member of the Murus Association, whose dedication ensured the successful completion of the exhibition before his retirement.



Beyond the sculpture and exhibition hall lies a larger message that preserving history is more than protecting old buildings or artifacts. It is about keeping alive the stories of people whose vision shaped communities and inspired generations.



For the descendants of Chief Onyeama N’Eke, the ceremony ensured that the voice of one of Enugu’s and Igbo’s greatest traditional rulers will continue to echo through history rather than fade with time.

World.title: Trump’s secret plane swap triggers questions and confusion
World.content:
US President Donald Trump speaks after signing executive orders in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on August 7, 2026. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP)

Donald Trump confirmed Tuesday that he secretly switched planes because of a threat to his life, after the Washington Post revealed the US president was smuggled out of Air Force One to a different aircraft on a catering truck.

“They wanted me to go in a different flight, a different plane — equal safety, but they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say,” Trump told reporters during a gaggle.

“I guess there was a threat out there. I didn’t really ask too much about it.”

The newspaper reported Monday that the secret operation reportedly smuggled Trump off Air Force One before the plane departed, still carrying journalists and top aides who remained at apparent risk of an Iranian strike.

Trump covertly exited the presidential plane while it was on the ground in Turkey on July 8.

Some traveling media expressed anger at having unwittingly served as decoys, while others complained about deception and lack of communication from the White House.

Trump boarded the presidential jet in full view of video cameras and photographers, with AFP pictures showing two supply containers at the front and rear of the aircraft.

But he then reportedly left the plane, stepping inside one of the cargo containers, to board a smaller US Air Force aircraft positioned nearby.

“I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” Trump told reporters. “Because that would be the plane I think that — that they would be more likely to go for.”

About a dozen journalists traveling in a separate section of Air Force One with no access to the president were unaware of the switch and flew out of Turkey on the plane despite the apparent threat from Iran, which is at war with the United States.

“Any consequential president has a lot of threats,” Trump said, brushing off concerns.

“I don’t worry about anything, to be honest. Whatever it is, you know my attitude: ‘Whatever.'”

– Shoulder-to-air missile threat? –

The Wall Street Journal reported Israel had briefed the US about a possible shoulder-to-air missile strike on Air Force One, adding that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was among senior officials and staff who remained on the plane.

Dispatches sent by pool media on board noted a Secret Service order that window shades be lowered during takeoff — an unusual instruction outside of combat zones.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday called for Congress to be briefed “on the Iranian threats against the president, the extraordinary measures taken to get him out of Turkey.”

Trump’s trip to the NATO summit had already raised eyebrows after he arrived on a luxury Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar and retrofitted to carry the US president.

But it was reportedly not fitted with anti-missile security systems and the old Air Force One was called into action.

Trump claimed at the time that the new plane was being sent ahead for US troops in Britain to tour, as a treat.

At a stopover in Britain, he returned to the Qatar-gifted plane for the flight to Washington.

Asked at the time why journalists had been asked to lower window blinds he said “because you’re probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with.”

“If I go, you go. Right?” Trump told reporters.

In 2000, Bill Clinton switched presidential planes at the last minute while traveling from India to Pakistan, using a decoy aircraft carrying Secret Service agents.

Joe Biden’s 2023 visit to Ukraine was also shrouded in strict secrecy during a long journey by plane and train, though he was accompanied by a reporter and photographer.

World.title: Osun Election: Police bar Amotekun, CJTF, hunters, neighbourhood watch
World.content:
We won’t allow criminality thrive in Osun - Amotekun Commander

ABUJA — The Nigeria Police Force, NPF, has barred the Western Nigeria Security Network, Amotekun, vigilante groups, Joint Civilian Task Force, CJTF, hunters’ associations, community-based security groups and neighbourhood watch outfits from participating in security operations during Saturday’s Osun State governorship election.

The Police said the non-state and quasi-security formations had no role in election security, including escorting electoral materials, guarding polling units, mounting checkpoints or bearing arms.

The Force, in a statement issued by its Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Ani Iniedu, on behalf of the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu, urged all concerned to comply with the directive in the interest of peace.

The Police warned political parties, candidates, supporters and members of the public against violence, intimidation and thuggery during the election.

It said recurring electoral offences such as ballot snatching, voter intimidation, vote buying and clashes between rival supporters would not be tolerated.

According to the Force, anyone involved in such offences, either as a direct perpetrator or sponsor, would be arrested and prosecuted irrespective of political affiliation or status.

The Police identified the NPF, Department of State Services, DSS, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, Nigeria Immigration Service, Nigeria Correctional Service and Federal Road Safety Corps, FRSC, among the authorised agencies for election security.

It said the joint deployment would cover all 30 Local Government Areas of Osun State, including polling units, collation centres, electoral materials, officials, observers, journalists and voters.

The Force also warned political parties, candidates and the public against engaging, arming or deploying any unauthorised security outfit for election-related activities.

“Any member or sponsor of such unauthorised outfits will be arrested and dealt with according to the law,” it said.

The Police further reiterated that firearms, dangerous weapons and other offensive materials were prohibited around polling units and collation centres, except those lawfully carried by accredited security personnel on election duty.

It said persons found involved in thuggery, obstruction of electoral officials, unlawful possession of election materials, hate speech or incitement to violence would be arrested and charged to court.

The IGP directed all commanders and personnel deployed for the election to operate professionally, impartially and firmly, in line with the rule of law and respect for human rights.

The Force also urged traditional rulers, religious leaders, civil society organisations, the media and accredited observers to report suspicious persons, movements or activities to the nearest security agency or established emergency channels.

The Police assured residents of Osun State, the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, political parties, candidates and other stakeholders of its commitment to providing a secure environment for eligible voters to exercise their franchise without fear or intimidation.

The Force said it would remain neutral, professional and resolute and would not allow any individual or group to undermine the peaceful conduct of the governorship election.

World.title: C’River pegs presidential campaign ads at N150m, govs N100m
World.content:
..PDP, ADC, others kick, say tariff outrageous, exorbitant

By Ike Uchechukwu

CALABAR — The Cross River State Signage and  Agency, CRISSAA, has fixed N150 million as the tariff for outdoor campaign s by presidential candidates ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Under the new tariff, governorship candidates are to pay N100 million, while senatorial, House of Representatives and State House of Assembly candidates are required to pay N50 million, N25 million and N5 million respectively.

The Director-General of CRISSAA, Ubong Sam, disclosed this during an interactive session with the Inter-Party Advisory Council, IPAC, in Calabar.

Sam also directed political parties to remove their campaign billboards and other advertising materials within 30 days after the declaration of election results.

He said the rates were moderate compared with what obtained in neighbouring states, adding that the agency remained impartial in its dealings with political parties and candidates.

He said CRISSAA had introduced measures to regulate advertising spaces and ensure fairness among political parties and candidates.

“We have tried to regulate advert space, by not allowing anybody to insult the integrity of anybody or party, by being fair in all ramifications, by giving advertisers opportunity to either dialogue or arbitration and not necessarily by litigation,” he said.

Sam warned that defaulters risked having their campaign materials removed, paying fines or facing prosecution before the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria, ARCON.

He said: “For defaulters having it at the back of their mind that ARCON fine is more than a million naira, there is no ARCON fine that is less than a million naira.”

On the deadline for removing campaign materials, the CRISSAA boss said political parties would have 30 days from the announcement of election results to remove their billboards and other campaign materials.

“Immediately after each election, at the expiration when results are announced, political parties are given 30 days to take off their campaign materials. Once it’s beyond 30 days, the advert materials become a nuisance,” he said.

The IPAC state chairman, Engr. Effiom Edet, backed the tariffs, describing them as fair, while the Special Adviser to the Governor on Inter-Party Affairs, Nkoyo Otu, assured stakeholders of transparency in the process.

However, the state chairman of the Action Democratic Party, Apostle Edet, and the Publicity Secretary of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, kicked against the tariffs.

They described the charges as outrageous and accused CRISSAA of attempting to shut out candidates from less financially buoyant political parties from using billboards for publicity ahead of the 2027 elections.

Speaking with Vanguard by telephone, the PDP spokesman, Mike Ojisi, said he was not part of any IPAC meeting where the tariffs were agreed.

“The tariff is outrageous, exorbitant and a ploy to prevent other political parties from carrying out massive publicity through billboards. The tariff is totally unacceptable,” he said.

World.title: Insecurity: AWPUF Accuses Alia of Abandoning Agatu, Hails Council Chairman Over Army Battalion
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent

The Agatu West Peace and Unity Forum, AWPUF, has accused Benue State Governor, Rev. Fr. Hyacinth Alia, of abandoning Agatu Local Government Area to the mercy of armed herders, saying claims that the area has been “reclaimed” are far from the truth.

The group was reacting to a report published in Idoma Voice Newspaper on August 5, 2026, headlined _“We Have Reclaimed Agatu From Armed Herders”which was credited to the Agatu Local Government Council Chairman, Ambassador Melvin James Ejeh.

In a statement issued in Agatu and signed by its President, Comrade Ebi Lucky, AWPUF said the position of the council chairman does not reflect the reality on ground. According to the forum, 15 villages sacked by repeated attacks remain deserted.

“To set the record straight, the fifteen affected villages have not returned to their ancestral homes and farming activities are not taking place in those areas as claimed by the Agatu Local Government Council Chairman,” the statement read.

AWPUF further alleged that since the attacks began, Governor Alia has neither visited Agatu nor made any public comment on the killings. The forum described the silence as an indication that the LGA has been left on its own.

“Let us ask Mr. Governor: Is Agatu not part of the State? When did His Excellency ever comment on the killings of our dear people of Agatu since the consistent attacks by Fulani herders?” the group queried.

The forum said it has, since 2024, repeatedly called for the deployment of security operatives to Agatu Western Zone, but alleged that all appeals to the state government have been ignored. It claimed the only intervention was short-lived.

“It is pertinent to inform the public that the 25 soldiers deployed to Agatu Western Zone were redeployed back to Obagaji, the Agatu Local Government headquarters, within two weeks of their deployment,” AWPUF stated.

Despite its criticism of the state government, the forum commended the Agatu Council Chairman, Ambassador Ejeh, for facilitating the siting of an Army Battalion in the area. AWPUF said the move would strengthen security and boost community confidence.

The group lauded the chairman for what it described as “proactive steps that have brought relative peace to parts of the local government” and for providing logistics support to security agencies. It noted that hosting the battalion connects security to livelihood and could encourage displaced persons to return to their farms and markets.

While commending Chairman Ejeh, AWPUF urged the Benue State Government to take decisive action to end the killings and facilitate the safe return of displaced persons. “What we need are proactive measures to stop the incessant killings of our people. Crediting failed responsibility is not healthy in a true democratic setting,” Comrade Lucky said.

World.title: West African Regulators Intensify Move to Build Regional Fuel Pricing, Trading Hub
World.content:
*NMDPRA: Infrastructure, capital, data critical to price benchmark

*Lokpobiri: Deregulation has unlocked investment in Nigeria’s downstream

*Eyesan says rising refining capacity, oil output good for market integration

*Verheijen: Why refining capacity alone can’t guarantee energy security

*S&P advocates more liquidity to make regional benchmarks work

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

West African petroleum regulators Tuesday intensified efforts to establish an integrated regional refined petroleum products market capable of supporting credible pricing benchmarks and positioning the sub-region as a major fuel trading hub.

The push formed the central focus of the 2026 West African Refined Fuel Market (WAFRFM) Conference, organised by the West Africa Regulators Forum (WARF), the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) and S&P Global Energy.

The conference, held under the theme: “Funding West Africa Infrastructure & Distribution to Create a Transparent Market for Regional Price Benchmarks,” brought together regulators, governments, refiners, traders, financial institutions, infrastructure investors and other industry stakeholders to deliberate on the development of the regional fuel market.

The discussions centred on the need to move beyond increased refining capacity to build the infrastructure, financing structures, regulatory systems, data architecture and market liquidity required to enable petroleum products to move efficiently across West Africa and allow prices to increasingly reflect regional market fundamentals.

Speaking at the conference, the Authority Chief Executive (ACE) of the NMDPRA, Mallam Umar Rabiu, said the region had made progress since the inaugural conference in 2025, but stressed that institutional developments must now be matched by investment and execution.

He said the 2025 conference had established a roadmap towards a West African refined products reference market, with emphasis on reliable refining capacity, stronger logistics and storage networks, interconnected ports, roads, rail and pipelines, harmonised standards, transparent market data and cross-border cooperation.

According to him, developments over the past year included the institutionalisation of regional regulatory cooperation through WARF, progress towards West African reference pricing and deeper collaboration with S&P Global Commodity Insights on market reporting and benchmark expertise.

However, Rabiu, who is the current chairman of WARF warned that a reference price alone could not create a trading hub.

“A reference price is not by itself a trading hub. A conference is not a market. Regulatory cooperation, important as it is, cannot substitute for the physical infrastructure, commercial liquidity, market information and operational excellence on which a credible trading hub must stand,” he said.

He identified infrastructure, capital, data and regulatory cooperation as critical foundations for creating a credible regional benchmark.

Rabiu pointed out that Africa has the resources, demand and increasingly the refining capacity, but needed to efficiently connect production to consumers through refineries, pipelines, storage terminals, jetties, ports, rail networks, roads, marine logistics, strategic reserves and digital trading platforms.

“The objective is not infrastructure for infrastructure’s sake. The objective is infrastructure that reduces the cost of moving energy, increases security of supply, improves inventory visibility, expands the number of credible market participants and creates the physical liquidity upon which transparent pricing depends,” he said.

Rabiu also urged investors to view the region’s infrastructure deficit as an opportunity, citing potential investments in pipelines, product transportation, storage, marine terminals, refinery expansion, road and rail logistics, gas infrastructure, digital commodity exchanges, product-tracking systems and integrated regional logistics corridors.

He noted, however, that capital would only flow into projects that were bankable, with predictable regulation, understood risks and sustainable returns. The NMDPRA chief also stressed the importance of operational efficiency, warning that infrastructure without operational excellence could create expensive bottlenecks.

“Our ports must become more efficient. Our terminals must improve turnaround times. Our pipelines and storage systems must operate safely and reliably. Our refineries must pursue sustained utilisation, reliability and competitive yields,” he said.

He further called for improved data transparency, noting that credible price discovery required sufficient transactions, willing participants, reliable reporting and confidence that market information reflected actual commercial activity. “Markets operate on information. Benchmarks operate on trust,” he said.

Also speaking, the Minister of State, Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, said Nigeria’s deregulation of the midstream and downstream petroleum sectors had created renewed investor interest and opened opportunities for greater regional integration.

According to him, the federal government took a bold decision to completely deregulate the downstream sector, creating an environment capable of attracting investment and unlocking the potential of the industry.

“Before this government came, nobody had the courage to turn around the downstream. Not even the military leaders had the courage. But at the breaking point, he (President Bola Tinubu) took the boldest decision of completely deregulating.

“Today, the midstream and downstream are completely deregulated. That is why we are seeing renewed interest,” Lokpobiri emphasised.

The minister said Nigeria must look beyond its domestic market and position itself to serve the wider West African market, arguing that the region could benefit from the country’s growing refining capacity.

He stressed the importance of processing resources locally rather than exporting raw materials and subsequently importing refined products at significantly higher costs.

“We export our raw cashews. We export our raw agro-products outside. They refine them. We process them. And we buy them back ten times the price,” he said.

Lokpobiri said Nigeria should use its growing refining capacity to capture a larger share of the West African market, but noted that this would require a sustainable pricing mechanism and stronger collaboration among countries and regulators.

For her part, the Chief Executive of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, said developments across Nigeria’s oil and gas value chain were creating an opportunity for deeper regional market integration.

Eyesan pointed to the increase in refining capacity, rising crude oil production and improvements in the gas sector as evidence of significant changes in the Nigerian petroleum industry.

“We are seeing a spike in refining capacity. We are seeing Nigeria not only meet its refining needs, but attempt to also export. That is unprecedented,” she said.

She added that Nigeria’s gas industry was moving from a position of total deficit towards bridging the supply gap, while crude oil production had also increased. “We are now able to cross the barrier that OPEC has set for us. That, again, is unprecedented,” she said.

Eyesan explained that the next step was to close the loop by integrating West African petroleum markets, stressing that countries could no longer afford to operate in silos. “The West African market must be integrated. We can no longer afford to operate in silos,” she pointed out.

She called for integrated regulatory systems and appropriate infrastructure across the value chain, arguing that the region needed to build ready markets and systems that connected rather than isolated individual countries and industries.

Also speaking, the Special Adviser on Energy to the President, Olu Verheijen, said West Africa’s challenge was no longer primarily a question of resources or refining capacity, but whether the region could develop the systems required to efficiently move energy from where it is produced to where it is needed. “Refining capacity alone, as big as ours is, does not create energy security,” she said.

Verheijen said refined products could only deliver economic value when they could be financed, stored, transported and distributed reliably.

“A refined product only delivers economic value when it can be financed, stored, transported, and distributed reliably. Without infrastructure, supply remains stranded. Without transparent pricing, investors price uncertainty rather than opportunity,” she said.

She said the region needed pipelines, ports, storage facilities, coastal vessels, trucking networks and trading platforms, as well as greater access to trade and infrastructure finance.

Verheijen said Nigeria was increasingly refining the majority of the petrol consumed domestically, with imports falling significantly, while refined products were increasingly reaching markets outside the country.

She said the next phase should focus on connecting the growing supply with regional demand through infrastructure and transparent markets.

Head of Platts, S&P Global Energy, Vera Bleu, in her intervention, said significant progress had been made towards developing regional price references over the past year, but stressed that market participants themselves must create the liquidity required to make regional benchmarks credible.

She said S&P Global had expanded its regional pricing assessments, including more frequent updates for petrol and other refined products in response to increased market volatility.

“We can give the foundations, we can make the reference prices available. It’s time for everybody in this room to take bold steps to really bring them alive,” she said.

Bleu said the challenge was that market participants would naturally continue to gravitate towards established international benchmarks because of their liquidity.

“The reality is you will have to create them. We can give the foundations, we can make the reference prices available. It’s time for everybody in this room to take bold steps to really bring them alive,” she said.

Deputy Governor, Operations, Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Emem Usoro, said a well-functioning and well-priced refined products market could create significant opportunities for the financial sector, particularly in mobilising long-term capital for refining, storage, transportation and other critical infrastructure.

She pointed out that such developments could strengthen capital markets, improve foreign exchange efficiency, boost intra-African trade and enhance investor confidence across the region.

World.title: Zacch Adedeji: When Academic Brilliance Runs Ahead of Judgment
World.content:
The recent outing by the Chairman of Nigeria Revenue Service, Mr. Zacch Adedeji, on Sunday Politics, was a blanket verdict on the characters of persons in the President Bola Tinubu administration. Olawale Olaleye writes.

After watching the Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), Mr. Zacch Adedeji, fumble on simple questions around basic principles of good governance and sound leadership, it’s easy to come to terms with the reality that, there are moments in public life when a single sentence tells you considerably more about an official than an hour-long interview ever could.

His recent outing on Sunday Politics, a Channels Television programme dedicated to Politics, Governance and Current Affairs, has just given credence to the saying that, it’s better to stay quiet and remain unassuming than to open one’s mouth and clear all doubts, sadly, shamefully.

For Adedeji, unfortunately, that moment arrived last Sunday. Appearing on Channels Television’s Sunday Politics, Adedeji undertook what ordinarily should have been an uncomplicated assignment: defend the economic policies of President Bola Tinubu.

His job was clearly cut out without equivocation. Explain the administration’s thinking, provide context to some of its difficult choices and, perhaps most importantly, reassure a population carrying an extraordinary burden that those in government understand their sacrifices.

Instead, somewhere along the way, the defence escaped him. What Nigerians got was something altogether different: a remarkable exhibition of how very easily intelligence can become separated from judgment.

Asked about the cost of governance and the lifestyle of those in power at a difficult economic moment, Adedeji offered, among other things, the fact that President Tinubu walks from his residence to his office as evidence that the President is not living extravagantly.

He said the President eats once a day, has spent long stretches without travelling abroad and hardly attends parties. Then came the sentence that ought to be studied in schools of public communication.

“How much is an Escalade that the president of Nigeria cannot afford?” he asked. How much is an Escalade? Really? That question, coming from the man who heads the institution charged with collecting revenue from Nigerians, was perhaps more revealing than Adedeji intended.

It was not merely the answer that was troubling. It was the frame of mind from which such an answer could emerge.

Nigeria is living through a severe cost-of-living squeeze. Even where macroeconomic indicators have begun to improve, the relief has yet to reach millions of households in anything resembling proportion to the sacrifices demanded of them.

Reuters reported only this week that many Nigerians continue to struggle with food, fuel and other essentials despite improving investor sentiment and other signs of macroeconomic stabilisation.

That is the audience Adedeji was addressing. Not economists at a seminar. Not a gathering of investment bankers. Not presidential aides sitting around a conference table in the Villa. Ordinary Nigerians.

Men and women, who calculate transport fares before leaving home. Families that revise food lists several times before reaching the market. Salary earners for whom the last week of the month has become an exercise in improvisation. Small-business owners confronted simultaneously by electricity costs, fuel costs, rent, taxes and weakening purchasing power.

And the chairman of the country’s revenue service looks into a television camera and asks them, in effect: How much is an Escalade anyway? Therein lies the tragedy. The question was never whether Tinubu could afford an Escalade. Adedeji either misunderstood the question put to him or chose to answer a more convenient one.

The issue is not whether Bola Tinubu, as a private citizen, possesses sufficient personal wealth to buy a Cadillac Escalade. That is beside the point.

A President may personally be able to afford 50 Escalades. He may be capable of buying a private aircraft, a yacht and whatever else catches his fancy. If lawfully acquired with private resources, that would be a different conversation entirely.

The question about the cost of governance concerns public resources. It asks whether a government demanding sacrifice from its citizens is itself demonstrating restraint.

It asks whether the political class appreciates the moral obligation to share, or at least visibly recognise, the burden of economic adjustment. It asks whether official expenditure reflects the gravity of the times.

It asks why the belt appears permanently tightened around the waist of the citizen while government always seems to find another hole through which its own waist may expand.

These are questions of leadership, symbolism and accountability. They cannot be answered by announcing the president’s personal purchasing power. Indeed, “the President can afford it” is precisely the wrong defence where public expenditure is concerned.

The Nigerian state is not Bola Tinubu’s private estate. Government vehicles are not justified by the personal net worth of their occupants. Public expenditure is justified by necessity, value, prudence and the public interest.

For the head of the nation’s revenue service, of all people, that distinction should require no explanation. Walking inside the Villa is not an economic policy. Then there was Adedeji’s fascinating evidence of presidential frugality: President Tinubu, he said, walks from his residence to his office.

One hardly knows where to begin. The President’s residence and office are within the heavily secured presidential complex. Walking between two points within that precinct may be healthy. It may even be admirable as a personal habit.

But what, exactly, does it tell us about the cost of government? Does the President’s walk reduce the number of official vehicles purchased by government? Does it shrink recurrent expenditure? Does it reduce the size of the bureaucracy?

Does it eliminate waste? Does it cut the cost of maintaining government fleets? Does it reduce the burden imposed on taxpayers? Does it put food on anybody’s table? The answer is obvious. But Adedeji just didn’t get it.

Imagine telling a man who has had to abandon his car because he can no longer comfortably afford fuel that the government understands sacrifice because the President walks from his residence to his office inside Aso Rock.

Imagine telling a woman rationing food portions for her children that the compelling evidence of government frugality is that the President eats once daily. These, interestingly, are personal choices, made sometimes on health ground.

They may have been intended as sympathetic anecdotes about the President’s work ethic. In another conversation, they might even have humanised him. But as answers to questions about the cost of governance, they were astonishingly tone-deaf.

There is a difference between defending a principal and embarrassing him with the defence. In this case, his defence became a damage to the president and the administration.

President Tinubu did not need that defence. Indeed, Adedeji’s intervention arguably created a problem where a more thoughtful answer might have earned the administration some credit.

He could have acknowledged the concern. He could have said that Nigerians were entitled to expect government to demonstrate the same discipline being demanded of citizens.

He could have provided figures showing reductions in particular areas of expenditure. He could have identified measures being implemented to rationalise government assets, travel, overheads or procurement. He could have argued that some expenditure associated with the presidency is dictated by security rather than luxury.

He could even have conceded that government must do more. Any of those responses would at least have engaged the substance of the question. Instead, Nigerians were invited to contemplate the affordability of an Escalade. And that is where education collides with emotional intelligence.

Adedeji is no academic lightweight. The Presidency itself announced him in 2023 as a first-class graduate of Accounting from Obafemi Awolowo University. His résumé includes service as Oyo State Commissioner for Finance, head of the National Sugar Development Council and presidential adviser on revenue before taking charge of the federal revenue authority.

This is exactly why the interview was so disappointing. Nobody disputes that a first-class brain can understand balance sheets. The question is whether it understands people.

Public administration is not an accounting examination. Nation-building is not solved by graduating at the top of a class. Leadership requires something that no university transcript can fully certify: judgment.

It requires knowing not only whether something is technically correct, but whether it is appropriate. Knowing when an argument, though available, should never be made. Knowing when triumphalism is dangerous.

It is also knowing the difference between explaining hardship and appearing to mock those experiencing it. That is the difference between book intelligence and public wisdom. And this is where Adedeji’s “book brain” appears surprisingly empty. It is not empty of knowledge, but empty, in that particular moment, of perspective.

Government cannot preach sacrifice from a luxury car. There is also a larger issue that Adedeji inadvertently reopened.

One of the enduring weaknesses of the Tinubu administration’s reform narrative has been the difficulty of persuading Nigerians that sacrifice is equitably distributed.

The administration can make a defensible economic case for removing distortions. Adedeji himself used the same interview to argue that subsidy removal, foreign-exchange reforms and other measures were necessary to address deep structural problems in the economy.

Those arguments deserve to be heard on their merits. But economic reform also has a moral component. If government tells people that an unsustainable subsidy must disappear because the country can no longer afford it, citizens are entitled to ask what government itself can no longer afford.

That is not populism. It is elementary fairness. A government cannot ask millions of people to downgrade their lives while its own political establishment appears determined to upgrade its tastes. It cannot sermonise about patience from behind tinted windows and expect universal applause.

It cannot repeatedly invoke fiscal discipline while the public associates political office with increasingly extravagant symbols of privilege. And it certainly cannot answer concerns about luxury with the astonishing proposition that the president is wealthy enough to afford the luxury being questioned.

Again, whether the President personally can afford an Escalade is irrelevant. Government is not a rich man’s club in which the personal wealth of officeholders determines the acceptable standard of public expenditure.

Government belongs equally to the Nigerian who cannot afford an Escalade, the Nigerian who cannot afford a second-hand Toyota and, more urgently, the Nigerian currently wondering whether he can afford the bus fare home. That is the citizen whose sensibilities public officials must never lose sight of.

The arrogance problem is another leg to it. There was something else buried inside that Escalade remark. “Please don’t embarrass this country,” Adedeji added after asking how much the vehicle costs.

That was perhaps even more disturbing. Who exactly was embarrassing the country? The journalist, Seun Okinbaloye, asking a legitimate question about the cost of governance? The citizens concerned about the lifestyle of their leaders?

Since when did questioning luxury in government become an embarrassment to Nigeria? A democracy begins to lose its moral compass when public officials treat scrutiny as insolence. Citizens are not subjects. They are not beneficiaries of the generosity of government. They fund government.

The President is not doing Nigerians a favour by being President. Ministers are not doing the country a favour by serving. Heads of agencies are not philanthropists who periodically dispense governance to a grateful population.

They are servants of the republic. The taxpayer has every right to ask questions about how public resources are deployed, whether the official being questioned earns a first-class degree or possesses ten doctorates.

Indeed, Adedeji’s own office makes sensitivity doubly important. The taxman cannot afford contempt. You cannot spend one part of the day persuading Nigerians that taxation is a civic duty and another sounding irritated that they dare ask how government spends what it collects.

Tax compliance ultimately rests on more than enforcement. It rests on legitimacy. People are more willing to surrender part of their income to a state they believe is responsible, accountable and conscious of their sacrifices. The language of tax administration therefore matters. So does humility.

Yet, there is still a defence to make — just not this one. None of this means the Tinubu administration has no economic story to tell.

Adedeji argued in the same interview that the government inherited severe economic distortions and that recent reforms have improved revenue and other fiscal indicators. He also said the philosophy of the tax reforms was to “tax prosperity” rather than poverty.

Fine. Make that case. Show the numbers. Demonstrate where revenue has gone. Show Nigerians the schools, roads, hospitals, infrastructure and social investments produced by increased collections. Explain what would have happened without the reforms.

Acknowledge what has not worked. State what government intends to correct. That is how serious governments communicate in difficult times. But spare Nigerians stories about how many times the President eats. Spare them lectures about his ability to buy an Escalade.

And please spare them the suggestion that walking a few minutes within the presidential precinct amounts to some extraordinary national sacrifice. That is not economic communication. It is political self-harm.

There is another important factor to further consider, and it is the danger of courtiers. Perhaps the larger lesson is for President Tinubu himself.

Every President needs defenders. But no President needs courtiers. Defenders interrogate facts before speaking. Courtiers interpret every question as an attack. Defenders know that acknowledging a weakness does not amount to betraying the principal. Courtiers believe loyalty requires pretending that no weakness exists.

And, eventually, courtiers become dangerous because they construct around power an alternative reality in which everything is wonderful, every criticism malicious and every public complaint evidence of ingratitude. That bubble is fatal to governments.

President Tinubu needs people around him who can tell him when Nigerians are hurting, not people competing to produce ever more inventive explanations for why Nigerians should stop complaining. He needs aides and appointees capable of reading a room.

He needs men and women who understand that economic reforms are not experienced as charts, indices and fiscal projections in Nigerian homes. They are experienced at fuel stations, supermarkets, school gates, pharmacies and markets.

Adedeji’s television appearance suggests this is a lesson some people in government still need to learn. A first class is not a licence for first-class insensitivity. This is what ultimately makes the episode painful. Adedeji is supposed to represent one of the administration’s brighter technocratic faces. That is why more should be expected of him.

Academic accomplishment should broaden perspective, not narrow it. Expertise should create clarity, not arrogance. A brilliant accountant should understand better than most that expenditure is not justified simply because somebody can afford it.

And a revenue administrator should understand better than most that every naira government spends originates somewhere — from taxes, oil receipts, levies, borrowing or other resources belonging ultimately to the Nigerian people.

The fellow asking, “How much is an Escalade?” may therefore wish to remember that, for millions of Nigerians, the real question today is much smaller.

How much is a bag of rice? How much is transport to work? How much is school fees? How much is rent? How much is medication? How much will it cost to feed the children tomorrow? Those are the questions occupying Nigerian minds.

Against them, the Escalade question does not merely sound insensitive. It sounds obscene. Public office demands more than certificates. It demands empathy, proportion, restraint and an instinctive recognition that power is held in trust.

When officials become so disconnected from the governed that legitimate questions about official luxury irritate them, something fundamental has gone wrong.

And when they begin to sound as though Nigerians should be grateful merely because those in power have agreed to govern them, then perhaps they have stayed too long inside the bubble of office.
