Kalasinga also announced that Linda Mwananchi would hold a rally in Homa Bay on August 16 despite local warnings. He said Sifuna had a right to campaign anywhere in Kenya.

He called for peaceful competition and warned against attempts to block the rally or restrict political activity in the region emphasising that Kenya is for everyone, constitutionally, peacefully and equally.

They two vowed to fight for the Linda Mwananchi name.

The Wamboka-Kalasinga push adds momentum to Sifuna’s campaign and pressures opposition leaders to unite before the 2027 election.

World.title: Kindiki defends government's development agenda in Mt Kenya
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Deputy President Kithure Kindiki and Lands Cabinet Secretary Alice Wahome at Gaichanjiru Catholic Church in Kandara, Murang’a, on August 10, 2026. [Boniface Gikandi, Standard]

Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has reiterated the government’s commitment to ensure equitable development.

Prof Kindiki said that President William Ruto’s government has initiated many development projects in Mt Kenya to transform livelihoods.

“Am advising the people against being deceived to leave the government to join the opposition where nothing is being provided,” he said.

The Deputy President said the road projects which had stalled have since been revived after the government released Sh176 billion owed to contractors to ensure completion of 6,000km.

He spoke at Gaichanjiru Catholic Church in Kandara, Murang’a, on Sunday, where he was the chief guest during celebrations to mark 100 years since the establishment of Gaichanjiru Mission Hospital managed by the Catholic Diocese of Murang'a.

Kindiki, who was accompanied by Cabinet Secretaries Alice Wahome (Lands) and Rebecca Miano (Tourism), said that the government has impacted the region with affordable houses estimated at 180,000 units, modern markets and student hostels that have created employment for hundreds of skilled and unskilled persons.

He said the church has a history of partnering with the government in matters concerning development and empowerment of the less fortunate in the community.

“In Murang’a the government has ensured all the projects that KeRRA under Eng Antony Mwaura was working on are completed to give the locals value for money,” said the DP.

During the event, the President gave Sh10 million for procurement of equipment for the health facility, where more than Sh20 million was raised.

Ruto also gave Sh 50 million and directed the Housing Department to facilitate construction of the hospital's ICU, HDU, theatre and laboratory

Kindiki lauded efforts by Wahome that have seen Murang’a County benefit from Sh27 billion programmes from her ministry.

“Murang’a through her efforts has 27 modern markets, Affordable Housing Programme units, and student hostels, programmes that have engaged hundreds of persons,” he said.

World.title: Charlene Ruto's Koito lights up Kilgoris
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto’s daughter, Charlene Ruto, is engaged to Tanzanian entrepreneur Isaiah Yunge.

The drums rolled, traditional songs filled the air and dancers swayed in colourful rhythm as Kilgoris was transformed into a spectacular theatre of love, culture, wealth and political power.

At the expansive Intonna Heritage Farm in Naserian Village, President William Ruto’s daughter, Charlene Chelagat Ruto, took a major traditional step towards marriage as the First Family hosted her Koito ak Chaik—a colourful Kalenjin engagement and farewell ceremony.

For hours, the skies above Kilgoris were punctuated by helicopters ferrying distinguished guests to the President’s family property, while luxury vehicles streamed through the gates carrying politicians, government officials, business personalities, relatives and friends.

On the ground, the mood was unmistakably festive. Traditional songs echoed across the expansive farm as dancers moved to the rhythm, colourful attire transformed the venue into a sea of elegance and culture, and guests embraced the joy of a ceremony that combined an ancient African tradition with the unmistakable grandeur of Kenya’s First Family.

It was romance wrapped in tradition—and tradition presented on a spectacular scale.

The guest list read almost like a roll call of Kenya’s political establishment. Leaving the Narok delegation was Governor Patrick Ole Ntutu, who joined Kilgoris MP Julius Sunkuli and former Narok Governor Samuel Tunai in celebrating the First Family on the special occasion.

The ceremony also brought together elected leaders from across Narok County, creating an impressive gathering of the county’s political establishment at the heart of Trans Mara.

From governors and Senators to MPs, the event brought together leaders from across the country. Top government officials and senior executives too came dressed for the ceremony

The fashion became part of the spectacle. Brown, maroon and other earthy tones dominated the scene, blending effortlessly with the traditional African setting. It was a celebration in which political leaders seemed determined to make an entrance as memorable as the occasion itself.

But beyond the political faces and the luxury was the heartbeat of the ceremony—culture. Traditional songs rang across the farm. Dancers moved with energy and precision, their performances adding colour and rhythm to a celebration centred on family and love.

The atmosphere shifted between moments of emotion and bursts of exuberance as relatives, friends and guests celebrated Charlene’s transition into a new stage of life.

The contrast was striking. Modern wealth arrived by helicopter, while ancient traditions were celebrated through song and dance. Luxury vehicles lined up outside as cultural performers entertained guests inside. Political heavyweights mingled with family elders.

Politicians arrive for Charlene Ruto's Koito in Kilgoris. [UGC]

And amid the glamour, the central message remained simple: Charlene and her fiancé, Isaiah Yunge, had brought together not just two families but two countries.

Yunge is a Tanzanian technology entrepreneur and digital innovation enthusiast associated with Goodsam Technologies and is a co-founder of Smart Kaya LLC, a smart-home technology venture.

He has been recognised among Forbes Africa’s 30 Under 30 and received the Queen’s Young Leaders Award in 2018. His interest in technology reportedly began at an early age. At 17, he was selected as a UNICEF Africa Youth Ambassador and participated in international advocacy around children's rights.

He later pursued training in sustainable business models through the Swedish Institute, studied Leading Change at Cambridge University and became an alumnus of the Harvard Ministerial Leadership Program.

For all its glamour, the heart of the celebration remained the centuries-old tradition of Koito. Among the Kalenjin, it is a significant engagement ceremony through which the families of the bride and groom formally meet, bless the relationship, exchange gifts and discuss dowry arrangements.

It is a moment when families begin the process of becoming one. The Chaik aspect gives the occasion an emotional dimension, symbolising the farewell of a daughter as she prepares to leave her parental home and begin a new chapter with her husband. Politicians arrive for Charlene Ruto's Koito in Kilgoris. [UGC]

For Charlene, the symbolism was profound. Surrounded by her parents, family, friends and some of the country’s most powerful political figures, she was celebrated not simply as the President’s daughter, but as a daughter taking a traditional step towards marriage.

The songs, dances and blessings gave the occasion an emotional warmth that stood in contrast to the scale of the event.

Yet there was no escaping the extraordinary display of wealth surrounding the celebration. Helicopters arriving overhead. Luxury vehicles streaming through the gates. High-ranking government officials and elected leaders arriving in motorcades. Elegant outfits and carefully coordinated colours.

It was a spectacle that demonstrated the resources, networks and influence available to one of Kenya’s most powerful families. The ceremony was therefore more than a social event.

For Charlene, however, beyond the helicopters, politicians, fashion and cameras was the quiet meaning of the day.

A daughter was being prepared to leave one home and begin another. Two families were being brought together.

Love was at the centre. Culture provided the rhythm. Wealth supplied the grandeur. And political power provided the spectacle.

For one unforgettable Saturday, Charlene Ruto’s Koito turned Kilgoris into a glittering stage where romance, tradition, influence and prosperity met under the Narok sky.

World.title: Police join protest victims' Sh25.75m reparations payout
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prof. Makau Mutua, Chairperson of the Panel of Experts on Compensation of Victims of Human Rights Violations. [File,Standard]

A protest reparations panel has approved compensation for 49 police officers, awarding them Sh25.75 million alongside payments to civilians who suffered human rights violations.

The Panel of Experts on Compensation of Victims of Human Rights Violations approved seven claims involving severe injuries, 37 for moderate injuries and five for minor injuries, according to an update issued Friday, August 7.

"In acknowledgement of the dedication by our uniformed officers to protecting the public, the Panel has resolved to grant appropriate compensation for the human rights violations they sustained during the period in question," the panel said.

The inclusion of police officers adds a new dimension to a compensation programme created against the backdrop of protests in which police conduct has faced scrutiny.

During protests between June 17 and July 7, 2025, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) recorded 65 deaths, 342 civilian injuries and 171 injuries to police officers.

IPOA said most of the deaths were linked mainly to police actions during crowd-control operations.

The compensation programme grew out of the National Dialogue Committee (NADCO) process, which sought to address political and governance tensions in Kenya.

The government later set aside Sh2 billion for victims of human rights violations linked to protests and other demonstrations between 2017 and 2025.

The panel reported that it has processed 680 claims and disbursed Sh896.1 million in compensation.

The panel listed three phases of payments as Sh448.7 million in the initial phase, Sh225.4 million in the second phase and Sh247.95 million in the third phase.

The latest phase covered 175 civilian victims and included 50 fatalities, 46 severe injuries, 49 moderate injuries, 21 minor injuries and nine economic-loss claims.

The panel reported total payments of Sh222 million for the phase.

However, 472 claims submitted through IPOA and KNCHR remain outstanding because applicants have not provided enough supporting documents.

The panel is working with IPOA regional offices to locate affected victims and their beneficiaries and obtain the documents required to process the claims.

The backlog includes 594 of the 600 economic-loss claims received by the panel. Only four have been processed and compensated.

The panel has also received nine claims under the sexual offences category. Eight have been processed and compensated while one remains pending.

Claims involving enforced disappearances remain under review because the panel says the cases require investigation and verification before they can be approved, referred for further investigation or declared ineligible.

The panel has also reclassified three claims from minor to severe after reviewing medical reports and additional submissions.

It approved above-scale compensation for five victims whose injuries it described as permanent and life-altering and said it would recommend that President Ruto include them in a government-funded lifetime medical scheme.

World.title: EACC arrests Kitui County Chief Officer over Sh17.48m procurement fraud
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kitui County Chief Officer Gladys Mami Kivoto and five company directors arrested by EACC. [Joh Muia, Standard]

The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) has arrested Kitui County Chief Officer Gladys Mami Kivoto and five company directors over alleged conflict of interest and procurement irregularities involving Sh17.48 million contracts.

In a statement on Thursday, EACC CEO Abdi Mohamud said investigations found that Kivoto, who served in the Departments of Agriculture & Fisheries and Irrigation, allegedly traded with the county through five proxy companies: Shanel Construction Ltd, ECO Stone Ltd, AZ Links Ltd, DTK Construction Ltd, and 4-Walls Ltd.

The companies were paid a total of Sh14.1 million by the county between the 2018/2019 and 2024/2025 financial years.

EACC further established that three of the directors, Josephine Mwikali Wambua of Shanel Construction, Makoma Wambua of AZ Links and Emmanuel Wambua of ECO Stone are relatives of Kivoto. There were also financial transactions between Kivoto and directors of DTK Construction and 4-Walls.

Following investigations, the file was forwarded to the DPP, who approved charges against nine suspects, including conflict of interest, abuse of office, money laundering, and corrupt procurement.

Those arrested are Gladys Mami Kivoto, Josephine Mwikali Wambua Director, Shanel Construction, Roselyne Kyambi Kilonzi Director, Shanel Construction, Mary Mueni Mbiti Director, DTK Construction & 4-Walls, Jonathan Kivondo Kieti Director, DTK Construction and Onesmus Munyao Nzioka Director, ECO Stone.

EACC directed Makoma Wambua of ECO Stone, Emmanuel Wambua of AZ Links, and Stella Nthenya Kioko of AZ Links who are reportedly in hiding to present themselves at the EACC Lower Eastern Regional Office in Machakos or the nearest EACC office for processing.

The suspects are expected to be arraigned at the Kitui Law Courts.

World.title: High Court orders striking nurses back to work
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Uasin Gishu County nurses strike over delayed payments and unfulfilled Collective Bargaining Agreement [Wycliff Kipsang, Standard]

Nurses across the 47 counties have been ordered to report back to work immediately or face legal action from the counties.

Justice Monica Mbaru of the Employment and Labour Court in Mombasa issued orders temporarily stopping the nationwide nurse strike that commenced on July 29, 2026, and ordered the Kenya National Union of Nurses and Midwives (KNUNM) to direct its members back to work.

Justice Mbaru said on Wednesday that any nurse absent from work without proper and lawful cause shall face disciplinary action.

This is after Mombasa County Government and its Public Service Board successfully enjoined the 46 county governments to make the order national.

“In the interim, the KNUNM (respondent) is hereby restrained from undertaking any industrial action relating to the strike notices dated July 21 and July 29 and shall direct all its members to resume duty forthwith and unconditionally to allow the court to address the claim herein on a priority basis,” said Justice Mbaru.

The judge ordered all county labour officers in the 47 counties to record attendance of nurses who report to work and compile a report in court on September 22, 2026.

“Any member of the KNUNM who will be noted by the County Labour Officer as absent from duty without lawful cause shall allow the counties to issue necessary notice to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken,” said Justice Mbaru.

In their petition certified urgent, Mombasa County claimed that the nurses strike has crippled services in public hospitals across all the 47 counties, thereby placing patients facing emergency and inpatient care at risk.

In Mombasa County, the nurses strike paralysed medical services at all medical facilities, including Coast General Hospital, Port Reitz Hospital, Likoni District Hospital and Shimo La Tewa GK Prison Hospital.

Mombasa County, through its Counsel Murtaza Tajbhai, said that the strike had turned from a labour disagreement to a matter of immense public interest.

Tajbhai said that the nurses’ union proceeded with the said strike despite the Mombasa Public Service Board inviting the KNUNM officials for talks to avert the said strike.

The union had raised concerns over the 2025-2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA), implementation of the 2017 Return to Work Formula and pension terms for Universal Health Coverage staff care guidelines for nurses and the reinstatement of 46 nurses dismissed in Kisii County.

However, in their petition, Mombasa County said that the said grievances could not be addressed by each county individually.

Mombasa County Service Board Chief Executive Officer Fadhil Maamum told the court in his affidavit that most of the demands required consultation with national institutions like the Salaries and Remuneration Commission, while others cannot be implemented immediately given their significant financial implications.

He said that nurses under Mombasa County have no salary arrears and had met some of the union’s demands through negotiations.

Maamum said that while the nurses’ grievances can be resolved, the patients do not have the luxury of time.

“Nurses are designated essential service providers under the Labour Relations Act and the industrial action was unlawful because the statutory dispute resolution mechanism had not been exhausted," said Maamum.

He said the court's intervention will allow for negotiations and safeguard the constitutional right to healthcare.

However, the Union said that the strike was after failed action by the counties to meet their agreed grievances despite continued negotiations.

The nurses said they will not be reporting to work unless guided by the union.

World.title: What Trump’s catering-truck escape says about a war that won’t end
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s use of a catering truck in a secret escape from a NATO country amid an Iranian threat is the latest embarrassing twist of a war that repeatedly defies his claims of victory.

The Secret Service did its job by using whatever method was necessary to spirit Trump out of Turkey in July, ultimately on an alternative jet to one that has been bringing presidents home safely since the 1990s.

But belated revelations about the drama, first reported by the Washington Post, kicked up a major new political storm. Most significantly, the ruse conjured up damaging new imagery about an unpopular war that Trump can’t end.

The existence of a potential threat against the president doesn’t in itself mean his war against Iran is a failure. But the spectacle of him leaving incognito after a NATO summit is likely to be interpreted overseas as a new affront to American power. It also raises this question: If Trump cannot guarantee his own safety on the territory of a major ally, how can his administration’s case that it has all but obliterated Iran’s military capability and regional terror threat be fully believed?

Iran has yet to comment. But its apparent success in metaphorically forcing Trump to take cover is a propaganda coup. For all the president’s bravado, the regime doesn’t seem to be heading for collapse or begging for a deal.

The hijinks at Ankara airport are just the latest occasion when reality has mocked the administration’s rosy war narrative.

Trump on Monday, for instance, insisted yet again that the Strait of Hormuz was “open now.” Yet the critical waterway remains effectively under Iran’s control, meaning that US forces have been fighting for months to return to the status quo — and open strait — that prevailed before the war.

Everyone has meanwhile lost count of Trump’s predictions that a deal is imminent, only for the stalemate to grind on.

In another sign of apparent US strategic disarray, the war that Trump declared won after a few days has seriously depleted US missile stocks, including nearly 80 percent of interceptors for a key missile defense system, CNN reported last week.

Trump ‘hates anything like this’

President Donald Trump holds a press briefing at the White House after a man with a gun stormed the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in Washington, DC, on April 25. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Oddly, given their position, presidents often travel through scruffy locations, since security precautions force them to enter buildings through underground garages, back entrances, kitchens and service elevators. So even the kingpin of gold-plated Mar-a-Lago may not have been too shocked to slum it in a hydraulic catering truck in Ankara.

But Trump’s clandestine departure from Turkey sits poorly with the president’s self-image as a winner and a strongman.

Even when bloodied and rumpled after an 2024 assassination attempt, he rose, pumped his fist and said “fight, fight.” When a gunman tried to rush the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April, Trump went on TV to insist he wouldn’t be intimidated and the show must go on.

“Donald Trump absolutely hates anything like this,” the president’s first-term communications director Alyssa Farah Griffin told CNN’s Phil Mattingly on “The Lead” Tuesday. “He hated when he had to go to the bunker because of the threat environment in the White House … He wanted to go back immediately to show he’s not scared, he’s not running.”

Griffin, now a CNN commentator, added, “This speaks to me that this was a very real threat. If he’s willing to take these measures and to do it. It speaks to the moment we’re in, in the Middle East.”

Trump’s tarmac bait-and-switch also fueled new controversy over the presidential plane fleet, since he’d previously abandoned plans to fly his new red, white, and blue jet donated by Qatar, which critics warn lacks sufficient security systems for a president. The president and the White House have denied that a threat led them to resort to a backup aircraft.

People board Air Force One at Ankara Esenboga Airport in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Then, there’s the issue of whether staff, Secret Service agents, journalists and crew were in mortal danger when they took off on a plane that Trump had been shown on television boarding minutes previously — before secretly leaving.

On Tuesday, Trump was asked by reporters why it was considered too dangerous for him to fly on one of the planes usually used as Air Force One while the same did not apply to members of the press.

“The plane that I flew on was at greater risk … because that would be the plane, I think, that they would be more likely to go for,” the president said.

But his comment didn’t answer the question at issue, because by climbing aboard the presidential jet, he’d given every impression he planned to travel on it — before his unannounced departure.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, told CNN’s Erin Burnett Tuesday that Trump “put people in harm’s way to save himself — that’s who Donald Trump is.”

Pritzker then tied the incident to the wider war, saying, “He’s willing to put troops in harm’s way … he slinked away literally in a catering truck while the reporters and his own staff were on a plane that apparently was under threat.”

Pritzker’s comments put the drama at the center of the midterm election battle. And there will likely be investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress in November.

Trump may spend the rest of his life facing threats from Iran

An Iranian flag is waved under a billboard with graphic showing Strait of Hormuz and the sewn lips of President Donald Trump, in downtown Tehran, Iran, on May 6. Vahid Salemi/AP

Trump, who has survived at least two direct assassination attempts, is likely to spend the rest of his life under the threat of an attack from Iran. His exposure dates to his first term, when he ordered an attack that killed Iranian general Qasem Soleimani. Iran’s incentive grew when Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in US and Israeli air strikes at the start of the current war.

Choreographed displays of defiance at Khamenei’s funeral in July saw protesters demand the death of the president. So there is good reason for the Secret Service to take any intelligence about possible attacks seriously. There have been past reports of killings of Iranians opposed to the Tehran government in Turkey, and the Iranian regime has been one of the world’s most prominent exporters of terrorism.

“I do find it entirely plausible that there might be a serious threat to the president by some Iranian-backed entity. The US, the UK, a number of European states have foiled or disrupted Iranian-backed attacks over the last several years, frankly going back decades,” retired US Army Lt. Gen. Karen Gibson said on “The Lead” Tuesday. “They’ve demonstrated an intent and a capacity to do this.”

Trump warned in July that 1,000 missiles were “Locked and ⁠Loaded and aimed at the ​Islamic Republic of Iran, with ​thousands of more to immediately follow” if it attempted or succeeded in assassinating him. In practice, any response to the death of a president would not be decided by orders he left behind, but by his successor, in this case, Vice President JD Vance. A need to restore US deterrence and credibility would likely mandate a massive US escalation.

Still, it’s notable that Trump did not respond to his indecorous departure from Turkey with an emotional response of his own. Perhaps his success in keeping it quiet until now saved face. But he has also consistently reached forks in the road and balked at mission creep that could result in heavy US casualties.

It’s possible that the Secret Service’s actions in Turkey may have averted an attack that could have drawn the US deeper into a quagmire.

But Trump’s furtive flight from Turkey makes it much harder for him to argue he’s made the world safer.

World.title: Trump declines to rule out declaring a national security emergency to control the 2026 election
World.content:
President Donald Trump in a new interview declined to rule out declaring a national security emergency as a means to try to assert more control over the 2026 midterm elections.

It’s merely the latest warning sign that Trump could try to mess with the election not just by baselessly claiming voter fraud and challenging the results afterward — as he did in 2020, leading to a violent riot at the US Capitol — but by trying to unilaterally take control before votes are cast.

In the interview, Wayne Allyn Root of Real America’s Voice pitched such a scenario to Trump. He suggested it as an alternative, given the Senate has failed to pass Trump’s coveted elections bill, known as the “SAVE America Act.”

“If they never get the SAVE America Act done, you have the right to declare a national security emergency for elections,” Root said. He added that “if you declare a national security emergency as the president of the United States, they can’t challenge it. It can only be overturned by a two-thirds vote by both houses of Congress. So if you do this in the next month, we will get photo ID, proof of citizenship (for voter registration) and a limit to mail-in ballots.”

It’s at this point that Trump cut Root off and coyly suggested such an option was indeed in play.

“Let me just say that stranger things have happened, OK?” Trump said. “I’ll leave it at that.”

Despite Root’s comments, it’s far from clear such a gambit would even work. And CNN has asked the White House for more detail on what the president meant.

Trump often responds to hypotheticals by declining to rule them out — no matter how extreme the proposal might be. So it’s possible to read too much into this.

But as CNN’s Jake Tapper has noted, there are plenty of signals that Trump at least aspires to try to exert more control over elections. And these methods often appear transparently geared toward helping Republicans.

A major one is the administration’s threat to have the US Postal Service not deliver mail ballots for states that don’t comply with its demand that they hand over their voter lists. This is a request that even many red states have rejected, citing privacy concerns.

Democrats are much more likely to use mail ballots, which Trump has baselessly connected to widespread fraud. So curtailing them could greatly help Republicans.

(Federal courts have blocked this Trump executive order, and the administration recently appealed to the Supreme Court.)

Trump has also gone to great lengths to try to substantiate his still-baseless claims of widespread fraud. That includes the administration seizing 2020 ballots in Fulton County, Georgia, and Trump’s recent primetime address about election security that some read as a statement of intent — a pretext for more direct federal involvement in elections, which are run by states.

President Donald Trump speaks about election security during an address to the nation from the East Room of the White House on July 16. Saul Loeb/Pool/Reuters

Ty Cobb, who served as White House counsel in Trump’s first term, said he interpreted the speech last month as a “predicate that he needs to declare an emergency.”

And Trump has occasionally said things, like he did in the new interview, suggesting he would like to take control of US elections.

Back in February, he urged his party to “take over the voting in at least 15 places,” adding: “The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting.”

The Washington Post also reported in March that pro-Trump activists were circulating a potential executive order that claimed Chinese interference in the 2020 election gave Trump emergency authorities over the 2026 election. And Trump’s primetime address focused on China, despite the tenuous evidence.

Trump’s intense focus on the “SAVE America Act,” which has never appeared to have a chance to pass but Trump has said is vital, could also be read as part of building the case for more drastic action.

But whether Trump could take over elections himself, as Root posits, is far from certain.

As CNN’s Marshall Cohen and Michael Williams reported in February, the Constitution makes it difficult for Trump to truly “nationalize” elections. Courts have overwhelmingly upheld the principle that states are in charge of elections.

Presidents generally have more authority to act unilaterally when national security is involved — hence the significance of invoking China — but some experts are skeptical that Trump’s effort would pass legal muster.

World.title: Iran’s supreme leader elevates military veterans willing to confront the US
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has boasted that his war in Iran has led to a “very rational,” “very different,” and “much more reasonable” leadership in Tehran. But the elevation of six hardliners to top security positions this week suggests the Islamic Republic’s new command may be neither moderate nor inclined to compromise.

The men now rising through the security establishment have spent their careers confronting enemies abroad and suppressing dissent at home.

The announcement of the senior appointments, purportedly made by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Monday, followed the naming of a new national security chief, Mohsen Rezaie, a day earlier.

Experts say the changes mark a shift in approach compared to the more cautious tone under Mojtaba’s father, Ali Khamenei, who was supreme leader until assassinated by Israel at the start of the war.

An image of “Team Mojtaba” featured on the front page of the Hamshahri newspaper on Tuesday. Hamshahri

It is both more aggressive toward external enemies and more vigilant toward internal dissent.

There are two parallel priorities, says Hamidreza Azizi at the Clingendael Institute, a think tank in the Netherlands: preparing the state for a more confrontational external environment and further securitizing the domestic sphere.

“The emphasis on offensive operations, unified command, and faster decision-making suggests that the leadership wants to move from Ali Khamenei’s traditionally more cautious approach to deterrence toward what could be described as offensive deterrence,” Azizi told CNN.

Most of the appointees have a background in intelligence, according to Saeid Golkar, associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga.

“The picture we are seeing is the Islamic Republic moving toward a security-dominated bureaucratic regime,” he told CNN.

The reshuffle reinforces the regime’s “current maximalist and hardline positions,” according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, “including absolute Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz, the removal of US troops from the region, and the development of Iran’s nuclear program.”

Rezaie has long called for resistance against the United States while acknowledging a place for negotiation.

In March he warned that “if the United States strikes Iran’s electricity infrastructure, this time the equation will not be ‘an eye for an eye’; rather, it will be a head, hands, and feet for an eye.”

And last month he claimed: “The United States has been trapped, it has fallen into the trap of Iran, but we will not let it go.”

Targeting Trump through the ballot box

Rezaie belongs to a faction of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) that believes “the only way to get concessions from the US is the continuation of fighting, exerting pressure on the US and a steady dose of pain on Donald Trump,” said Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East politics at George Washington University.

His elevation feeds into the overall Iranian strategy of prolonging the conflict with the US and ensuring that Trump’s allies face defeat in the midterm elections, Azodi told CNN.

“The current leadership in Tehran is far more risk-taking,” according to Vali Nasr, author of “Iran’s Grand Strategy.”

That leadership believes that Iran’s “weak” response to the killing by the US in 2020 of Qasem Soleimani, the leader of Iran’s elite Quds Force, was one reason Trump escalated pressure in his second term, according to Nasr.

Soleimani was targeted by a US missile in Baghdad at the end of the first Trump term. Iran did not retaliate directly, despite furious rhetoric.

This new group of leaders is more willing to use “Iran’s own military capabilities directly, and challenge adversaries without the same level of restraint,” says Israeli analyst and Iran-watcher Danny Citrinowicz.

“This shift should be especially concerning when it comes to the nuclear issue. A significant number of voices inside Iran believe that Ali Khamenei’s strategy of maintaining a strategic ‘limbo’ – avoiding both escalation and resolution, ultimately weakened Iran more than it protected it,” Citrinowicz posted on X.

‘Granular’ domestic security strategy

One of the new appointments brings back a veteran intelligence figure as the head of the Basij volunteer militia, which is under the Guards’ control and was heavily involved in the brutal suppression of protests in January.

Hossein Taeb – a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei – “was a particularly controversial and divisive figure during his tenure as head of IRGC Intelligence, closely associated with the hardline security apparatus’s repression of dissent,” wrote Sina Toossi, senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, on X.

The United States sanctioned Taeb in 2010 for his involvement in suppressing protests the previous year after a presidential election widely thought to have been rigged.

His new mandate “calls for strengthening the Basij’s ‘public intelligence network,’ exploiting modern technologies, and expanding neighborhood organization” of the militia, Toossi said.

In a picture obtained by AFP from the Iranian news agency Tasnim, Hossein Taeb attends a meeting in Iran’s capital, Tehran, on June 24, 2018. Hamed Malekpour/Tasnim News/AFP/Getty Images

This amounts to “an attempt to make intelligence and internal security much more granular: pushing collection, detection and early warning deeper into neighborhoods, local social networks and mosques,” according to Babak Vahdad, an independent researcher.

That is significant “after a war in which penetration, covert networks, sabotage and intelligence failures became one of the Islamic Republic’s most serious vulnerabilities,” he added.

In part, the appointments could be an effort by Khamenei – who has not been seen or heard from directly since being chosen as supreme leader in March – “to instal allies in influential positions in case growing economic pressures prompt another public uprising,” according to Golkar.

Given his long absence from public view, analysts are unsure whether Khamanei is indeed the architect of the new set-up.

But the combination of Taeb, Rezaei, Ahmad Vahidi – now commander of the IRGC – and other security veterans “indicates a leadership increasingly relying on experienced intelligence and military figures to consolidate the system after the war,” Azizi told CNN.

“It is not a complete break with Ali Khamenei’s approach, but it does represent a harder and more explicitly confrontational version of it.”

CNN’s Aida Karimi contributed to this article.

World.title: Thailand tightens gun controls after deadly school shooting
World.content:
Bangkok —

Thailand is suspending new gun permits and tightening its firearm controls after last week’s deadly school shooting, in which a 14-year-old boy killed eight people before turning the gun on himself.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul issued the directive on Tuesday, ordering government officials to “urgently elevate firearm control measures across the entire system,” according to a statement from his office.

The measures include temporarily suspending the issuance of gun purchase permits, re-reviewing all permits still pending approval, and suspending new “welfare gun” programs – which allow eligible public officials, including civil servants and politicians, to buy discounted weapons.

Government agencies will also now inspect gun dealers nationwide and verify sales records; inspect ammunition at shooting ranges to check that they’re following regulations; and “accelerate crackdowns on illegal firearms, rigorously prosecute offenders, and request maximum penalties from the court,” the directive read.

The statement also lays out broader reforms that will take longer to legislate, such as increasing penalties for offenders, tightening ammunition controls for gun dealers and ranges, and requiring that gun permits be renewed on a more frequent basis.

An initial compensation of 1 million baht (about $30,166) has been approved for six of the deceased victims, the statement said.

Officials prepare to pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, on August 11, 2026, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson, before he killed six others at his school and then turned the gun on himself. Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

The mass shooting has shone a new spotlight on Thailand’s high levels of gun ownership, both licensed and unlicensed.

Last Friday, the 14-year-old gunman first killed his grandparents at their home, where he also lived, before opening fire at a secondary school and killing six people there. He then killed himself. It was the country’s worst mass shooting since 2022.

Police said on Sunday the gunman had previously had an air gun confiscated by a teacher last year, and had watched violent content online, using social media to learn how to use a firearm. The firearm he used is believed to have been his grandfather’s.

Thailand has the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in Southeast Asia, with around 15 guns per 100 people. Its firearm death rate is similarly elevated, second in the region only to the Philippines.

Countries with higher gun ownership rates tend to see correspondingly higher firearm death rates. Multiple studies link easy access to firearms with more frequent gun-related deaths, including through suicide, homicide and unintentional injury.

As well as reigniting debate about gun control in Thailand, the shooting has put a focus on mental health for students and young people.

The Ministry of Education said it would develop new safety protocols in the coming months, including mental health screenings and a system to refer at-risk people to specialists, drills for emergency response plans, a drive to stamp out bullying and better detection to stop items from being taken into schools.

Mass shootings elsewhere in the world have often led to stricter gun control measures. Serbia and New Zealand, two nations with comparatively high gun ownership rates, both tightened rules and brought in gun amnesty drives following horrific massacres in recent years.

The outlier remains the United States, where gun violence and rates of mass shootings are among the highest in the world, with little progress made on tighter laws in the face of strong lobbying and constitutional protections.

World.title: Trump tries new line of attack on Democrats, calling them ‘jihadists’
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Monday that “jihadists” are being elected “all over the place” — trying a new, incendiary line of attack against Democrats with the midterm election just three months away.

“Well, the one thing is, we have jihadists being elected all over the place,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, without specifying who he was talking about or offering evidence of his claims.

“We have this whether it’s communism, jihadism,” Trump added.

The president has frequently cast Democrats and democratic socialists as communists, looking to portray the party as increasingly extreme headed into November — even though portrayals of even the party’s most liberal candidates as communists are far from reality.

But calling them “jihadists” is a new escalation, which Trump acknowledged in his remarks Monday, recounting that a “friend of mine called up,” and told him, “’You know, really, you should use the word jihadist because that’s what’s happening.’” The president’s escalating rhetoric comes amid broad lines of attack from others in the GOP seeking to paint Muslim candidates as anti-American.

Trump said that, “as an example,” some of the candidates he termed “jihadist” are coming from countries like Somalia. The president has repeatedly criticized Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who was born in Somalia, came to the United States as a child and is now a naturalized citizen. Trump has previously advocated for sending Omar and another Muslim congresswoman “back from where they came.”

He’s also unleashed increasingly provocative rhetoric against Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, saying at a campaign event in Las Vegas last week that he’s “full of sh*t” and is a “hater of Jews and hater of Israel,” without offering evidence. El-Sayed, who is Muslim, has been critical of the Israeli government.

On Monday, Trump posted on Truth Social an image of El-Sayed with Sen. Elizabeth Warren in a Native American headdress, with the caption, “Pocahontas and ‘Abdul’ want to take your stuff, and Crash the Economy!!!” And over the weekend, Trump shared an image of himself and first lady Melania Trump alongside a photo of El-Sayed and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, who wears a hijab. The caption read: “Two very different America’s.”

In an interview on CNN’s Sate of the Union with Jake Tapper, El-Sayed agreed that the two images offered differing visions of America.

“Yeah, he’s right. One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other but joint in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you. Or, two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good thing,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, you got two different visions of America.”

And it’s not just Trump engaging in that sort of rhetoric. Shortly after El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination last week, national Republicans repeatedly started referring to him by his full name: Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

Previously, Trump has accused Democrats of being taken over by “godless Communists” who pose an existential threat to the country. And while the democratic socialist movement appears set to push the Democratic Party further to the left, the tenets of socialism — much less democratic socialism — are still far removed from the communist ideology that Trump has loudly, and inaccurately, portrayed as a rising threat.

This story has been updated with additional details.

World.title: Former Syrian President Assad sentenced to death in absentia
World.content:
AP —

A Syrian court sentenced ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad along with his younger brother to death in absentia on Tuesday for crimes against humanity and war crimes during Syria’s 14-year conflict that left about half a million people dead.

The sentences at the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus are the first against Assad or members of his inner circle since the Assad family’s five decades in power came to an end 20 months ago.

“Bashar Assad used state agencies to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity,” said judge Fakhareddine al-Aryan during a court session that was aired live on state TV.

Also sentenced to death in the same case was Assad’s maternal cousin Atef Najib, who was convicted of overseeing a crackdown in the southern province of Daraa that led to the uprising and later the civil war.

Atef Najib appears in court in Syria on Tuesday. Syrian Ministry of Justice

Amid tight security, Najib stood inside a cage wearing a prisoner’s uniform as the judge read the sentence. A crowd of people gathered outside the courthouse in central Damascus to hear the verdict.

Assad and his brother Maher fled to Russia after the government’s fall in December 2024 and received political asylum. Syria’s new rulers have asked Russia to hand the Assads over.

Najib, who was sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury in April 2011, was later detained and is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.

Najib is a former Syrian army brigadier general who was head of the Political Security Branch in southern Syria’s Daraa province under Assad in 2011.

During his tenure, more than a dozen teenagers who scrawled anti-government graffiti on a school wall in Daraa were arrested and tortured. The case became a catalyst for mass protests against the repressive policies of Assad’s security forces.

The protests were met by a brutal government crackdown and spiraled into a 14-year civil war that ended with Assad’s ouster in a lightning rebel offensive.

Maher Assad was a former commander of the Syrian military’s 4th Armored Division – which Syrian opposition activists have accused of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, in addition to running its own detention centers.

World.title: Trump loves data centers. Americans hate them
World.content:
If there’s a true populist issue built for this moment in time, it might be opposition to AI data centers. Lawmakers and candidates from both parties across states are increasingly positioning themselves as critics of data center proliferation.

And recent primary results suggest it’s a pretty potent issue.

There is, however, one big exception to the growing political stampede away from data centers: President Donald Trump and his administration officials, who are bear-hugging them.

It’s merely the latest political head-scratcher from the president, given the growing volume of polls showing just how much Americans hate data centers and overwhelmingly don’t seem to want them in their communities.

Trump’s defenses of data centers have grown substantially in recent weeks. He’s not only pitched them as vital to competing with China on artificial intelligence, but as win-wins for the US communities that welcome them.

Trump loves data centers

Back in March, the administration debuted an initiative called the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which aimed to get developers to voluntarily promise that data center construction wouldn’t raise people’s energy bills.

But even at the time, Trump downplayed the need for his executive action. He suggested data centers weren’t really raising energy bills in the first place.

“They need some PR help, because people think that if a data center goes in there, electricity prices are going to go up,” Trump said.

Last month, he sharply criticized Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul for signing an executive order halting the construction of new data centers. Trump on social media called them “big, strong, bold, and Money Machines” and “Cash Cows, with Lower Taxes and Record Setting Jobs.”

Last week, he told Fox News that “any community that turns down AI is making a big mistake,” claiming data centers would reduce taxes and make property values go up.

He called it “a tremendous thing” and even seemed to marvel at how anybody could oppose them.

“It’s almost like there’s a campaign against, you know, data centers,” the president said.

And then in an interview with Punchbowl News later in the week, he took aim at GOP-controlled Texas, which moved to more strongly regulate data center construction.

Trump said data centers could be “bigger than oil.”

“I don’t think they’re unsightly,” he added. “I mean, I’m looking at some of these data centers — the most incredible buildings I’ve ever seen. They go for two-and-a-half, three miles.”

But the American people really don’t like them

Virtually everything Trump is saying is at odds with where the American people are.

Americans opposed the construction of new data centers 45 percent-16 percent in a Reuters-Ipsos poll in June.

And the margins grew significantly when it came to building them in their communities. The margin against grew to 59 percent-10 percent when the data centers were within 10 miles of the person’s home. Gallup in March showed 7 in 10 Americans opposed building data centers “in your area.”

The passion is clearly on the side of the critics.

Only between 3 percent and 7 percent strongly supported the construction of data centers in their areas in the above polls, while between 44 percent to 48 percent strongly opposed them.

While 61 percent of Americans said data centers were necessary in the Reuters poll, 77 percent wanted them to be built in remote areas away from communities.

The Sabey Data Centers Seattle Data Center campus in Tukwila, Washington, US, on Saturday, July 11, 2026. David Ryder/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Despite Trump’s claims that data centers are economic boons and potentially “bigger than oil,” just 50 percent of Americans think they create jobs and are good for the economy. And only 1 in 6 feel that way strongly, saying that describes data centers “very” or “extremely” well.

Despite Trump’s claim that data centers aren’t or wouldn’t make electricity more expensive, 77 percent said they were doing just that in Reuters/Ipsos polling earlier in June, while two-thirds said the same in a March Pew Research Center poll.

And finally, all told, Americans said by a whopping 71 percent-29 percent margin that the costs of data centers outweighed the benefits, according a Marquette Law School poll in May.

Most notably: All of these polls suggest it’s a remarkably bipartisan aversion. Republicans are somewhat more likely to see the benefits of data centers and welcome them in their communities, but they’re strongly against them, too.

The bipartisan campaigns against and efforts to rein in data centers

That bipartisanship has made itself clear in how the issue has been addressed across the country — and not just in New York and Texas. Bills banning data center construction have been proposed in 15 states, spanning from deep red to deep blue.

The issue also featured prominently in both parties’ gubernatorial primaries in Kansas last week, with critics winning both primaries. (The Democrat who won, state Sen. Cindy Holscher, disowned a previous vote in favor of data center construction and strongly backed a moratorium.) Both parties’ gubernatorial nominees in Ohio also back a moratorium.

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and House candidate William Lawrence played up the issue on their way to primary victories in Michigan last week. And Democratic Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong looks to do the same Tuesday after making the issue her calling card.

They’ve all seemed to sense the rare issue that truly galvanizes — both because it directly impacts Americans in their communities and, they worry, is exacerbating their already increasing costs.

But Trump seems to be making a different calculation.

World.title: Trump says the US has “mine swept the entire” Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States has swept the Strait of Hormuz for mines and claimed the US Navy has full control of the vital waterway.

“It’s open now. Look, the only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States Navy,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.

“They will, on occasion, drop a mine, and we find the mine,” the president added. “You know, we’ve mine swept the entire strait, as you probably maybe heard, maybe you didn’t hear.”

He added that the United States controls the strait “100%.”

Earlier Monday, Trump applied a new condition to talks with Iran, saying he would require compensation from the country for past misdeeds after Tehran said US compensation was required to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said an agreement with Oman to manage the strait would not be enough to reopen the waterway unless the United States meets the list of conditions.

World.title: Liberia: Five LDEA Leadership Changes in Two Years—Senator Konneh Warns Liberia Cannot “Change the Figurehead” and Cure the Cancer
World.content:
MONROVIA— President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s decision to replace the leadership of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency marks the latest turn in a revolving door that has seen the agency change hands five times in just over two years.

By Obediah Johnson, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The appointment of retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. as Director General-designate comes as the LDEA and Liberia’s wider security establishment face perhaps their most serious credibility crisis in years.

But for Senator Amara Konneh, the latest change raises a question that goes beyond the credentials of the incoming director: Can Liberia fix a deeply troubled security institution simply by repeatedly changing the person at the top?

Konneh’s answer is no.

“Changing the leadership at LDEA does not automatically fix the cancer eating away at our security system,” the Senate Public Accounts and Audit Committee chairman warned Tuesday.

His argument goes to the heart of Liberia’s ongoing cocaine crisis. The country has recorded cocaine seizures valued at more than US$336 million, including an approximately US$317 million shipment intercepted in the VOA Community in Paynesville and a roughly US$19 million consignment seized at Roberts International Airport.

The investigations have generated allegations involving individuals connected to the security and law-enforcement establishment, triggered internal investigations and produced leadership changes.

Now, President Boakai has turned to Ziankahn, a retired military general and former Defense Minister, to restore stability and credibility to an agency that has experienced extraordinary leadership turbulence.

But the question remains whether another change at the top can address what critics describe as deeper institutional weaknesses.

Five Changes, One Troubled Agency

The significance of Ziankahn’s appointment is best understood against the backdrop of the leadership changes that preceded him.

Since taking office in January 2024, President Boakai has overseen five changes involving the top leadership of the LDEA—three director-general-level appointments and two periods in which officials served as Officer in Charge.

The revolving door is striking, particularly because the fight against illicit drugs was one of Boakai’s prominent campaign commitments.

After his inauguration, Boakai moved quickly to appoint Abraham Kromah, a veteran security officer who had previously served as Deputy Commissioner of Police for Operations under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

Kromah arrived with a reputation as a tough law-enforcement officer, and his appointment was initially welcomed by many Liberians who expected him to bring a more aggressive approach to the fight against drugs, particularly the synthetic drug commonly known as Kush.

Instead, his tenure became embroiled in an internal management crisis.

A public confrontation involving Kromah and his deputies, Hassan Fadiga and Gbawou Kowou, escalated into a physical altercation and resulted in their suspension. The administration subsequently ordered an investigation, and following the submission of the report, Kromah and his deputies were removed.

But the report was never made public. That unresolved issue continues to hang over the agency. For the public, the unanswered question is simple: What did the investigation find? The absence of a public explanation has contributed to a recurring problem within the LDEA—major decisions are announced, but the underlying findings are often kept from public view.

Peters Leaves With a Warning

Following Kromah’s removal, Christopher K. Peters Sr. was appointed Officer in Charge of the LDEA on June 4, 2024. Peters’ tenure was brief.

Although he pointed to drug seizures worth more than US$4 million and lengthy prison sentences secured against traffickers, he resigned only months after taking office.

His resignation letter, addressed to then-Minister of State Sylvester M. Grigsby (now deceased), offered perhaps one of the clearest diagnoses of the agency’s institutional weaknesses.

Peters argued that winning the war on drugs required strategic reforms, enhanced training, additional personnel, adequate funding and sustained support from key partners. He also stressed the need for leadership capable of promoting calm, maturity and teamwork within the agency.

His resignation became effective October 31, 2024. Whether his recommendations were fully acted upon remains an open question.

Souh Returns—Then Leaves

Peters was succeeded by Anthony Souh, another experienced law-enforcement officer and former LDEA Director General during the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf administration, when Boakai served as Vice President.

Souh returned to the agency with institutional experience and familiarity with Liberia’s drug-enforcement challenges.

But his return did not produce lasting stability. About a year later, the Boakai administration removed Souh and other senior LDEA officials, paving the way for another restructuring.

Again, the cycle continued.

Then Came Biago

The next major leadership arrangement brought Fitzgerald T. M. Biago, a Deputy Commissioner of Police, into the agency’s leadership.

On August 28, 2025, President Boakai appointed Biago, a Deputy Commissioner of the Liberian National Police, as Officer-In-Charge. He led an interim management structure alongside Ernest T. Tarpeh of the National Security Agency and Patrick B. Kormazu of the LNP following the removal of Souh and other senior officials.

Nearly a year later, his leadership was thrown into controversy after activist Martin K. N. Kollie alleged that Biago had received a vehicle as a gift from Leroy Harris, a suspect in the US$317 million cocaine investigation.

Biago denied involvement in the drug allegations and stepped aside to make himself available for investigation.

A Ministry of Justice review did not establish his involvement in narcotics trafficking. But the government said the review identified ethical concerns, prompting President Boakai to indefinitely suspend Biago from the Liberia National Police and order a more detailed investigation.

Again, the distinction is important: the government did not establish that Biago was involved in the narcotics trade, but it found ethical concerns serious enough to warrant further action. And again, the LDEA was left with a leadership problem.

Now comes Ziankahn.

The retired major general brings perhaps the strongest national-security credentials of any of the recent LDEA appointees.

He became the first post-war Liberian Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia, appointed in 2014 after the restructuring of the military following the civil war. He had enlisted in the newly restructured Armed Forces of Liberia in 2006 and rose through the ranks before becoming Chief of Staff, a position he held from 2014 to 2018.

He subsequently served as Liberia’s Minister of National Defense under former President George Weah and later became Military Advisor to President Boakai.

Analysts say his appointment represents a significant shift in the profile of LDEA leadership. The administration appears to be betting that Ziankahn’s military and national-security experience can bring discipline, stability and strategic direction to an agency that has repeatedly struggled with internal turmoil. But that is precisely where Konneh’s warning becomes relevant.

A Revolving Door at the LDEA

Ziankahn’s appointment marks what amounts to the fifth leadership change at the LDEA in roughly two years under President Boakai—three director-general-level appointments and two individuals who have served as Officer in Charge.

The frequency of those changes raises a fundamental institutional question: If leadership keeps changing but the underlying vulnerabilities remain, is the problem really the person at the top?

The “Self-Policing” Problem

Senator Konneh argued that institutions implicated in allegations surrounding a major criminal investigation should not be left to investigate themselves.

“Institutions with heavy corruption and cartel allegations cannot investigate themselves,” he said, calling for an open, credible and independent inquiry into high-ranking individuals allegedly connected to the narcotics network.

That demand strikes at the heart of the cocaine investigations.

The magnitude of the seizures has transformed the issue from an ordinary drug-enforcement matter into a national security question.

A shipment valued at hundreds of millions of dollars does not move through international supply chains, ports, airports and local communities without sophisticated organization, financing, logistics and access.

That inevitably raises questions about whether criminal networks operated entirely outside the state—or whether individuals with access to official systems may have facilitated, enabled or shielded elements of the trade.

Those questions cannot be answered merely by replacing one agency director with another. They require investigators capable of following the evidence wherever it leads. And that means senior officials cannot be treated differently from ordinary suspects simply because of their positions.

Ziankahn’s Appointment: A Strong Man for a Weak System?

There is little doubt that Ziankahn brings considerable experience to the position. The retired major general previously served as Liberia’s Minister of National Defense and, more recently, as Military Advisor to President Boakai.

His background gives him significant exposure to national security operations and strategic decision-making. That experience could prove valuable to an agency that has been battered by leadership instability and public distrust.

But experience alone does not answer the central problem.

The question is whether Ziankahn will inherit an agency capable of functioning independently—or an institution whose credibility has been damaged by allegations that reach beyond its current leadership.

Konneh acknowledged Ziankahn’s credentials while making clear that his appointment does not erase the unresolved questions.

“We wish Gen. Ziankahn success in his Senate confirmation and in his tenure, but we will observe closely,” he said.

That may ultimately become the defining test of the new LDEA leadership.

Ziankahn will not merely be judged by the number of drug seizures under his watch. He will be judged by whether his tenure produces an agency in which investigations are insulated from political influence, evidence is protected, officers are held accountable, and no official is considered untouchable.

World.title: Liberia’s Drug Crisis: Accountability Must Begin Within the Security Sector
World.content:
Senator Amara Konneh’s latest intervention raises an important question that Liberia can no longer afford to avoid: Can the government effectively fight transnational drug trafficking while simultaneously confronting allegations of corruption within the very institutions responsible for fighting it?

By E. W. Cooper, contributing writer

I believe the answer must be yes—but only if the government is prepared to apply the same standard of accountability to everyone.

This is not about protecting the opposition, defending the government, or creating political scapegoats. It is about protecting Liberia’s national security.

The reported US$317 million cocaine seizure is not an ordinary criminal matter. It involves alleged transnational criminal networks, international partners, substantial financial resources, and allegations involving individuals within Liberia’s security architecture. That requires an investigation that is professional, evidence-driven, and insulated from conflicts of interest.

I therefore agree with Senator Konneh on one fundamental principle: there must be no sacred cows.

But accountability must be based on evidence.

If an officer is accused of accepting money, investigate the financial trail.

If an officer claims he was instructed to escort a shipment, examine the communications records.

If someone is alleged to have facilitated communication between detained suspects and an international network, examine the phones, financial transactions, surveillance footage, and other available evidence.

If an official is accused of interfering with an investigation, determine exactly what action was taken, when it occurred, and whether it violated the law.

And if allegations are made against the Inspector General or any other senior official, those allegations should receive the same objective scrutiny.

Recusal Is About Integrity

This is where my position remains consistent.

When serious allegations begin pointing toward an official who has a significant role in overseeing an investigation, recusal can be an act of institutional integrity rather than an admission of guilt.

The objective is not to remove someone because they have been accused. The objective is to ensure that the person being questioned is not simultaneously in a position to influence the investigation into those questions.

If the official is innocent, an independent process can establish that.

If the allegations are unsupported, the official’s credibility can be restored.

And if evidence establishes wrongdoing, the law should apply.

That is precisely why an impartial process matters.

International Assistance Should Strengthen, Not Replace Liberia

There is another important point.

International involvement in a case of this magnitude should not be interpreted as evidence that Liberians are incapable of investigating their own country. Liberia has capable law-enforcement and security professionals.

International partners can provide specialized expertise, intelligence, forensic capabilities, financial investigations, and transnational investigative connections that are particularly valuable in organized-crime cases.

But Liberian institutions must remain part of the process.

The objective should be partnership—not institutional surrender.

The President’s Test

President Boakai now faces an important test of leadership.

The public does not simply need arrests. It needs to see a process that is credible.

The President must demonstrate that accountability is not determined by rank, political affiliation, personal relationships, or institutional loyalty.

If someone is innocent, clear them.

If someone violated administrative rules, discipline them.

If someone committed a crime, prosecute them.

And if the evidence leads to someone at the highest level of government or security institutions, follow the evidence there as well.

That is what the rule of law means.

The government should not fear the truth. The truth, properly established through evidence and due process, ultimately protects legitimate institutions.

The greatest danger would be for Liberia to investigate this matter selectively—protecting some, sacrificing others, and allowing public pressure rather than evidence to determine the outcome.

This investigation should not be about Cocaingate as a political slogan.

It should be about establishing exactly who knew what, who did what, who benefited, who facilitated the operation, who attempted to obstruct the investigation, and whether anyone within Liberia’s security apparatus compromised the Republic for personal gain.

Follow the evidence.

No sacred cows. No scapegoats. No selective justice.

Just truth, accountability, due process, and the rule of law.E. W. Cooper is a Law enforcement supervisor, Homeland Security & Emergency Management professional, and a Criminal Justice scholar.

World.title: U.S. Signal to Liberia’s Drug War Carries Extra Weight After Record Busts — and a Cloud Over Its Chief Enforcers
World.content:
The U.S. Embassy meeting between Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny and Liberia’s top police officials — Inspector General Gregory Coleman and EPS Director Sam Gaye — comes at a fraught moment: a $19 million cocaine bust in July was followed by a record $317 million seizure implicating senior police officers themselves, some now facing charges. Coleman has also faced unproven allegations of ties to the trafficking network, making the embassy’s emphasis on “accountability” read as pointed encouragement rather than blanket endorsement.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia- By any measure, U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny’s meeting with Liberia National Police Inspector General Gregory O.W. Coleman and Executive Protection Service Director Sam Gaye should have been a routine diplomatic courtesy. Instead, it lands at one of the most consequential moments in Liberia’s modern anti-narcotics effort — and its timing, coming just as President Boakai reshuffles the LDEA’s leadership for the third time in two years, makes it read as something closer to a signal than a formality.

Why the timing matters

The meeting follows two extraordinary seizures in the space of a few weeks. In July, security personnel intercepted six cargo boxes at Roberts International Airport disguised as textiles and seasoning cubes; inside were nearly 200 compressed blocks of cocaine, ultimately valued around $19 million — a case that drew public criticism after delays in identifying suspects raised fears that individuals connected to the shipment had already fled the country. Weeks later came a seizure of a different order of magnitude entirely: nearly four tonnes of cocaine, worth an estimated $317.7 million, recovered from what investigators described as an organized, sophisticated, and well-funded trafficking network that may have operated in Liberia for more than six years. Authorities later incinerated 4.2 metric tons of the drug, sending what Coleman called a message that Liberia was no longer “a place of comfort” for traffickers.

What has made the second bust politically explosive, however, is who it implicated. Coleman confirmed that Liberia’s chief of highway patrol and the head of the major crimes unit face charges, with a deputy police commander at the main airport also under suspicion — meaning the very institution now meant to lead enforcement, the Liberia National Police, has senior officers accused of facilitating the trafficking it is supposed to stop.

The credibility problem the U.S. visit runs into

That is precisely why Zadrozny’s meeting cannot be read purely as encouragement. Coleman himself has become a subject of serious, if unproven, allegations. In a July 15 letter to Zadrozny, CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee requested U.S. backing for an international investigation, alleging that Coleman took vehicles from a drug cartel and distributed them to President Boakai, Vice President Koung, and the presiding officers of the Legislature, and separately that the 2024 removal of former LDEA head Abraham Kromah was orchestrated by Coleman to protect a cartel he was allegedly connected to, and that Coleman later maneuvered Fitzgerald Biago — his own deputy at the police — into the LDEA’s top job. Koijee’s broader argument was structural: that repeatedly installing senior police officers atop the drug agency has blurred the LDEA’s independence and concentrated excessive influence within Liberia’s security apparatus.

Notably, Boakai’s own government has now partly validated that structural critique without validating the corruption allegation. Monday’s Executive Mansion release states that the Justice Ministry’s probe into Biago “did not establish any involvement… in illegal narcotics trafficking” but did identify unspecified “ethical concerns” — landing in a gray zone that neither clears the LDEA leadership pipeline of suspicion nor confirms the most serious claims against it. Biago’s own departure now repeats the very pattern Koijee flagged: a police-to-LDEA pipeline replaced, once again, by another appointee — this time a retired general rather than a police officer, which may itself be read as an attempt to break that cycle.

What the U.S. statement does — and doesn’t — say

Read against this backdrop, Zadrozny’s language is carefully calibrated. It reaffirms partnership and frames Liberian institution-building as serving “regional stability” and the “enduring friendship” between the two countries — standard diplomatic register. But it also pointedly addresses itself to “law and order” and “a just and accountable legal system,” phrasing that functions as quiet pressure on Coleman and Gaye specifically to see the investigations — including into their own ranks — through to a credible conclusion, rather than as an unqualified vote of confidence in current leadership.

The U.S. has skin in this game beyond diplomacy: earlier reporting has linked American law enforcement, including the Department of Justice, to the broader trafficking investigation tied to the record cocaine seizure, and West Africa’s role as a transit corridor — now carrying an estimated 30 percent of Europe-bound cocaine, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime — makes Liberia’s enforcement capacity a matter of direct interest to Washington and European partners alike, not just Monrovia.

The stakes for the investigation ahead

For Ziankahn’s incoming LDEA leadership, the practical effect of the U.S. engagement is likely to be twofold: continued technical and possibly intelligence-sharing support for dismantling the trafficking network behind the record bust, paired with implicit international scrutiny of whether Liberia’s own police leadership — the officials the U.S. just met with — can be trusted to police itself.

Whether Coleman and Gaye emerge from the ongoing probes as central figures in prosecuting this case, or as subjects of it, may do more than any embassy statement to determine whether Liberia’s “war on drugs” produces lasting institutional reform or simply another rotation of the same personnel through different chairs.

World.title: Guinea Border: Time for Government to Level with the Liberian People
World.content:
Since February, Liberia’s border with Guinea has seen repeated incursions, a flag removal, troop deployments, and the displacement of thousands of residents in Lofa County. President Boakai has pursued the right diplomatic path — tripartite summits, joint technical commissions, a special envoy — but the public has received only sporadic updates since. This editorial argues that quiet diplomacy without public transparency risks eroding trust at home and, given West Africa’s history, could let a manageable dispute harden into something far more dangerous. It calls on the government to communicate more regularly and plainly with affected communities, not just with counterparts in Conakry.

FOR NEARLY a year now, communities along Liberia’s border with Guinea have lived with a question their government has not fully answered: what exactly is happening on our land, and what is being done about it?

PICTURE A FAMILY in Sorlumba, in Foya District, going about an ordinary morning — tending a farm plot, walking to a river crossing they’ve used their whole lives — when armed soldiers from across the border appear and declare the ground beneath their feet belongs to someone else. That is not a hypothetical. It is close to what residents there say happened earlier this year, when Guinean soldiers reportedly crossed into Liberian territory, seized construction equipment from a Liberian road contractor, and — most provocatively — ordered the removal of the Liberian flag that had flown at the riverbank for decades, even through the years of civil war. ￼ For people who lived through that war, watching their flag come down was not an abstract diplomatic incident. It was personal.

THE BARE FACTS, as they have trickled out through news reports rather than official candor, are troubling enough on their own. Alleged incursions in February sent panic through border communities. Guinea responded to the rising tension not with reassurance but with troop deployments to the frontier, and Liberia’s own rights commission later found that the affair had displaced thousands of residents and exposed serious gaps in both border protection and regional diplomacy. Thousands of displaced people is not a statistic to file away — it is thousands of individual decisions to grab what could be carried and walk away from home, uncertain when, or whether, it would be safe to return.

TO ITS CREDIT, the Boakai administration did not let the crisis spiral into confrontation. President Boakai joined his Guinean and Sierra Leonean counterparts in Conakry in March for a tripartite summit that produced commitments to dialogue, joint technical commissions on border delimitation, and a pledge to convene a full Mano River Union summit within a month to “revitalize” the organization. In June, Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah reaffirmed that Liberia remained committed to resolving the dispute through diplomacy, and that a special presidential envoy had been dispatched to follow up on the Conakry commitments.

THESE ARE THE RIGHT instincts. Nobody serious wants Liberia and Guinea shooting at each other over a riverbank in Foya.

BUT GOOD INSTINCTS are not the same as good governance, and here is where the government’s approach has fallen short: the Liberian public still does not know, in any real detail, where things stand. The promised MRU summit, floated for July, has come and gone without a clear public accounting of whether it happened, what it produced, or why it may have slipped. The joint technical commissions on border delimitation — the actual mechanism that would settle, once and for all, whose land is whose — have operated largely out of public view.
