World.title: The hurdles facing Canada's planned pandemic-busting lab
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Experts say Canada’s plan to build a $267-million medical countermeasures laboratory in Winnipeg is a vital step toward heading off future pandemics, but they warn the facility faces steep hurdles around long-term funding, staffing and governance.

The federal government announced a $10.2-million design contract for the facility last week, with the finished building slated to open in 2033 next to Winnipeg’s National Microbiology Laboratory (NML).

While the lab aims to bridge a critical gap in testing early-stage vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostic tools, health researchers caution that a brand-new building will accomplish little without sustained, decades-long investments in human talent.

"It's one thing to have a building, but it's another thing to have the human resources that will make it a world-class centre," said Dr. Joanne Liu, a physician and professor at McGill University's School of Population and Global Health, and former international president of Médecins Sans Frontières.

"It's safe to say that in principle it's not a bad idea, but then you would need to really walk the talk of countermeasures."

The planned countermeasures lab will be built next to the National Microbiology Laboratory, in Winnipeg. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)

Fixing the preclinical bottleneck

The facility would add capacity for preclinical trials — lab and animal testing — within Canada’s research and development pipeline. That would give scientists a dedicated place to test, for example, small batches of a promising vaccine before scaling up to clinical trials.

For now, according to NML chief operating officer Steven Guercio, space constraints mean the NML sometimes repurposes lab facilities meant for research into the most volatile pathogens — such as Ebola — in order to do preclinical tests.

Industry and academic partners would both potentially be able to use the lab spaces, Guercio said, "with the appropriate agreements in place and the appropriate screenings and vettings."

Keith Fowke, scientific director at the Canadian Institutes of Health Research's infections facility in Winnipeg, noted that Canadian university researchers frequently hit a "roadblock" when trying to move vaccine discoveries into early human safety trials because Canada lacks local cleanrooms to make test batches.

To experts, expanding Canada’s capacity in this regard is a no-brainer. In fact, health officials have been talking about it for at least a decade, said Gary Kobinger, a former NML scientist who led the team that co-developed the world’s first successful Ebola vaccine , and now directs the Level 4 Galveston National Laboratory at the University of Texas.

"Like anything else, better late than never," he said in an interview with CBC News. "It's good news that they are moving."

What matters most for the project, according to Kobinger, is stability in the longer term. "The important move is committing to that activity. If you build a $300-million building, hopefully you are also planning to inject funding to advance those products over the following 10 years."

Sustaining funding in 'quiet times'

McGill’s Liu had a similar take, noting that investing in pandemic research can be politically popular during a pandemic, but the key moments are when there isn’t an immediate health threat.

"You have to have the vision of investing from beginning to end on a virus and the countermeasures necessary for it, and then carry on for several years — even during the quiet times when it's off everybody's radar," Liu said.

Existing facilities in the National Microbiology Laboratory are sometimes repurposed to be used for preclinical trials due to a lack of dedicated space. (Submitted by the National Microbiology Laboratory)

Of particular concern to Liu is cuts made to staff at the NML just last year. "We have lost a lot of talent," Liu said, positing that those cuts could affect the NML's ability to bring in the world-class researchers it would need to have relevance.

"If you want to re-attract talent, you need to not only promise a building, but promise funding to get a team to do the research, pay the salaries of the people doing the work, and fund the research itself," she said. “We're talking about millions and millions of dollars."

In a statement emailed to CBC News, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) said that it "re-prioritized and streamlined some programs, and in some cases discontinued work" as part of a post-pandemic recalibration.

"The NML has ongoing funding to strengthen medical countermeasures capacity in Canada, and specifically to expand pre-clinical research," the agency wrote, adding that it has a "robust talent pipeline."

Red tape and governance risks

Kobinger warned of a "huge risk" if the countermeasures lab is run entirely by the government, given the potential for red tape or funding challenges.

He invoked Canada's handling of the Ebola vaccine as a cautionary tale. While scientists at the NML successfully developed the life-saving vaccine in the 2000s, it happened amidst a culture of cutbacks , and as federal officials struggled with technology transfer and commercialization. Canada ultimately licensed the rights to a small U.S. company, which was later acquired by pharmaceutical giant Merck to handle mass manufacturing and global distribution.

Gary Kobinger, shown working at a lab at Université Laval in 2020, says, 'There is a huge challenge with governance within government.' (CBC News)

Kobinger also pointed to the Biologics Manufacturing Centre (BMC) — a $130-million vaccine facility built in Montreal during the COVID-19 pandemic — as a recent example of operational delay. As of 2024, the plant still had not produced any shots . Operations were transferred to a not-for-profit entity in 2023, but the National Research Council confirmed that it still provides $17 million each year to keep it running.

PHAC defended its record, pointing to $2.5 billion in federal investments since 2018 aimed at rebuilding Canada's life sciences sector. The agency noted that commercial hand-offs do not rest on public health officials alone, pointing to a new federal agency, Health Emergency Readiness Canada, specifically tasked with bridging reasearch and development with private industry.

But for Kobinger, adding new agencies and building labs will mean little if Ottawa repeats past mistakes with patents and paperwork.

"A lot of this project will depend on the vision of the person leading it and how they make it work within government," he said.

World.title: Air force's 1st new refuelling jet won't be delivered until late 2027
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's air force will have to wait until the end of next year before it receives the first of four new air tankers critical to refuelling fighter jets in the Arctic.

The Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) has for the first time outlined the state of the CC-330 Husky fleet purchased to replace its aging Airbus 310s.

The wide-body jets are the backbone of the air force's intercontinental fleet, flying troops and the prime minister around the globe.

But it's their role as flying gas stations that matters so much as Canada looks to boost continental defence.

A spokesperson for the Department of National Defence said in a statement to CBC News that the first new aircraft will be "delivered to the RCAF in late 2027."

In July 2023, Canada purchased nine Airbus A330s for approximately $3.6 billion — five used jets, which saw less than 10 years' service with Kuwait Airways, and four brand new planes.

Until now, the department had not disclosed how many of the new aircraft would be delivered by next year.

3 used jets delivered

So far, three of the used Airbus planes have arrived, in their original airline configuration.

They are being used to transport passengers, including the prime minister, around the world. However, one has already gone into a scheduled heavy maintenance at Mirabel Airport.

The fourth is in Switzerland getting a new interior and defence components, and the fifth is in Spain to be refitted as an air tanker.

The first new-build tanker is in testing in Spain, while the other three new builds are in production in Toulouse, France.

Royal Canadian Air Force fighter jets perform air-to-air refuelling from a CC-150 Polaris in 2021. The Polaris is not equipped to refuel F-35 fighters. (Aviator Avery Philpott/Canadian Armed Forces)

The RCAF's fleet of CF-18s and soon its new F-35s need air tankers to stay on patrol over the Arctic. Fighter jets quickly burn through fuel, and frequently work with air tankers to extend the time and distance they can stay aloft.

This role was highlighted during the FIFA World Cup games in Toronto this summer.

One of the air force's aging air tankers was able to help CF-18s stay aloft over the stadium for hours at a time.

Canada's new tankers will have the boom and hoses necessary to refuel all NATO equipped aircraft.

The aircraft they are replacing lacked the large boom, essentially a long metal pipe, used primarily for aircraft designed for the U.S. Air Force including the C-17 cargo plane and the F-35.

Defences for PM's new plane

There has been recent talk about threats to the aircraft of world leaders .

The air force confirms the new V-VIP Airbus, the used jet currently being refitted in Switzerland for use by the prime minister, will have a "self-protection suite" to help protect the aircraft from missile attack.

This system could include a system of lasers, flares and aluminum foil meant to confuse or defeat an incoming missile.

Much of the components from this system won't be visible to the naked eye but there will be a few telltale bulges around the skin of the aircraft.

The air force expects plane spotters and foreign governments to take note of them, and what their capabilities may be.

In a statement to CBC News, the air force says initial operational capability for the CC-330 Husky fleet is planned for 2028-29, and full operational capability of all nine jets will follow by 2032-33.

Right now the jets are based in Ottawa, but new facilities are being built in Trenton, Ont., and Edmonton.

Old fleet in service until 2030

The RCAF's fleet of five smaller Airbus A310s, also known as the CC-150 Polaris, started as Wardair passenger jets in the late 1980s.

The former Airbus 01, which served the last three prime ministers, is now a museum piece in Trenton.

WATCH | Canada chooses Swedish surveillance plane maker: Ottawa passes on U.S. bids to buy Swedish surveillance plane | Duration 1:54 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada has entered negotiations to purchase the Saab GlobalEye early warning aircraft from Sweden rather than a competing Boeing model, as his government tries to reduce a reliance on U.S. military technology.

Another A310 was written off after a parking lot incident in 2023 in Guam.

The Canadian jet rolled back and collided with a nearby parked French cargo plane, seriously damaging both aircraft. A flight safety investigation found the parking brakes on the Airbus were only designed to hold for 12 hours, and after that period would give way.

The investigation board cited the lack of chocks being installed around the aircraft's wheels, crew fatigue and checklist design as the factors that led to the incident. The report said no one was injured in the incident.

The remaining three aircraft will stay in service until 2030.

World.title: From last place to the post-season? Here's how the 2026 Blue Jays could pull it off
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. It's been a frustrating season for the Toronto Blue Jays after the team made it all the way to Game 7 of the World Series last year, but a winning surge in the past two weeks has kept their playoff hopes alive. The CBC's Greg Ross has more on the Jays' turnaround and their chances of making it to the post-season. Prime Minister Mark Carney says "you've got to believe" the Toronto Blue Jays can still make the playoffs. But can they, really? The Jays have played some scrappy baseball lately, as the team finds itself on the fringes of playoff contention with a quarter of the season to go and it's still possible they might find a way to the post-season in the anemic American League. Toronto beat the Boston Red Sox tonight, in a 5-3 victory that improved their season record to 58-63 and kept the team in the hunt for a potential playoff spot. Thanks for the sweater, Karla.

My message to Jays Nation: you've got to believe. pic.twitter.com/oP6IQ9dHmJ —MarkJCarney "At this point, you just kind of throw everything other than winning out the window and show up every day and try to win," Jays infielder and all-star Ernie Clement told CBC News, earlier Tuesday. There are a half-dozen teams, including Toronto, that are within four games of the last wild-card spot in the wider American League — and the Blue Jays would have to leap past all of them to secure a return to the post-season. Here's a look at why the Jays are where they are with just over 40 games to go, and what they have to do to get back to the post-season. From the World Series to last place? That's the reality: Toronto has gone from a team that competed for a World Series title last fall to a team curently sitting in last place in the American Leage East. They can't win the division at this point, so that means they'll have to claim a wild-card spot to reach the post-season. WATCH | The end of an era for some Toronto fan favourites: Blue Jays lose fan favourites in big trades | Duration 2:09 Less than a year after competing for the MLB championship, the Toronto Blue Jays made some big trades ahead of the deadline, including fan favourites Daulton Varsho and pitcher Kevin Gausman. The win over Boston Tuesday night improved Toronto's season record to 58-63 — 12 fewer wins than they had at the same point last year. At present, the Tampa Bay Rays lead the AL East, followed by the New York Yankees in second place, and the resurgent Boston Red Sox — who put together lengthy win streaks in July and August — in third. The Baltimore Orioles (with a 58-62 record) and the Jays sit in fourth and fifth place. Just 2 teams have done it According to Elias Sports Bureau, the official statistician of Major League Baseball (MLB), there are just two teams that have stood at 58-63 through 121 games — the same record the Jays have right now — that went on to make the playoffs in the wild-card era: The 2024 Detroit Tigers and the 2009 Minnesota Twins. Randy Robles of Elias Sports Bureau believes "there's some hope" for the Jays, noting that if there ever was a year for a struggling team to still have a chance, it would be this one, when so many American League teams have been playing so poorly. Blue Jays rookie Charles McAdoo runs the bases at Toronto's Rogers Centre after hitting a solo home run in Monday's game against the Boston Red Sox. (Getty Images) What it will take Toronto has begun to claw its way to a better record, claiming series wins against the Washington Nationals, the St. Louis Cardinals, the Houston Astros and the Philadelphia Phillies in the past couple of weeks. That winning trend has to continue for the team to have a shot at the post-season: "They gotta get to .500," Robles told CBC News, referring to the point when a team has won as many games as it has lost. The Texas Rangers, the team currently sitting in the third wild-card spot the Jays are vying for, was only one game above the .500 mark prior to Tuesday's matchups. All the teams seeking to take the Rangers' spot — Toronto included — currently have losing records. Summing up the challenge the Blue Jays face in climbing the standings, Toronto Star baseball columnist Mike Wilner saw a certain parity in the teams involved in the wild-card fight. "Every team in front of the Blue Jays kind of stinks," Wilner told CBC News. "The problem is, the Blue Jays kind of stink, too." Dylan Cease is the ace of the Blue Jays' starting pitching staff and in the hunt for a Cy Young Award this season. (Paul Beaty/The Associated Press) Cease leads the rotation The Jays are thin on starting pitching right now, but the rotation includes pitching ace Dylan Cease, the newly acquired José Soriano, Shane Bieber, as well as veteran Max Scherzer. Cease is on the hunt for a Cy Young Award, and has been in the midst of a sizzling run this summer that included bid for a no-hitter in July that he carried into the ninth inning. He started Tuesday's game against Boston, going five innings and striking out seven. Soriano was solid in his recent Blue Jays debut. Bieber, who missed most of the first half of the season, has been battling for consistency since rejoining the team in June. Scherzer has had two decent starts for Toronto this month — and the team will be counting on him to deliver more if they have a shot at a wild card. "We have a job to do: Every time we come to the park, we've got to win," Scherzer told CBC News. In the bullpen, the Jays will continue to look to closer Louis Varland and workhorse reliever Tyler Rogers in high-leverage situations. Rookie pitcher Spencer Miles, as well as relievers Braydon Fisher and Mason Fluharty will also be key to any push for the post-season. Kazuma Okamoto rounds the bases after a July 28 home run at Nationals Park. The rookie is leading the Jays in home runs this year with 24. (Brad Mills/Imagn Images/Reuters) What about the bats? Hitting has been a real problem for the Blue Jays this year. The team sits near the bottom of the major leagues in terms of home runs, runs scored and on-base percentage. Only two Blue Jays have a double-digit home run total: Kazuma Okamoto (24) and Springer (12). Last year, Toronto had four players who swatted 20-plus homers. This year, they'll be fortunate to have two.

World.title: You can stream AI TV 24/7 on Roku now
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Artificial intelligence has made movies and music, and now it also has its own TV channel on popular streaming platform, the Roku Channel.

Roku did not publicly announce the addition of Fairground AI Creator TV — fully AI-generated content, 24/7, for free — on its streaming platform. Instead, Cord Cutters News was the first to report its inclusion in Roku's lineup.

But if the online backlash is any indication, viewers might be inclined to change the channel.

"Roku is giving the masses what they never asked for: an unending conveyor belt of AI slop," wrote Frank Landymore of Futurism , a science and technology news website.

Bradly Shankar of MobileSyrup, a Canadian tech news website, was just as critical .

"[Roku's] a nice option to have in this oversaturated and increasingly expensive streaming market. But enshittification comes for us all, and Roku is sadly no exception."

LISTEN | Are we in a golden age of free TV?: Cost of Living 9:05 Are we in a golden age of free TV? A growing number of people are tuning in to free streaming channels like Tubi, Pluto TV and Plex to watch re-runs of Baywatch or movies like Meth Gator. It may not be first-rate content, but as Nick Logan explains, for young viewers in particular, you can't beat free.

Fairground AI is a FAST channel, meaning a free, ad-supported streaming television.

There are about 200 FAST channels available on the Roku Channel in Canada, though Fairground AI is not currently one of them. The company has not said whether there are plans to bring the channel to Canada.

Roku cashes in on streaming

Roku is one of the world's most popular streaming companies. Fox reached an agreement to buy the company in a deal worth $22 billion US in June, giving it access to over 100 million global households using the platform.

The new channel comes amid a proliferation of AI-generated content. Earlier this year, Tribeca Festival became the first major film festival to feature an AI-generated movie . Toy giant Hasbro announced in June it would create AI-powered versions of its popular characters , citing unauthorized AI use of its intellectual property. Human web traffic is also declining against AI, according to internet data .

Roku told CBC News Tuesday it provides "customers with a variety of streaming options," in response to an inquiry about the AI channel and the backlash.

AI channel's CEO expecting 'same evolution' as YouTube

The Roku Channel isn't Fairground AI's only platform — the company's website says it's slated to stream on five TV and FAST platforms starting this month.

On its website, Fairground AI calls its channel "the first FAST channel dedicated exclusively to AI-generated content."

Colin Petrie-Norris, Fairground AI's founder and CEO, told CBC News that the channel is also on electronics company LG's streaming platform, but did not say what other platforms the channel is slated to appear on.

"Overall, we've seen really strong interest by streaming platforms of all types in the medium," he said.

Fairground AI has said its channel is slated to appear on more platforms, but has not publicly disclosed all of them. (Giordano Ciampini/The Canadian Press)

Petrie-Norris is convinced the AI doubters and skeptics will come around eventually.

"When YouTube first launched, its early creators were written off as being limited to 'dogs on skateboards' and low-quality user-generated content," he said.

"YouTube creators today are now mainstream personalities driving billions of dollars for the entertainment industry. We believe the same evolution will happen with Fairground's AI creators."

Why do people watch TV?

Roku's adoption of an AI channel does not surprise Fenwick McKelvey, a professor of information and communication technology policy at Concordia University in Montreal.

"Streamers are looking to lower costs and raise time on platforms, and this looks like the inevitable direction," he said, adding it remains to be seen whether viewers will like the channel.

He said Roku made a name for itself partly through the popularity of its screensavers, which suggests not everyone wants to have engaging content on their screens. The channel may function for many viewers as a more dynamic screensaver.

"One of the things that's really important is we often miss why people watch TV," he said. "There's lots of ways that television is just something people have on in the background."

Late last year, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission updated its definition of Canadian content to exclude fully AI-generated content.

WATCH | An education professor explains: What does AI baby slop look like? | Duration 1:56 An education professor and kids’ content creator explain characteristics of low-quality, hastily produced, generative-AI video content that’s proliferating online.

The regulator said in its updated definition that "while AI may serve as a potential tool to assist in the creation of Canadian content, the Commission is of the view that humans should hold creative control to support economic opportunities and remuneration for Canadians creators."

But McKelvey said many difficult questions on AI generated content have not been addressed, such as the AI industry's often dubious record adhering to copyright laws and privacy protections. In May, Canada's privacy commissioner found that AI company OpenAI was not compliant with Canadian privacy laws when it trained its chatbot, ChatGPT.

The Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists has also consistently opposed replacing human performers with AI and has repeatedly called on the government to pass more laws regulating AI.

And so, what remains unsolved are the "fundamental issues about how artists get paid, or how do we pay for culture," McKelvey said.

"Largely, the business-first, economic opportunity of AI has trumped most other social concerns."

World.title: CUSMA breakdown could mean hundreds of thousands of jobs, a trillion dollars lost: report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As trade talks aimed at avoiding fresh U.S. tariffs continue, a new report is warning that the breakdown of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement would lead to hundreds of thousands of job losses and major economic impacts on both sides of the border.

The report, prepared for the Canadian American Business Council by Oxford Economics — an independent economic advisory firm — and released Monday, analyzed the likely result of three different outcomes of the ongoing trade talks between the U.S. and Canada.

The scenarios were a status quo situation where current tariffs remain in place, a scenario where the CUSMA agreement breaks down, and one where CUSMA is successfully renegotiated and the trading relationship improves.

In the event that CUSMA were to end, a projected 214,000 American and 102,000 Canadian jobs would be lost, the report said, compared to the status quo scenario.

But if CUSMA were renegotiated successfully, the U.S. and Canada stand to add jobs — 137,000 and 98,000 of them, respectively.

"It means real jobs and security and stability [lost] at a time where affordability is front and centre for so many Canadians and Americans," Beth Burke, the CEO of the Canadian American Business Council, told Power and Politics in an interview Tuesday.

Burke says the findings highlight just how important the trading relationship between the U.S. and Canada is to the success of both countries.

"This relationship matters," Burke said.

The impacts also extend beyond jobs. According to the report's estimates, the breakdown scenario would impact the GDP of both countries, costing the U.S. economy $1.04 trillion US and costing Canada $271 billion Cdn by 2035.

The pace of inflation would likely pick up in both countries in the immediate and long-term, while growth of real disposable income would be stunted, especially on the Canadian side.

A successful negotiation paints the opposite picture in the report's projections — more disposable income for citizens on both sides of the border, slower inflation and GDP gains of billions for both countries.

WATCH | Hundreds of thousands of jobs on the line if CUSMA dies, says business council CEO: Hundreds of thousands of jobs on the line with trade talks: business council | Duration 8:37 A report released on Tuesday by the Canadian American Business Council presented the likely economic consequences of three possible outcomes of CUSMA negotiations. The findings indicated that hundreds of thousands of jobs on either side of the border hang in the balance of the ongoing trade talks. Power & Politics speaks to the CEO of the Canadian American Business Council, Beth Burke, about why the ongoing discussions on the ground in Washington matter.

On the U.S. side, manufacturing industries would be hit hardest in the report's worst-case scenario — including losses in auto, wood product and metal product manufacturing. Hubs for that kind of work including Iowa, Michigan, Kentucky and Alabama would suffer as a result, the authors suggest.

And in Canada, the manufacturing hubs of Quebec and Ontario would feel the pain most if CUSMA broke down, as the report says manufacturing industries would take the biggest hit at home, too.

Trade reps still trying to cut a deal

The report comes as the Aug. 19 deadline looms for new 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian products — from honey to plywood to hyacinth bulbs — that make up about five per cent of Canada's exports to the U.S.

Officials are still working to cut a deal that would curb new tariffs before then.

Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette speak during a press conference on the roof of the Canadian Embassy in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. LeBlanc is back in Washington today speaking with his U.S. counterpart ahead of next week's looming tariff deadline. (Kelly Geraldine Malone/Canadian Press)

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc was slated to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer today — their third meeting in as many weeks. According to sources recently briefed on the matter, LeBlanc and his counterpart are aiming to present U.S. President Donald Trump with a possible trade deal as early as Monday.

That timeline would give the president at least a day to make a decision on the deal ahead of the deadline for the new tariffs to come into effect.

Burke says she's glad to see talks continuing, and added that Canadians should be prepared to see concessions made on both sides for a deal to be reached.

"That's what a negotiation means, that there needs to be movement from both ends to get to the right place," she said.

WATCH | Canadian businesses rush goods to U.S. ahead of new 50% tariffs: Canadian businesses rush goods to U.S. ahead of new 50% tariffs | Duration 2:00 Canadian companies vulnerable to new 50 per cent U.S. tariffs are rushing shipments and hoping a breakthrough deal will avert the punishing levies before the August 19 deadline.

When Trump's administration first threatened the tariffs last month in a series of presidential proclamations, it cited grievances over Canada's alleged discrimination against U.S. dairy products, retaliatory auto tariffs and provincial alcohol bans.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that negotiators were discussing "all strategic sectors" with their counterparts in the hopes of making a deal.

But if a deal isn't reached and fresh 50 per cent levies do come into effect next week, they're expected to hit manufacturers in central Canada hardest.

Another new report out yesterday from Oxford Economics predicts that manufacturers of cement and concrete would feel the biggest impact, followed by paper product makers, with wood, computers and electronics, plastics and rubber manufacturers also being among the hardest hit.

“Manufacturers that face the stiffest tariff hikes, rely heavily on exports to the U.S., and whose products are easier to substitute away from would face the heaviest impact,” wrote the report's co-authors, Tony Stillo, director of Canada Economics, and Michael Davenport, a senior economist.

Ontario, New Brunswick and Quebec would be the hardest-hit provinces according to their analysis, because of their dependence on these manufacturing sectors, while Saskatchewan, Alberta and Newfoundland and Labrador would better dodge the new tariffs.

World.title: Author Marina Nemat follows the light in her new novel
World.content:
Article content

It tells you a great deal about Iranian-Canadian author Marina Nemat that she is able to speak these words with such gentle conviction. She has never shirked writing about the unspeakable horrors she suffered as a teenager at the hands of the Iranian government. So she knew she would again be entering dark places when she decided to honour the memory of a much-loved grandmother in her new novel, Mistress of the Persian Boarding House. But in writing it, Nemat was, as always, drawn to the light at the end of the tunnel. Goodness, she insists, can still prevail in the midst of evil.
