Hidalgo’s Industrial Engine

Hidalgo’s 8.2% growth makes it the clear national leader in the first quarter of 2026. This is according to the ITAEE state-level indicator.

The state sits just north of Mexico City. Its economy is heavily weighted toward secondary activities.

That sector includes manufacturing, construction, energy generation, and industrial production. It grew 16.5% year-on-year.

That extraordinary pace powered the state’s overall expansion.

What is driving that surge? The research points to a broad-based industrial push, not a single project.

Energy infrastructure, manufacturing plants, and construction activity all appear to be contributing. This is a notable shift for a state historically overshadowed by neighbors like Mexico State or Puebla.

If you are an expat or investor looking for pockets of dynamism, Hidalgo is where the momentum is concentrated.

Chiapas: A Modest Contrast

Chiapas, at the opposite end of the spectrum, grew about 2.0% in the same quarter. That is positive — it is not a contraction.

But it is far below Hidalgo’s pace and roughly in line with the national average. Chiapas has long been one of Mexico’s most economically challenged states.

It has high poverty rates and a limited industrial base. Its economy leans more on agriculture, tourism, and remittances.

Those sectors did not see the same kind of industrial boost.

The contrast matters for anyone living in or invested in Latin America. Mexico’s economy is not a single monolith.

It is a collection of regional economies moving at very different speeds. When you see national GDP forecasts of 1.1%–1.8%, remember that those numbers mask wide variation.

Hidalgo is growing at a pace that would be impressive even in a booming global economy. Chiapas is barely keeping its head above water.

That divergence has real consequences for property prices, job markets, and business opportunities.

Why the Gap Matters to You

If you are an expat, a nomad, or an investor in Latin America, the regional split in Mexico should shape your decisions. A state growing at 8.2% is likely to see rising demand for housing, commercial space, and services.

Hidalgo’s industrial expansion could mean new jobs, higher wages, and better infrastructure. All those factors make a region more attractive for living or doing business.

Conversely, a state growing at 2.0% may struggle to generate new opportunities. Property values or business prospects there may lag.

This is not about predicting the future. It is about reading the present more accurately.

National averages flatten the picture. The ITAEE data shows that Mexico’s economic center of gravity is shifting.

At least in the short term, it is shifting toward industrial states like Hidalgo. For anyone deciding where to relocate, invest, or start a venture, that kind of granular information is more useful than a single national GDP figure.

The gap between Hidalgo and Chiapas is not an anomaly. It is a signal of how Mexico’s economy is restructuring.

Mexico’s Fastest-Growing State: A Regional Outlook

Mexico’s fastest-growing state in Q1 2026, Hidalgo, offers a counterpoint to the national slowdown. The country as a whole is forecast to expand just 1.1%–1.8% this year.

Hidalgo’s 8.2% growth shows that industrial policy, energy investment, and manufacturing can still deliver outsized results in specific regions. The secondary sector’s 16.5% jump is the engine behind that performance.

It suggests that states with a strong industrial base are better positioned to ride out a sluggish national economy.

For Chiapas, the 2.0% growth is a reminder that not all Mexican states share the same momentum. The gap between the two states — more than six percentage points — is among the widest in the country.

Whether that gap narrows or widens will depend on factors like infrastructure investment, energy policy, and private-sector confidence. For now, the data is clear.

If you are looking for growth in Mexico, look north of the capital, not south.

Frequently Asked Questions

What made Hidalgo grow so fast in Q1 2026? Hidalgo’s growth was driven by secondary activities — industry, construction, manufacturing, and energy. That sector grew 16.5% year-on-year. It is the state’s economic engine. Its strong performance powered the overall 8.2% expansion, the highest in Mexico. How does Chiapas compare to Hidalgo? Chiapas grew about 2.0% in the same quarter. That is well behind Hidalgo’s 8.2%. Chiapas did see positive growth. But it was roughly in line with the national average and far below the industrial surge seen in Hidalgo. Is the national GDP forecast relevant to these state numbers? Yes, but only as a backdrop. Mexico’s national GDP is forecast to grow around 1.1%–1.8% in 2026. That national figure masks wide regional variation. Hidalgo is growing far faster, while other states may be growing slower. For local decisions, state-level data is more useful than the national average.

Sources: INEGI (ITAEE, Q1 2026); Mexican state economic reports, 2026.

World.title: Fonseca and Cerúndolo Drawn Into the Same Cincinnati Quarter
World.content:
The 2026 Cincinnati Open draws were released Tuesday, and Latin America’s two most prominent men landed in the same crowded section of the bracket. Brazil’s João Fonseca, seeded 23rd, and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, seeded 20th, were both placed in the third quarter headed by American Taylor Fritz, a section that also contains 2019 champion Daniil Medvedev, 2021 runner-up Andrey Rublev, Norway’s Casper Ruud, American Brandon Nakashima, Belgian Zizou Bergs and wildcard Marin Čilić, who won the tournament in 2016.

The two cannot meet before the quarterfinals. Both will have to survive a section stacked with former Masters 1000 winners to get there. The draw arrives under unusual circumstances. World Nos. 1 and 2 Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, who won the last two men’s titles at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, are both absent, Sinner with a knee injury and Alcaraz with a wrist injury.

Their withdrawals leave the men’s field without the two players who have decided nearly every major hard-court event of the past two seasons. Alexander Zverev, the 2021 champion, acknowledged the shift in an assessment of the field, noting Sinner’s record streak of 34 consecutive Masters 1000 match victories and six titles this year.

“I think it does change things a little bit, especially with Jannik not being here,” Zverev said. “But for me, it doesn’t change much. I still want to compete against the best.” Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo, seeded 22nd, drew a different assignment. He was placed in Zverev’s quarter alongside Flavio Cobolli, the rising Spaniard Rafael Jodar, American Tommy Paul, Valentin Vacherot of Monaco, Belgian Alexander Blockx, Hubert Hurkacz and Denis Shapovalov.

Peru’s Ignacio Buse, seeded 29th at 21 years old, sits in the bottom quarter. That section is headed by second seed Félix Auger-Aliassime and includes Ben Shelton, Lorenzo Musetti, Americans Learner Tien and Frances Tiafoe, France’s Ugo Humbert and Arthur Rinderknech, Stefanos Tsitsipas and 2017 champion Grigor Dimitrov.

Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry is seeded 26th. All 32 seeds receive a bye into the second round. Argentina again brought the region’s largest delegation, with eight men across the seeded and unseeded ranks. One of them has already made an impression on this swing.

Thiago Agustín Tirante beat Fritz in the Round of 64 in Montreal, an upset that cost the American the tournament he entered as a favorite and that now shadows the quarter Fritz heads in Ohio. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio is the region’s only player in the main draw. She opens against American Taylor Townsend, with the winner advancing to face world No. 2 Elena Rybakina.

It is an unforgiving path for a player who has spent the season rebuilding her ranking, though Townsend is beatable and the reward for an upset would be the highest-profile match of Osorio’s summer. Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia, listed on early entry publications, will not appear.

The former world No. 10 announced last week that she will not play again on tour this year and intends to return in 2027 using a protected ranking, after a season that produced a 4-19 record and eight consecutive losses. Four Latin American women entered qualifying instead. Argentina’s Solana Sierra went out Tuesday evening to Japan’s Aoi Ito, 6-1, 6-1, leaving Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska and Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa to chase the twelve main-draw places on offer.



In the men’s qualifying, 36-year-old Argentine Marco Trungelliti came through his opener against Sebastian Ofner in three sets, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien and Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía were still in action late Tuesday. Main-draw play begins Thursday and runs through Aug. 23, the last significant test before the US Open. For a region sending fourteen players to Ohio, the answers about form and readiness will come quickly.

World.title: Costa Rica Runs Its National Evacuation Drill Wednesday
World.content:
At 10 a.m. Wednesday, offices, schools, hotels, clinics and government buildings across Costa Rica will empty into the street at the same time. Nothing will be wrong.It is the eighth national evacuation drill, and if you are in a building when it starts, someone will ask you to leave it. Follow them, take the stairs, and expect to be back at your desk or in your room within ten or fifteen minutes.

You do not need to have signed up to be swept along by it. If your hotel, your child’s school or your workplace registered, you are taking part whether or not anyone told you in advance.If you want to actually use the exercise rather than just stand outside for it, there are three steps.

Register at simulacro.cr, write or update an emergency plan for your household or business, then evacuate at 10 a.m. Wednesday and report that you did it through the Simulacro CR app. The middle step is the one that matters and the one most people skip. A plan means deciding now who collects the children, where everyone meets if the house is unsafe, which route you take if the usual road is blocked, and what you would grab on the way out.

Standing in a parking lot for ten minutes teaches you nothing if you have never answered those questions. This year’s exercise works differently from previous ones. Rather than everyone rehearsing the same scenario, you practice for the hazard that can actually reach where you are. Eight are on the list — earthquake, flood, landslide, volcanic eruption, tornado, hurricane, fire and tsunami.

The reason for this change is more common sense than anything else. Practicing a tsunami evacuation in Cartago is wasted effort, and practicing an earthquake drill on a beach where the real problem is the water arriving twenty minutes later teaches the wrong reflex. What you rehearse should match what is likely to happen where you live.

Unfortunately, turnout is running behind last year. The emergency commission counted 350,000 people signed up as of August 3, against more than 1.4 million who took part in 2025 — the highest participation on record. Keep in mind that registration and participation are not the same thing and sign-ups tend to surge in the final days, but the gap is wide.

Alejandro Picado, president of the Comisión Nacional de Emergencias, has pointed to emergencies elsewhere as the argument for taking it seriously, noting that Costa Rica deals with emergencies constantly and that knowing how to act is a civic responsibility rather than an optional extra.

Expect some public services to slow. The Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones will run the drill at its main offices, its warehouse in Desamparados, the Civil Registry archive in Los Yoses and all 32 regional offices, with more than a thousand people involved at the main site alone, including members of the public who happen to be mid-transaction. If you have paperwork to do Wednesday morning, do it early or do it Thursday.

The app is worth downloading before Wednesday rather than during it. It carries information about the exercise and is how you log your participation afterward, which is how the commission measures who actually took part. Monday’s magnitude 7.4 earthquake in Colombia, which killed more than a hundred people and closed three airports, is a reminder of why Costa Rica runs this exercise at all. Emergencies do not schedule themselves, and the ten minutes you spend outside on Wednesday are the cheapest preparation available.

World.title: Bench warrant cancelled for Lorenzo Tzul after he explains missed court because he was in jail
World.content:
Bench warrant cancelled for Lorenzo Tzul after he explains missed court because he was in jail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A bench warrant issued for Lorenzo Tzul after he repeatedly failed to appear in court has been cancelled after he explained that he had been serving time in prison during part of the period he missed his court dates.

Tzul appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was asked to explain his absence from proceedings in a pending case.

Tzul told the court that he had been incarcerated for possession of a controlled drug and claimed that while at the Belize Central Prison, he informed prison authorities that he had a court matter scheduled, but was not taken to court.

The Senior Magistrate questioned why his $1,500 bail should not be revoked. Tzul told the court that he was released from prison around his birthday on July 4 and was now trying to do better.

Because of his previous failure to appear, the court also sought to have his surety notified. While bail money can be forfeited when an accused person breaches bail conditions, the court did not take that action against Tzul’s sister, who had stood surety for him.

The Magistrate ultimately cancelled the bench warrant and allowed Tzul to remain on bail.

Tzul was then provided with 11 pages of disclosure, and his case was adjourned to October 20, 2026, when the matter is scheduled for trial.

World.title: Joel Hamilton granted $1,500 bail after allegedly wounding 72-year-old father
World.content:
Joel Hamilton granted $1,500 bail after allegedly wounding 72-year-old father

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Ladyville resident Joel Hamilton has been granted bail in the sum of $1,500 as he awaits trial on a charge of wounding his 72-year-old father.

Hamilton appeared before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was provided with seven pages of disclosure. His trial has been set for October 8, 2026.

Hamilton had been on remand at the Belize Central Prison for more than two months in connection with the alleged June incident. Bail was granted at $1,500 plus one surety of the same amount, which he was able to meet.

The court imposed several conditions on his release. Hamilton is not to contact his father and must report to the Ladyville Police Station every Tuesday and Friday. He must also remain living with his sister in the Spanish Town area of Ladyville and cannot change his residence without first obtaining permission from the court. Additionally, he is not to be arrested and charged with any offence while on bail.

Hamilton is accused of causing a wound to his father during a family dispute.

When he first appeared in court, Hamilton entered a guilty plea with an explanation. However, after the prosecution’s facts were read to him, he appeared uncertain as to whether he agreed with the allegations. The Magistrate subsequently entered an equivocal plea of not guilty on his behalf.

Bail was initially denied after the prosecution raised concerns about the age and safety of the alleged victim, who had been residing in the same household as Hamilton.

Hamilton’s matter is scheduled to return to Court #2 for trial on October 8, 2026.

World.title: Belize City man fined $1,500 after beating motorcyclist following traffic collision
World.content:
Belize City man fined $1,500 after beating motorcyclist following traffic collision

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-two-year-old Keiron Garbutt was fined $1,500 after pleading guilty to a charge of harm stemming from an altercation following a traffic collision in Belize City.

Garbutt appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he admitted intentionally and unlawfully causing harm to a 46-year-old man on July 30, 2026.

According to the man, he was riding his motorcycle on George Street when a green motorcycle, allegedly driven by Garbutt from the direction of Bishop Street, collided with him at the intersection.

The man reported that when he stopped and questioned Garbutt about the collision, Garbutt got off his motorcycle and punched him in the face. The man further alleged that Garbutt produced a pocket knife and threatened to stab him in the throat.

The man later alerted two police officers in the area and was taken to the Precinct 1 Police Station, where he was issued medico-legal forms. Garbutt was subsequently detained and charged with harm. No charges were brought against either man in relation to the traffic collision.

In mitigation, Garbutt told the court that the complainant had crashed into him, saying he did not understand why the incident had occurred. When questioned by the Magistrate, however, Garbutt acknowledged that he had harmed the complainant and accepted responsibility for his actions.

For his guilty plea, Garbutt was fined $1,500 plus $5 cost of court. He has until November 30, 2026, to pay the fine, or he will serve five months in prison in default.

World.title: Belize and regional judiciary heads back CCJ; raise grave concern over leaked internal communications
World.content:
Belize and regional judiciary heads back CCJ; raise grave concern over leaked internal communications

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The heads of several Caribbean judiciaries, including Belize, have expressed “grave concern” over the leak of internal communications from the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ), amid reports of significant disagreements among judges of the regional court.

In a joint statement, the heads of judiciary of Barbados, The Bahamas, Belize, Guyana, the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago said they have taken note of recent reports concerning internal correspondence and matters relating to the administration and functioning of the CCJ.

The judicial leaders said they would not comment on the merits of statements or allegations attributed to individual judges, or on the Court’s internal deliberative and administrative processes. They nevertheless expressed serious concern over the apparent breach of confidentiality that resulted in internal communications being disclosed publicly.

The statement follows reports, first published by the Trinidad Express, based on leaked emails said to reveal disagreements between five of the CCJ’s six sitting judges and CCJ President Justice Winston Anderson. The reported allegations include concerns about Anderson’s management style, judicial decision-making and changes to panels hearing cases. No independent finding has established the allegations as fact. (News Room Guyana)

The CCJ has defended the independence and integrity of the Court, cautioning that allegations concerning judicial deliberations and institutional governance could be misunderstood when presented without their full context. (News Room Guyana) The Guyana Bar Association has also condemned the unauthorised disclosure of the correspondence while declining to take a position on the substance of the matters contained in it. (Ignite News)

The regional judiciary heads reaffirmed their confidence in the CCJ, describing it as a vital regional institution and stressing that its authority depends on public confidence in the independence, impartiality, integrity and competence of its judges. They also reaffirmed their commitment to protecting the institutional integrity of the Court and maintaining public trust in the region’s judicial systems.

World.title: Social partners demand representation from all organizations during meeting with cabinet; reiterate request for independent valuation reports
World.content:
Social partners demand representation from all organizations during meeting with cabinet; reiterate request for independent valuation reports

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI), Belize Network of Non-Governmental Organizations (BNN), National Evangelical Association of Belize (NEAB), and National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB) have responded to Government’s invitation to meet with Cabinet regarding ongoing concerns over the proposed acquisition.

In a joint statement, the four social partners welcomed meaningful engagement with Government on the matter.

The social partners, however, reiterated that any consideration for a meeting must include representation from all four organizations, noting that they have been acting collectively on the issue. They said this is necessary to ensure that discussions reflect the positions and concerns raised jointly by the social partners.

The organizations also pointed to outstanding requests for information, including financial statements and independent valuation reports. They said these documents, among other requested information, remain pending and are necessary for them to properly review and assess the matter.

The social partners said they look forward to receiving the requested information and being given a reasonable amount of time to examine it before participating in further discussions with Cabinet.

In addition, the social partners welcomed the Public Utilities Commission’s willingness to engage in further discussions and respectfully called on the Commission to respond to the requests outlined in the social partners’ August 6, 2026 statement.

They further reiterated their commitment to collective action in support of the public interest and said they remain open to meaningful engagement with Government.

World.title: Social Partners insist all four groups be included in Cabinet talks on BTL-Smart deal
World.content:
Social Partners insist all four groups be included in Cabinet talks on BTL-Smart deal

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize’s Social Partners say they are prepared to engage with the Government over the proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications Limited, operator of Smart, by Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL), but are insisting that all four partner organizations be included in the discussions.

In a joint statement issued Tuesday, the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI), Belize Network of Non-Governmental Organizations (BNN), National Evangelical Association of Belize (NEAB) and National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB) acknowledged Government’s invitation for the BCCI and NTUCB to meet with Cabinet on Thursday, August 13. However, the organizations said any meeting must include representatives of all four Social Partners because they have been acting collectively on the matter.

The groups also say several requests for information remain outstanding, including financial statements and independent valuation reports. They maintain that they should be given reasonable time to examine the information before participating in discussions with Cabinet.

Government announced Tuesday that the Social Security Board, Public Utilities Commission and BTL were invited to make presentations to Cabinet on the proposed acquisition, while the BCCI and NTUCB were invited to appear on Thursday. Cabinet says it intends to hear from the various stakeholders before deliberating on the matter and announcing its position following its meeting on Tuesday, August 18. (Belize Press Office)

The controversy surrounds BTL’s proposed approximately $80 million acquisition of 100 percent of Speednet’s shares. BTL’s Board gave preliminary approval to the transaction earlier this month, subject to continued due diligence. (Love FM) The Social Partners have publicly opposed the acquisition in its present form, raising concerns about transparency, competition and the public interest. (Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry)

The Social Partners also welcomed the PUC’s willingness to continue discussions but referred the regulator back to the requests contained in their August 6 statement as the basis for further engagement. They reiterated that their collective actions are intended to protect the public interest.

World.title: International News: Messi takes break from football following father’s death
World.content:
International News: Messi takes break from football following father’s death

By Zoila Palma: Inter Miami star Lionel Messi has temporarily stepped away from football following the death of his father, Jorge Messi.

The Argentine forward is expected to remain in his native Argentina as he spends time with his family during this difficult period.

Jorge Messi played a significant role throughout his son’s career, supporting Lionel from his early days in Argentina and helping him pursue opportunities in Spain.

He remained closely involved in Messi’s career through his years at Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, while also helping to protect his son from the pressures surrounding his global fame.

Messi reportedly returned to Rosario after the World Cup to spend time with his father as his health declined. Following Jorge’s passing, the Inter Miami star has decided to remain with his family and has not been given a specific date to return to the club.

World.title: Weather experts monitor 2 disturbances in Atlantic
World.content:
Weather experts monitor 2 disturbances in Atlantic

By Zoila Palma: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) is monitoring two areas of disturbed weather over the Atlantic, including a tropical wave in the central tropical Atlantic that has a growing chance of developing into a tropical depression later this week.

The first system is located about 550 miles southwest of the Cabo Verde Islands, where disorganized showers and thunderstorms are associated with a tropical wave.

The NHC says environmental conditions are expected to become more favorable for development over the next few days as the system moves westward to west-northwestward across the central tropical Atlantic.

The system has a 40% chance of development within 48 hours and a 70% chance within seven days. If it develops, the NHC says a tropical depression will likely form during the latter half of this week.

Meanwhile, a trough of low pressure about 750 miles east-northeast of Bermuda has also produced an area of showers and thunderstorms that has become somewhat more organized.

The system has a 20% chance of development over the next 48 hours and through seven days as it moves eastward at about 20 mph.

The NHC expects the system to encounter cooler waters later this week, which should end its chances of formation by Thursday.

World.title: US$25-m yacht bet
World.content:
Jamaican American businessman Denton Douglas is confident that within three years a boatbuilding plant he is establishing in Jamaica will be an international success.Photo: Karl Mclarty

JAMAICAN American businessman Denton Douglas is embarking on an ambitious plan to take his boatbuilding business to Jamaica and is prepared to spend US$25 million, initially, to make it a success.

Douglas, who operates Monarch Yachts — a Florida-headquartered company which began operations in China and now operates two plants in Turkey — is pushing to open a yacht-building and repair facility in Jamaica and is confident that within three years it will become profitable while employing scores of Jamaicans.

“I want Jamaica to be a manufacturing hub. Over the years we have been mainly on primary goods; we export bananas, we export ore, but we never make something. We import our cars. We import everything else. I want to move Jamaica from that primary [producer] to a manufacturing hub, and I think we have the know-how. For sure we have the skills, and we have the logistics to do it,” Douglas told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

“We make luxury yachts, commercial boats like fishing boats. We also have ferries… for shuttling people… and our biggest business now are military boats, which is surprisingly patrol boats. We have a line of patrol boats and we have a contract for a country in Africa to do 20 to 40 small ferries… and about 10 patrol boats… We want to do that here because those are easy to build,” added Douglas, who wants to start operating locally before the end of this year.

The Munro College graduate, who received a track scholarship to study at Howard University in the United States in 1988, worked on Wall Street for years before moving into the boating business some 20 years ago.

“When I was in China we were price-competitive, [but] my idea was this: Anyone can come cheaper than you are; they can cut more corners and be cheaper. So I changed my business to quality, meaning… no one in the world can make a better yacht,” declared Denton, who now designs and builds yachts for some of the world’s super-rich.

He said Monarch’s services, which include yacht design, construction, brokerage, charters, and refits/repairs, can all be done in Jamaica, which would be convenient for many of the company’s clients.

“I want to come here and build yachts. Why? First, to be selfish. I fly 12 hours every time to Turkey and Italy to the shipyard, or 21 hours to China. An hour and a half [from Miami to Jamaica] is a lot better than flying so long,” said Douglas.

He pointed out that a customer in the US can jump on a plane in the morning, view his yacht in production in Jamaica and be back in the US the same day, something that cannot happen where he now operates in Turkey.

In addition, it will be much cheaper to build a yacht in Jamaica and ship it to the US.

“For example, my 45-footer, to take it from Turkey to the United States, it’s US$50,000. If I build that same boat here, I’m saving that much money. To take that boat from China is another US$25,000, so that’s US$75,000,” said Douglas as he pointed to the practicality of operating on the island.

According to Douglas, he is now in talks with local authorities to identify a site to set up shop, and while he would love it to be based in St Elizabeth, where he is from, for practical reasons the main shipyard will be in the eastern end of the island — either the Corporate Area, St Catherine, or Portland.

“We need access to skilled labour and access to a port. The key thing is an airport, so if an American businessman comes to Jamaica, comes to see his boat, [he can] fly in [to Jamaica in] the morning, see his yacht, and fly back. So we need somewhere that’s close to an airport where you have access to skilled labour,” said Douglas.

He added that, while his shop will be in one location, the operation could be islandwide as Monarch will operate differently from the American yacht companies which manufacture everything in a single plant.

“I want to adopt the European model, where the shipyard may be in Kingston, but the woodwork could be in St Elizabeth. The piping could be somewhere else, so the wealth and the labour skills are spread throughout Jamaica. So everyone benefits, not just one area,” declared Douglas.

He told the Observer that the plan is not just to build boats, but to establish an ecosystem that will include carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and others who will contribute to all aspects of the production of the yachts.

Douglas said he has already made contact with the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) which are helping with his application for a special economic zone (SEZ) designation, while Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) has already indicated its readiness to help with the training of workers.

“What I would do first is take a bunch of Jamaicans to China and Turkey and teach them on-the-job how it works. Then, once they get a basic understanding of whether it’s aluminium welding, steel welding for marine, or fibreglass, or epoxy work, then they will come back and start working.

“And so it will be maybe 15 to 20 foreign nationals and the rest Jamaicans. If it’s 100 Jamaicans, it will be 10 foreign nationals. It’s more of a teaching model, not a working model,” said Douglas.

“It’s just once we get the right people who can learn and are extremely meticulous, then we’ll be successful. The goal is never to have a lot of foreigners working at the shipyard. It’s always to have them teach us at the shipyard. That is the only way I’m going to do it. If I was going to have a lot of foreigners, I might as well stay where I am in Turkey,” Douglas explained.

He said Monarch will be prepared to pay the tuition for Jamaicans to study at CMU and work for the company for a period under a bonded arrangement.

“But I expect many of them to move on to companies in Germany and Italy because they will be able to pay them more. One of the highest-paid engineers on a yacht now is Jamaica[n],” said Douglas.

World.title: Rewarding resilience
World.content:
From left: Executive director at Sandals Foundation Heidi Clarke; consultant paediatrician at Falmouth Public General Hospital Dr Kerry-Ann McKenzie; Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett; and director of operations at Sandals Foundation Karen Zacca engage in conversation during Tuesday’s launch of Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica 2026 at AC Hotel Kingston. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

CONSULTANT paediatrician at Falmouth Public General Hospital Dr Kerry-Ann McKenzie was visibly moved, Tuesday, as she welcomed the Sandals Foundation’s annual Island Challenge, which will raise £100,000 to replace paediatric and neonatal equipment destroyed by Hurricane Melissa.

Operating out of Trelawny, a parish still recovering from last October’s devastation, McKenzie shared that even after the hospital replaced its roof, the paediatric unit’s Accident and Emergency Department looked forlorn, with only one bed to spare.

“We were pretty much very badly affected by Hurricane Melissa, and our paediatric unit was destroyed. We lost everything; every incubator, every monitor, every bed except one, our departments, where we fight every single day for the lives of our smallest, and our future leaders of our country were devastated,” said McKenzie, her voice trembling slightly.

She was extending her thanks to the Sandals Foundation during the launch of the annual Island Challenge at the AC Hotel Kingston.

Beginning October 2, the four-day expedition will take 30 athletes from the United Kingdom and 15 Jamaican participants across Trelawny, St Ann, St Mary, and St Andrew, where they will trek, hike, and paddle around the island to raise funds for paediatric equipment at Falmouth Public General Hospital.

McKenzie told the launch that doctors and nurses have been resilient in the face of disaster, showing up daily despite not having the equipment to provide comprehensive care. She noted that she was happily anticipating the addition of the medical instruments.

“Jamaicans are resilient. We are a resilient people, and we’re a resilient health facility. With the help of Sandals Foundation, we are going to show forth brighter than what we were previously.

“But resilience can’t buy an incubator. It can’t replace a cardiac monitor. It cannot give us back the beds that we lost. That’s why we’ve joined the Sandals Foundation now in this Island Challenge in getting us the essential equipment that we need for our paediatric and neonatal units at the Falmouth Public General Hospital,” she said.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer, McKenzie explained that the paediatric unit was badly in need of beds, incubators, resuscitators, and monitoring equipment such as pulse oximeters, vital signs monitors, as well as phototherapy lights, warming blankets, and cooling blankets.

“We’ve struggled, but we have been able to keep the department afloat despite the lack of resources. We’re really looking forward to getting the extra help that we need to do what we need to do. We’ve had to do a lot of transfers out because we just don’t have the capacity to keep as many children as we want. But there are scenarios where we can’t get babies out and we’ve really had to take our hand and make fashion. It’s been an exhausting journey, but this is the beginning of a new one, so I’m so excited,” she said.

The head paediatrician also extended her gratitude to athletes participating in the event, telling the launch that their contribution to the hospital’s recovery was invaluable.

“To every runner, every hiker, every donor, every partner standing with us today, on behalf of every child that will pass through the doors of Falmouth Public General Hospital, and every family who will sit beside them holding their hands, we say thank you. You’re not just raising funds. You’re giving our children a lifeline, a fighting chance. You’re rewarding our resilience. And it will go a long way in making sure that we’re able to offer the care that they need,” she said.

Delivering her remarks, executive director at Sandals Foundation Heidi Clarke spoke of the event’s importance. She said the past three challenges raised £300,000 across Antigua & Barbuda in 2023, Saint Vincent & the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025 collectively, benefiting about 1,800 babies.

“I’m very excited to see this finally come home to Jamaica, and as our road to recovery continues here in Jamaica, we know it all too well and [so do] the dedicated teams at the hospitals. It has been a difficult and long road, but with many partners, we’ve been able to work together to make things come to life. We have to recognise, more than ever, the strength of our health care systems are what matter and make communities stronger. Everybody in this room today helps to make events like this possible. And we could not be more grateful,” she said.

Meanwhile, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett told the launch that the testimonial from McKenzie very nearly moved him to tears, hailing the event as a well-needed lifesaving mechanism.

“The passion that drives the Island Challenge, for example, is a powerful one. Because it’s not just one of physical fitness, discipline, dexterity, agility, and ability to use GPS (global positioning system) to navigate through and find your places. It’s not just about that only. It’s about why you do it…

“In the end, you will say, ‘I’m not here for me. I’m here because of others.’ And so what the foundation is doing is demonstrating practically that we are here for others. And tourism connects others,” said Bartlett.

World.title: ‘Mikie’ Bennett: ‘It was a different kind of excitement’
World.content:
Record producer, composer, vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Mikie BennettKarl Mclarty

The first time Mikie Bennett heard a song he wrote played on the radio he shelved his ambitions of a corporate career. That song was Irons In The Fire, recorded in 1980 by Home T 4, the group in which he was a member.

“I had to pull over. My arms were shaking. It was a thing, like, ‘I want more of this, I need this. This is what I want to live for,’ ” he recalled.

Bennett has lived for music since then, establishing himself as a songwriter/producer for major acts like Dennis Brown, Maxi Priest, Shabba Ranks, Cocoa Tea, and J C Lodge.

His work have been recognised by the Jamaican Government, which has made him a member of the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer class for his contribution to the music industry.

When he was informed of the national honour, Bennett said two people instantly came to mind — his mother, Ivy Bennett, and his aunt Amy Picart, her sister.

Ivy Bennett was a literature teacher, who encouraged her son to read more, which nurtured his love for writing.

Amy Picart was a librarian with a meticulous nature, who later managed his Grafton recording studio in east Kingston.

Bennett says while he has received music industry awards, it is not on the same level as national recognition.

“When I got the phone call it was a feeling I wasn’t prepared for; it was a different kind of excitement. A wonderful feeling,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

A Kingston College (KC) graduate, Bennett seemed destined for a conventional nine-to-five job after tertiary studies in business administration from West Indies Teachers’ College (now Northern Caribbean University).

But his music career thrived during the 1980s and 1990s, considered by music pundits as the most creative period in dancehall music.

He co-wrote several of that era’s biggest hit songs, including Temptress (Maxi Priest); Housecall, Mr Loverman (Shabba Ranks); Pirates Anthem (Home T, Cocoa Tea, Shabba Ranks); Can You (Brian and Tony Gold); and Telephone Love by J C Lodge.

Bennett was raised in Vineyard Town, a middle-class community. His neighbours included the Chung brothers, Geoffrey and Mikey, who were respected session musicians/producers.

His biggest musical influence, however, was producer Gussie Clarke, another KC old boy who operated the Music Works label and studio.

Bennett credits Clarke with showing him the business side of things, including publishing and the importance of assembling a solid production team.

In the 1990s, Bennett also worked with producers Lloyd “King Jammy” James, Steely and Clevie, and Bobby Digital. Those associations were also invaluable.

“Jammys has golden ears, but the day-to-day guidance came from Bobby Digital. They knew who they were recording music for. They knew the kind of rhythms the people wanted. And they knew the communication style to reach them,” said Bennett. “They also knew how to take a chance with something different.”

Mikie Bennett is one of nine music industry figures who will receive national honour and awards.

Guitarist Earl “Chinna” Smith, singer Stranger Cole (posthumously), producer Robert Livingston, and deejay Mr Vegas, will also receive the OD (Officer Class).

Percussionists Norman “Bongo Herman” Davis and Lawrence “Larry” McDonald; Carlyle Palmer, co-founder of Jet Star Records in the United Kingdom; and Shirley Findley-Willis, are recipients of the Badge of Honour for Meritorious Service.

Though the assignments take effect on Independence Day, August 6, the annual Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards will this year take place on National Heroes’ Day on October 19 at King’s House in St Andrew.

World.title: Committing to CCJ would be reckless, says Tavares-Finson
World.content:
Tom Tavares Finson

President of the Jamaican Senate, King’s Counsel Tom Tavares-Finson says it would be extremely reckless for Jamaica to commit to the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) as its final appellate court given the turmoil currently gripping the institution.

The Trinidad Express reported earlier this week a series of allegations made by judges of the CCJ, including allegations of dictatorial tendencies in the running of the court and a series of inter-personal conflict.

Tavares-Finson says no less than a public enquiry is required to deal with the issues facing the CCJ.

While acknowledging that inter-personal conflicts is not unusual for a court, he said the allegation surrounding the convening of panels to achieve pre-desired outcomes is troubling and must be treated seriously.

Tavares-Finson says the Opposition People’s National Party, whose insistence that Jamaica must accept the CCJ as its final appellate court has stalled the island’s constitutional reform process, should state clearly whether it maintains its position despite the turmoil which has gripped the regional court.

World.title: WATCH: 20 families homeless after early morning demolition in Trelawny
World.content:
Flattened structures in Coopers Pen, Trelawny after a demolition crew tore down 20 housing units in the area on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Some 20 families in Coopers Pen, Trelawny, have been left homeless after a demolition team reportedly tore down about 20 housing units in an early-morning operation Tuesday.

The residents say they have been before the courts since 2009 for the parcel of land that some say they have occupied for more than three decades.

Residents said the demolition crew arrived on the parcel of land shortly after 3:30 am, catching them off guard and leaving little time to save their belongings.

The team reportedly arrived with two excavators, sledgehammers, pickaxes and other equipment, and was accompanied by a strong contingent of police personnel.

Residents said they received no prior warning before the demolition began.

They also claimed that, before leaving the area, members of the demolition team warned that they would return in the coming weeks to continue the operation.

World.title: Tougher water fines
World.content:
Water level in the Mona reservoir last week.

SEVEN parishes will face a water prohibition from Monday, August 17 as the Government moves to tighten restrictions amid worsening drought conditions.

At the same time, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is set to approach the executive and legislature to punish violators with stiffer fines.

“As we had to do after the first incident that took place with Rio Cobre, where we had to shift the fine, we now have to take the same approach with fines in relation to water prohibition,” Samuda told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“Because of the present forecast and warning associated with El Niño, we will have to move with unprecedented speed, and we will have to engage first the Cabinet and then Parliament in the coming weeks to facilitate this,” Samuda added.

On Monday, Samuda’s ministry, through the National Water Commission (NWC), announced that the water prohibition orders will apply to Kingston, St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine and will remain in force until further notice.

“Under the orders, no person shall use or cause water supplied by the NWC to be used for non-essential or unusual purposes. Prohibited activities include:

• irrigation or watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms;

• refilling or supplying of ponds or swimming pools and/or for use other than normal domestic services such as drinking, cooking, washing, bathing, and sanitation;

• washing of vehicles by the use of a hose;

• watering or washing of roadways, pavements, paths, garages, or out-rooms;

• any activity requiring excessive or unusual quantities of water,” the ministry release stated.

The ministry said the decision followed a high-level stakeholder meeting earlier Monday with the NWC and the Meteorological Service, which confirmed that rainfall levels remain critically low and temperatures continue to soar.

Underscoring the necessity of the measure, Samuda said, “We understand that there is some disproportionate economic impact on commercial operations, such as car washes, and we have not taken this decision lightly. Ultimately, our priority is to maintain supply to critical services, especially schools, as we prepare for the September reopening.”

He further advised that sanctions will be applied to individuals and entities found in breach of the prohibition order, noting “these penalties are intended to ensure compliance and protect the integrity of Jamaica’s water supply during this critical period”.

The current fine for breaching an NWC prohibition order is $1,000. Failure to pay the court-ordered fine results in imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Samuda’s reference to the Rio Cobre was the action taken by the Government after chemical spills that resulted in fish kills that affected several species and impacted other aquatic organisms four years ago.

In January 2025 he successfully piloted a Bill in the House of Representatives which approved amendments to the Natural Resources Conservation Authority (NRCA) Act and the Wild Life Protection Act to allow for significant increases in fines and related custodial sentences.

Under the Acts, depending on the severity of the offence, as adjudicated by the Supreme Court, corporate bodies may now be subject to a fine of approximately $10 million, individuals in breach of the Acts may face a fine of up to $5 million or serve a term of imprisonment up to five years, subject to the jurisdiction of the parish courts.

On Monday, Samuda told the Observer that the request he will be taking to Cabinet and Parliament is to “move the fines in line with what was done for bodies corporate and individuals under the NRCA Act breaches.

The naturally-occurring El Niño climate pattern, which began in June and is expected to peak later this year, has already amplified unprecedented temperatures across the world.

Some 33 countries recorded their hottest July since records began, according to a detailed analysis of billions of data points from Copernicus’s ERA5 climate model.

The severe drought has triggered food security concerns worldwide.

Last week, the United Nations World Food Programme said that Central America is expected to be the region hardest hit in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity.

Including the Caribbean, the agency estimates that an additional 16 million people could face food insecurity by the end of 2027.

World.title: Who hurt the child?
World.content:
AN announcement by the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) that it is fast-tracking the installation of security cameras at Glenhope Place of Safety, even as it probes the injuries suffered by a one-year-old boy who had been in its care, has been welcomed by attorney Denise Hinson who is adamant that somebody needs to be held accountable for how the child came to be injured in such a manner.

“The questions still need to be answered. This should not be pushed under the rug. I’m angry, and I think that someone needs to explain why a one-year-old defenceless child, a Jamaican child, looks as if he was in an MMA (mixed martial arts) fight,” Hinson told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The attorney is representing the mother of the child who is before the court for immigration issues.

She said the child’s injuries captivated the attention of the St Catherine Parish Court last Friday when the matter was called up before Justice Roneiph Lawrence.

Hinson said the child’s Haitian mother, Fabienne Cherisma, who was recently arrested for overstaying her visa alongside her husband who is said to have used fraudulent documents to obtain Jamaican citizenship, were on Friday brought before the court so it could make a further order for the child to remain in the custody of the State.

However, Hinson said when the child was presented to the court, both parents went into shock.

“The child was taken to court with [healing] black and blue bruises under both eyes; what seemed to be burn marks to the right cheek and chin; swelling of the face, especially to the right cheek; and scratches to the nose. Both eyes were bloodshot in the corners. A medical shown to the court by the CPFSA officer who brought the baby to court, described the injuries as ‘non-accidental’,” Hinson told the Observer.

The attorney said that when the mother saw her child she “screamed and began to cry uncontrollably and the father collapsed. They had to be removed and later returned to the dock”.

Hinson said the court was also “visibly disturbed by the doctor’s findings and the injuries on the baby’s face”.

She said the CPFSA officer, when pressed by the judge about the cause of the child’s injuries, “informed the court that when she asked, on arriving to collect the child, she was told that he had hit his face on the crib”.

The attorney, in making a successful bail application on behalf of the mother, who was released on humanitarian grounds, however countered that, “both eyes were bruised and that could not have occurred if the child simply fell out his crib”.

“I also pointed out that the child is in danger where he is and that he needed his mother. My focus is really to get to the bottom of how the child received those injuries at Glenhope. Also, the bruises were healing and the burn mark almost completely healed. However, the child didn’t see a doctor until the day before court, on August 6, 2026. I need help in finding out when and how the child was injured and why the child wasn’t taken to the doctor until the day before the scheduled court date,” Hinson declared.

The attorney said she is in discussion with the child’s mother to determine the legal options available to her as she presses for answers regarding her son’s health. Hinson told the Observer that her client is adamant that the “child was in perfect health when removed from [their] home”.

The CPFSA issued a statement to the media on Monday saying “the incident is being investigated and is being treated with utmost urgency and importance”.

The agency stated that it “takes a zero-tolerance approach to all forms of child abuse” and said, based on the outcome of the investigation, it stands ready to execute all measures or sanctions regarding child abuse, in keeping with the Child Care and Protection Act (CCPA 2004).

Furthermore, the CPFSA said under its 2025–2027 strategic framework it established an islandwide initiative to equip residential child care facilities with security cameras, ensuring high safety standards are maintained across all locations.

“In light of the recent incident however, deployment has been prioritised to fast-track installation at the facility in which this incident has taken place,” the agency pledged.

World.title: Rock-born DJ Damage scores BMI Trailblazers award
World.content:
DJ Damage BMI Award.

JAMAICAN-BORN Leonard “DJ Damage” Douglas is celebrating career-defining achievements as the creative force behind Without You, a chart-topping single by Jevon Dewand and The Trap Starz.

The single, which reached #1 on Billboard’s Gospel Airplay Chart in February, was recognised as one of the year’s most-performed gospel songs at the Broadcast Music, Inc (BMI) Trailblazers of Gospel Music Awards on July 21 in Nashville, Tennessee.

The milestones are an international breakthrough for DJ Damage, whose two-decade career has taken him from Jamaica’s sound system culture to the global music stage.

The Atlanta-based DJ played a multidimensional role in the success of Without You, which is recognised as an urban, hip hop praise anthem, contributing as a songwriter, scratch DJ, producer, background vocalist, and featured performer in the accompanying music video.

The Billboard #1 capped an extraordinary 33-week run that saw Without You reshape the gospel and urban radio landscape, including a 12 per cent surge in radio spins during its climb to the top spot, and a #26 placement on the Billboard Year-End Top Gospel Airplay Chart.

“Reaching the Billboard #1 spot was nothing short of a dream come true. For a kid from Jamaica to achieve that level of recognition on one of music’s most prestigious charts is a milestone I don’t take lightly,” he said. “It represents both my personal achievement and a moment of pride for Jamaica and the Caribbean as a whole. Very few creatives from our region have ever stood at that height, and I’m deeply grateful and humbled to be among them.”

DJ Damage has built a career behind the scenes of the music industry, spinning for Grammy Award-winning R&B group 112; touring with American rap rock band Gym Class Heroes; and sharing stages with artistes including Swizz Beatz, DJ Khaled, Rick Ross, Ashanti, Sean Paul, Vybz Kartel, Mavado, Buju Banton, Beenie Man, and Bounty Killer.

Jevon Dewand credits DJ Damage’s versatility and musical instincts as key ingredients in the success of

Without You.

“He has a great ear for music. Sight is a blessing and vision is a gift. I saw the vision in him,” said Dewand. “DJ Damage knows all types of music, and he’s very versatile in all genres. Most DJs play music but can’t make it music. He can.”

While Billboard recognition and the BMI Award mark two of the biggest moments of his career, DJ Damage says the journey began in Prospect, Clarendon, where he first dreamt of making it in music. His breakthrough came years later in Stony Hill, St Andrew, when he convinced promoters to let him perform with R&B group 112.

“That night in Stony Hill was everything. It was me taking a chance and betting on myself. I knew that if I could just get my foot in the door and get on that stage with 112, my skills would reach the right ears,” he said.

They did.

“I still DJ for 112 to this day. From there I took the momentum to Jersey City and began DJ’ing with Gym Class Heroes, and it just kept building. Every connection, every show, and every risk led to the next opportunity. I went on to DJ for Shai, joined a sound system called Diamond Movements, and had the privilege of performing alongside legends across reggae, dancehall, R&B, hip hop, and more. That one night in Stony Hill set everything in motion.”

That momentum eventually led to an introduction from Wayne Wonder, which opened doors to King Promotions, touring opportunities with producer and songwriter Jazze Pha and, in 2023, performing before an audience of over 60,000 people during hip hop’s 50th anniversary celebration.

“It was electrifying. There’s really no other word to describe it. To me, standing on one of hip hop’s greatest stages, surrounded by some of the biggest names in the culture, celebrating 50 years of a genre that was born from Jamaican sound system culture, as a Jamaican DJ was priceless,” he said. “Every obstacle, every sacrifice, every door that was closed before one finally opened, all of it flashed in that moment. Not many DJs will ever have that experience. And standing there, I knew without a doubt that it was exactly where I was supposed to be. That feeling is truly indescribable.”

DJ Damage hopes his story encourages the next generation of creatives to dream bigger than their circumstances.

“These are moments I worked for over 20 years. I started with nothing but a chance and a will to prove myself. I hope young creatives across Jamaica and the Caribbean will see this win and know that if they have a dream and don’t know if it’s possible, it is.”

Following his latest achievements, DJ Damage will continue his momentum with a performance at the 41st Annual Stellar Gospel Music Awards on August 15 at the Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina. The awards ceremony will be later aired on BET.

World.title: Merz’s deal with the Taliban alarms Afghan dissidents in Germany
World.content:
Under pressure from the rising far right, Berlin is letting Taliban officials staff Afghan missions in exchange for more deportations. Activists say the arrangement puts them at risk.

Zarmina Paryani and her four sisters fear they may soon have to again face the persecutors they fled from in Afghanistan — and this time inside Germany.

Paryani and her sisters were imprisoned twice in Kabul for protesting against the Taliban after the Afghan militants retook the capital in 2021, the 27-year-old said. After going into hiding for several months, the family eventually made their way to Germany in search of safe haven.

But now, Berlin has struck a Faustian bargain that allows the Taliban to deepen its diplomatic foothold in Germany in return for cooperation on deporting Afghan migrants back to Afghanistan. For Paryani and other Afghan activists who resisted the Taliban at home, the arrangement is giving their former persecutors new leverage over their lives in exile.





“It’s hard to accept that my fate and my affairs are being discussed with the very same representatives whose oppression, prisons, whippings and violence I fled from,” Paryani, who worked as a midwife in Kabul and now lives in western Germany, told POLITICO.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government first struck a deal with the Afghan government announced last October that gives Taliban officials control of diplomatic missions in Berlin and Bonn in exchange for permission to return Afghan migrants directly to Afghanistan. That cooperation was deepened early this summer with a deal that allows more Taliban officials to work in Germany in return for cooperation on additional deportation flights — now up to three per month.

Under the new deal, Germany has expanded deportations to include not only Afghan men convicted of crimes, but also, more broadly, Afghan men with no protected status or legal right to remain in Germany.

The agreement with the Taliban makes Germany an outlier in Europe, making it the first EU country to allow Taliban-appointed officials to work in diplomatic missions inside the country. Before the agreement, Western-oriented Afghan officials representing the former government in Afghanistan had remained in charge.

The arrangement comes as Merz’s government grapples with rock-bottom approval ratings and the rise of the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, now the country’s most popular political force, according to polls. The AfD’s surge comes ahead of two elections in the former East Germany, where the far-right party is ahead in polls by wide margins. In one of those states, Saxony-Anhalt, the party may take real governing power for the first time since it was founded in 2013, a result that would serve as a great humiliation for the conservative Merz, who was elected chancellor last year partly on a promise to crack down on migration.





The AfD’s rise is piling pressure on the chancellor to deliver on his election pledge to deport more migrants — even as he insists that working with the Taliban does not legitimize a regime notorious for its human rights abuses. Overall, Afghans are the third-largest group of refugees or people who have fled war to come to Germany, behind Ukrainians and Syrians.

“We are not extending a hand to this Taliban regime,” Merz said in the German parliament in June. “Rather, we are seeking cooperation at the necessary technical level, which is in our country’s national interest.”

‘Nightmares’ and ‘psychological distress’

For Afghan rights activists in Germany, one of the worst consequences of Berlin’s deal with the Taliban is that it may particularly put at risk some 35,000 Afghans who came to Germany under special humanitarian programs for people deemed especially vulnerable to the Taliban. They include Paryani and her sisters in addition to thousands of human rights activists and Afghans who worked with the German military during its nearly two-decade presence in the country.

Paryani and others fear they will have to face the Taliban when attempting to renew their Afghan passports — which they need to extend their humanitarian visas — at Afghan diplomatic missions. Another 321,000 Afghans live in Germany as refugees or with other forms of protected status. They do not necessarily need Afghan passports, unless they want to apply for a permanent residence status.

More generally, activists and refugees also fear the Taliban, with their growing presence in Germany, could gain access to personal information held in databases in German missions, including details about their families, making them susceptible to blackmail and extortion.

Afghan activists speak at a protest camp at Berlin’s Alexanderplatz on August 15, 2025, the fourth anniversary of the Taliban takeover. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

“Given my personal history and my stance on extremism, I am concerned for my safety and that of my family,” one former teacher from Afghanistan granted anonymity due to his fear of retribution from the Taliban told POLITICO.

The former teacher, who lives in Germany with a humanitarian visa, said German immigration officials have asked him to renew his expired Afghan passport, a request that he fears will force him to deal directly with his persecutors.

“This situation continues to cause me significant psychological distress,” he said. “Sometimes I wake up at night because of nightmares related to the Taliban and this situation.”

‘Vulnerable to blackmail’

With its handling of the Taliban, Merz’s government is setting a precedent that will be closely watched by other EU countries. Government officials in Austria and Belgium have said they’re watching Germany’s cooperation with the Taliban closely. Taliban officials also held talks focused on deportations with the EU Commission in June in Brussels.

But Hamid Nangialay Kabiri, the former head of the Afghan consulate in Bonn, who quit last September in protest over the initial deal allowing Taliban officials to serve in diplomatic missions in Germany, warned that the German government’s decision to cooperate with the Afghan regime would come back to haunt it — and that the Taliban would use their new leverage over Germany to advance their interests in Europe, including by building networks that intimidate dissidents.

“They are destroying my country, and now they are coming here,” he said. “They are not thinking of diplomacy. They have a lot of plans in their mind.”





It’s a sentiment politicians inside the left-leaning opposition also share.

“The German government has made itself vulnerable to blackmail,” Schahina Gambir, a lawmaker for the Greens who was born in Kabul, told POLITICO. “We’re seeing recognition through the back door. The Taliban are being granted access to embassies, they’re being granted immunity, they’re given channels for dialogue — and at the same time, the situation for women and girls in Afghanistan is getting worse and worse.”

There are already signs that the Taliban are exercising their newfound leverage.

Last May, Kabul unexpectedly halted a deportation flight at the last minute, seemingly seeking to extract additional concessions from the German government. A couple of weeks later, Berlin announced the terms of the latest agreement allowing additional Taliban-appointed officials to work at diplomatic missions in Germany.

Officials in Berlin depicted the new deal as a victory and a practical necessity, allowing for more deportations.





“To increase the number of repatriations, more passports must be issued, more identities must be verified, and so on,” Martin Giese, a spokesperson for Germany’s foreign ministry, said at the time. “To this end, it will also be necessary for more consular officials to be involved.”

But Paryani, the Afghan midwife who fled to Germany with her four sisters, said the Taliban would use their new power to torment them in the country they had sought safety in.

“A Taliban member once wrote to me: ‘Just wait until our embassy in Germany reopens. Then we’ll find you there,'” she said of a comment that had surfaced under one of her social media posts about two years ago. She then deemed it irrelevant because it seemed so unrealistic.

“Today, I feel as though that threat has become a reality,” she said.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s Balkan fumble
World.content:
Since Zelenskyy’s visit, Vučić threatened to physically redirect the Iber River that runs from Serbia to Kosovo in retaliation for Kosovo demolishing Serb-owned houses along the reservoir’s shore. Such a move would drain the reservoir supplying much of Kosovo’s water and crucial cooling capacity to its largest power plant.

In addition, Serbian Foreign Minister Marko Djurić and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama exchanged barbs on X, with the latter accusing Serbia of being in “a political bubble” and being in denial over the fact that “Serbia lost Kosova” long ago.

Kosovo was an Albanian-majority southern province of Serbia for most of the 20th century. Its people held broad political rights under socialist Yugoslavia until a decade-long Serb crackdown on dissent led to the armed conflict of 1998-99. A three-month NATO bombing campaign drove Serbian forces out and made the province a U.N. protectorate.

Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and, to date, it is recognized by over 100 nations, including the U.S., U.K. and 22 of the 27 EU member countries. It is also a potential EU candidate country, submitting its application in December 2022.

The country’s status has long been a favorite talking point for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has used it to justify invading Georgia in 2008 and annexing Crimea in 2014. Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said he took note of Zelenskyy’s views “with regret” and that such rhetoric echoes “Russia’s attempts to invoke Kosova as a precedent.”

As for why Ukraine’s leader would wade into the intractable Balkan issue at all, it likely comes down to weaponry.

World.title: Farage vs. Binface: Inside the Clacton by-election circus
World.content:
The feeling that the town has been made to look daft was apparent even among those preparing to vote once again to return the Reform UK leader to parliament. And it’s not the rival candidate wearing a trash can on his head that they’re holding responsible for the “farce.”

Thursday may not be the end of the matter, either. A parliamentary investigation into Farage’s alleged failure to declare millions of pounds of donations in the run-up to his 2024 election could mean yet another by-election — and a tougher battle for the right-wing populist next time around.

Bid for absolution

This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents.

Ordinary punters, he argued, should be the ones to have their say as he faced mounting questions over undeclared donations. The gamble was that such a vote would absolve him of wrongdoing in the eyes of the public, regardless of the findings in two parliamentary probes — one over a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, and the other into support from a convicted fraudster. Farage has denied wrongdoing in both instances, arguing that help was given in a personal capacity.

Reform UK Party Leader Nigel Farage gestures as he speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners on August 10, 2026 at Royal Horseguards Hotel in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

But Britain’s main political parties took one look at this ploy and opted out. That’s how Count Binface, one of the most enthusiastic inheritors of a rich British tradition of standing as a satirical candidate in elections, ended up as Farage’s most high-profile rival.

Others risking their £500 deposit to get their names on the 90-cm-long ballot paper include rival jokesters with names ranging from Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap. Broadcast rules mean the 34-strong candidate list needs to be read in full at every mention of Farage’s by-election on TV.

World.title: Breakfast looks a lot more expensive under new EU pesticide plans
World.content:
Even under more plausible scenarios envisioned by the researchers, in which external growers get on board to varying degrees, consumer prices would rise and EU agricultural imports decline. Though that would in turn boost domestic production, with exact numbers depending on producers' willingness to adapt.

The findings lay out an unpalatable political choice for Brussels: Keep angry farmers' tractors off the streets, or hit consumers' wallets as they fulfill basic needs at the grocery store.

The proposed residue ban, which is part of the food and feed safety simplification package, is popular with European farmers seeking a level playing field with foreign growers — after all, it was partly designed to appease their ire over the EU's trade deal with the Mercosur bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. In order to avoid leaving any residue on fruits and vegetables, producers would essentially have to stop using the substance in question.

However, critics say it clashes with global trade rules, as it essentially imposes EU rules on foreign producers, which is known as a mirror clause.

A wide range of international producer groups argue that the proposed ban goes beyond existing health protections in order to push a one-size-fits-all approach, ignoring the reality that growers around the world face different pests, climates and farming conditions.

“The choice is between berries that are available all year round — healthy, safe and at a fair price — or limited production at a high price,” said Amine Bennani, president of the Moroccan Association of Red Fruit Producers.

World.title: Swarming jellyfish overrun French nuclear plant on same date two years in a row
World.content:
Three fishing vessels are now “constantly patrolling off the coast of the plant" to conduct "preventive fishing operations [...] 24/7,” the company added.

Tuesday’s jellyfish invasion comes a the latest in a series of climate change-driven incidents that have affected French nuclear energy during a particularly infernal summer.

Nuclear power plants are typically built by rivers or on coastlines so they can use nearby water sources to cool their reactors. But a record number in France this summer have been forced to temporarily shut down due to heatwaves and droughts affecting their water supply.

Rising sea temperatures have made jellyfish swarms more common along the French coast in recent years, and those swarms can affect a plant’s ability to bring in seawater — which is what happened at Gravelines. Following last year’s incident at the plant along the North Sea, EDF installed cameras and deployed fishing boats to monitor the situation.

While the vessels “prevented a massive influx of jellyfish” on Saturday and Sunday, they were eventually overwhelmed as the swarm grew from “about 100 kilograms” to “several dozen tons,” the French state-owned utility giant said.

Opponents of nuclear energy were quick to jump on the incident.

“This only highlights that nuclear power plants are ill-equipped to deal with the consequences of climate change,” the French branch of Greenpeace said in statement.
