World.title: Yettel announces useful 4G and 5G mobile network development at Sziget Festival 2026
World.content:
Yettel has prepared 20 per cent more mobile network capacity for this year’s Sziget Festival than it did last year, with the additional capacity roughly equivalent to the needs of a town the size of Szombathely. The cost of building and operating the extra network has exceeded HUF 50 million, Balázs Mang, Yettel’s director of technical strategy, told a press conference at the festival on Tuesday.

30 engineers and service specialists worked on the new system

He said a team of 30 engineers and service specialists had been working on the system’s design, operation and round-the-clock monitoring since the initial planning stage. The work began in May.

For a mobile communications provider, he said, ensuring a reliable service at an event of this scale was particularly challenging because between 70,000 and 80,000 people used their devices simultaneously across an area of 0.7 square kilometres.

Festival-goers also uploaded considerably more photographs, videos and live content than they would under normal circumstances. While uploads typically account for less than 10 per cent of downloads, that figure can reach 30 per cent during the festival’s busiest hours.

Total 4G and 5G capacity increased at Sziget Festival

Working with its network infrastructure partner Cetin, Yettel has expanded last year’s 31-sector network and increased total 4G and 5G capacity by 20 per cent. Within that figure, capacity on high-speed 5G cells using the C-band frequency has risen by 40 per cent.

Mr Mang described this as particularly favourable given current energy pressures, saying that modern 4G and 5G network equipment operated far more efficiently. The latest technologies require less cooling and can handle the same volume of data while using fewer resources, he said.

The provider is supplying the additional network through 144 mobile-cell capacities at 21 locations during the festival, he added. The so-called microcells operating across the island typically cover sectors measuring between 100 and 200 metres.

He also said that, according to last year’s figures, peak-hour mobile traffic increased by 10 per cent over the previous year during the festival as a whole, with 40 per cent of it carried over the 5G network. 5G accounted for 25 per cent of total data traffic, and specialists expect that figure to approach 30 per cent this year as compatible devices become more widespread.

Free Wi-Fi zone with mobile-phone charging points

Judit Tőzsér, Yettel’s director of corporate communications, said that, as the official telecommunications partner of one of Europe’s largest music and cultural events, the company had set up a free Wi-Fi zone equipped with 15 mobile-phone charging points.

If you missed: Sziget Festival kicked off – West European police help Hungarian colleagues

Tamás Kádár, the festival’s chief organiser, said this was an exciting year for Sziget because the festival had once again come under Hungarian ownership. Its founder, Károly Gerendai, had returned, the management had become co-owners, and a group of investors with whom the organisers had worked for many years had also been brought into the festival’s ownership structure.

He added that the comfort of festival-goers would become an increasingly important consideration at European festivals, and that this included being able to use mobile phones without interruption.

Yettel was providing Sziget with extensive technological and other support in this area, he said, helping the festival deliver an outstanding experience for its guests.

World.title: New, thrilling – but deadly – routes emerge in drought-stricken Hungary
World.content:
Drought-stricken Hungary is opening up a series of intriguing new, but deadly routes even for fit and experienced hikers. Several people have already found themselves in trouble, and the latest incident came perilously close to ending in tragedy.

She almost sank into the mud

A few days ago, it was reported that a 35-year-old woman from Dunaújváros nearly disappeared into the vast expanse of mud at the shrinking Lake Velence after deciding to cross it. An off-duty police officer and a local resident eventually pulled her to safety, after which paramedics took her to hospital for further examination, the Hungarian police wrote.

The incident is a stark illustration of the dangers facing drought-stricken Hungary. As lakes and rivers recede, previously inaccessible areas are opening up, creating what may appear to be exciting new opportunities for walks and excursions. In reality, most of them are extraordinarily hazardous. Had no one nearby heard the woman’s cries for help, she would almost certainly not be alive to recount the experience as a warning to others.

Lake Velence drying out, but the mud can be extremely dangerous. Photo: Facebook/Élhető Velence Egyesület

Record-low water levels are also exposing places that had previously remained hidden, prompting magnet fishers and collectors to set out in search of discoveries. Most recently, a German Second World War motorbike was found on the banks of the Danube in Budapest, alongside various other items of equipment and human remains. Elsewhere, warships, bombs and other objects have emerged from the water – all of which may pose a danger to virtually anyone other than trained specialists.

New, but deadly routes in the Danube riverbed and in Lake Velence

Walking along the exposed banks of the shrinking Danube, or attempting to wade across Lake Velence, may seem tempting. But the receding waters have created dangers that have never previously been encountered. Experts warn that a single wrong step could put someone’s life at risk.

Entering the lakebed at Lake Velence remains prohibited, and the area becomes particularly dangerous beyond 100 metres from the shore. Although the surface may look completely dry, cracked and hard in many places, this is merely a thin crust. Beneath it, the mud may still be wet, soft and sticky.

Gábor Kürti, alias Kükü, the chairman of the Hungarian Bicycle Club, crossed the lake with special equipment he dragged with him after he studied carefully his route from the air. Photo: Facebook/Kürti Gábor Dezső

The lakebed may also contain so-called mud wells, which can be as much as two or three metres deeper than the lake’s average depth, according to Blikk.

Panic can make you even more vulnerable

Several people have already had to be rescued from the mud at Lake Velence this year. A young woman and a man from Budapest both got into difficulty; the latter was freed by water police before receiving medical attention.

One of the greatest dangers posed by the mud is the vacuum it can create around a person’s legs. The harder someone struggles and tries to move their feet, the deeper they may sink. Decomposing organic matter can also release dangerous gases, including methane and hydrogen sulphide, while the lakebed may contain shards of glass, rusty metal objects and fishing hooks.

If you missed: Did the Danube run dry in Budapest and Paks because the Slovaks diverted it?

Rescue operations are far from straightforward. Lifeguards do not approach those in trouble on foot, but use boats, ladders, planks, ropes and other equipment. Panic and unnecessary movement can make the situation even worse.

It may look dry and shallow at first

The Danube’s unusually low water level can be just as deceptive. Wide stretches of riverbank have been exposed at several points, attracting walkers and even cyclists. But the clay banks are being eroded from below by the river’s current, creating apparently solid ledges of earth that may collapse without warning, infostart.hu wrote.

The German WWII motorcycle that emerged from the record-low Danube last week. Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

This is particularly dangerous because someone standing in water only a few centimetres deep could suddenly plunge into several metres of fast-flowing water. The cold can cause cramp, while the current may sweep a person away – or carry them beneath a collapsing section of riverbank.

The danger at both locations lies precisely in the false sense of security created by ground that appears dry or water that seems shallow. Experts therefore warn that exceptionally low water levels do not make a river or lakebed safer. On the contrary, they can expose hidden hazards that remain invisible under normal conditions.

Deadly new routes emerge fromt the Danube. Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

World.title: Shock as young man joins women taken ill en masse at Budapest concert and recounts his ordeal
World.content:
One moment he was partying with his friends; the next, he was walking towards the toilets. After that, his next memory was of lying on a bed with a doctor standing beside him, a number marked on his stomach. This was not the opening scene of a horror film but a real-life ordeal – and it happened the day before yesterday at a Budapest on the Hajógyári Island, the site of the Sziget Festival. No one yet knows exactly what happened: were the young people drugged, or was something else behind the incidents?

Many fell ill at Budapest concert

The concert did not form part of the Sziget Festival, although it was held on the festival’s main stage, where the illnesses occurred.

Sziget organisers issued a statement on Sunday condemning what had happened, but stressed that they had nothing to do with the DJ OTI – Balázs Sebestyén – concert, which was not included in the Sziget Festival programme. The concert was nevertheless held on Sziget’s main stage, and at one of the high points of the party Balázs flew in front of a Sziget logo, leading many people to associate the two events.

Both Sziget and Balázs expressed their regret and stressed the importance of human life. Károly Gerendai, Sziget’s lead organiser, added that he and his colleagues would try to investigate exactly what had happened more thoroughly. He said he knew of 20 cases among the 100 people who had received medical attention, while tens of thousands had attended the event.

Balázs Sebestyén, alias DJ OTI, on the main stage of Sziget Festival. Source: Facebook/DJ OTI

Hours missing from his life

An affected man told Index on Tuesday how he had experienced the events. The man, who is in his thirties, said he had not drunk much alcohol, yet had ended up in a condition for which he still has little explanation: three or four hours had disappeared completely from his memory.

One moment he was partying with his friends; then he set off for the toilets and remembers nothing after that. His next memory was of lying in a room with a doctor standing beside him. He does not know how he got there, nor who helped him reach the medical facility. He assumes that, when he regained consciousness, someone may have explained what had happened to him, but none of that information remained with him.

One of the most shocking details only became clear to the man later. Once he had recovered further, he noticed that a huge number had been written on his stomach in marker pen. His pockets had been emptied, and his phone and identity documents were returned to him in a transparent plastic bag.

Professional care, followed by illness

According to Index, the number written on the skin is an identification method used at mass events. If someone is unconscious or unable to communicate, the number is used to link the patient to their medical records and to the belongings found on them.

Our previous article concerning the issue – Young women collapse one after another at Budapest concert: police investigate as victims recount same story

The man came round in the detoxification unit operating at Sziget. This is the observation area where people who are severely intoxicated or under the influence of psychoactive substances are kept under medical supervision until their condition stabilises. The festival has a fully equipped medical centre, including a triage unit, internal medicine and surgical treatment rooms, a resuscitation unit, an inpatient area and a detoxification unit, supported by an emergency team of around 50 people.

All victims received professional medical care. Photo: depositphotos.com

But the ordeal did not end with the night. The man said he felt extremely unwell throughout Sunday, adding that he had never felt so ill in his life.

Following the incident, the Budapest Police Headquarters launched an investigation on suspicion of drug possession and questioned witnesses. However, no toxicology results have yet been made public to prove that the man or anyone else was given a psychoactive substance without their consent. Many people suspect GHB – commonly known in Hungary as “gina” – but the substance leaves the body quickly, although it can be detected in hair at considerable expense.

World.title: Breaking – New Hungarian President elected: “Hungary’s future cannot be built on revenge” – read his full message below
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament elected András Baka, the former head of the Supreme Court, as President of the Republic on Tuesday. Baka, the candidate of the ruling Tisza Party, was elected head of state with 140 votes in favour and 6 against in a secret ballot. Orbán’s Fidesz and the KDNP did not participate on the vote. Baka will assume office on the eighth day following the announcement of the election result.

Hungarians cannot avoid confronting the past at the beginning of a new era, Baka, the president-elect said in a speech to parliament on Tuesday. In his address after his election, Baka emphasised the need to understand “how the nation reached this point”. The president-elect said Hungary had “wasted a generation’s worth of time, slipping from a model student during the time of the democratic transition to the ranks of lagging nations”.

He said that he had accepted the nomination “because I think that Hungary has arrived at a point in its history when it needs to seriously contemplate the operation of the state, constitutionality and the country as community.” Baka, who was the sole candidate for the post, said the National Assembly’s decision to elect him was “a great honour, recognition and exceptional trust. The candidacy itself was also unexpected, overwhelming and an honour,” he said.

Photo: MTI

Past regime failed to meet basic democratic rule-of-law requirements

Baka said that before 2026, the Hungarian state had failed to meet one of the most fundamental requirements of a democratic rule-of-law system: the genuine separation of powers and a functioning system of checks and balances.

Baka said Hungary had developed a system in which a single party had captured the state and its institutions, culminating in years of governance by decree that largely bypassed parliament. “It is the responsibility of us all to ensure such a system never emerges again in Hungary,” he said.

Expressing national unity means political neutrality, but never neutrality on values

Expressing the unity of the nation first and foremost means political neutrality, but it must never mean neutrality on values, he said. Baka said that a modern, democratic society was inherently diverse, with coexisting worldviews, political convictions, lifestyles and interests. “There may even be deep, sometimes irreconcilable divisions among them,” he said.

Here are some photos from the Parliament:

As president, Baka said, he must represent this diverse community and always acknowledge the legitimacy of differing views, as well as the right of both majority and minority positions to be heard. The president’s role, he said, was not to manufacture consensus where none exists, but to represent the idea that “citizens with differing views are equal members of the same nation.“

A democratic institution’s authority is defined by its ability to remain true to its function, even in situations of conflict, he added. A democratic institution’s authority did not come from operating without conflict, but from its ability to stay true to its mission even amid disputes. He added that he intended to uphold this principle as president.

New President Baka could stand up firmly to PM Magyar – so why is the opposition attacking him so viciously?

Constitution’s stability hinges on broad societal ownership

A constitution’s stability rests on its being regarded as belonging to the broadest sections of society, Baka said. He warned that once again drafting a constitution “solely as the document of a temporary majority” would result in repeating the mistake the consequences of which Hungary was now attempting to rectify.

Drafting a constitution required more than mere parliamentary legislation, he said. “A wide-ranging societal and expert debate, genuine political consensus, and a process that in itself reflects the democratic culture the new constitution will later be tasked with upholding” was also necessary, he said.

World.title: Budapest in deep trouble: more threatening individuals on streets, cheap drugs becoming increasingly widespread
World.content:
The mayors of Budapest’s inner districts have united in warning the government that it must immediately begin filling vacant police posts, saying local authorities can no longer cope with the large numbers of threatening people and groups arriving in the capital from the countryside. They also said that some of these people exchanged empty bottles for cash before using the money to buy cheap, extraordinarily harmful drugs and alcohol. At present, the authorities are virtually powerless to deal with them.

They come from the countryside to make money and buy drugs

Dávid Vitézy, now the Minister for Transport, proposed – when he was still a Budapest council member and the MOHU bottle-return scheme was being introduced – that the Budapest municipality install bottle-collection bins in the inner districts. Not everyone, he argued, would seek out a redemption point where they could receive 50 forints for an empty mineral-water or soft-drink bottle.

The proposal was implemented, and the yellow bins still accept bottles today. However, while the initiative may have led to the collection of bottles, it may also have given a further boost to the presence of threatening individuals and groups on the streets.

The mayors of Ferencváros, Erzsébetváros, Józsefváros and Terézváros, as well as Újlipótváros, have joined the initiative launched by Imre László, the Democratic Coalition mayor of District XI. Among other demands, they are calling for more police officers, broader powers and additional funding to tackle the problem. According to the mayors, at least 3,000 police officers are missing from the streets, and they cannot be replaced with overtime payments or municipal resources, Blikk reports.

Meanwhile, Budapest as a whole is facing an increasingly serious social, mental-health and public-order crisis on its streets. The problem is particularly visible around railway stations and major transport hubs. In District XI, for example, complaints from residents have increased in recent months. The district says the bottle-return scheme is bringing increasing numbers of people to Budapest from the countryside in an attempt to make money by collecting bottles.

More drug users on the streets

The problem, however, is not confined to bottle collecting. District mayors say that more and more drug users are appearing on the streets, including people whose behaviour may be influenced by severe mental-health problems. Some spend the money earned from collecting bottles on alcohol or drugs, further undermining residents’ sense of safety.

The leaders of the inner districts say the emergence of cheap, new types of drugs is particularly alarming because they can trigger serious psychiatric problems among users. Keleti and Nyugati railway stations, Népliget, Blaha Lujza Square and several other busy transport hubs therefore require special attention, but there are not enough police officers to resolve the problems.

The Nyugati railway station in Budapest. Photo: Daily News Hungary

Long-term solutions are impossible through temporary redeployments. In an overstretched system suffering from staff shortages, any worker taken from one location will sooner or later be missed at their previous post. In addition, an effective support system is needed to address the social problems underlying homelessness and addiction.

Gergely Karácsony, the Mayor of Budapest, recently highlighted this point, noting that the problem has implications not only for public safety but also for health and social services. Most people cannot afford to pay the fines imposed on them in any case, and instead “convert” them into detention or community service.

Joint proposals submitted to the Government

The mayors have also drawn up a joint package of proposals. Among other measures, they would introduce a 30 per cent Budapest allowance for police officers serving in the capital to make the postings more attractive, while calling for a continuous police presence at problematic transport hubs.

If you missed: Aggressive ‘zombies’ everywhere: Is a new drug claiming victims in Budapest? Inner-city leaders sound the alarm

The municipalities are also seeking greater influence over the regulation of national tobacco shops and want to expand the scope for holding people accountable on the basis of CCTV footage.

The mayors further reported that municipal wardens and civil-guard patrols funded by district budgets have extremely limited powers. For example, they cannot even check people’s identities, meaning they have no way of knowing whether they have encountered someone who is wanted by the authorities.

Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

The district leaders say that, alongside reinforcing the police, access to night shelters must also be made easier. They believe Budapest’s municipalities are no longer able to tackle the simultaneous problems of homelessness, addiction and public disorder using their own resources, and are therefore calling for immediate state intervention.

World.title: ARVAL ROMANIA: Less ownership, more access: how the new generation of entrepreneurs is changing the demand for corporate mobility
World.content:
News from Companies

Operational leasing intention rises to 49% in Romania, 13 points above the European average. The strongest appetite comes from small and medium-sized companies, with 54%, according to the Arval Mobility Observatory 2026 Barometer.

Arval Romania, part of the BNP Paribas Group and a major player in full-service leasing and mobility solutions for companies, presents an in-depth analysis of one of the most relevant signals captured by the 2026 edition of the Fleet and Mobility Barometer: 49% of companies in Romania intend to introduce or increase the use of operational leasing in the next three years, up from 42% in 2024 and 13 percentage points above the European average of 36%.

SMEs, the engine of operational leasing in Romania



Beyond the aggregate figure, the structure of this increase is relevant. Thus, the intention to operate leasing is more strongly supported by small (54%) and medium-sized (48%) companies than by large ones (37%), a reversal of the classic pattern, in which large corporations led the way, and SMEs followed. For years, operational leasing has been perceived as a tool for large corporate fleets, with dedicated administration departments and sophisticated procurement processes. Data from the 2026 edition show that the center of gravity of demand has shifted: the small and medium-sized business segment has become the engine of the market.



The move is even more remarkable as it takes place in a market where ownership remains the cultural norm, from housing to company assets. Against this background, the fact that Romanian entrepreneurs in the SME segment choose access over ownership when it comes to business mobility indicates a change in mentality with lasting potential, beyond immediate financial calculations.



At the same time, the general market context supports the same direction. The 2026 edition of the Barometer shows a moderate optimism of local companies regarding fleet dynamics: one in four companies expects the fleet to grow in the next three years, and 65% expect it to remain at the current level. In parallel, the electrification of fleets and adaptation to restrictive policies on combustion engines are the main challenges equally mentioned by 41% of respondents. In an environment where companies must simultaneously navigate the technological transition, regulatory uncertainty and cost pressure, formulas that transfer risk and complexity to a specialized partner are becoming increasingly attractive, and operational leasing is, by construction, such a formula.

"We see a change of mentality at the level of decision-makers. The new generation of entrepreneurs and managers in SMEs is made up of people who already operate on the logic of subscription, in personal and business life alike, from streaming services to the software through which they run their companies. The question I ask myself is no longer 'what do I own?', but 'what do I have access to and how much does it cost me monthly?'. Brought into the fleet decision, this reflex fundamentally changes the relationship to the company car: for a small business, operational leasing means access to a new fleet without capital immobilization. The cost becomes a predictable operational expense, and the money remains in the business." explains Roxana Lupescu, General Manager of Arval Romania.

The company car, from the balance sheet to the benefits package



However, the change goes beyond the scope of financing and touches the role that the car plays within the company. The barometer thus highlights a transformation of employee mobility: in 2026, companies are moving from simply expanding the available solutions to repositioning mobility as a central element in human resources and sustainability strategies. Social responsibility factors are invoked by 44% of respondents as motivation for these initiatives, and 42% mention HR aspects, namely attracting talent, improving well-being and supporting hybrid work models. In other words, the company car migrates from the balance sheet to the benefits package and becomes a tool through which the organization attracts and retains people.

"Customer requirements have changed accordingly: flexibility at the time of upgrade, digital settlement, 36 to 48-month contracts. At the same time, for employees, mobility becomes a benefit, and a benefit must be flexible, easy to manage and scalable with the team, exactly what operational leasing offers by its nature." adds Roxana Lupescu.

Less ownership, more access, a trend that is consolidating



Taken together, the data of the 2026 edition outlines a market at the beginning of a substantial transition. The demand for operational leasing is growing and changing its structure, with SMEs as the driving force; employee mobility is part of HR and sustainability strategies; and the company car redefines its role, from an asset to be managed to a service to be used and a benefit to be offered.

"The outlook remains one of growth. With an intention to use 13 points above the European average and with an SME segment that has just entered the maturity phase, the potential of operational leasing on the local market is far from being exhausted. The direction is clear, from ownership to use, and the pace of this transition is given, for the first time in the history of this market, by small and medium-sized companies." concludes Roxana Lupescu.

The Fleet and Mobility Barometer is conducted annually by the Arval Mobility Observatory. For the local market, the 2026 edition is based on over 300 interviews with decision-makers in Romania, part of a global survey carried out in 33 countries, with over 10,000 respondents.

*This is a press release.

World.title: Wizz Air opens base in Romania’s Brașov, launches four additional routes
World.content:
Budget carrier Wizz Air is opening a base at Brașov-Ghimbav International Airport with one Airbus A321neo aircraft and will add four new destinations from the central Romania city starting this winter.

Starting in December, passengers will be able to fly from Brașov to Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden, Chișinău, Barcelona and Madrid.

The Nuremberg route will resume on October 26.

Wizz Air operates flights from Brașov to London, Budapest, Dortmund, Rome, Milan, Naples, Memmingen, Warsaw and Katowice.

The airline began operating in Brașov in August 2023, shortly after the country’s newest airport opened. Since then, it has carried more than 800,000 passengers, it said.

The airline currently operates 231 routes from 14 airports in Romania, connecting passengers to 83 destinations in 26 countries.

“The opening of our tenth base in Romania is a proud moment for Wizz Air, especially after we recently celebrated 20 years of operations in the country. We are delighted to further expand our presence in Brașov by allocating a modern Airbus A321neo aircraft, launching several new routes and bringing the total number of WIZZ connections to 15,” András Radó, Head of Communications at Wizz Air, said.

Wizz Air's Romanian network began with flights from Târgu Mureș before expanding to Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Timișoara, Craiova, Sibiu, Iași, Constanța, Suceava, Satu Mare, Bacău, Brașov and, most recently, Oradea, where operations started in March 2026.

World.title: Romania’s Constitutional Court to review biodiversity strategy law
World.content:
Romania’s Constitutional Court will review on August 12 the law implementing the National Strategy and Action Plan for Biodiversity Conservation 2026-2030, alongside the recently passed Integrity Law, with both measures linked to milestones under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The biodiversity legislation was referred to the Constitutional Court by the Alliance for the Unity of Romanians (AUR) after the Parliament approved the strategy with amendments, including changes proposed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and criticized by environment NGOs.

Environmental organisations have criticised the final version, arguing that parliamentary amendments removed or weakened mechanisms intended to implement Romania’s biodiversity commitments.

The Federation of the Natura 2000 Coalition Romania and the Institute for Public Policies (IPP) said in a joint analysis that several amendments reduced the ambition of the strategy and, in some cases, incorrectly reproduced Romania’s existing commitments as statutory provisions.

Among the changes highlighted by the organisations is the reduction of the target for protected areas from 30% to 25%. The target for areas under strict protection was also reduced from 10% to 5%.

The amendments also changed the mechanism for removing artificial barriers from watercourses. Under the adopted version, such interventions would require a government decision and several additional approvals, according to the organisations.

The biodiversity strategy was initially approved by the government but was subsequently cancelled and transferred to Parliament following pressure from the PSD, amid concerns that the party would otherwise refer the measure to the Constitutional Court.

The Parliament adopted the National Strategy and the National Action Plan for Biodiversity Conservation 2026-2030 at the beginning of August. The legislation is considered an important PNRR milestone, with failure to complete the required reforms potentially putting associated European funding at risk.

The Constitutional Court's review comes amid wider disputes over PNRR-related legislation. The court is also examining the Integrity Law, which has been challenged over provisions concerning asset declarations by life partners and the retroactive termination of mandates held by elected officials.

World.title: Romania’s centrist parties fail to reach consensus on public sector wage law
World.content:
Romania’s centrist parliamentary parties failed to reach an agreement on the draft unitary wage law for public sector employees during talks convened by president Nicușor Dan on August 11, according to sources cited by G4Media.

The deadlock puts at risk EUR 771 million in grants under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), as the legislation is a milestone that must be adopted by August 31.

The talks brought together president Dan and the leaders of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), National Liberal Party (PNL), Save Romania Union (USR) and Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), amid disagreements over the reform of public sector pay.

Formally, a major obstacle is the financial impact of demands made by trade unions, which are supported by the PSD, according to the cited sources. Separately, analysts argue that a more transparent and consistent framework for remuneration across the public sector could reduce the influence of trade unions, political leaders and senior public officials over discretionary bonuses and other supplements that have contributed to the complexity of the current pay structure.

The parties are continuing negotiations in an effort to find a formula that would allow the milestone to be completed by the deadline.

One option under discussion is to submit the draft law to Parliament next week or, at the latest, within two weeks, leaving limited time for its adoption before August 31.

The negotiations follow repeated warnings from the government that the deadline for completing the RRF milestone is approaching. Interim Labour Minister Dragoș Pîslaru said on August 10 that this was the final week in which a political agreement could be reached in time for the reform to be adopted and promulgated by the end of August.

(Photo: Aaron Amat/ Dreamstime)

World.title: Romania’s Hidroelectrica reports 62% y/y profit surge in H1
World.content:
Hidroelectrica (BVB: H2O) recorded in the first six months of 2026 operational and financial results significantly above the results recorded in the same period of 2025, against the backdrop of a normalized hydrological regime, as well as the reconfiguration of the revenue structure as a result of the increased contribution of the supply segment, the company announced on the evening of August 11 in a note to investors.

Net electricity production was 7,070 GWh, up 17% compared to H1 2025. This increase was mainly due to the hydrological conditions in the first quarter of 2026. Net profit surged by 62% y/y to RON 2.57 billion (EUR 490 million). The company's capitalisation is RON 81 bn (EUR 15.5 billion), following a 46% y/y rise in its share price.

Key results from the first semester of 2026 compared to the first semester of 2025:

Operating profit increased by 65%, up to 2,893 million RON

Net electricity production increased by 17%, to 7,070 GWh

Revenues increased by 40%, up to RON 6.05 billion

Operating margin of 48%, up 18%

Net margin of 43%, up 16%

Net profit rose by 62%, to RON 2.57 billion

Adjusted EBITDA, up 51%, to RON 3.32 billion

Earnings per share, 62% higher, at 5.72 RON/share, from 3.53 RON/share

Share price up 46% y/y to RON 180

According to the company's information, Hidroelectrica applied a prudent commercial policy, actively managed price and volume risks, and dynamically calibrated the production-purchase mix, maintaining a solid financial position and results in line with the evolution of energy markets.

"The supply portfolio continued to grow, confirming the repositioning towards a hybrid model, with stronger commercial anchoring and an expanded customer base. Market purchases increased, with market risk being managed through phased contracting and commercial discipline. Operational efficiency, optimising the production-purchase mix, developing RES and storage projects, to reduce structural exposure to hydrological variability and strengthen long-term resilience remain priorities for the group in the coming period," the report reads.

Hidroelectrica is the largest renewable energy producer in Romania, managing a portfolio of 188 hydroelectric power plants with a total capacity of 6.4 GW, as well as the Crucea wind farm, with 108 MW installed.

World.title: Romania seeks EU support to manage electricity shortage and extend coal power use
World.content:
Romania has asked the European Commission and the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) to provide support as the country prepares to shut down Cernavoda's second reactor, while also seeking permission to keep several coal-fired units operating beyond their planned shutdown deadline of August 31.

Secretary of State at the Ministry of Energy Cristian Bușoi said Romania activated the "early warning" mechanism on August 7 and notified the next level, a "crisis situation", on August 10 under Article 14(2) of Regulation 941/2019, according to Agerpres.

Bușoi raised the issue at the European Commission's Electricity Coordination Group meeting on August 11, presenting Romania's electricity situation, the imminent shutdown of Cernavoda Unit 2 and measures adopted by the government to manage the supply risk.

Romania asked the European authorities to assess available generation capacity, balancing reserves, cross-border interconnection capacity and the ability of neighboring electricity systems to provide support if regional conditions deteriorate further.

EU officials indicated that member states would co-ordinate to ensure Romania, Hungary and Slovenia can cover their electricity needs during peak hours. Under the arrangements discussed, Romania could receive up to 4,000 MWh, which is over 50% of the country’s peak consumption.

Separately, Bucharest is seeking an extension of the permitted operation of coal-fired power plants that are scheduled to close under Romania's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

Bușoi said the planned August 31 closure of the Turceni 5 unit, covered by PNRR milestone 119A, would be particularly difficult given the current electricity supply situation. He said Romania was seeking European Commission approval to continue operating four coal-fired units beyond the deadline.

"The closure, on August 31, of the Turceni 5 coal group, part of milestone 119A, is extremely problematic in the current situation," Bușoi said, adding that Romania would continue seeking agreement to operate four units after August.

The available coal-fired capacity at Turceni, Rovinari and the two Craiova units amounts to almost 900 MW of net generation capacity, Bușoi said, describing it as an important reserve as Romania prepares for the loss of Cernavoda's second reactor.

World.title: Ukraine seeks to re-establish grain corridor through Moldova to Romania's Constanţa port
World.content:
Moldova’s Ministry of Infrastructure and Regional Development (MIDR) is in talks with the Ukrainian side regarding the railway transport of grain in transit through the national territory to the port of Constanţa in Romania, announced Moldpres, citing MIDR. The annual freight under discussion stands around 4.5 million tonnes.

According to Reuters, citing sources from both countries, Kyiv has asked Chisinau for a transport tariff reduced by 50% compared to the list prices charged by Moldovan Railways, and the two sides are still discussing terms and volumes.

MIDR assured that any decision will seek economic benefits for both parties, while the shares of the port operators in Romania potentially involved in the transfer have increased.

The institution argued that the Moldovan Railway has an important economic opportunity to attract additional volumes of freight, and the application of temporary tariff reductions for large transport volumes is a practice used internationally.

"Under the conditions of this tariff reduction, at the level currently discussed with the Ukrainian side, the additional volumes that will transit the Republic of Moldova will generate a good profit for the Moldovan Railway," MIDR noted.

In Romania, the shares of port operators Socep and Comvex, listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, increased by up to 12% after information regarding a possible railway corridor for the transport of Ukrainian grains to Constanţa, where the two companies operate.

Socep (SOCP) shares rose 11.8% on Tuesday, August 11, and Comvex (CMVX) shares rose 8.3%, after Reuters wrote that Ukraine was analysing the transport of grain by rail through Moldova to Constanta.

"Investors are probably counting on the handling of larger volumes by the companies present in the port of Constanţa, which already has a history in recent years for the transit of large volumes of Ukrainian cereals," said Antonio Oroian, broker at Goldring, cited by Ziarul Financiar.

Former head of Moldovan Railways Oleg Tofilat estimated that such a corridor could handle 4.5 million tons per year, while Ukrainian estimates indicate about 10% of the country's exports. The Agriculture Ministry in Kyiv has reduced its export forecast for the 2026-2027 season to 38-40 million tons, from 43 million, due to Russian attacks on ports.

For now, there is no publicly announced agreement, and the actual volumes depend on negotiations and the available railway infrastructure.

Comvex handled 5.09 million tons through its grain terminal last year, up from 4.79 million tons in 2024. In its annual report, the company writes that demand for logistics services for Ukrainian goods, which was still present at the beginning of 2024, disappeared in 2025. Comvex has a storage capacity of about 212,000 tons and is working on an expansion of 28,000 tons.

Socep, for its part, reported port traffic of 815,000 tons for the first quarter, 11.2% below the level of the same period last year. The company is building its own grain terminal.

World.title: Romania’s sole nuclear power plant prepares to shut down due to low Danube flow
World.content:
Romania’s Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant has initiated the technical procedures preceding the controlled shutdown of its second nuclear reactor, the so-called Unit 2, due to the very low flow of the Danube. The river water was essential for the cooling of the pumps used by the plant.

The shutdown of Unit 2, scheduled for Thursday, August 13, represents the complete closure of the facility in Cernavodă. The nuclear power plant, operated by Bucharest Exchange-listed company Nuclearelectrica (BVB: SNN), shut down Unit 1 in late July for the same reason, as drought persists in the Danube basin.

Sorin Rândașu, deputy general manager of Romanian Waters, said that the critical threshold of -230 cm water level had been reached at Cernavodă. “In the coming period, the plant will be shut down; it is inevitable. It will be shut down for about two weeks, as an estimate. In the next five days there will be no rain at all in the Danube basin, according to the data we have,” Rândașu told Digi24.

Previously, the state secretary in the Ministry of Energy, Cristian Bușoi, also stated that Unit 2 at Cernavodă will not be able to remain in operation throughout August.

To compensate for the loss of energy, the Rovinari 4 energy unit of the Oltenia Energy Complex will be restarted and integrated into the national power grid.

However, without nuclear energy, which ensured roughly 20% of Romania’s consumption, the country will have to reduce consumption and increase expensive energy imports, especially in the evening. The phased limitation of consumption for certain large industrial consumers, in the 7 PM and 11 PM interval, is the last measure in the order of priority and could be applied, according to the authorities. Household consumers are not targeted by the consumption limitation mechanism, the same source added.

However, Romania’s Energy Ministry again appealed to the population, public institutions and economic operators to limit their energy consumption between 7 PM and 11 PM. A similar call had been issued last week and echoed by prime minister Ilie Bolojan.

Separately, through a stock exchange announcement issued on Tuesday, August 11, Nuclearelectrica drew attention to a series of Notices of the Existence of a Force Majeure Event by the Constanța Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Navigation and Agriculture (CCINA), applicable in the case of electricity supply contracts. This means that the company may not be able to fulfill contractual obligations.

“Nuclearelectrica will send to its contractual partners an estimate regarding the duration of the period during which it will not be able to fulfil its obligations. Nuclearelectrica will make all commercially reasonable efforts to minimise the effects of the Force Majeure Event,” the company stated.

World.title: Letter from London: From Burnham’s Bounce to Ghost Ships in the Danube
World.content:
Greetings from London, where we are all enjoying, or at least experiencing, the “Burnham Bounce”.

No, it’s not an expensive hairstyle, a dance move, isometric exercise, or body modification. It’s a lift in the opinion polls for the ruling Labour Party.

It’s attributed to the easy, breezy style of its new leader, our new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, whose relatively jargon-free form of communications has lifted his party out of its former doldrums to the stratospheric-sounding level of 28 per cent support in the polls.

There was a time when the two ‘big beasts’ of the British party system, the Labour and Conservative parties, both cruised along at around 40 per cent in the polls. That left the small fry – mainly Liberals and various nationalists – to fight over the remaining 20 per cent.

But times have changed. These days, 28 per cent is a stellar achievement for one of the two major parties.

World.title: US Right-Wing Heritage Foundation Promotes Changes to Bosnia’s Peace Agreement
World.content:
A report published in February by Germany’s Der Spiegel, Sweden’s Aftonbladet and the environmental campaign group BLOOM detailed what BLOOM described as “harmful links between the European conservative right and Trumpist circles”, indicating that some European parliamentarians have come under American influence as Washington attempts to shift the political balance in Brussels rightwards.

BLOOM researcher Alessandro Mazzotti told BIRN that the Heritage Foundation’s isn’t just seeking political connections on the far right of the European parliament, but also within European People’s Party, EPP, which brings together centre-right parties and is the largest political group in the EU.

The report also highlights a meeting between Manfred Weber, president of the EPP, Jorgen Warborn, a member of the Swedish Parliament, and representatives of the Heritage Foundation.

“The Heritage Foundation acts as a kind of intermediary in this shift of the EPP toward a more radically right-wing position,” said Mazzotti.

An important figure connecting people within this lobbying environment, Mazzotti claimed, is Croatian MEP Zeljana Zovko of the centre-right Croatian Democratic Union party, which is part of the EPP. He claimed that Zovko has opened many doors for the Heritage Foundation.

Zovko provided support for the Heritage Foundation’s TradFest in Zagreb. “Over the past three or four years she has been one of the leading representatives in the European Parliament for the European People’s Party. Essentially the first point of contact between the EPP and Heritage. She was really the person who started this cooperation, this dialogue,” said Mazzotti.

Zovko has publicly met with Heritage representatives on multiple occasions, including Primorac.

According to Mazzotti, Zovko is the first person to have created the link between the Heritage Foundation and the EPP – a link that today influences cooperation between Brussels and the Trump administration.

Zovko told BIRN that critical sentiment towards her is partly caused by her role in the EU’s trade agreement with the US, as well as her role as the EPP’s chief negotiator in Brussels’ talks with Washington.

“I am the EPP negotiator, that is why I am also in the area of defence and trade and that is why all the attacks are there. I am the contact person for Congress and all the [American] foundations. I am the key person in the EPP for relations with everyone in the US Congress and I talk to all the foundations,” she said.

“As the vice-president of the EPP group in charge of EPP diplomacy, my duty includes maintaining contacts with all the relevant interlocutors. I open the doors and that is my nature – you have to communicate with everyone, not only with Heritage and America First, but also with the left foundations,” she added.

In her view, a revision of the Dayton Agreement is not currently a realistic option.

“I advocate for full implementation, respect for the Dayton Agreement and the spirit of the Dayton Agreement. It is not being respected; if it were, Croats would have their own member of the presidency and they would have a fair electoral law,” she said.

Critics have alleged that the election victory of the current Croat member of the tripartite Bosnian presidency, Zeljko Komsic, relied on more Bosniak voters rather than Croats, and hence does not represent the will of the Croat people in the country.

However, as Zovko pointed out: “For a revision [of Dayton], you need to have the other two peoples [Serbs and Bosniaks] on your side. The Serbs would not agree to that, and the Bosniaks in this set-up would not agree to a more profound revision either.”

World.title: Kosovo Pays the Price as Serbia Stalls Cross-Border Electricity Transmissions
World.content:
Amid an ongoing energy crisis and mounting financial costs, Kosovo has renewed its call on the European Union and the Energy Community for South East Europe to pressure Serbia to make cross-border transmission capacity available, after Belgrade again failed to meet its commitment to do so.

The Energy Community, a Vienna-based international organisation that oversees compliance and dispute resolution in the energy sector across the Western Balkans and the Black Sea region, set a July 1 deadline for Serbia to provide Kosovo with cross-border transmission capacities.

The ultimatum, which stemmed from a Ministerial Council decision, reminded Belgrade of its need to “ensure compliance with Energy Community law”.

World.title: Montenegro Police Raid Nets 50 Foreigners, ‘Hundreds’ of Digital Devices, and Cash
World.content:
Montenegrin police said on Tuesday they were checking on more than 50 foreign nationals, most of them Ukrainian citizens, who they found when raiding a large house in the Mareza area of Podgorica.

Police also said they seized hundreds of digital devices, “sophisticated equipment” and a large amount of cash.

“Police officers, based on previously undertaken proactive activities, located and identified the facility – a large house in Mareza, Podgorica – after which they entered the building in accordance with the law,” a Police Directorate statement said.

According to police, they found more than 50 foreign nationals inside the house and carried out a search of the premises, documenting equipment and other material relevant to the investigation.

“During the activities, several hundred digital devices and other elements of sophisticated equipment were found, and their quantity and scale were such that, for adequate relocation, they had to be transported by a cargo motor vehicle,” police said.

Police said a large amount of cash was also found and that its origin and possible connection to the activities under investigation would be checked.

The authorities said they were examining the legal basis on which the foreigners are staying and working in Montenegro, their activities and movements, the purpose and manner of use of the seized equipment and devices, and any possible links to illegal activities.

“Given the complexity of the case, the director of the Police Directorate has formed an Operational Team composed of several groups of police officers specialised in cyber security and high-tech crime, financial investigations and money laundering, international operational cooperation, as well as foreigner and migration affairs, with the strong support of the National Security Agency,” the statement said.

Police added that they were taking action in coordination with the State Prosecutor’s Office to establish all the facts and could not comment further at this stage..

“Having in mind the interest of the proceedings and the complexity of the criminal investigation, the Police Directorate is not in a position at this moment to provide more details, so as not to jeopardise the further course of the preliminary investigation,” the statement said.

World.title: Serbian Firefighters Douse Wildfire in Deliblato Sands After Seven-Day Blaze
World.content:
A fire blazing in Serbia’s Deliblato Sands for seven days has finally been brought under control, Milos Milenkovic, Assistant Head of Serbia’s Fire and Rescue Units Directorate told the state broadcaster RTS on Tuesday.

The Deliblato Sands, Deliblatska Pescara in Serbian, is the largest continental sandy terrain in Europe, covering around 350 square km in southeast Vojvodina, Serbia’s northern province – a nature reserve nicknamed Europe’s Sahara.

The wildfire broke out amid an intense heatwave and prolonged drought affecting Serbia and much of the Balkans, with temperatures reaching around 40 degrees Celsius. The hot and dry conditions, coupled with strong winds, have significantly increased the risk of wildfires and complicated firefighting efforts.

World.title: Why Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky Has a Kosovo Blind Spot
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s first official visit to Serbia at the weekend prompted understandable debate and reaction about Kyiv’s relations with Belgrade.

Serbia nominally supports Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and Serbian-origin ammunition has reached Ukrainian forces through third countries. Yet Belgrade has not joined the European Union’s sanctions regime against Russia and continues to maintain close political and economic ties with Moscow. Serbia's domestic political and public environment also remains overwhelmingly receptive to Russia-sympathetic narratives.

Ukraine has practical reasons to engage with Serbia. But should this come at the cost of Kyiv politically distancing itself from Kosovo, its continued policy of not recognising Kosovo’s independence, and staying silent about Serbia’s efforts to undermine Kosovo’s security and international agency?

Kosovo has supported Ukraine consistently since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. It adopted sanctions against Russia, aligned itself with the Western response to Russian aggression, including recognising Ukraine’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to self-defence.

World.title: Turkish Parliament Overwhelmingly Approves PKK Disarmament Law
World.content:
Turkey’s parliament approved the much-heralded framework law that provides a legal basis for disarming the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party, PKK, on Monday regulating the judicial procedures for people linked to it and marking the most comprehensive legislative step yet to end the four-decade-long conflict.

“Brotherhood will grow even stronger; therefore, once the terrorist organisation seeking to come between us is eliminated, Turkey will become even stronger,” Abdulhamit Gul, Parliamentary Deputy Group Leader of the ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, told reporters after the vote.

The “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration” passed easily, with 467 votes in favour. 88 MPs against and six abstentions.

Support came from the ruling AKP, its nationalist ally, the Nationalist Movement Party, MHP, the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the pro-Kurdish and Islamist HUDA PAR, some MPs from the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, some members of the New Path parliamentary group and several independents.

The new law lays out the legal framework for the post-disarmament process, including temporary judicial provisions for eligible people convicted of, or investigated over, PKK-related offences.

It includes mechanisms such as supervised release, sentence postponement and judicial supervision under specified conditions following the organisation’s dissolution and disarmament.

The law stipulates that its provisions take effect only after Turkey’s National Security Council, MGK, has determined that the PKK and its affiliated structures have fully disbanded and surrendered all weapons.

The opposition right wing Good Party rejected the bill entirely. “[The law] is for paving the way for [President Recep Tayyip] Erdogan to remain president for life.” Musavat Dervisoglu, its leader, said in parliament.

The new main opposition New Party did not adopt a unified decision. Party leader Ozgur Ozel allowed his MPs a free vote, and 54 of its 91 MPs voted against the law.

“I am not against peace. I want terrorism to end, the guns to fall silent, and the Kurdish issue to be resolved through democratic and peaceful means,” New Party MP Mahmut Tanal said in a written statement before the vote. However, he said he would vote “no” because he did not trust the government, stressing its harsh crackdown on the opposition and other critics.

Ozel announced that the senior party leadership had voted in favour.

The legislation follows political developments that began earlier. In February 2025, jailed PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to lay down its arms. His appeal followed an unexpected peace initiative by Devlet Bahceli, leader of the MHP, a key ally of Erdogan’s AKP.

The initiative led to the establishment of a parliamentary commission and regular visits to Ocalan by a delegation from the pro-Kurdish DEM Party. The new framework law is regarded as the closest Turkey has come to establishing a comprehensive legal basis for ending the decades-long conflict.

More than 40,000 people have been killed since fighting between the PKK and Turkish security forces began after Ocalan founded the group in 1984.

World.title: Why Emigrants Prefer Democracies and Leave Illiberal States Behind
World.content:
Several years ago, in Gorazde in eastern Bosnia, I had a discussion with a young man who had a job and in general was in a good position in his hometown. He told me he had recently visited a cousin in Sweden, and that, while he had a decent life, he suspected he might emigrate there anyway, to start over.

He noted that it felt good to be able to walk down the street in that country, or be able to turn on the TV, and not see the same politicians he was not able to escape when in Bosnia.

This anecdote would fit well in Justin Gest’s new book, Democratic Drain: Global Migration and the Struggle for Democracy, which explores the motivations for, and impact of, the outflow of people from less democratic societies to more democratic – and more successful – destinations.

World.title: Accommodation Owners Claim Croatian Local Host Campaign Started Late
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – The Croatian Tourist Board is satisfied, but accommodation owners are claiming that the Croatian Local Host campaign started too late.

“We’re extremely satisfied with the results of the first Local Host label campaign,” stated Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ). Croatia very successfully recorded 12.4 million arrivals from the beginning of the year to the end of July.

Ana Roksandic/Poslovni reports that eight million impressions and almost 500 completed reservations are the results of the first joint promotional campaign by the Croatian National Tourist Board and the Booking.com platform dedicated to Croatian family accommodation and hosts gathered under the Croatian Your Host/Local Host label.

The campaign “Experience real Croatia” ran during the months of June and July on the markets of Germany, Austria, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary. At its heart were the actual local hosts themselves and the authentic experiences they offer their guests, the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) announced.

room for improvement

So far, over 3,570 properties with over 21,170 beds have joined the Croatian Local Host project. The largest number of properties with the Local Host label are located in Istria, on the Kvarner and in Split-Dalmatia County. Looking by destination, the highest numbers are in Crikvenica, Dubrovnik, Pula, Rovinj and Medulin.

“All of our activities are aimed at protecting genuine family accommodation that has been building Croatian tourism for generations and giving special value to our tourism offer. These hosts are precisely the foundation of Croatian tourism, which is why their protection will continue to be our focus,” revealed Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport, adding: “For the first time, we ‘ve also carried out a national promotional campaign dedicated exclusively to family accommodation, and the first results are already visible through 6 percent better occupancy, which confirms that the market recognises the value of authentic hospitality.”

the coast, of course, dominates the campaign

The largest number of properties with the Local Host label are situated in Istria, on the Kvarner and in Split-Dalmatia County.

As HTZ stated on its official website, the “Your Host” (Local Host) label enables hosts to stand out among numerous private accommodation providers and reach guests looking for an authentic and hospitable experience. Label holders can also use the official Local Host visual identity, and their offer can be included in HTZ promotional activities on foreign markets and digital channels. The label also provides them with guidelines for further raising the quality and sustainability of their business. However, among family accommodation providers there are also questions about the criteria for obtaining the label and its real impact.

“In fact, this label tries to make a distinction between such hosts and landlords where the guest often has no contact with the host at all. They arrive, get a code for the key, enter the apartment and leave, and you practically don’t even know who stayed in your accommodation. When you have the Local Host label, you should be present in the place where the property is located. Not necessarily at the address itself, but you should live, or have your residence, in that town or place. If, for example, you rent out a holiday home in Šibenik-Knin County and live in Split, you will not be able to get that label, regardless of the fact that you are available to the guest in that holiday home.

The reason is that your address of residence is not in the municipality or city where the property is located. Obviously there is still a little room for fine-tuning there, but there are people who already have that label and who work exactly like that – they are truly present and available to their guests,” said Ante Glavaš, vice-president of the Croatian Association of Family Accommodation (HUOS), adding: “However, some people in residential buildings have also received these labels. On what principle that happened is not clear to us.”

has this label led to higher occupancy rates?

HTZ says the label leads to higher occupancy: “In addition to an initially higher occupancy rate, properties that are part of the Local Host programme in 2025 recorded further positive progression: their occupancy grew by 5.74 percent compared to the previous year, while the occupancy of properties that are not part of the programme grew by only 0.6 percent. In the first five months of 2026 the occupancy of properties that are part of the Local Host programme, both in absolute terms and in terms of growth rate, remains higher compared to properties that are not in the programme relative to the same period of the previous year.”

However, one label holder we spoke to said the campaign did not have a particularly promotional effect on her property because it was carried out during June and July. Olinka Gjigaš, director of the Tourist Board of the City of Križevci and holder of the “Your Host” label in the Municipality of Kalnik, stressed that she is speaking from personal experience about the campaign’s impact: “I can’t really say there were any changes because the campaign started quite late. At the time when the promotion was being filmed, I already had 90 percent of the dates booked. I saw that the minister spoke about six percent growth, which surprised me – I wonder how that was even calculated.”

HTZ, however, rates the campaign results significantly more positively. “We’re extremely satisfied with the results of the first Local Host label campaign on the Booking.com platform, as well as with the overall effect of the promotional activities aimed at this label so far,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of HTZ, adding that the Local Host project is continuously gathering an ever larger number of hosts. HTZ will continue promotional activities in the second half of the year, when a new wave of the campaign on the domestic market will follow from mid-August to the end of October.

5.74 percen is how much the occupancy of Croatian Local Host properties grew compared to last year, which arguably isn’t much.

istria takes the lead

In a broader context, the Local Host results come at a time when Croatian tourism has been constantly recording a positive continuation of the season. According to data from the eVisitor and eCrew systems, from the beginning of the year to the end of July Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays, which is one percent more than in the same period last year. On the Adriatic 56.1 million overnight stays were recorded, or 0.5 percent more, while on the continent, including Zagreb, more than three million overnight stays were recorded, with growth of one percent.

In July alone, 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays were recorded. Compared to July last year, the number of arrivals increased by 2.5 percent and the number of overnight stays by one percent. The most guests came from Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary.

Istria retained its leading position among the counties with 16.7 million overnight stays in the first seven months, followed by Split-Dalmatia County with 11.1 million and Kvarner with 9.7 million overnight stays. Among destinations, Dubrovnik, Rovinj, Poreč, Split and Umag lead.

World.title: June Sees Drop in Overnight Stays in Croatian Commercial Accommodation
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – June saw a drop in overnight stays in Croatian commercial accommodation recorded, with Istria County outperforming the rest of the country.

A mixed picture could be garnered when looking at overnight stays realised in Croatian commercial accommodation facilities in June this year. Jutarnji reports that a total of 3.0 million tourist arrivals and 13.5 million overnight stays were recorded. Compared to June 2025, tourist arrivals were down by 6.6% and overnight stays by 6.1%, according to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS).

the germans (of course) lead the way

Of the total overnight stays realised, domestic tourists accounted for 8.9% and foreign tourists for 91.1%. Domestic tourists recorded 387 thousand arrivals and 1.2 million overnight stays, which is 11.8% more arrivals and 11.7% more overnight stays than back in June 2025. Foreign tourists recorded 2.6 million arrivals and 12.3 million overnight stays, which is 8.9% fewer arrivals and 7.5% fewer overnight stays than back in June 2025.

The highest number of overnight stays realised by foreign tourists in June 2026 was achieved by tourists from Germany, totalling 2.7 million overnight stays, or 22.1% of all foreign overnight stays. Compared to June 2025, their overnight stays were down by 28.1%. On average, they recorded 7.7 overnight stays per arrival.

After German tourists, the largest shares of foreign overnight stays were held by tourists from Austria (10.3%), Slovenia (9.9%), Poland (8.8%), the Czech Republic (6.6%), the United Kingdom (5.3%) and Italy (3.8%). Compared to June 2025, increases in overnight stays were recorded by tourists from Italy (5.0%), Slovenia (3.9%), Poland (3.2%), the Czech Republic (2.4%) and the United Kingdom (1.2%), while tourists from Austria had 6.0% fewer overnight stays.

istria county outperformed the rest of the country in june this year

In June 2026, Istria County once again recorded the highest number of overnight stays in the country, totalling 4.3 million, or 31.9% of all overnight stays in Croatia. Despite being the county with the most tourist overnight stays, overnight stays in Istria County fell by 10.0% compared to June 2025. Domestic tourists in Istria County recorded 219 thousand overnight stays (15.9% more than in June 2025), while foreign tourists recorded 4.1 million overnight stays (down 11.1% from the previous year’s June).

After Istria County came Split-Dalmatia County with 2.7 million overnight stays (20.0% of the Croatian total) and Primorje-Gorski Kotar County with 2.2 million (16.4%). Compared to June 2025, overnight stays were down 7.5% in Primorje-Gorski Kotar County and 1.7% in Split-Dalmatia County.

In June 2026, the highest number of overnight stays was recorded by tourists in two age groups: those under 14 years of age and those between 55 and 64 years of age. Each of these groups recorded 2.2 million overnight stays, accounting for 16.2% of the total.

World.title: More and More Filipinos Are Working in Croatia
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – More and more Filipinos are being registered as living and working in Croatia, with the vast majority employed in the tourism and trade sectors.

As Jadranka Dozan/Poslovni reports, over the first seven months of this year, a total of 106,400 permits were issued to citizens of third countries (countries outside of the EEA), of which almost two-thirds were for work in tourism and construction.

The number of issued work permits is reportedly falling, but Interior Ministry data doesn’t show the real number of workers from abroad. The latest data from the Ministry of the Interior on permits issued to foreign workers from so-called third countries only confirmed the continuation of the year-on-year decline in their overall number. This is partly a consequence of the fact that since March last year the maximum duration of permits has been extended from one to three years.

this “decline” isn’t straightforward

How much of this alleged decline is explained by that change in legal rules, and how much is contributed by generally tightened rules or some other reasons (such as meeting part of the need for workers through increased work engagement of domestic pensioners or, for example, returnees to Croatia), the Interior Ministry statistics don’t reveal.

In the first seven months of 2026, a total of 106,400 residence and work permits were issued to citizens of “third countries”, which is 7.5 percent less than last year. Looking only at July, almost 23 percent fewer were issued than last year.

seasonal employment

So far in 2026, the share of permits for seasonal jobs increased significantly, they’re actually up by 40 percent compared to last year – while those for new employment are down 31 percent, and permit extensions are up around 10 percent. Looking only at the month of July, Interior Ministry data reveals that a total of 12,282 positive decisions were issued for imported labour (compared to 15,905 in the same month last year). Almost every fourth of these, or more than 3,000 permits, was given for seasonal work, while just over 9,000 relate to new employment (just under 4,500) and permit extensions (just under 4,800).

40 percent is how much the number of permits for seasonal jobs has risen this year compared to last year, and it’s far from insignificant. Looking at the situation by activity, almost two-thirds of permits go to the two sectors where the import of workers is normally the most massive, tourism and hospitality, as well as construction. This applies both to those issued last month and to the total number issued since the beginning of the year. However, in construction there are 17 percent fewer this year than in the first seven months of last year, while in tourism and hospitality activities there are 5.4 percent more.

Of the other three most represented sectors when it comes to importing workers, an increase in the number of issued permits in 2026 is recorded only in trade. This also contributes to changes in the structure of issued permits in terms of the origin of workers. By far the largest growth is recorded for those issued to Filipinos – almost 50 percent higher than last year. Filipino workers, in addition to the tourism sector, are most often engaged by employers from the trade sector.

misleading statistics

The Interior Ministry’s records of work permits, however, fail to reveal many things and are certainly not the best indicator of the real situation regarding how many workers from third countries there are in Croatia. Experts on migration and demography have been pointing out the problem of recording foreign workers in general for a long time.

On the occasion of the recent publication of data by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics on migration for 2025, one of the more active among them, Tado Jurić, once again warned about the methodological challenges in this area. From the official data of the Interior Ministry and the CBS (according to which 56,700 immigrated foreign citizens were recorded last year), no one can say with certainty how many of them are actually in Croatia because these are records of different phenomena, he says.

For that reason, the number of insured persons in the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO) is usually considered a somewhat more authoritative indicator. In its records in the middle of this year there were a little under 151,000 insured persons who are citizens of third countries (more precisely, with travel documents of those countries), which is about 29,000 more than at the end of last year. Although these are insured persons (which does not automatically mean employees), this is still roughly the indicator closest to reality, and it roughly implies that every 12th person who works and/or pays contributions in Croatia is a foreigner.

“practically half of croatia’s foreign workforce comes from africa and asia”

Given that practically half of the foreign workforce in Croatia today comes from Asia and Africa, migration experts have long emphasised that this requires active management of the processes, both in the context of integration and policies aimed at stronger activation of one’s own potentials. Due to low labour productivity in the public sector, it is often pointed out that there are certain employment reserves there for the entrepreneurial sector, but reforms of that kind do not come easily.

World.title: Almost All Istrian Beaches Have Excellent Quality Seawater
World.content:
August the 12th, 2026 – Almost all Istrian beaches have excellent quality seawater according to the latest measurements, with only four lagging behind.

The sea at Istrian beaches continues to be of exceptionally high quality. In the sixth examination of this year, conducted from the 28th of July to the 6th of August, as many as 98.2 percent of the seawater samples received an excellent rating. Index reports that the sea was sampled at a total of 222 measuring points on beaches from Savudrija to Brestova.

During the process of seawater sampling, the sea temperature ranged between 24 and 29 degrees, while the air temperature was from 24 to 33 degrees.

only four locations were less than exceptional

Excellent swimming seawater quality was recorded at 218 measuring points. Good quality was also recorded at one location, in Ližnjan at Matićev Pisk below the hotel. At three locations, the sea received a satisfactory rating only. These are AC Kažela – FKK in Medulin, Tarska vala in the Tar-Vabriga area, and the location near Hotel Molindrio in Poreč.

bacteria measuring

When examining the seawater, the quantities of intestinal enterococci and the bacterium Escherichia coli are determined as indicators of microbiological pollution. During the sampling process, meteorological conditions, sea temperature and salinity, as well as any visible pollution, are also recorded.

Based on the results of individual samples, the sea is classified as excellent, good or satisfactory. The results of all individual examinations are available via the online application of the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition.
