World.title: Are we on the verge of World War III?
World.content:
We seem to have avoided the Thucydides Trap. The inevitable conflict triggered by the insecurity in the world’s leading power created by the rise of a challenger has not yet materialized. Don’t get too comfortable, however, now, the talk is of World War III.

Last week, Politico’s National Security Daily warned that “connections between many of the world’s conflicts are multiplying” and “officials, analysts and investors are increasingly asking whether humanity is on the verge of World War III.”

My instinct upon reading that was to skip to the next item in that daily mailer. Conflicts are spreading and superpower confrontation is a possibility, but world war? Come on! Still, warning signs are flashing and it’s worth asking how close we are to a global conflict, and what it means to be slouching and sliding toward a wider, perhaps world, war.

World.title: Mexican man arrested over attempt to smuggle some 200 lizards into Japan
World.content:
Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department said Wednesday it arrested a 23-year-old man after he tried to smuggle some 200 lizards into Japan by hiding them inside socks in a suitcase.

Daniel Isaac Velasco Baltazar, who is of Mexican nationality and whose place of residence and occupation are unknown, has admitted to the allegations of attempted import without permission, police said.

Baltazar is alleged to have attempted to bring in the lizards, including nine Mexican alligator lizards, from South Korea without declaring them at customs on Saturday.

International commercial trade of Mexican alligator lizards is strictly controlled under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora.

Tokyo police said they received an anonymous tip in late July saying Baltazar was trying to smuggle lizards in time for a reptiles exhibition and sales event.

The Tokyo Customs officers who had been on alert at Haneda Airport inspected his suitcase and found some 200 lizards squeezed into 22 pairs of socks. One of them was dead.

The suspect reportedly told investigators that he had purchased them in Mexico at roughly ¥560 ($3.50) to ¥750 each.

Mexican alligator lizards that inhabit alpine regions in Mexico are scarce in Japan and are said to be traded at around ¥100,000 each.

The lizards found in the suitcase appeared to include other species as well, and authorities are investigating the details.

Translated by The Japan Times

World.title: Nvidia’s show of financial force soothes credit markets
World.content:
Six of the biggest names in finance are helping Nvidia ease some of the investor anxiety that’s been building for weeks over its swelling commitments to backstop the artificial intelligence boom.

The early signs came after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced Monday that the coalition of major investment firms including BlackRock and Goldman Sachs Group were lining up more than $500 billion to help fund the AI build-out. The group will independently judge individual deals and their own participation level, while Nvidia’s contribution will be relatively limited, and only factor into some deals.

The idea is that outside money, sophisticated eyes on deals and Wall Street’s stamp of approval should help alleviate worries that Nvidia was inflating an AI asset bubble with circular financing. In less than three weeks, a gauge of the chipmaker’s credit risk had nearly doubled on concern that while loans to customers would bring more sales, they risked causing pain later if those customers fail.

World.title: Intervention and higher rates might not be enough to stop yen from weakening
World.content:
The coordinated intervention by Japan and the United States to support the yen has bumped up hard against reality, the $70 billion or so committed to strengthening the currency all but ineffective as fiscal questions continue to hang over the market.

“It’s still just intervention,” said Tsuyoshi Ueno, executive research fellow at NLI Research Institute. “It doesn’t really change economic fundamentals.

“The market knows that, which is why the yen is now sliding back again after the initial gain.”

World.title: Parkour helps Singapore’s elderly boost agility, strength
World.content:
Parkour may conjure images of boisterous teenagers swinging between buildings ⁠in urban settings, but a coach in Singapore is using the techniques to teach better balance to the elderly, drawing millions of social media views.

How to keep an aging population of 6.1 million healthy amid rising ​life expectancy is a key challenge for the city ‌state, which joined ‌the ranks of the “super-aged” in 2025, when ​more than a fifth of its people were aged 65 or more.

After three years of parkour, Betty Boon said she could ⁠haul her own luggage up steep stairs in Japanese train stations, freeing her from ⁠reliance on her husband or son.

“That was wonderful, I just discovered that I could do that,” said ​the 69-year-old retiree, who felt ⁠the classes were also a good way to keep in touch with friends while boosting ⁠her strength, flexibility and ​heart health.

Interest in the classes, called Movement ​Singapore, has exploded recently, said coach Tan Shie Boon, who ​founded ‌them in November 2017.

He was prompted to do so after a 64-year-old woman expressed interest in taking up the sport to resolve balance issues, and managed to ditch her support trolley ‌to walk unaided after just two months of practice.

“I think some of my students (have) grown through the years in terms of strength and so they are able to showcase abilities that are not normal for, ​say, ​a 60-year-old or 70-year-old,” added Tan, 33.

Parkour is an ​intense discipline that teaches individuals how to fall and avoid debilitating ⁠injuries that could cause the elderly to lose confidence in their own mobility, he said.

The contrast between a sport widely seen as very risky and the age of participants might ​have piqued the public’s curiosity, Tan said, after Movement Singapore’s Instagram page went viral.

“Just keep proving to yourself that you can do more than you think you could,” he added.

World.title: JAL plane crash victims mourned 41 years after accident
World.content:
Bereaved family members and others mourned on Wednesday the victims of the 1985 crash of a Japan Airlines jumbo jet on a mountain in Gunma Prefecture.

They went on a memorial hike to the Osutaka Ridge in the village of Ueno — the site of the crash 41 years ago that claimed 520 lives.

The hikers prayed for the deceased in front of memorial markers scattered along the trail.

World.title: Ikarigata closer to emulating older brother Fujinokawa than many think
World.content:
Newer fans, who have only discovered Japan’s national sport in the past few years, could be forgiven for thinking that rapid progress to the top of the banzuke is the norm for sumo’s biggest names.

Given how quickly men such as Onosato and Aonishiki went from promising youngsters to superstars, that would be a reasonable assumption.

With numerous other marquee wrestlers in recent years having success at the collegiate and amateur levels, it might also appear as if future yokozuna and ōzeki can easily be identified while they are still teenagers or even younger.

World.title: Myanmar ramps up civilian attacks with airborne weapons, U.N. says
World.content:
Myanmar’s military is increasingly using drones, motorized paragliders and other low-cost aircraft to attack civilians, United Nations investigators said, even as the country’s rulers seek to project stability and gain legitimacy after a military-run election.

The report by the U.N.-established Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar released Tuesday said attacks continued to rise from July last year, with a notable escalation ahead of elections held in December and January. The vote helped elevate then-junta chief Min Aung Hlaing to the presidency in April after his military seized power in a 2021 coup.

The military increasingly relies on motorized paragliders, gyrocopters and drones for low-altitude strikes using unguided explosives, including mortar shells, according to the report. In several incidents in Sagaing region, paraglider pilots cut their engines as they approached targets and glided silently, giving civilians less warning and time to seek shelter.

Investigators also said casualties were exacerbated by so-called “double-tap” aerial attacks, in which the military strikes a target and then attacks again shortly afterward, apparently targeting first responders, people helping the wounded and those trying to flee.

The mechanism said its investigations showed the frequency and intensity of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by Myanmar’s military and various armed groups continued to escalate over the past year. It also collected “extensive evidence” of arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence in military-run facilities, including cases linked to a 2025 law criminalizing criticism of the elections.

Myanmar’s military spokesman, Brig. Gen. San Nyo Win, did not immediately respond to a request to comment on the report.

The findings undercut efforts by the military-backed government to portray the election as a return to civilian rule after the coup. The military’s proxy party dominated the vote, with major opponents excluded and former civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in detention. Western governments largely rejected the process as neither free nor fair.

Min Aung Hlaing has stepped up diplomatic outreach since becoming president, visiting China, India, Laos and Thailand. While he has pledged to restore normal ties with members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, he’s also dismissed the bloc’s stalled peace plan for Myanmar and accused some members of “unconstructive discrimination.”

World.title: How Hong Kong can unlock the real value of its Asean trade boom
World.content:
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has a role to play in Hong Kong’s plans for its economy. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu signalled as much when he touched on the city’s first five-year plan in his August 7 meeting with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn.

For businesses, however, the central question is not whether Hong Kong-Asean economic ties will continue to grow. They will. The harder question is who will capture the value that growth creates.

Asean has been Hong Kong’s second-largest trading partner since 2010. In 2025, merchandise trade reached HK$1.67 trillion (US$212.8 billion), accounting for 15.3 per cent of the city’s global goods trade, while Hong Kong’s direct investment stock in Asean exceeded HK$670 billion at the end of 2024.

These figures describe a mature economic relationship. They also conceal an uncomfortable truth: enormous trade volumes do not necessarily generate a large pool of profit.

Goods can be re-exported through Hong Kong while most of the value remains elsewhere. Re-exports generate legitimate business for ports, freight forwarders, insurers and banks. Yet if a shipment changes hands only on paper or through financing arrangements before moving on, Hong Kong captures just a thin slice of the transaction.

The larger margins accrue in the services surrounding the goods: trade finance, treasury management, insurance, intellectual property, legal contracts, arbitration, supply-chain data and regional headquarters. Hong Kong’s Asean opportunity therefore depends less on moving more containers than on attaching more high-value services to each transaction.

World.title: Man injured as fire engulfs 2 huts, 4 speedboats at village in Sai Kung
World.content:
A man has suffered minor burns in a fire that spread to two huts and four speedboats in Hong Kong’s Sai Kung.

The Fire Services Department said it received multiple reports of a blaze that broke out near a minibus terminus in Po Toi O village at 8.33am on Wednesday. It was classified as a No 1 alarm fire, the lowest in Hong Kong’s five-tier system.

Firefighters arrived at the scene 14 minutes later and found a man, aged about 60, who had suffered minor burns to his right hand, it said. He received treatment at the scene by paramedics.

A photo shows the charred remains of one of the boats. Photo: Handout

The fire, which affected two huts and four speedboats, was extinguished less than an hour after it was reported.

Photos released by the department show thick black smoke rising from boats moored near waterfront structures, with firefighters battling the blaze from floating platforms and fireboats.

Several badly burned vessels, including one reduced largely to its metal frame, can also be seen in photos showing the fire’s aftermath.

Po Toi O is known for its seafood restaurants. Its sheltered bay is also a popular lunchtime stop for people arriving by boat.

World.title: Limited burning of paper offerings at funeral parlour since weekend power outage
World.content:
A prolonged power outage since Sunday has forced a funeral parlour to limit burnings of paper offerings due to poor ventilation, though some of its other services have resumed.

Power was restored at Global Funeral Parlour in Hung Hom on Wednesday, with lights and air conditioning returning across its five floors and large fans and air coolers deployed to further cool the premises.

But the burning of paper offerings, a traditional ritual in Chinese funerals, remained limited as the building’s exhaust ventilation system had not been fully restored, with repair work still ongoing, according to a staff member.

“We try not to burn too many paper offerings for now, because the exhaust ventilation is still a bit weak,” the staff member told the South China Morning Post.

Funerals proceeded inside two halls, while notices about the power situation remained posted near the passenger lifts.

Tung Wah Group of Hospitals (TWGH), which runs the venue, said initially that the outage had affected lighting, air-conditioning and exhaust ventilation systems on certain floors, as well as lifts used to transport bodies.

World.title: Snooker star Jimmy White becomes Hong Kong resident through talent scheme
World.content:
Snooker star Jimmy White, known as “The Whirlwind”, has become a Hong Kong resident through an official talent scheme, and has revealed plans to establish a snooker academy in the city to nurture local talent.

The Hong Kong Immigration Department announced on Wednesday that the English player recently obtained his identity card and took up residency through the Quality Migrant Admission Scheme, joining fellow stars Judd Trump and Ronnie O’Sullivan.

Appearing in a video posted on the department’s Instagram page, White also recalled his appearance alongside comedy star Stephen Chow Sing-chi in a 1991 Hong Kong film, and expressed hope of catching up with his “old friend”.

White’s compatriots – high-profile English snooker star, seven-time world champion Ronnie O’Sullivan and the current world number one Judd Trump – also became Hong Kong residents in 2024 through the same talent scheme.

Speaking about his future plans in the city, White said he would want to promote snooker at his best.

“My plan in Hong Kong is to maybe open a snooker academy and find the snooker talent of Hong Kong, promote snooker as much as I can,” he said in the video.

White also shared an anecdote about his connection to the city tracing back to the early 1990s.

World.title: Hong Kong student avoids jail for seditious graffiti in commercial complex toilet
World.content:
A Hong Kong student has been spared jail for seditious acts in breach of the domestic national security law , after a court ruled that his good background, young age and the limited impact of his offences constituted “exceptional circumstances”.

Leung Kai-lok, 19, is potentially the first person to avoid a custodial sentence for violating the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance , although he was incarcerated for four weeks before sentencing.

West Kowloon Court on Wednesday gave the defendant 1½ years of probation after finding him guilty of inciting hatred towards authorities by scrawling anti-government messages in a commercial building toilet last year.

The order requires Leung, who is now pursuing a higher diploma in digital media at a vocational school, to attend psychiatric and psychological counselling and take part in community activities and courses at his probation officer’s instructions.

The court also ordered the student to pay HK$1,500 (US$190) in cleaning expenses to the China Hong Kong City commercial complex in Tsim Sha Tsui.

He pleaded guilty to three counts of criminal damage for writing graffiti inside a men’s toilet at the complex, where he worked as a part-time clerk for the city’s Vanuatu consulate, between July 17 and 21, 2025.

World.title: Hong Kong authorities charge woman who allegedly kept 136 dogs without licences
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities have charged a woman on suspicion of keeping 136 dogs without valid licences at a shelter previously investigated for alleged animal cruelty, the South China Morning Post has learned.

The Agriculture, Conservation and Fisheries Department (AFCD) said on Wednesday that it had commenced prosecution after conducting a raid in response to complaints about the shelter in Yuen Long district.

“During the operation, a total of 136 dogs were suspected of being kept without valid licences,” a spokesman said.

Authorities have issued a court summons to the woman, with the case expected to be mentioned in Tuen Mun Court on September 2.

The woman will be prosecuted under the Rabies Ordinance, which mandates that an owner or handler must have a licence for any dog over five months old, to be renewed every three years.

Anyone convicted of keeping an unlicensed dog faces a maximum fine of HK$10,000 (US$1,270).

A source said the suspect and the dog shelter had previously been investigated for alleged animal cruelty.

World.title: Extreme heat grips Hong Kong as labour groups urge district-level index
World.content:
Hong Kong remained gripped by extreme heat on Wednesday with temperatures reaching 37.5 degrees Celsius (99.5 Fahrenheit) in parts of the city, prompting labour representatives to urge authorities to introduce a district-level index to better protect outdoor workers.

The Very Hot Weather Warning and the Amber Heat Stress at Work Warning have been in effect throughout Wednesday, with parts of the New Territories including Yuen Long reaching a maximum of 37.5 degrees, Sheung Shui 37.2 degrees, Ta Kwu Ling 37.1 degrees, according to the Hong Kong Observatory.

The sustained heat followed Sunday’s record-breaking 36.9 degrees – the highest since the Observatory began keeping records in 1884. Yet the lowest-level amber heat stress alert for outdoor workers remained in place, drawing criticism of the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning System.

Li Wing-foo, chairman of the Staffs and Workers Union of Hong Kong Civil Airlines, said heat stress warnings should be issued at a district level rather than relying solely on territory-wide readings.

He noted that areas such as the northern New Territories and the airport apron could run far hotter than urban stations.

“The airport apron is wide open and fully exposed. It should have its own independent reading so employers can roll out targeted protections for staff,” he told a radio programme.

World.title: Hong Kong is no longer a Western playground – and it’s not looking back
World.content:
When it comes to bad prognostication, no one can beat Fortune, which came up with the mother of all “Hong Kong is doomed” narratives. In June 1995, the magazine ran its infamous “The Death of Hong Kong” cover story, predicting its demise following the 1997 handover to China.

Stephen Roach , veteran China watcher and former chairman of Morgan Stanley Asia, seems determined to follow in its footsteps.

Who can argue with that? You and I are very different from our younger selves. We all have to change and adapt. Not changing with the times in this day and age is positively suicidal, at least with your career.

As it is with people, so it is with cities. As mainland China emerges as a superpower, how can Hong Kong not change with the rest of the nation, and for the better?

Do you know what next-door Shenzhen was like in the mid-1960s when I was born? Well, it didn’t exist as an economic entity, and certainly did not register anywhere in the then global economy.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Saving China’s Vanishing Fields of Knowledge
World.content:
Every summer, millions of Chinese high school students who have just completed the national college entrance examination, or gaokao, face a pivotal decision: which university and major to choose. At the same time, media outlets and social platforms fill with debate over which fields of study offer the best employment prospects and financial returns. Driven by pragmatism, students tend to favor majors that lead to well-paid or stable careers, such as computer science, software engineering, medicine, and accounting.

At the other end of the spectrum are disciplines that appear to have little practical value and remain unfamiliar to most people, including Western Xia studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, silk manuscript studies, and Dunhuang studies. In recent years, these fields have come to be grouped under the poetic term “lengmen juexue,” often translated as “niche and endangered disciplines.”

The phrase combines two concepts. Lengmen, or “niche disciplines,” refers to traditional humanities fields with small research communities that attract limited scholarly attention and produce results slowly. Juexue, or “endangered disciplines,” refers to fields of exceptional cultural significance that require highly specialized expertise and risk disappearing as senior scholars retire. In other words, lengmen describes their circumstances, while juexue reflects their value. A true niche and endangered discipline must satisfy both conditions: it has only a small community of researchers while preserving an irreplaceable body of cultural knowledge at risk of being lost.

Many of these disciplines have a long history. Fields such as philology, Confucian classics, epigraphy, bibliography, ancient musicology, and calendrical studies were once central to Chinese scholarship but gradually became marginalized following the introduction of Western academic disciplines in the modern era. The term juexue itself dates back more than a thousand years. During the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), the philosopher Zhang Zai (1020–1077) wrote in his “Hengqu Yulu” of the need “to ordain conscience for Heaven and Earth, to secure life for the people, to continue the lost teachings of past sages, and to establish peace for all future generations.”

Today, however, “niche and endangered disciplines” is more than a descriptive label. It has become an institutional framework within Chinese academia. In 2016, President Xi Jinping called for greater attention to marginal disciplines with high cultural value and significance for Chinese heritage during a speech at the Seminar on Philosophy and Social Sciences in Beijing. Quoting an old Chinese saying, he argued that resources maintained over the long term prove their worth when they are eventually needed.

That vision took institutional form in 2018, when the National Social Science Fund of China established a dedicated funding program for niche and endangered disciplines. Since then, the Ministry of Education, the Chinese Academy of History, and other institutions have launched related initiatives. One flagship funding program provides around 350,000 yuan ($52,000) for individual research projects and about 800,000 yuan for collaborative projects, placing these disciplines on a similar footing to other major National Social Science Fund initiatives.

These disciplines contribute little to GDP growth and seem far removed from everyday life. So why do the state and the academic community devote such significant resources to supporting them?

The answer lies in their role in helping Chinese civilization understand itself and sustain its continuity. Civilizations do not endure by chance. Their longevity depends not only on creating new knowledge but also on preserving and interpreting their past.

These disciplines address fundamental questions about China’s history. Why were oracle bone inscriptions written the way they were? How was the millennia-old “Book of Documents” passed down through the centuries? How did ancient Chinese societies observe the skies and develop calendars? What does the Library Cave at the Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang reveal about cultural exchange? Such questions may seem remote, but they form the foundation of a civilization’s understanding of its own history.

These disciplines also safeguard cultural continuity. The longevity of the Chinese civilization has depended on generations of scholars who continuously compiled classical texts, interpreted ancient scripts, and preserved knowledge. Without this work, vast collections of cultural heritage might survive physically while becoming increasingly difficult, or even impossible, to understand.

These disciplines also shape China’s cultural narrative. Research into frontier history, ethnic writing systems, and Chinese texts preserved overseas extends beyond academic inquiry. It informs historical interpretation, cultural identity, and international exchange.

In short, niche and endangered disciplines preserve the historical memory of Chinese civilization. Once sustained by only a handful of scholars, they have become an important part of China’s broader cultural strategy.

So what qualifies as a niche and endangered discipline? There is no definitive list. Instead, the category has steadily expanded. It initially included fields such as oracle bone studies, Dunhuang studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, and ancient script studies. More recently, it has broadened to encompass the history of ancient Chinese science and technology, ancient astronomy and calendrical studies, ethnic scripts, Chinese texts preserved overseas, frontier history and geography, and research on exchanges between China and other civilizations. Today, these disciplines are generally grouped into four broad categories: ancient scripts and extinct languages; traditional classics and endangered classical studies; ancient specialized histories and niche skills; and research on China’s frontiers and its exchanges with other ancient civilizations.

Why has the category expanded? Not because more disciplines have become obscure but because there is growing recognition that many specialized fields are indispensable to understanding Chinese civilization.

Take ancient astronomy and calendrical studies. Without them, it would be difficult to understand how ancient China developed its calendar, organized agricultural production, and structured political authority. Likewise, without research into historical ethnic writing systems, countless documents produced by frontier peoples would become unreadable. Moreover, dedicated funding programs provide specialized institutions and researchers with the long-term support needed to sustain this work.

State support has already produced significant results. The Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, for example, has published major works including “Heroic Epic and Oral Tradition” and “Translations of Sanskrit Literature.” These works preserve and interpret historical texts, making them accessible to modern scholars and readers. Meanwhile, digital technologies are increasingly being used to collate ancient texts, digitize documents, and recognize historical scripts, greatly improving research efficiency. Even so, significant challenges remain.

The greatest challenge is not funding but time. One scholar may spend three decades studying just a few dozen oracle bones. Another may devote an entire career to deciphering a script that disappeared more than a thousand years ago. A third may spend decades reconstructing an ancient calendar.

Mastering a niche and endangered discipline often requires decades of training, yet an entire field can disappear within a single generation. Early Chinese astronomy, for example, demands expertise in ancient astronomy and calendrical systems, the ability to decipher ancient scripts, and a deep understanding of history. The barriers to entry are therefore exceptionally high. Since the deaths of leading scholars such as Bo Shuren (1934–1997), Xi Zezong (1927–2008), and Chen Meidong (1942–2008), the field has weakened significantly, with few young researchers able to replace them. Sustained institutional support is therefore essential.

These disciplines also sit uneasily within a modern research system that rewards speed and measurable output. Their work progresses slowly, while public awareness remains limited and relatively few young people are willing to commit to careers that require decades of patient study.

Protecting niche and endangered disciplines therefore requires training and evaluation systems tailored to their unique characteristics. Only then can more students be encouraged to enter these fields, allowing scholars to devote themselves to the long-term work of preserving and expanding humanity’s understanding of China’s past.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from International Dunhuang Programme and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.title: China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.content:
China’s central Henan province issued a notice last week urging companies to ensure employees take their full paid annual leave and encouraging employer flexibility around workers leaving early on Fridays, domestic media reported Wednesday. The move was designed to encourage travel and spending on holidays and weekend getaways.

However, on Friday, local authorities said that the notice contained “inaccurate wording” and had “not undergone proper approval procedures,” and in response to public concerns, would be revised and reissued.

The original notice required employers to simplify leave approval procedures and called on company leaders to “lead by example” by taking time off themselves. It also clarified that all employees are entitled to the same paid annual leave regardless of whether they are permanent, temporary, dispatched, or contracted workers.

In addition, it encouraged employees to maximize their breaks by combining leave with weekends and public holidays, and said those with school-age children should receive priority when applying for leave during school breaks.

Henan is among several provincial-level regions that have introduced measures this year to better enforce paid annual leave, in line with China’s latest and first specific five-year plan on boosting consumption, approved by the State Council in July.

The Henan notice sparked heated discussion on social media, jumping to the trending topics list on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users voiced support and called for a nationwide rollout of the policy. Others took the opportunity to criticize a long-standing workplace culture in the country that promotes skipping leave to demonstrate dedication.

“I no longer have to lose pay to travel,” an employee who has worked at a state-owned enterprise in the Henan city of Luoyang for 10 years told Sixth Tone. “We were so excited when we saw the news that afternoon, and everyone cheered when our company issued (its own) notice the next day.”

She said taking time off previously meant losing a significant portion of her salary. “Now, (the notice) makes me feel more motivated to work,” she said. “People will complete their tasks more thoroughly before going on leave.” The employee added that she is already planning to combine her annual leave with the weeklong National Day holiday, at the beginning of October, for a longer break.

Two private-sector employees in Henan, however, told Sixth Tone that they had yet to receive any notice of a change in annual leave from their companies.

Similar notices have also been issued this year in the northern port city of Tianjin, the eastern provinces of Zhejiang and Anhui, the northwestern province of Shaanxi, and the southwestern province of Guizhou.

Many notices state they aim to change “unhealthy workplace norms,” while attempting to allay workers’ concerns that taking leave could affect their pay, performance evaluations, or chances for promotion.

In 2025, Lü Guoquan, a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and then an official with the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, said only around 57% of China’s workers entitled to paid annual leave actually take it.

Under national regulations implemented in 2008, employees with one to 10 years of cumulative work experience are entitled to five days of paid annual leave; those with 10 to 20 years receive 10 days; and those with more than 20 years receive 15 days.

“To fundamentally change the situation, China also needs routine labor inspections, accessible channels for workers to defend their rights, and better job rotation systems to reduce operational pressure on employers,” Song Xiangqing, vice president of the Commerce Economy Association of China, told domestic business outlet Caijing.

In January, China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security also announced that it would revise national regulations to promote better enforcement of the paid leave system.

“Paid leave is no longer simply about work-life balance or employee welfare,” state-run Guangming Daily wrote in a commentary published Thursday. “It has become part of the country’s strategy to boost consumption and expand domestic demand. Only with sufficient, uninterrupted, and predictable time off will people have both the time and willingness to spend.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Horstgerlach/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.title: Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.content:
China’s industry associations are revoking hundreds of honorary designations that have increasingly been used as marketing tools.

In late July, the China Cuisine Association announced that all previously awarded titles — including “Chinese Culinary Master” and “Chinese Catering Service Master” — along with related certificates and uniforms, were now invalid. The association also revoked all honorary designations awarded to cities — such as the “capital of” and “hometown of” certain dishes. Local governments are now officially barred from using them in any form of publicity.

The revocation of the titles triggered renewed interest among social media users. This week, they questioned the reliability of the “National Stir-Fried Meat King” title awarded to restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, after discovering it was conferred following an online public vote on photos and videos submitted by contestants.

The title has not yet been revoked, though, in response, the China Cuisine Association said they will “communicate after reviewing relevant materials,” domestic media reported.

Originally intended to recognize exceptional craftsmanship, “master” titles were once rare state honors. But in the early 2000s, industry associations across the tea, ceramics, and jewelry sectors, and many others, began creating their own titles, allowing businesses to charge a premium by creating the perception of higher-quality products and services. However, numerous shadowy practices also emerged around the honors, including honorary title certificates being openly sold on e-commerce platforms.

Since the beginning of this year, at least a dozen national and local industry associations covering sectors ranging from cosmetic surgery to jade carving and wedding services have revoked or abolished previously-conferred honorary titles containing words like “master.”

An increasing number of industry associations began nullifying their own honorary titles after the Social Work Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Ministry of Civil Affairs jointly released new guidelines on governing social organizations’ awards and commendations in mid-July.

The guidelines, which took effect on Aug. 1, imposed stricter eligibility requirements on organizations seeking to present awards. It also prohibits organizations from charging fees for recognition programs or partnering with, or outsourcing such activities to, for-profit entities.

China has gradually tightened oversight of awards and commendations organized by social organizations over the past decade, with its first regulations governing the practice taking effect in 2012.

Restrictions were tightened further in 2018, when award programs using national designations such as “China,” “Chinese,” and “national” became subject to stricter controls. In 2022, authorities required organizations seeking to launch honorary recognition programs to hold at least a 4A rating, the second highest on the country’s social organization rating scale.

Lu Zhen, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of Beijing-based Hylands Law Firm, told local media that rather than eliminating professional evaluations altogether, the regulations are intended to draw a clearer distinction between professional qualifications and commercialized honorary awards.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An  for restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, at a shopping mall in Beijing, May 23, 2024. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018862/Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.title: Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018862/Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.content:
Ask anyone to name a Chinese video game character, and chances are they will say Chun-Li. That is both her achievement and the problem.

When Japanese gaming giant Capcom debuted her character in the 1991 arcade game Street Fighter II, Chun-Li was an Interpol officer. But it was her blue qipao, double buns, and devastating kicks that made her famous.

Those details made Chun-Li instantly recognizable, but they also turned her Chinese identity into spectacle — graceful, formidable, and framed for the male gaze. Her image was already so familiar by 1993 that Jackie Chan could parody her in his film “City Hunter” without explanation.

The arcade era rewarded that kind of instant legibility. Fighting-game characters were built from bold silhouettes, familiar archetypes, and minimal backstory. In Japanese developer SNK’s 1994 arcade fighting game The King of Fighters ’94, Chin Gentsai was the drunken, disheveled old man cast as the quintessential kung fu master. Chinese culture was visible, but largely reduced to type: exotic, recognizable, and stripped of psychological depth.

It would take another generation of games for Chinese characters to move beyond such tropes. By the mid-2010s, globally popular multiplayer titles were reaching vast Chinese audiences, whose size and commercial importance made their expectations harder to ignore. As Chinese characters became more common, players increasingly expected them to feel culturally grounded rather than assembled from stock signs.

When American video game developer Blizzard released the first-person shooter Overwatch in 2016, its Chinese hero, Mei-Ling Zhou, seemed to mark a step beyond the old archetypes. A climatologist from Xi’an in northwestern China, Mei wears polar expedition gear and is portrayed as affable, resilient, and determined to protect both people and the planet.

Yet while Mei is more fully drawn than the arcade characters before her, her Chinese identity remains largely incidental. Her nationality adds diversity to Overwatch’s global cast without meaningfully shaping her inner life.

Nearly a decade later, Overwatch introduced its second Chinese hero, Wuyang Ye. A 19-year-old from the southwestern Sichuan province, he attends the fictional Wuxing University, whose colleges draw on the five traditional Chinese elements. Yet the most revealing detail is also the most ordinary: Wuyang is a college student, a figure immediately familiar to much of the game’s Chinese audience.

Overwatch also gave its characters linguistic markers of where they came from. In the English-language version, an allied Mei shouts “Freeze, don’t move!” when using her ultimate ability; an enemy Mei delivers the warning in Mandarin. For Chinese players, the switch allowed her nationality to be heard rather than merely listed in her biography.

By the time Wuyang appeared, simply hearing a Chinese character speak Chinese was no longer enough. In a 2025 promotional trailer, he dismisses a challenge with “xiao case,” a Chinese-English expression roughly equivalent to “piece of cake.” Some Chinese viewers found the line playful; others argued that a student from Sichuan should instead use the local expression “le ge hao long” — “this one’s easy.”

The disagreement was minor, but it showed how expectations had changed. Players expected his language to reflect where he came from and who he was.

In 2026, Wuyang’s elder sister, Anran Ye, joined the Overwatch roster. Associated with the element of fire, she is forceful, impatient, and quick to challenge her younger brother. Their exchanges introduce sibling rivalry, parental pressure, and family expectations, giving both characters a social world beyond their individual backstories.

This marks the clearest break from Mei. Mei’s Chinese identity is conveyed largely through nationality and language; the Ye siblings’ emerges through family relationships and everyday behavior. Anran feels familiar not as a symbol of China but as the demanding older sister who refuses to let her younger brother coast.

The 2020 tactical shooter Valorant, developed by U.S. video game company Riot Games — owned by Chinese tech giant Tencent — offers a different kind of Chinese character. Sage is built around protection rather than aggression: she heals injured teammates, raises defensive barriers, and can revive fallen allies. Players often call her “mom,” a playful nickname rooted less in her nationality than in the trust inspired by her abilities and calm authority.

Three years later, Valorant introduced its second Chinese character, Iso, a hired gun from the southwestern megacity of Chongqing. His abilities are built around single combat, allowing him to isolate opponents and force them into one-on-one fights. The contrast with Sage is immediate: Sage protects and restores her team, while Iso is aggressive, self-contained, and designed to fight alone.

Iso’s reveal trailer featured “Renegade,” an original track by Chinese rappers 99 God and C103, grounding the character in contemporary Chinese music without relying on traditional costume or martial-arts imagery.

Neither character is expected to represent China as a whole or reduced to a single cultural type. Together with Mei, Wuyang, and Anran, they mark a broader shift in global competitive games, where Chinese characters increasingly appear as individuals rather than national symbols.

Chinese culture has also become more visible beyond character rosters. In League of Legends, developed by Riot Games, and Honor of Kings, developed in China by Tencent’s TiMi Studio Group, players can buy skins inspired by Chinese mythology, clothing, and decorative motifs.

But visibility alone was not enough. Anran’s trailer presented her as fierce and commanding, while her in-game model appeared cuter and more delicate.

Chinese players objected to the mismatch, and Blizzard later announced changes to the design. The response showed that players were judging not merely whether Chinese elements were present but whether the character remained consistent with the world and personality the game had established.

From Chun-Li to the Ye siblings, and from Sage to Iso, Chinese characters in global competitive games have begun to move from spectacle to self. They are no longer recognized only through costume, accent, or archetype. Players now debate how they speak, how they look, where they come from, and whether those details add up to a convincing person.

In the years ahead, perhaps the misty canal towns of Jiangnan, in eastern China’s lower Yangtze region, will appear on a new arena map, Miao embroidery on a tournament skin, or Tang dynasty poetry woven into a champion’s identity. But such details will matter only when they do more than decorate.

When culture is lived rather than labeled, a Chinese figure stops being a symbol. They become someone players can root for, and perhaps someone who brings them closer to their own roots.

(Header image: Visuals from Street Fighter, Blizzard, and Riot Game, reedited by Sixth Tone)
