World.title: Taiwan condemns ‘dangerous’ planned Chinese navy drill with Indonesia to its east
World.content:
CHINA-TAIWAN CONFLICT. Chinese and Taiwanese flags are seen in this illustration, August 6, 2022.

The mid-August drill at an unspecified location east of Taiwan would be a 'navigation exercise' with an Indonesian navy ship, a highly unusual move given China does not generally hold exercises with foreign militaries near Taiwan

TAIPEI, Taiwan – Taiwan‘s government has condemned “dangerous” planned Chinese navy drills with an Indonesian warship off the island’s east coast, saying Beijing was trying to create a false impression to the international community that it controls those waters.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, and in June began coast guard patrols off the island’s east coast, causing anger in Taipei and concern in Washington and some other Western capitals.

China’s defense ministry said on Tuesday the drill, to take place in mid-August at a location east of Taiwan it did not detail, would be a “navigation exercise” with an Indonesian navy ship, a highly unusual move given China does not generally hold exercises with foreign militaries near Taiwan.

The Indonesian navy and defense ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Late on Tuesday, Taiwan’s China-policy-making Mainland Affairs Council said the drill was a “military provocation” and Beijing should “immediately stop this dangerous behaviour that undermines the status quo.”

Following a recent series of Chinese actions, including so-called “routine law-enforcement patrols” to the east of Taiwan, China is now attempting to conduct military exercises with “relevant countries” in waters east of Taiwan, it said in a statement.

“This is, in reality, political manipulation, ‘exercises in name, expansion in fact’, aimed at creating a false impression before the international community that the Chinese communists have jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan,” it added.

Taking lawmaker questions at parliament in Taipei on Wednesday, Wu Tien-jen, assistant deputy chief of the general staff for intelligence, said the Indonesian warship China said would take part was on its way back from Japan rather than coming specifically to drill with the Chinese navy.

The ship was some 70 to 80 nautical miles off Taiwan’s east, in the Pacific, he added.

“Militarily this does not have a direct impact on Taiwan,” he said. “It has a geopolitical significance.”

Taiwan’s foreign ministry said separately that it had asked for a “clarification” from Indonesia on its taking part in the drill.

Taiwan holding annual war games

Taiwan is in the midst of its annual Han Kuang war games, where it simulates how to beat back an attempted Chinese attack.

China’s announcement came as US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby met with Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin at his Jakarta office on Tuesday.

Sjafrie told Colby that expanding defense cooperation with the United States is not intended to establish a US military base in Indonesia, his office cited him as saying.

China recognizes no sovereignty claims by Taiwan’s government and its military operates around the island on an almost daily basis.

Like most countries, Indonesia has no formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the island is home to more than 300,000 Indonesian migrant workers.

Taiwan’s government says only the Taiwanese people can decide their future and has repeatedly denounced Chinese military pressure. – Rappler.com

World.title: Luxury condo resilience: Half of Ayala’s Laurean buyers staying despite pause
World.content:
Despite construction grinding to a halt amid higher costs and uncertainty from the Middle East war, half of Laurean Residences’ deep-pocketed buyers are choosing to stay rather than take a refund or move to another Ayala project

MANILA, Philippines – Ayala Land (ALI) put one of its boldest luxury bets on pause this year. And yet many of the people who had already bought into it are willing to wait it out.

Around half of the buyers of Laurean Residences have chosen to stick with the project, ALI chief operating officer Mikhail Cruz said during the property giant’s H1 briefing on Monday, August 10. When the Makati tower was suspended, ALI earlier gave buyers the option to refund or transfer their payments to other Ayala Land developments.

ALI president and chief executive officer Margarita Bautista-Dy previously said they could revisit the Laurean project by the middle of 2027, as reported by The Philippine Star.

The decision to stay on — despite there being no definite plans yet on when construction will restart — gives evidence that the very top end of the residential market may be proving more resilient than the broader condominium market.

Ayala’s own numbers show the importance of its higher-end segment. Its premium residential sales reservations reached P31.5 billion in the first half, down just 8% year-on-year, while its core segment plunged 38% to P14.9 billion. Cruz said premium demand “continues to be resilient.”

There is also evidence beyond ALI’s projects. Metro Manila ranked third globally for luxury residential price growth in 2025. Luxury home prices in the capital region rose 17.5% year-on-year, behind Dubai’s 25.1% and Tokyo’s 58.5%, according to Knight Frank.

From carpark to P28-billion luxury tower

The spot that is now ground zero for the soon-to-rise Laurean Residences was once the Dela Rosa 2 Carpark, a decidedly less glamorous but daily fixture for people working in the Makati central business district.

The redevelopment began in 2024. Along with the demolition of the parking structure went a portion of the Dela Rosa Elevated Walkway attached to it, breaking a familiar pedestrian route through the CBD. The 1.1-kilometer walkway historically connected Greenbelt toward Makati Medical Center. Through SM and Ayala’s network of malls and walkways, commuters could continue toward the Ayala Station of the Metro Rail Transit Line 3.

For the thousands of commuters who used that route every day, what replaces the old carpark has a lot to live up to.

GREEN. Artist’s rendition of the Dela Rosa Gardens mixed-use redevelopment, which includes an urban park. Photo from Ayala Land

Ayala’s answer is Dela Rosa Gardens, a 1.3-hectare mixed-use redevelopment planned around the new Bank of the Philippine Islands headquarters, Laurean Residences, retail and civic spaces, and a 2,700-square-meter urban park.

Laurean itself was conceived as one of Ayala Land Premier’s biggest Makati bets, with an estimated P28-billion sales value.

The 65-storey tower was planned to contain just 388 residences, ranging from 72-square-meter suites to two- to four-bedroom homes as large as 402 square meters, along with “rare” bi-level villas. More than half a hectare was set aside for club-like exclusive amenities.

In its initial announcement for Laurean, which has since been taken down from Ayala Land’s website, the developer pitched the project as an “urban sanctuary” for a particularly discerning slice of the luxury market. Ayala said Laurean was designed to offer the feel of a private in-city club while remaining right at the heart of Makati’s business district.

And the old walkway? Ayala said Laurean would eventually reconnect to it, with direct access to the Dela Rosa elevated walkway forming part of the project’s pitch on walkability and connectivity.

Buyers initially came quickly. Laurean had already generated around P10.4 billion in presales by the time Ayala broke ground in February 2026, as reported by the Inquirer. Latest presales figures have since hit P11 billion, ALI confirmed to Rappler as of Tuesday, August 11.

Only months after its strong start, construction and sales were paused.

Ayala blamed worsening uncertainty from the Middle East conflict, saying rising cost pressures and increasingly unpredictable delivery timelines made it difficult to execute Laurean with the certainty it promises customers.

ALI trims residential inventory

Laurean aside, ALI has also made progress in working down its broader residential inventory.

The value of its unsold residential stock, excluding Laurean, has fallen steadily from P214 billion in 2024 to P110 billion by June 2026. That is equivalent to about 15 months of inventory, already better than the roughly 18 months Ayala carried before the pandemic.

Still, there is plenty left to sell. In terms of value, about 75% of the remaining inventory is in premium developments.

Ayala launched no residential projects in the first half specifically so its sales teams could work through existing stock. Despite having nothing new to launch, they generated P22.3 billion in second-quarter residential take-up, a performance that management called encouraging in a “hyper-competitive” market. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Ralph Recto quote on taxing Alex Eala’s prize money is fake
World.content:
In an email to Rappler, Recto’s office debunked the circulating quote, saying the executive secretary would ‘never make this statement’

Claim: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said the prize money of Filipina tennis star Alex Eala should be subject to tax.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted by Facebook user Ado Paglinawan on August 8. As of writing, it has reached more than 2,400 reactions and 3,200 shares.

The quote card cites Recto as saying, “Prize money ni Alex Eala, dapat sumailalim sa tax.”

(Alex Eala’s prize money should be subject to tax.)

The quote card was reposted by various Facebook accounts and pages across different groups. Other graphics, bearing the same quote, also emerged online.

The facts: The quote circulating online is fake. This was confirmed by the Office of the Executive Secretary in an email to Rappler on August 11.

“This is the latest product of a well-financed fake news industry targeting the Executive Secretary. Obviously, no such statement was made. Kahit kailan, hindi niya sasabihin ‘yan (He will never say that),” Recto’s office stated.

Eala’s prize money: The Filipina tennis star has dominated news headlines after winning her first-ever Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Tour crown in the Washington Open.

On Monday, August 3 (Tuesday, August 4, Manila time), Eala defeated world No. 3 Jessica Pegula of the United States for the title.

Her victory raised her world ranking to No. 20 — eight spots higher than her previous ranking a week before, marking her biggest ranking jump since her breakthrough into the top 35 in February.

Eala’s title victory earned her prize money of $252,000 (around P15.4 million). This brings her earnings from competitions this year so far to $1.5 million, or more than P93.3 million.

However, Eala’s winnings are still subject to tax in the country where the tournament is held. For example, foreign players who win in the United States, which is the host country of the Mubadala DC Open, are generally subject to a withholding tax of 30%.

Alex Eala at the Canadian Open: Following her Washington title run, Eala sought to extend her hot streak at the Canadian Open in Toronto.

However, fatigue from consecutive matches and an ankle injury appear to have caught up with the young tennis star, as Eala’s stint ended after falling to world No. 14 Belinda Bencic of Switzerland in the round of 16 of the tourney. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: To the Youngest Person in the Room….
World.content:
To all the youngest people in the room,

I hope you know that it is always better to be in that room than to convince yourself you do not belong there. There will be rooms where everyone seems to know more than you do. Rooms where people speak with far more confidence you have yet to find, where their names are more familiar and yours is not. Where you wonder if someone will eventually notice that you are younger, less experienced, and perhaps not supposed to be there. When these thoughts find their way into your mind, stay. Stay even when you are doubting whether to speak up, do it. Stay even if you’re not certain on what comes after. Stay no matter what. Because being young has never meant that you have nothing to say. To be young is to live in the strange gap in between being told that you are the future of our nation and being reminded that you are not quite ready yet. We are told to dream big, but sometimes told that we are too young to understand how the world works. We are encouraged to speak up, yet questioned when our opinions challenge those who came before us. Sounds familiar?

And yet, here we are. Yet, here YOU are.

The Filipino youth have always found ways to make themselves heard. You cannot deny that you at least tried to volunteer, create, write, protest, teach, vote, and show up. We make things out of what we cannot explain and communities out of what we cannot change alone. We find one another online and offline, in classrooms, streets, workplaces and spaces where you people are simply trying to make sense of the world.

But I hope despite all these, you remember that you do not have to change the world every day.

Sometimes, simply surviving a difficult academic year or career is enough. Sometimes choosing to try again after failing is enough. These things count, way more than you think.

There is so much pressure placed on young people to become extraordinary. We are constantly asked what we want to be, where we see ourselves in five years. Even asked what we want to be when we grow up as early as the age of five. Somewhere along the way, we can forget that we are allowed to simply become.

You do not need to have your life figured out at twenty. You do not need to know exactly where you are going at eighteen, twenty-two, or even twenty-five. You are allowed to take the longer road. Allowed to outgrow dreams that once felt like they were supposed to define you.

And when you find yourself in a room where you feel like the youngest there, remember this, you are there for a reason.

Seize every opportunity. Ask questions. Make mistakes. Let yourself be humbled by what you do not know yet. But do not make yourself feel smaller simply because someone else in the room has been there longer.

Every person in any room was once the youngest too.

So to every young Filipino who is still figuring things out, keep showing up.

Show up to the classrooms even when you feel behind, in communities even when you are unsure of what you can contribute, and most importantly, show up in conversations that matter. Take up space, but make space for others, too.

You are more than the country’s future. And if you are ever standing outside a room, wondering whether you are too young and inexperienced, I hope you choose to walk through the door.

Because it is better to be the youngest person in the room than to spend your life outside it, waiting until you feel ready. You may never feel ready, but walk in anyway.

From a fellow youth, Happy International Youth Day!

World.title: Kazakhstan Updates Astana Master Plan to Meet Demands of Fast-Growing Capital
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s government has approved an updated master plan for Astana through 2035, effective Aug. 8, setting out how the capital will accommodate a population projected to reach nearly 2.3 million while expanding housing, schools, transport and utilities.

The plan comes as Astana continues to expand rapidly, driven by sustained population growth. The city had approximately 300,000 residents when it became the capital in 1997. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, by June 1, its population had reached nearly 1.67 million.

Government projections now put the population at 1.97 million by 2030 and 2.28 million by 2035, meaning the capital could add nearly 600,000 residents within the next decade.

Planning for a city of more than 2 million

The updated master plan uses Jan. 1, 2025, as its baseline, with 2030 designated as the first construction phase and 2035 as the final planning horizon. The document’s baseline population is 1.528 million, a level Astana has already exceeded.

The plan sets out where residential, social, recreational and industrial areas will develop and how they will be supported by transport and engineering infrastructure. It also covers land-use restrictions, reserve territories, environmental protection, emergency resilience and functional zoning.

By 2035, working-age residents are projected to account for 59.5% of the population.

Planning also extends beyond the city’s administrative boundaries. The document takes into account Astana’s growing links with the surrounding agglomeration, where transport networks, utilities, housing and social infrastructure are increasingly interconnected with the capital.

Fivefold population growth since capital relocation

Astana’s development has accelerated sharply since Kazakhstan moved its capital from Almaty to Akmola on Dec. 10, 1997. The city was renamed Astana the following year and officially presented as the new capital on July 6, 1998.

Its population passed one million in 2018 and reached about 1.35 million by the beginning of 2023. Today, Astana has more than five times as many residents as it did when it became the capital. By 2035, Astana’s population is projected to be more than seven times its 1997 level.

Internal migration has contributed significantly to that expansion, with Astana remaining one of Kazakhstan’s main destinations for people relocating from other regions.

Housing, utilities and redevelopment

Housing construction will remain central to accommodating the city’s growth. The master plan sets a target of 30 square meters of housing per resident by 2035, requiring the total housing stock to reach approximately 68.3 million square meters.

Expansion will include both new construction and redevelopment of existing areas. The plan provides for the removal of dilapidated and unsafe housing where necessary, along with garages and some low-rise buildings in districts designated for renovation.

The master plan will also underpin more detailed development programs for electricity, heating, gas, water supply, sewage and stormwater systems, as well as Astana’s comprehensive transport scheme.

The master plan will also serve as the basis for more detailed programs covering electricity, heating, gas, water supply, sewage and stormwater systems, as well as the city’s comprehensive transport scheme. These plans will guide future construction, neighborhood renovation and the redevelopment of residential, industrial and utility areas.

Schools, public spaces and the next stage of growth

Population growth will place particularly strong pressure on schools and kindergartens.

By 2035, Astana is expected to require preschool capacity for 159,194 children. The plan provides for the construction of 206 kindergartens.

School demand is projected to reach 182,423 additional places by 2030 and 256,170 by 2035. To address that need, the plan envisages 123 schools during the first construction phase and another 55 by the end of the planning period.

Beyond new housing and infrastructure, the plan sets a framework for green and recreational areas, public spaces, renovation of established districts and the preservation of historic buildings and cultural heritage sites.

It also includes measures to protect water bodies, improve environmental conditions and guide future rules on compact development and neighborhood renewal.

World.title: Kazakhstan Economy Grows 4.1% as Non-Oil Sectors Expand
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s economy grew 4.1% in the first seven months of 2026, maintaining the pace recorded in the first half of the year despite an 8.9% decline in oil production, reported the Ministry of National Economy on Aug.11.

According to preliminary data from the Bureau of National Statistics (BNS), oil production totaled 53.2 million tons from January through July. Against that decline, the non-oil sector expanded by an estimated 5.4%.

Manufacturing remained among the strongest-performing sectors, growing 9% over the seven months. The fastest increases were recorded in pharmaceuticals at 38.5%, fabricated metal products at 35%, chemicals at 26.9% and mechanical engineering at 22%. Food production rose 13.9%, while building materials increased 9.4%. Growth was also recorded in construction at 15.3%, transport and warehousing at 7.4%, trade at 5.9%, agriculture at 5% and communications at 4.3%.

The figures point to a broader distribution of economic growth at a time when weaker oil output would normally weigh more heavily on overall performance. Economist Ruslan Sultanov said the latest data suggest growth is being generated across several parts of the economy rather than moving entirely in line with oil production.

“Growth is becoming more distributed. The BNS data show an interesting configuration: declining oil production is so far coinciding with the overall GDP growth rate being maintained. This has been possible because several sectors are growing simultaneously,” Sultanov wrote on his Tengenomika Telegram channel.

He also noted that high growth rates in individual industries do not necessarily mean they make an equally large contribution to GDP.

“What matters is their weight in the economy, the absolute volume of output and their ability to maintain this momentum over a longer horizon. The next point of assessment for the economy will be the quality of this growth: whether manufacturing, construction, transport, agriculture and trade can maintain their momentum and generate a sustainable contribution to GDP as conditions in the commodity sector change,” he said.

According to the ministry, the changing composition of growth reflects the gradual diversification of Kazakhstan’s economy, including stronger industrial capacity, development of transport infrastructure, support for domestic producers and small and medium-sized businesses, and increased investment in non-oil sectors. Oil extraction accounted for 7.8% of GDP in 2025.

Independent business indicators also point to activity across a broader range of sectors. In its second-quarter Business Activity Index report published July 28, Halyk Finance said the index stood at 55.2, above the neutral level of 50 that separates expansion from contraction, with growth recorded across manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, agriculture and most other major sectors. The index for small and medium-sized businesses reached 55.3.

The seven-month figures also show an improvement from earlier in the year. According to an April report by the Halyk Finance analytical center, Kazakhstan’s economy grew 3% year on year in the first quarter of 2026, when oil production fell nearly 20%, while manufacturing expanded 8.5%. By January-May, growth had reached 3.7%, according to a June 15 report by the International Monetary Fund.

The IMF projected Kazakhstan’s economy to grow approximately 4.6% in 2026, while identifying potential oil export disruptions, global uncertainty and inflationary pressures as key risks to the outlook.

World.title: Kazakhstan Considers Baku-Supsa Oil Route Amid CPC Disruptions
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is considering additional oil export routes through Azerbaijan and Georgia, including Baku-Supsa, after temporary restrictions on crude intake by the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) in July prompted the diversion of some volumes to alternative routes.

During the restrictions, some Kazakh oil was redirected through the Aktau port, the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline toward China and the Atyrau-Samara route, reported Kazinform, citing Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry spokesperson and adviser to the minister, Assel Serikpayeva.

“Additional export options under consideration include transportation through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan system, trans-Caspian shipments through Azerbaijan and the Baku-Supsa route,” she said.

Kazakhstan currently transports approximately 1.5 million tons of oil per year through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline. According to Serikpayeva, Azerbaijan has expressed readiness to increase its intake of Kazakh oil to 2.2 million tons annually.

Under the BTC route, Kazakh oil is shipped across the Caspian Sea from Aktau to Azerbaijan before entering the pipeline, which crosses Georgia and reaches the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan in Türkiye.

Baku-Supsa provides another route through Azerbaijan and Georgia, reaching the Supsa terminal on Georgia’s Black Sea coast. Kazakhstan considered using the corridor in 2025, when the ministry said its potential use would depend on commercial terms, operational efficiency and agreements between the companies involved.

The search for additional capacity comes as Kazakhstan continues to rely heavily on CPC for crude exports. The pipeline carries oil from western Kazakhstan to a marine terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk. According to the ministry, 64.8 million tons of oil were exported through the route in 2025, out of Kazakhstan’s total oil exports of 78.7 million tons.

The route faced several disruptions in July. The Tengiz-Novorossiysk system resumed operations on July 8 following scheduled maintenance, while loading at the CPC marine terminal was later suspended after drone attacks on tankers on July 19 and 20.

Kazakhstan has previously redirected oil when CPC capacity was constrained. In December 2025, KazMunayGas rerouted approximately 300,000 tons through alternative channels, including shipments toward China and through the BTC system. Kazakhstan also exports oil through the Atyrau-Samara and Atasu-Alashankou pipelines and across the Caspian through the Aktau port.

World.title: Fewer Births, Better Chances: Kazakhstan Advances in Newborn Care
World.content:
ASTANA —Kazakhstan recorded nearly 150,000 births in the first half of 2026, down approximately 7% year on year, while neonatal mortality fell to 3.9 per 1,000 live births in 2025, the lowest rate in Central Asia, according to the Bureau of National Statistics and the Ministry of Healthcare.

The decline in births follows a broader downward trend in Kazakhstan’s total fertility rate, which measures the average number of children a woman would have over her reproductive years. A demographic review by the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund (UAPF) shows the rate fell from 3.32 children per woman in 2021 to 3.06 in 2022 and 2.57 in 2025. The review described declining fertility as part of a broader global trend.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, 335,000 children were born in Kazakhstan in 2025, with boys accounting for 51.5% of births and girls for 48.5%. The country recorded 64,700 deaths from January through June, resulting in a natural population increase of 85,100 people.

While the birth rate has been declining, the ministry data show improving outcomes for newborns requiring specialized medical care, particularly premature babies and children born with severe congenital conditions.

Survival improves in complex neonatal cases

Over the past five years, mortality among newborns with severe congenital conditions has fallen more than threefold, from 22% to 6.9%, while postoperative survival has risen to 93%. Approximately 1,400 operations are performed on newborns each year, with specialized care available at perinatal centers across Kazakhstan.

The ministry attributes the improvement to the development of obstetric and neonatal services, the introduction of modern medical technologies and the work of specialized medical teams. Such treatment can be particularly demanding for premature babies, who require specialized preparation before surgery and intensive care afterward.

Neonatal and pediatric surgeon Zhenis Sakuov told The Astana Times that successful treatment depends on coordination across the entire medical team.

“Operating on newborns is difficult, and operating on premature babies is even more difficult because they require specialized preparation for surgery. (…) The operation itself is complex, the postoperative period is complex, and they need specialized care afterward. This is teamwork,” he said.

About 17,000 premature babies were born in Kazakhstan last year, with each receiving a range of specialized medical care, according to the ministry.

Earlier diagnosis expands treatment options

Advances in neonatal care increasingly begin before birth. Modern prenatal diagnostics can detect many congenital conditions between 18 and 20 weeks of pregnancy, allowing doctors to determine how the pregnancy and delivery should be managed and prepare a medical team to assist the child immediately after birth. When fetal abnormalities are identified, expectant mothers are referred to specialized perinatal centers, where doctors determine the timing and method of delivery and prepare a treatment plan in advance.

This approach has also expanded through one-day clinics at fetal health centers. According to the ministry, since their introduction in 2024, prenatal screening coverage has increased by 10%, detection of fetal abnormalities by 12%, and childhood disability has declined by 8%.

Treatment in some cases can now begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, or the intrauterine correction of certain fetal conditions, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

For some conditions, treatment can begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, which involves correcting certain fetal conditions in the womb, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

After birth, about one-third of newborn surgeries are now performed using minimally invasive techniques. Kazakhstan has also used extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) since 2022 to support patients in critical condition with severe respiratory failure.

“Intensive care is developing, as well as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, anesthesiology, and diagnostics. All of this significantly increases children’s chances of recovery and a good quality of life. And most importantly, many families today can receive high-tech medical care without leaving Kazakhstan,” Pediatric Cardiac Surgeon Tlektes Nashkenov told The Astana Times.

The ministry’s data show survival rates of 80% to 90% for children born with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, 85% to 95% for esophageal atresia and more than 90% for gastroschisis. Mortality among premature babies with necrotizing enterocolitis has fallen more than 2.5 times as diagnostic and surgical treatment has improved.

World.title: eGov GPT Expansion Advances Kazakhstan’s Digital Government Push
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to expand its AI-powered eGov GPT assistant so that services available through it account for approximately 70% of citizen requests by the end of 2026, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said at an Aug. 11 government meeting.

The assistant currently provides access to 50 of the most frequently requested government services, which together account for approximately 30% of citizen requests. Since its launch in April, eGov GPT has been used more than 150,000 times. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the ministry and government agencies to increase the number of services available through the assistant to 150 by year-end.

The system allows users to describe their situation in ordinary text rather than search for the appropriate form, certificate or government agency. The assistant identifies the relevant service, prepares the required application and provides the result.

“eGov GPT should become a universal AI assistant for all matters involving interaction between the state and citizens,” said Madiyev.

The expansion is part of Kazakhstan’s broader effort to integrate artificial intelligence into public services under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, approved in June.

“The year of digitalization and artificial intelligence marks the starting point for achieving this goal. In June, the nationwide Digital Qazaqstan strategy was approved, with the digitalization of public services identified as one of its key priorities,” said Bektenov.

The Aug. 11 meeting, chaired by Bektenov, focused on developing an AI-based public service ecosystem and implementing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to accelerate digital transformation across the economy and public administration. The government is also seeking to make interactions with citizens and businesses increasingly digital and proactive.

Government agencies shift to QazTech

All government agencies are now working with QazTech, Kazakhstan’s unified platform for developing digital public services, while the migration of existing information systems continues under a two-year government plan. The platform has been operating since April 1 and is designed to shorten the development and launch of new digital services from several years to several weeks.

“This year, 39 systems are scheduled for migration, with work on 36 nearing completion. Another 25 systems are being migrated or developed outside the plan, while 10 systems are already fully operational on the platform. This means the work is progressing ahead of schedule, and today all government agencies are already working with QazTech,” said Madiyev.

A moratorium on creating new government information systems outside QazTech has also been in effect since the beginning of 2026. The move is intended to consolidate digital development within a common technological environment, reduce duplicative systems and establish shared standards across government agencies.

Kazakhstan launches eGov 3.0

The government has also launched eGov 3.0, an upgraded version of Kazakhstan’s electronic government portal built on the QazTech platform.

According to Madiyev, the previous eGov portal had reached the limits of its technological capacity, prompting the launch of eGov 3.0 on the QazTech platform. The upgraded portal simplifies services by removing unnecessary requirements and steps, with several of the most frequently requested services already available in the new format.

The modernization is aimed at simplifying access to public services while reducing pressure on government digital infrastructure as demand for online services continues to grow.

According to the latest United Nations e-government survey published in 2024, Kazakhstan ranks 24th among 193 countries in the E-Government Development Index, with a score of 0.9009, placing it in the UN’s “very high” e-government development group.

World.title: What Lies Behind Kazakhstan’s External Debt
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s external debt rose 7.5% year on year to $182.8 billion as of April 1. External liabilities of the government and state-controlled institutions jumped 39%, while private-sector debt remained virtually unchanged and intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment declined 5.5% in one year.

The National Bank defines external debt as debt obligations of Kazakhstan’s residents to nonresidents. The measure covers both public- and private-sector liabilities and includes debt regardless of the currency in which it is denominated.

From April 1, 2025 to April 1, 2026, gross external debt increased from $170 billion to $182.8 billion, up $12.8 billion, or 7.5%. Intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment fell from $92.5 billion to $87.4 billion, a decline of 5.5%. As of April, $19.2 billion was owed by banks, an increase from $14.6 billion a year earlier.

Public external debt rose from $14.7 to $18.9 billion in a year. The figures show that most of Kazakhstan’s external liabilities remain outside the government balance sheet. The latest National Bank data points to sovereign and state-controlled borrowers accounting for a growing share of the increase since the start of 2025.

Kazakhstan’s external debt is predominantly long term, with 87.1% carrying an original maturity of more than one year. According to the National Bank, that limits immediate liquidity pressure, but it does not remove longer-term risks, as refinancing and servicing costs can rise when global financial conditions tighten. Loans and borrowings from nonresidents make up 69.2% of the total, while debt securities held by foreign investors account for 13%.

By creditor jurisdiction, the Netherlands accounted for the largest share of Kazakhstan’s external debt as of April 1, at approximately $40.8 billion, followed by the United Kingdom at $19.8 billion, Russia at $16.7 billion, China at $13.8 billion and the United States at $11 billion.

The figures should not be interpreted as direct bilateral government lending, however, as they include corporate and intercompany liabilities and may reflect the jurisdiction through which financial claims are held or administered. In the case of the Netherlands, data from the National Bank shows that of $41 billion total, government debt is only $21 million, banks – $11 million and intercompany debt – $38.23 billion, so roughly 94% of Kazakhstan’s debt recorded against the Netherlands is intercompany FDI debt.

External debt of Central Asian countries excluding Turkmenistan increased by 34.9% over the past five years, reaching nearly $290.8 billion in 2025, according to data from the CIS Statistical Committee and the Eurasian Economic Commission. Kazakhstan accounted for 62.5% of the total.

Despite having by far the largest external debt stock in Central Asia, Kazakhstan’s general government debt burden remains comparatively moderate. The International Monetary Fund data put general government gross debt at around 24.9% of GDP, compared with 27.5% in Uzbekistan and 37.4% in Kyrgyzstan.

The size of the debt, however, is only one measure of fiscal vulnerability. Economists also look at the cost of servicing it, its currency and maturity structure, and how borrowed funds are used. A country with a relatively high debt ratio can remain financially stable if investors retain confidence and debt-service costs remain manageable.

World.title: New Security Architecture: Future of Abraham Accords and  Emerging Strategic Landscape for Kazakhstan
World.content:
On July 22, Washington hosted an important hearing of the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa, titled “Building a New Regional Security Architecture: The Next Phase of the Abraham Accords.” American lawmakers, diplomats, and experts, including Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel, gathered at the Capitol to discuss the broader transformation of the framework under the auspices of the White House.

The hearing, together with the current geopolitical agenda, made one trend increasingly clear: the Abraham Accords have moved decisively beyond the confines of the Middle East and are evolving into a broader international coalition, with Kazakhstan assuming an important precedent-setting role.

The discussions in Congress provide valuable insight into the key trends likely to shape the future development of the Accords and help define Astana’s place within this emerging international architecture.

Resetting the framework: From a regional pact to a “Club of Power”

Speakers before Congress emphasized that the Abraham Accords have demonstrated their resilience even under the most difficult circumstances following the October 2023 crisis. The current strategy of the Donald Trump administration rests on two major pillars.

The U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal

The long-anticipated agreement on civilian nuclear cooperation between Washington and Riyadh has now been concluded. On July 22, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed an agreement establishing a framework for long-term cooperation on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

The significance of the agreement extends well beyond the energy sector. It represents an important element of the broader U.S. strategy to build a new regional architecture in which economic integration, advanced technology, energy cooperation, and security partnerships increasingly complement the normalization process associated with the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, the nuclear agreement should be viewed separately from the question of Saudi-Israeli normalization. While normalization remains an important strategic objective for Washington, the two tracks are not identical. The conclusion of the nuclear agreement nevertheless strengthens the broader strategic framework within which future regional arrangements may develop.

Expanding the Geographic Scope

The second pillar is the expansion of the Accords beyond their original Middle Eastern framework. Bringing influential states from outside the Arab world into the process demonstrates that the platform can serve as a broader mechanism for international cooperation, reinforcing its relevance, resilience, and legitimacy.

The Central Asian dimension: why do the Accords matter for Kazakhstan?

Kazakhstan’s formal accession to the Abraham Accords in November 2025 was highlighted at the congressional hearing as an important diplomatic precedent. Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel and a prominent American expert on the regional normalization process,emphasized in his testimony that Kazakhstan’s decision helped dispel skepticism about the framework and demonstrated its appeal beyond the Arab world, particularly among moderate Muslim-majority states.

Against the backdrop of today’s geopolitical turbulence, participation in the Accords offers Kazakhstan three strategic opportunities.

Diplomatic Balancing and Multi-Vector Foreign Policy

Positioned at the intersection of Russian and Chinese interests, Astana can use the platform as an additional instrument for diversifying its international partnerships. This allows Kazakhstan to broaden its network of strategic partners without entering into direct confrontation with regional powers or Tehran.

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s engagement with the Abraham Accords should not be interpreted as a departure from its traditional multi-vector foreign policy. Rather, it reflects an adaptation of that policy to a rapidly changing global environment.

Experts increasingly point to a shift from a largely passive model of maneuvering between major powers toward a more active model of pragmatic and sovereign balancing, in which foreign policy is increasingly anchored in the protection of national interests and economic security.

Under this approach, diversification is not an end in itself. It is a strategic instrument designed to preserve Kazakhstan’s sovereignty, expand its room for maneuver, reduce excessive dependence on any single external partner, and secure access to capital, technology, markets, and critical infrastructure.

Participation in the Abraham Accords therefore fits within the broader evolution of Kazakhstan’s foreign policy: not a rejection of multi-vector diplomacy, but its modernization in response to a more fragmented, competitive, and unpredictable international system.

A Direct Track to Washington

Demonstrating support for U.S.-backed peace and normalization initiatives can strengthen Kazakhstan’s standing in Washington. This is particularly important for safeguarding long-term American investment in Kazakhstan’s energy sector and critical minerals, while also helping the country navigate the risks created by global tariff disputes and geopolitical fragmentation.

For Astana, closer engagement with the United States through emerging regional frameworks can therefore serve both diplomatic and economic purposes. It creates an additional channel for dialogue with Washington while reinforcing Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of maintaining diversified external partnerships.

A Pragmatic Economic Foundation

The expanding framework can provide Astana with access to new sources of capital and technology. Wealthy Gulf states, particularly the United Arab Emirates, can contribute financing to major infrastructure and connectivity projects, while Israel offers advanced expertise in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, water management, agricultural technology, and resource efficiency.

For Kazakhstan, therefore, the value of the Accords lies not simply in diplomatic symbolism. Their importance increasingly rests on the possibility of connecting different pools of capital, technology, infrastructure, and political influence within a broader international framework.

At the same time, as experts at the hearing made clear, Kazakhstan retains its sovereign position. Participation in the Accords does not alter Astana’s commitment to a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or its support for humanitarian efforts. Kazakhstan can therefore participate in the emerging framework while maintaining its established position on the Palestinian issue.

The future of the Abraham Accords lies in their transformation from a primarily regional political and security framework into a broader international network encompassing security, connectivity, logistics, energy, investment, and technological cooperation under U.S. leadership.

The developments of 2026 suggest that this transformation is already underway. The expansion of the Accords beyond the Arab world, Kazakhstan’s participation, and the newly concluded U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement all point toward an emerging architecture that is considerably broader than the original normalization framework.

For Kazakhstan, the Abraham Accords are therefore becoming more than a symbolic diplomatic gesture. They represent an additional instrument of the country’s long-standing multi-vector foreign policy — one that can help Astana diversify strategic partnerships, attract new investment and technology, deepen its engagement with Washington and the Gulf states, and strengthen its resilience amid growing geopolitical competition.

The strategic opportunity for Kazakhstan lies in turning its early participation into practical cooperation — transforming diplomatic positioning into tangible economic benefits, technological partnerships, and greater geopolitical resilience.

The author is Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform, an independent think tank based at Astana International University.

World.title: Sport’s Next Generation Won’t Choose Sides, Says Phygital International CEO
World.content:
ASTANA — Phygital sport’s future will depend on building lasting local ecosystems, developing a new generation of athletes skilled in both physical and digital competition, and establishing itself as a distinct international sporting movement, Phygital International CEO Daniel Merkley said in an exclusive interview with The Astana Times.

The Games of the Future 2026 powered by Samruk Kazyna (GOTF 2026) concluded in Astana on Aug. 9 after 12 days of competition across eight disciplines. With the event over, attention is turning to what comes next for phygital sport and how it can develop beyond major international tournaments.

Drawing on more than 20 years of experience working on Olympic and Paralympic events, Merkley said phygital sport has much to learn from established sporting institutions, particularly in governance, athlete-centered development and trust.

“One of the greatest lessons from the Olympic and Paralympic Movement is that lasting success comes from strong governance, clear values and a commitment to serving athletes first. Major sporting movements are built over decades through trust, consistency and collaboration, and those principles are just as relevant for phygital sport,” said Merkley.

“At the same time, we should not assume that because something has always been done a certain way, it is the right approach for a new generation,” he added.

For Merkley, strong governance – the rules, decision-making and accountability behind how a sport is organized – will be essential to building international credibility. However, he emphasized that the emerging movement should not simply reproduce the structures of traditional sport.

“Rather than asking young people to adapt to traditional sport, we can meet them where they already are. That means embracing technology, creating more engaging experiences for athletes and fans, and building a model that reflects how younger generations participate, compete and consume sport today,” said Merkley.

“Ultimately, our goal is not to replace traditional sport. It is to create something complementary that learns from its strengths while being confident enough to evolve in its own direction,” he said.

Astana’s legacy will be measured in years

According to Merkley, the most meaningful outcome for Kazakhstan will not be found in final scores, viewing figures or the scale of the event itself.

“The real measure of success won’t be what happens during these 12 days of competition. It will be what happens over the next three, five or even 10 years. If, in a few years’ time, Kazakhstan has more young people participating in phygital sport, a growing calendar of competitions, stronger links between sport, education and technology, and a new generation of athletes developing both physical and digital skills, then we’ll know these Games have created something that lasts,” he said.

He noted that impact could extend beyond organized competition, particularly as Kazakhstan places greater emphasis on innovation, technology and artificial intelligence. An event linking sport with digital skills can introduce young people to opportunities beyond the competition itself.

“If these Games encourage more young people to engage with technology, develop new skills and see opportunities at the intersection of sport and innovation, that is a powerful legacy in itself,” said Merkley.

He said Phygital International also works with host cities and partners to support continued development after the flagship event ends, to create local structures capable of sustaining participation and attracting future investment.

“Ultimately, success means leaving behind a stronger phygital ecosystem that continues to inspire young people, attract investment and create new opportunities long after the closing ceremony,” he said.

A new type of athlete

That distinction is also reflected in the demands placed on competitors themselves. In phygital sport, athletes compete across digital and physical stages within the same discipline. Depending on the format, a video game result can carry into football, basketball, combat sports or another physical contest, requiring competitors to perform effectively in both environments.

For Merkley, that combination is beginning to produce athletes who no longer fit neatly into the traditional distinction between gamers and sports competitors.

“What makes phygital athletes unique is that they cannot rely on excellence in just one environment. They have to combine elite gaming ability with high-level physical performance, while also being able to transition seamlessly between the two under competitive pressure. That demands technical skill, tactical intelligence, physical fitness, mental resilience and adaptability in equal measure,” said Merkley.

As competition develops, he expects training systems to become increasingly specialized around those combined demands. Coaches could prepare athletes for both stages, supported by sports science in areas such as physiology, biomechanics, psychology and performance analysis tailored specifically to phygital competition.

“I think we’re witnessing the emergence of a new type of athlete – one who develops physical excellence and digital mastery in parallel. (…) I also believe we’ll see more young athletes developing physical and digital skills side by side, rather than feeling they have to choose between traditional sport and gaming,” he said.

Becoming a category of its own

Phygital sport currently sits at the intersection of several industries, combining elements of international sport and entertainment while connecting traditional sports organizations, esports and technology companies.

“I don’t think those possibilities are mutually exclusive. Phygital sport has the potential to become a recognized international sporting movement while also delivering world-class entertainment and creating meaningful connections between traditional sport, esports and technology. What is important is that we do not define ourselves solely by comparison with existing models,” he said.

His long-term ambition is for the Games of the Future to become one of the world’s leading international sporting events while developing an identity that does not depend on resembling the Olympics, esports tournaments or any other existing model.

“Achieving that will require disciplined choices. We must protect sporting integrity, maintain high competitive standards and continue building trusted relationships with athletes, publishers, sports organizations, governments and commercial partners,” Merkley said.

“If we can balance those priorities, I believe phygital sport can become one of the defining sporting movements of the next generation,” he added.

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”
