World.title: Mecca defence pact: new opportunities for South Caucasus and Azerbaijan
World.content:
Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

The joint defence agreement signed in Mecca on 7 August marks an important step towards shaping the region’s security architecture, establishing collective defence commitments between three leading Muslim-majority states.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the agreement. It stipulates that an armed attack on one party will be treated as an attack on the other two.

The agreement also has the potential to influence the future security architecture of the South Caucasus.

Context of the Mecca joint defence agreement

The agreement builds on the Saudi-Pakistani Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed in September 2025. Official statements describe it as a purely defensive mechanism that does not target any country, including Iran, and has no religious or sectarian basis.

The parties stress that the agreement remains open to expansion. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that, technically, the deal resembles Article 5 of NATO. He said the parties plan to establish a ministerial-level committee and a secretariat based in Saudi Arabia. Erdogan’s vision includes expanding the initial three-member group and potentially involving other countries, including Egypt.

The strength of the agreement lies in the complementary advantages of its members. Turkey has NATO’s second-largest army and a developed defence industry, particularly in unmanned aerial vehicles. Saudi Arabia has significant financial resources, energy reserves and a unique symbolic status in the Muslim world. Pakistan, meanwhile, has a large and experienced military and is the only Muslim-majority country with nuclear weapons.

At the same time, the agreement does not establish an integrated command structure like NATO’s. The parties are still working out its operational details.

Prospects for expansion and the South Caucasus

In comments to Report on 9 August, Fidan said he did not rule out a similar joint defence agreement with South Caucasus countries.

He highlighted Turkey’s strategic role as a link between the Middle East, the Caucasus, the Mediterranean and Europe. He also said that completing the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia could open new security and economic opportunities. In the future, this could create conditions for a similar mechanism.

The statement does not amount to an official invitation. However, it opens the door to discussions about long-term scenarios for the region.

Azerbaijan’s position and the question of ties with Israel

Azerbaijan already maintains close relations with all three members of the agreement. The 2021 Shusha Declaration provides for mutual assistance with Turkey. Turkey, Azerbaijan and Pakistan also cooperate in a trilateral format, including summits held in Lachin in 2025. Defence industry cooperation is expanding, while Saudi Arabia’s investment interest is growing. Although Baku remains outside the formal agreement, it maintains privileged relations with all three capitals.

Israel is a particularly important issue in this context. Some social media posts have claimed that Azerbaijan would supposedly “give up recognition of Israel” if it joined the agreement.

Azerbaijan’s strategic partnership with Israel – including arms supplies that played an important role in the 2020 war, oil exports, intelligence cooperation and technology – is long-standing and stable.

There is no evidence in official sources that the members of the Mecca agreement have demanded or made it a condition for Azerbaijan to sever ties with Israel or withdraw its recognition of the country. Baku has repeatedly shown that it can act as an unofficial mediator between Turkey and Israel. Formal participation in the agreement could test this balance, but Azerbaijan’s current policy prioritises a flexible, multi-vector foreign policy. Claims that “Azerbaijan must give up recognition of Israel to join the agreement” are not supported by specific evidence and remain rumours for now.

Benefits and risks in the context of multi-vector policy

Potential benefits for the South Caucasus and Azerbaijan include stronger collective deterrence, expanded defence industry and technological capabilities, an influx of Saudi capital, synergies with the Middle Corridor, stronger symbolic ties between Turkic and the broader Muslim worlds, and greater strategic autonomy amid questions surrounding external security guarantees.

Azerbaijan could benefit from closer ties among its partners without formally joining the agreement, while retaining room to manoeuvre in its relations with the West, Israel, Central Asia and other partners.

There are also risks. These include the possibility of becoming involved in Middle Eastern conflicts, including tensions involving Iran; potential pressure on relations with Israel and Azerbaijan’s image in the West; and possible negative effects on the peace process with Armenia or ties with Iran and Russia. Another risk is the new format’s institutional immaturity, particularly the absence of a clearly defined commitment to automatically deploy military forces.

Azerbaijan’s tradition of an independent, non-aligned foreign policy makes full membership in the agreement in the near future unlikely.

Likelihood of joining and the limits of Azerbaijan’s multi-vector policy

Azerbaijan’s multi-vector foreign policy does not mean automatically distancing itself from new regional initiatives. Baku seeks to balance the interests of its partners and tends to join new platforms when suitable opportunities arise. Azerbaijan’s decision in 2026 to join the Board of Peace, established at the initiative of US President Donald Trump, as a founding member provides a practical example of this approach. Close ties with Turkey and Pakistan, the trilateral Turkey-Azerbaijan-Pakistan format and the Shusha Declaration could also increase Baku’s interest in the Mecca format.

The 2026 war with Iran demonstrated the practical limits of this balance more clearly. Azerbaijan officially declared neutrality, repeatedly stressed its support for Iran’s sovereignty and said its territory was not being used against third countries. However, several international media outlets, including CNN, reported that Israeli special forces and intelligence structures were allegedly deployed on Azerbaijani territory during the war. Baku called these claims “completely unfounded”.

Several think tanks, including the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), described Azerbaijan’s position as a “carefully maintained balance between its officially declared neutrality and practical rapprochement”. Turkey’s decision not to take part in the war and its advice to Baku to maintain a cautious position also influenced this approach.

This dynamic takes on additional significance in the context of the Mecca agreement. The agreement’s principle that “an attack on one is an attack on all”, along with Saudi Arabia’s response to Iranian strikes during the war, shows how collective defence commitments can operate during periods of real tension. Azerbaijan’s deep strategic partnership with Israel, its allied relations with Turkey and Pakistan, and its expanding ties with Saudi Arabia have led some experts to believe that this rapprochement could increase Baku’s interest in formats similar to the Mecca agreement.

For Azerbaijan, therefore, the main question is not so much whether to join the agreement, but how to benefit from closer ties among its existing partners – Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Israel – without taking on formal commitments. This is precisely the flexibility that its multi-vector policy provides.

Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

World.title: Number of Iranian companies in Georgia up 510% since 2012 – EPRC
World.content:
Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

According to data from the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the number of Iranian companies in Georgia has increased by around 510% since 2012, exceeding 12,800 by 2025–26.

EPRC says the figures are based on data from Geostat and the National Bank of Georgia. The organisation also notes that despite the sharp rise in the number of companies, foreign direct investment from Iran into Georgia has remained relatively low in recent years.

“Between 2013 and 2024, Iranian investment totalled $41 million. Although this is more than in the previous period, the amount per company remains quite small,” EPRC said.

According to the organisation, net foreign direct investment from Iran stood at -$0.65 million in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2025 put the figure at around $0.4 million.

EPRC estimates that Iran’s share of total foreign direct investment in Georgia remains small, according to official statistics.

The centre says Iranian companies registered in Georgia are mainly involved in small-scale trade, real estate transactions, services, construction, logistics and re-export.

“Most of this activity involves small and medium-sized businesses and is less connected to large-scale manufacturing, industrial or technology projects,” EPRC said.

The organisation notes that the activities of these companies have not led to significant job creation. It also says that dozens of companies are often registered at the same address.

According to EPRC, tourism has seen the most notable growth in economic activity linked to Iran. Between 2022 and 2024, tourism revenues from Iran rose from $91.1 million to $151.1 million, an increase of 65%. However, tourism revenues fell by 17.8% in 2025.

Why the number of Iranian companies is growing much faster than investment

The centre believes that the rapid increase in the number of companies, alongside relatively low levels of investment and official financial flows, raises questions about the true scale of their activities.

“Why is the number of Iranian companies growing much faster than investment and official financial inflows overall?” EPRC asks.

The organisation says that, given that a significant part of Iran’s financial sector operates under international sanctions, economic transactions may be taking place through alternative and potentially less transparent financial channels.

EPRC notes that if some economic activity takes place outside the traditional banking system or with limited transparency, this makes it harder for the state to effectively monitor financial flows. It also increases the risks of sanctions evasion and money laundering.

The centre also points to international practice, where such models are sometimes associated with nominal or so-called “paper” companies. These companies are officially registered, but their actual economic activity may be very limited.

According to EPRC, such companies are sometimes used for re-export operations, intermediary financial transactions, or to circumvent sanctions and regulatory requirements in different countries.

“When the number of companies grows rapidly but this is not accompanied by a corresponding increase in investment, production, exports or employment, questions arise about the real economic significance of their activities,” the organisation said.

EPRC also points to the visa-free regime between Georgia and the EU, saying that this could make the country more attractive to Iranian citizens and businesses.

According to the centre, the US sanctions imposed on Shelbit, a cryptocurrency company registered in Georgia and owned by an Iranian citizen, highlight the range of possible ways to circumvent sanctions.

EPRC believes that, in light of this case and the sharp increase in the number of companies opened in Georgia by Iranian citizens, the current figures should be viewed with additional risks in mind.

Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi’s new zoo ready to welcome visitors – video
World.content:
The new Tbilisi Zoo will open to visitors in August 2026. Construction began after the 2015 floods, and the zoo is opening in stages. Although work is still under way, visitors will soon be able to explore the new site.

One of Tbilisi Zoo’s best-known residents, Shani the lion cub, has already moved to the new zoo.

___________________________________________

___________________________________________

As David Taktakishvili, deputy director of Tbilisi Zoo, explains, the new zoo covers a large area, and the site is being developed in stages. Some animals have already been moved, but construction of the enclosures is still under way. Construction and infrastructure work will therefore continue after the zoo opens.

The zoo administration believes the public should already have the opportunity to see for themselves how a new-generation zoo is taking shape and how much better the animals will live in their new environment.

When the new zoo opens to visitors, the Caucasus biogeographical zone will be accessible to the public. In the future, the zoo will bring together spaces representing different regions of the world. At the first stage, however, the focus will be on the local flora and fauna of the Caucasus. Visitors will see red deer, bison, bears, wolves and other local species in this zone.

Construction of the African zone is currently under way. The new zoo will gradually add other biogeographical zones in the future.

In recent years, the role of zoos has also changed significantly. Today, one of their main functions is nature conservation, including protecting, breeding and caring for endangered species. The new, modern facility will serve this purpose and, in the future, will become not only a place for visitors but also an important wildlife conservation centre.

Admission prices will remain unchanged: free for children under three, 2 lari ($0.76) for children aged three to 12, and 4 lari ($1.53) for visitors aged 12 and over.

Some animals will remain at the old zoo, which will continue to operate as usual.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

New Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgian opposition figure investigated for ‘treason’ over comments on Abkhazia war
World.content:
Giorgi Baramidze case

Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation into comments by Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, about the war in Abkhazia. The case concerns charges of treason and actions that threaten state interests. The investigation focuses on his account of how prisoners of war were treated during the early stages of the conflict. Baramidze made the comments on a podcast, triggering a political backlash. The de facto authorities in Abkhazia have also reacted to his remarks.

What did Baramidze say?

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, discussed the war in Abkhazia on Yago Khvichia’s “Birth of Georgia” programme.

Speaking about the exchange of prisoners, he said:

“We did not take prisoners, we had no prisoners, we executed them.”

The remark prompted a strong reaction from government officials. Baramidze later clarified several times what he meant.

He said he was referring to the early stages of the war, when the Georgian side did not yet have a regular and organised army. Baramidze later explained that people enraged by the deaths of their relatives in the fighting did not take enemy fighters prisoner.

“At first, the situation was as follows: people who were enraged after their mothers, fathers and relatives had been killed did not take prisoners during the fighting but killed them instead. That is the bitter truth about the early stages of the war. I know this because I personally took part in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze said.

According to him, the situation later changed. The Georgian side began taking prisoners, which made exchanges possible. Baramidze said that around 200 Georgian prisoners were eventually brought home as a result.

“My deputy and I could not have exchanged 200 Georgian prisoners if our side had not taken any prisoners at all,” he added.

Baramidze also denies that his comments were directed against the Georgian army or the state as a whole. He insists that he was referring specifically to the situation during the early stages of the war.

At the same time, he stressed Russia’s responsibility, saying that the Russian Federation acted as an aggressor and occupier in the wars of 1992–93 and 2008.

Why has the prosecutor’s office opened an investigation?

Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office opened the investigation at the request of the State Service of Veterans Affairs.

According to the agency, prosecutors are investigating the case under Articles 307¹ and 318 of the Criminal Code. The first concerns treason, while the second covers actions that threaten Georgia’s state interests.

The prosecutor’s office said:

“The investigation began following an appeal from the State Service of Veterans Affairs concerning comments made by Giorgi Baramidze, a member of the United National Movement. The case concerns his remarks about the war in Abkhazia and the prisoner exchange process, which he made on Yago Khvichia’s programme ‘Birth of Georgia’.”

As part of the investigation, prosecutors also summoned Koba Kobaladze, head of the State Service of Veterans Affairs, for questioning.

Baramidze sees the investigation as political persecution.

“The prosecutor’s office has opened a case against me for ‘betraying Georgia’! I am not afraid of your persecution, let alone your dirty propaganda!” he wrote on social media.

What does the government say?

Members of the Georgian Dream party do not consider Baramidze’s remarks simply an unfortunate choice of words. They argue that such statements could harm Georgia’s national interests and international standing.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described Baramidze’s comments as morally unacceptable. As for the legal assessment, he said the relevant authorities should make that decision.

“As for the legal aspect, the relevant authorities will determine that, but from a moral standpoint, what this man said is simply disgusting,” Kobakhidze said.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili linked Baramidze’s remarks to a broader political context. He said the opposition had previously promoted what he called a harmful narrative about Georgia’s 2008 war, and that the same was now happening with the war in Abkhazia.

Alexander Tabatadze, chairman of the parliamentary Defence and Security Committee, said Baramidze’s comments could damage Georgia’s international standing.

He argued that such remarks could be used against Georgia. Tabatadze also said the wording insulted veterans of the Abkhazia war and those who were killed in the fighting.

The opposition also criticises the remarks

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Baramidze’s comments were inaccurate. However, he argued that an incorrect statement did not amount to treason.

“What was said is not true… I don’t know where this story came from. In my view, the words got ahead of the meaning, and that is not good. But treason and a crime are different things, and this is not how they are committed,” Gvaramia said.

He said he had no doubts about Baramidze’s patriotism. He described the prosecutor’s investigation as political persecution.

Shalva Kereselidze, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, called Baramidze’s remarks politically inappropriate and unworthy of a statesman.

“This is a statement unworthy of a statesman, and it is inappropriate both politically and from a human standpoint,” Kereselidze said.

The United National Movement, meanwhile, says the investigation is entirely politically motivated. The party also pointed out that Baramidze fought in the wars in Abkhazia and Ukraine.

“While the Kremlin regards Giorgi Baramidze as an enemy and persecutes him, the Georgian Dream government is accusing the same person of treason,” the party said in a statement.

Expert: “Baramidze’s account does not match the facts”

Conflict expert and former state minister Paata Zakareishvili has questioned the factual accuracy of Baramidze’s account.

Zakareishvili himself worked on prisoner exchanges during the Abkhazia war. He said Baramidze’s account differed so sharply from the realities of the time that he initially thought Baramidze was referring to a different war.

He also disputed Baramidze’s claim that he took part in the work of the prisoner exchange commission.

“Baramidze mentions this commission, but to be honest, he did not take part in its work,” Zakareishvili said.

He noted that documents exist detailing the commission’s work, but Baramidze’s name does not appear in them.

At the same time, Zakareishvili questioned the legal grounds for the investigation. In his view, false or exaggerated statements should not provide grounds for criminal prosecution.

“I still believe that Baramidze does not deserve punishment. I will do everything I can to prove that he was not a member of the commission. His comments are simply speculation, nothing more,” Zakareishvili said.

He also said he was ready to provide the prosecutor’s office with the information he has.

How the case moved beyond the domestic political conflict

The de facto Abkhaz foreign ministry has already responded to Baramidze’s remarks.

The ministry used his comments to reinforce its own historical narrative about the conflict. Its statement described the 1992–93 war as Georgia’s armed aggression against Abkhazia.

Sukhumi also criticised the investigation into Baramidze.

“It is clear that this criminal prosecution should serve as a warning to anyone prepared to speak openly about Georgia’s armed aggression and the crimes committed during it,” the statement said.

Giorgi Baramidze case

World.title: ‘Regional stability is main achievement’: assessing Washington peace summit one year on
World.content:
Washington peace summit: one year on

“The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is visible and tangible to everyone,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in a statement marking the events of 8 August.

A year ago, on this day, Washington hosted a historic peace summit, with US President Donald Trump acting as mediator. Yerevan and Baku initialled a peace agreement, signed a declaration on the TRIPP project – a transit route through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan (the “Trump Route”) – and signed a number of bilateral documents with the United States.

Pashinyan said the peace agreement “awaits signing and ratification”. He added that practical work on TRIPP would begin in the near future and become a “major regional and international event”.

The prime minister congratulated the people of Armenia and Azerbaijan on the landmark date of 8 August.

“Finally, we have a day that brings peace rather than stirs up our emotions,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also issued a statement, highlighting the “courage and foresight” shown by both countries over the past year.

“We look forward to further progress towards lasting and durable peace in the South Caucasus,” the secretary of state said.

Pashinyan held phone calls with Donald Trump and Ilham Aliyev.

Armenian analysts said the main outcome of the Washington summit was the establishment of stability in the region.

They noted positive developments despite what they described as Baku’s “aggressive agenda”, including its calls for Azerbaijanis to return to what it calls “Western Azerbaijan”. The term refers to almost the entire sovereign territory of Armenia.

Pashinyan on unresolved issues and how to make “peace irreversible”

In his address to the nation, Pashinyan once again said that peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been established.

“But this, of course, does not mean that we have already reached the end of the road in implementing the peace agenda,” he added.

According to the prime minister, the following issues remain unresolved:

signing and ratifying the peace agreement,

delimiting the Armenian-Azerbaijani border,

“the continued detention of our compatriots in Azerbaijan” [referring to 19 Armenian prisoners held in Baku].

He also said that 8 August 2025 had marked a turning point, dividing Armenia’s history into the periods “before and after this date”. Pashinyan described the period before 8 August as a dead end, while the period since then has offered “limitless opportunities”.

Pashinyan said the main political and social-psychological result of the Washington summit was that “the wheel of our history has once again fallen into our hands”.

He identified the implementation of the “Trump Route” project as another major outcome:

“It will not only end Armenia’s blockade in the very near future and become the backbone of Armenia’s and the region’s economy, but will also help Armenia and Azerbaijan start seeing each other not as an obstacle, but as a route and as a neighbour.”

The transit route was named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” after the mediator, as the Armenian and Azerbaijani authorities had been unable to reach an agreement on the issue for several years.

Pashinyan also outlined steps that Armenia and Azerbaijan should take to make the peace between them irreversible:

“We need to put an end to discussions about the ‘right of Armenians to return to Nagorno-Karabakh’ and the ‘return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan’. Azerbaijan, for its part, needs to end discussions about ‘Western Azerbaijan’ and the ‘right of Western Azerbaijanis to return’. This is an issue that both Armenia and Azerbaijan must resolve in the name of our generations’ right to live together in peace.”

“We hope to see further progress”, Rubio says

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that over the past 12 months, the United States had continued to work with Armenia and Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of the TRIPP project. According to Rubio, the transit route is gradually becoming a reality:

“Engineering work on the railway has already begun in Armenia, while construction of the highway and railway linking Azerbaijan with Armenia is nearly complete.”

He stressed that TRIPP is not simply an infrastructure project but also an important link in the Trans-Caspian trade route. It could drive new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries.

“It is a factor that opens up new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries. It is also an example of how economic cooperation can strengthen peace after long-standing disputes have been resolved,” Rubio said.

He added that peace had created an opportunity to deepen relations between the United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan. This, he said, would contribute to the economic prosperity of all three countries.

Thanks to Trump

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked him for organising the peace summit and for signing the peace declaration adopted by the Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders as a testament to the agreement. He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington. They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: 'He was there': Witness rejects claim by farmer accused of triple murder
World.content:
A man who told a triple murder trial jury that he and his family were shot by Queensland cattle farmer Darryl Valroy Young has angrily rejected claims the farmer was never at the alleged shooting.

Ross Tighe, 34, was the first witness to be called in the trial of Mr Young in the Supreme Court in Townsville.

Mr Young is charged with the attempted murder of Mr Tighe and the murder of his brother Graham Tighe, mother Maree Schwarz and stepfather Mervyn Schwarz.

Mr Young has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Mr Young is accused of killing Ross Tighe's mother, brother and stepfather. ( ABC News: Carole Howlett)

The jury trial has heard that Mr Young is accused of using a rifle to shoot the four family members when they attended the gate of his Bogie cattle property for a meeting on August 4, 2022.

Mr Young’s lawyer Anthony J Kimmins told jurors the farmer never saw the Tighes or the Schwarzes, who worked a neighbouring cattle station, on that day.

Mr Kimmins asked jurors to consider if anyone else had a motive to kill.

Mr Young's lawyer told jurors he denied ever seeing the Schwarzes or the Tighes on the day they were shot. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

'He was there'

Mr Kimmins began his cross-examination of Ross Tighe on Tuesday afternoon and concluded it on Wednesday by suggesting Mr Young was never at the gate at the time of the alleged shooting.

“Could I suggest to you Mr Tighe that on the morning of August 4, 2022 at around 8am Darryl Young was not at the front gate of the premises but you, your brother and your parents were there?" he asked.

Defence lawyer Anthony J Kimmins (right) is representing Mr Young. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

Mr Tighe raised his voiced, said "he was there" and told Mr Kimmins to repeat the question.

“Darryl was at the front gate,” Mr Tighe yelled.

Earlier Mr Kimmins questioned Mr Tighe on a range of topics.

The court viewed photos of the shirt Mr Tighe was wearing on the day he said he was shot, as well as a photo of the driver's seat in the car he said he drove while wounded.

Mr Kimmins asked Mr Tighe about the absence of a bullet entry hole on his shirt and the absence of blood in the car.

“Entry holes aren’t really that big — it didn't bleed that much,” Mr Tighe said.

Mr Tighe was also asked whether he had made a civil claim against Mr Young for injuries suffered, which he confirmed.

Ross Tighe gave evidence via video link from the Mackay courthouse on Wednesday. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Criminal past

The court heard Mr Tighe had a history of drug use and had been charged with the possession of both cannabis and MDMA as well as obstructing police.

Mr Tighe answered questions about his criminal history but was critical of Mr Kimmins.

"Scraping the bottom of the barrel a bit," he said.

Justice Christopher Johnstone warned Mr Tighe against commenting on the line of questioning.

The court heard that after one of Mr Tighe’s convictions he lost his gun licence which he confirmed but said he could not pinpoint when that happened.

Mr Kimmins also asked Mr Tighe if he ever grew cannabis or assisted anyone to grow cannabis.

He did not answer and instead claimed legal privilege.

The Supreme Court Trial in Townsville is expected to run for three weeks. (ABC North Queensland: Rachael Merritt)

Texts shown

Text messages exchanged between Ross Tighe and his former partner, who cannot be named for legal reasons, were also shown to the court.

"What has this got to do with anything?" Mr Tighe asked.

Mr Kimmins asked if one message from Mr Tighe’s ex-girlfriend indicated the couple, who had a young child, was struggling financially while working for his family’s cattle business.

"I am stressed about having no money," the message from his then-girlfriend read.

"We were trying to save more money," Mr Tighe explained to the court.

The court was shown Mr Tighe’s tax return from 2021-22 which stated that he had earned $35,688 over 12 months with the majority of the income from his family’s business.

The court was also shown messages between the couple which made mention of physical violence and a domestic violence order (DVO).

In his evidence, Mr Tighe denied he had been physically violent towards the woman and denied that he had a DVO placed on him.

Mr Tighe finished giving evidence on Wednesday.

The trial continues.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies, league star Brian Smith dies of cancer
World.content:
Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.

Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.

Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.

"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.

"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."

Australia's 999th Wallaby's Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.

"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.

"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.

"So, yeah, very sad."

After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.

Australian forward Angus Bell - in Wallabies camp in Townsville - paid tribute to his former high school coach and mentor Brian Smith. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.

"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.

"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.

"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

AAP

World.title: Former Hurricanes cricketer jailed for abusing 15yo girl
World.content:
A former Hobart Hurricanes cricket player will serve 10 months in prison for sexually abusing a child.

WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual abuse.

Aaron William Summers, 30, pleaded guilty to two counts of penetrative sexual abuse of a young person and one count of grooming in June in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, after having previously pleaded not guilty.

In court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in jail, suspended after 10 months, meaning he will leave prison in April next year.

Justice Helen Wood told the court that Summers met the victim at a Hobart Hurricanes cricket match in 2017.

The following month, the 15-year-old girl attended another game and spoke to Summers, who was 21 at the time.

Aaron Summers was playing for the Hobart Hurricanes when he met the 15-year-old girl. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

The pair began messaging on social media, and Summers arranged to pick her up from her home later that night.

The court heard he drove her to a local primary school, laid down a blanket, and sexually abused her twice.

Justice Wood told the court that Summers knew she was under the age of 17 and at high school, but did not ask how old she was.

"She thought they were meeting to talk; in reality, she represented a sexual opportunity to him," Justice Wood said.

"She was vulnerable because of her age and innocence; he had said nothing to warn her of his real motives."

The grooming charge related to social media conversations between Summers and the girl, in which Summers sent explicit photos of himself and requested photos from her.

"As a community, we look up to sportspeople; young people are likely to admire them, see them in a positive light," Justice Woods said.

"His role as a sportsperson gave him contact with young people, and enabled the commission of his crimes; this is an aggravating factor."

In November 2021, Summers pleaded guilty to charges in the Northern Territory, including possessing and transmitting child abuse material and transmitting communication with someone under 16 with the intention of procuring the recipient to engage in, or make, sexual activity.

Summers served three years and 11 months in prison in the NT. He was arrested on the day of his release and extradited to Tasmania to face these charges.

Cricket career 'at an end'

Justice Wood said Summers had experienced social isolation, loneliness and depressive symptoms while playing cricket in Tasmania and was spending excessive time on social media.

She said once he moved to the Northern Territory, he had established a successful career playing cricket in Australia and overseas and had a high profile.

"Due to the crimes, his future as a professional cricketer is at an end," she said.

Twenty months of the sentence was suspended, meaning Aaron Summers (left) is set for release in April next year. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Justice Wood said that Summers has accepted responsibility for his crimes and understood the impact his offending has had on his victims.

In the NT, he completed an intensive sex offender treatment program, which involved over 100 sessions, in which Justice Wood told the court he engaged appropriately and gained insight into his offending.

Justice Wood said when deciding on his sentence, she considered the lengthy jail time he had already served in the NT after the Tasmanian crimes were committed, and the significant progress he has taken towards his rehabilitation.

"[The] understanding he has about the harm he has caused and he is motivated to regain his life," she said.

Justice Wood imposed a sentence of two-and-a-half years, backdated to June 28 of this year, due to the time he has spent in remand.

She suspended the last 20 months of the sentence, with strict conditions, such as obliging him to comply with his probation officers and submit to psychological treatment.

The court heard that Summers would likely return to Western Australia, where he is from and his family live, to serve out his suspended sentence once he is able to leave prison in April next year.

World.title: Coroner says off-road racing needs stronger fire safety rules
World.content:
A coroner investigating an off-road racing crash that killed two people in Victoria's north-west is recommending stronger fire safety requirements for vehicles and competitors.

On September 4, 2022, Gerald Hoekstra, 46, and Ede Taric, 50, were competing in the Desert Enduro Race at Rainbow, about 400 kilometres north-west of Melbourne, when Mr Hoekstra lost control of their vehicle and crashed into a tree.

The vehicle rolled, landed on its side and was engulfed in flames.



Two competitor teams stopped to help, and saw Mr Hoekstra attempting to exit the vehicle.

They unsuccessfully tried to douse the flames with fire extinguishers.

Both the driver, Mr Hoekstra, and passenger, Mr Taric, died at the scene.

In her investigation, Coroner Ingrid Giles explored the circumstances that caused the crash and subsequent fire, the attempts to extinguish the fire, associated safety equipment, and the ability of the men to exit their vehicle after the crash.

Ms Giles found that both men had survived the initial crash, but died when fire "rapidly engulfed the vehicle".

She found the fire could not be extinguished until the local Country Fire Authority (CFA) arrived 12 to 13 minutes later, and said that their deaths were "unspeakably tragic".

Fire extinguishers 'inadequate', coroner finds

The men had been racing in a modified Can-Am Maverick X3 side-by-side buggy, which could reach speeds of 130km/h and had been fitted with hand-held fire extinguishers as well as two auxiliary 35-litre fuel tanks.

In her report, Ms Giles said the vehicle had been inspected by a scrutineer on the Friday prior to racing, and was confirmed to be compliant with requirements laid out by Motorsport Australia (MSA).

During the investigation, Victoria Police's arson chemist, forensic officer John Kelleher, said the fire was likely caused by heat from the buggy's catalytic converter igniting fuel that had spilled around the vehicle after the crash.



"Having seen the buggy and watched the video footage of the fire starting, there is no doubt that the cause of the fire was the ignition of petrol vapour rising from the spilled fuel puddling beneath the filler," Mr Kelleher said at the time.

"The position of the catalytic converter and its location immediately above the spilled fuel raises the possibility that it was the source of ignition."

The Desert Enduro car race was held at Rainbow in north-west Victoria. (Motorsport Australia)

Ms Giles found the fuel tanks had been installed correctly, and were compliant with safety requirements at the time.

However, the tanks had a plastic fuel cap and filler neck that protruded from the buggy's safety cage, leaving them "vulnerable to damage", she said.

Upon collision, the cap detached from the filler neck on one of the tanks, which did not contain a reflux valve — a one-way valve that automatically closes if the tank is up-ended.

Ms Giles said given the filler neck was not fitted with a reflux valve, petrol flowed freely and was able to combust easily.

"I consider that, had a reflux valve been present, the fire would have most likely been prevented, in that the fuel would not have spilled freely from the tank,” she said.

MSA regulations at the time required each competing vehicle to be fitted with a hand-held fire extinguisher, which Ms Giles found to be "inadequate" given the fire could not be safely extinguished without the CFA's help.

Ms Giles said a plumbed-in fire extinguisher system may have been more effective.

“Plumbed-in systems are primarily designed to provide the occupants with an immediate extinguisher response that can increase the amount of time available to extricate from the vehicle during an incident, and limit the effect of the fire on the occupant," she said.

Decisive action

At the time of the event, MSA also required vehicles to be designed so racing crews could exit their vehicle within 10 seconds during an emergency.

However, it was up to competitors to comply with the requirement, which was "not formally assessed".

“At the time of Gerald and Ede’s collision, there was no mandatory self-extrication time frame, and no testing was performed of competitors' ability to do so," the coroner found.

Ms Giles credited MSA for making changes following Mr Hoekstra's and Mr Taric's deaths, and said its decisive action had "obviated the need for an extensive suite of coronial recommendations".

Since the incident, MSA has mandated reflux valves in fuel tanks, banned any structures protruding outside safety cage structures, and doubled the required capacity for hand-held fire extinguishers for off-road racing events.

Ms Giles said that while MSA had introduced the implementation of mandatory plumbed-in fire extinguisher systems, an extended roll-out period of three years risked competitors' lives.

"The lives of off-road racing competitors who do not already have such a system remain at greater risk in the event of a fire – and, in my view, unnecessarily so," she said.

The coroner recommended that before the end of the 2026 racing season, MSA and the Australian Auto-Sport Alliance should require all off-road vehicles participating in sanctioned off-road events to be fitted with plumbed-in fire extinguisher systems.

She recommended mandatory testing of all competitors involved in racing competitions to ensure each occupant could self-extricate within 10 seconds.

Ms Giles also recommended MSA develop improved guidance for race organisers as to what constitutes "appropriate firefighting equipment" at the paddock areas of an event.

World.title: Gun clubs should be trained to detect radicalisation, inquiry told
World.content:
Gun clubs must be better equipped to spot the signs of radicalisation in members who may risk committing violent acts, a shooting organisation official and psychologist says.

Witnesses before the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion have this week painted a picture of the tools available to disrupt someone on the path to radicalisation.

Daniel Gregg works with people at various stages of radicalisation in his work as a psychologist in New South Wales, and is also the secretary of a shooting association.

He said gun clubs were uniquely positioned to intervene early in a person's path to radicalisation, and should be trained to detect the warning signs.

"If you taught clubs to notice those things and then refer those to the more appropriate pathways that we could be preventing further radicalisation," he said.

"We don't want bad actors in our organisations … because we wear the collective consequences if something goes wrong.

"Clubs are often called to coronial inquests and the last thing I wanted to do was be called to a coronial inquest and I hadn't done enough."

People becoming radicalised in weeks, inquiry told

Mr Gregg said he had implemented a behavioural screening framework at his own gun club, which involved a prospective member being interviewed and assigned a mentor to guide them through club and legislative requirements for firearms owners.

Commissioner Virginia Bell AC SC put to Mr Gregg that further firearms restrictions may be needed as part of the response to the Bondi Beach terror attack.

"It may be that Australia would be better off if it had a more restrictive approach to people being able to obtain a licence to use, albeit at a sporting club, weapons of the kind that were used at Bondi," she said to him.

Mr Gregg disagreed more firearms restrictions were needed. (Facebook: Rothwell Professional Industry Indoor Pistol Club)

Mr Gregg said he disagreed.

"A lot of what I am seeing from those on extremist pathways is that people can come through because they are self-radicalising, they have no [criminal] background … they have no markers that law enforcement would be able to pick up," he said.

"If you had more stricter pathways, you would still have people who would meet the requirements and get through, and they'd still be vulnerable to radicalisation."

In his work as a psychologist, Mr Gregg said he had previously observed people who were recruited by an extremist network typically became radicalised over a period of 12 to 18 months.

He said that shifted post-COVID, with people who self-radicalised becoming committed to an ideology in as little as two to four weeks.

Public awareness push for support helpline

The inquiry has also considered initiatives to help people spot the signs of radicalisation in their workmates, friends and family.

Through its website and helpline, Step Together directs people to resources about violent extremism, and general services which may offer support.

Countering violent extremism expert Michelle Grossman conducted a review of the program, which is run in NSW and delivered across the country.

Professor Grossman said Step Together played an important role in the countering violent extremism landscape, but not enough people knew about its existence.

"I actually think we need a saturation campaign around violent extremism in Australia," she said.

Michelle Grossman has called for a widespread awareness campaign. (Supplied: Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion)

"Violent extremists do not arrive from another planet, they are not beamed down on a spaceship, they are ordinary people in families, in our workplaces and in our schools.

"If we do not have the public awareness to be able to recognise and take steps towards addressing harms on many levels, then I believe we are doing ourselves a national disservice."

Professor Grossman said such an awareness campaign must be widespread, instead of isolated to certain groups.

"I feel quite strongly that the softly, softly approach, that more refined targeted approach, I think we're past that point," she said.

"I think some of the tragic and horrific events that we've seen recently in Australia have really clarified that for me. I don't think that we can afford anymore to have that."

'Tunnel vision' for extremism

NSW Department of Communities and Justice director Heather Jackson said work was underway to raise the profile of Step Together.

She also discussed the role of the state's Engagement and Support program in helping people and families vulnerable to violent extremist influence.

Ms Jackson said the age of eligibility for the program had been lowered from 14 to 10 in recent years to respond to the growing demand for the service.

"Unfortunately, in the last few years the landscape was indicating that there were young people, children 10 years and above, that were indicating capacity, capability and willingness to undertake a violent extremist event," she said.

Ms Jackson said the program worked to foster a sense of connection and belonging in participants who had developed "tunnel vision" for ideologically motivated extremism.

World.title: 'Chakra balancing' massage was indecent assault, court rules
World.content:
A former senior firefighter has avoided imprisonment for indecently assaulting a woman he was providing a professional massage to.

Valentine Ansett, 55, was found guilty in a Hobart Magistrates Court hearing earlier this year of indecent assault and assault with indecent intent, at his massage business in Hobart in 2024.

Magistrate Robert Webster said the assault with indecent intent, where Ansett placed his hand on the woman's genital region over a sarong, was during the "chakra balancing" part of the massage.

"[Ansett] admitted in a police interview that this technique was not something he was taught to do, not something he normally did," Magistrate Webster said.

The indecent assault involved him touching her breasts.

Victim's life 'profoundly impacted', court hears

Magistrate Webster said that Ansett had had a "long and distinguished" role in the Tasmania Fire Service (TFS), serving as a professional firefighter for more than 30 years, and had been an acting district officer for the TFS.

Ansett was stood down from that role in 2024, and his massage business has closed.

"[His] future employment situation is uncertain," he said.

" You are a person of otherwise good character; the offences are therefore in my view out of character. "

He said although Ansett was cooperative with police and sorry about the impact the offending has had on the woman, "you still do not consider you have done anything wrong."

"She was in a very vulnerable position … in the context of a therapeutic relationship, she ultimately placed trust in you," Magistrate Webster said.

"You breached that trust while she was vulnerable for your own sexual gratification."

A victim impact statement was read aloud to the court last week, during sentencing submissions.

"My life has been profoundly impacted by the assault," the prosecutor told the court on behalf of the victim.

She said she has been depressed and nearly took her life on two occasions.

"I miss the old me … brave, free and trusting," she said.

Magistrate Webster recorded a conviction and sentenced him to three months' imprisonment, wholly suspended for 18 months, meaning he will only go to jail if he commits another offence in that time.

Ansett's lawyer indicated that he had already filed an appeal of the conviction to the Criminal Court of Appeal, which will be mentioned in the Supreme Court of Tasmania in September.

World.title: 'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate
World.content:
Trent Robinson won't be raging about the inequality of the tax breaks afforded to the PNG Chiefs, even if he believes the NRL's open market is no longer a "level playing field".

After Penrith winger Brian To'o became the sixth player wooed by the start-up franchise's tax-free wages, Panthers coach Ivan Cleary declared clubs "can't compete" with the bounty the Chiefs can provide from 2028.

Cleary revealed he was in tears when To'o informed him he would leave Penrith to join the Chiefs, who critics — led by South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett — have said now have an unfair advantage in attracting talent.

The salary cap has been an equaliser of talent but Bennett has claimed the NRL has eroded the competition's fairness by giving the Chiefs such an upper hand.

The Chiefs' advantages are in contrast to the few concessions afforded to the Perth Bears, who will enter the NRL next season.

Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

"It's not a level playing field and I think you can see that," said Sydney Roosters coach Robinson.

"We've got (it on) one (hand) where we feel like it's not a level playing field and the other where we feel like they need more assistance.

"We're going to debate … but do we want our game to grow?

"We're not going to stop at 19 (teams) … we should own the Pacific.

"If we want more money in the game, want to expand, we need more teams, so I think it's a positive thing — players are going to go."

Penrith were the latest club to feel that pinch when they gave To'o, who enters the last 12 months of his deal in November, a seven-day window to explore his options for 2028.

Premiership-winning Panthers Jarome Luai and Brian To'o will reunite in 2028 at the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The winger signed with the Chiefs without visiting PNG, joining Jarome Luai, Connor Watson, Alex Johnston and Zac Lomax in agreeing to deals with the NRL's 19th side.

Loading Instagram content

"I had a little moment the other day, just very sad that Bizza's going to be going," the usually stoic Cleary said.

"There would've been a few (tears) … It's just hard to imagine 'Biz' playing in any other jersey. But there's a few guys out there that I thought the same."

Since their rise to premiership dominance in 2020, the Panthers have become accustomed to salary cap pressure squeezing out key players.

But they are especially vulnerable after 2027, with the cashed-up Chiefs emerging just as they battle to hold on to co-captains Isaah Yeo and Nathan Cleary, as well as premiership players Paul Alamoti, Liam Martin and Moses Leota.

"I think everyone knows with the Chiefs, it's hard to match that stuff," Cleary said.

"It's not your average club, but if players want to go there, you can't compete."

Asked whether the Chiefs had unfairly skewed the player market, Cleary recalled some wisdom from Marty Gurr, who was on the coaching staff during his early playing days at Manly.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remember when I first played 35 years ago, my first coach said to me 'rugby league isn't fair'," Cleary said.

"I think he was right. I've worked that out along the way. Whether it's fair or not, that's what the game's gone with. I can understand it."

Since overcoming the initial emotional blow of To'o's impending exit, Cleary has turned his attention to Penrith's task of retaining their stable of stars before September.

"We're very hopeful of having a few of them done (soon), you definitely don't want to be going into the finals doing this sort of stuff," he said.

AAP

World.title: Judge allows changes to dates of alleged Alan Jones assaults
World.content:
The judge in radio broadcaster Alan Jones's criminal trial has allowed changes to the date range of alleged indecent assault offences in the second week of proceedings, after witnesses gave conflicting timelines.

The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 20 counts of assault with act of indecency and two counts of sexual touching relating to six alleged victims between 2003 and 2020.

Prosecutors had alleged the first complainant to give evidence, Complainant J, had been 18 or 19 when Mr Jones allegedly kissed him and touched him on a trip to Fitzroy Falls, the broadcaster's NSW Southern Highlands property.

Charges relating to the trip to Fitzroy Falls are alleged to have occurred at some time in 2004, according to the Crown's original case.

But prosecutors have successfully argued to expand the possible dates of some of the alleged offending to any time between 2004 and April 2006, meaning Complainant J may have been between 18 and 21 years old.

Mr Jones and the witnesses were given an early mark as lawyers argued. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Mr Jones was given an early mark from the NSW Local Court on Wednesday, and witnesses were sent home as lawyers argued about changing the offence date ranges.

The court had heard Complainant J, who was an emerging athlete at the time, did not remember the date he allegedly confided in his then-girlfriend that Mr Jones had been "touching" him.

He said he thought the visit to Fitzroy Falls, where he alleged Mr Jones asked him to wear a "robe and nothing else" before kissing and touching him, was around 2004.

But his ex-girlfriend has since given evidence that Complainant J came to her house and told her about the alleged offending straight after the Fitzroy Falls trip, which she said was in 2005 or early 2006.

Dates of alleged offending expanded

Prosecutors argued that "time is not of the essence" in relation to the charges, and that the Crown's case was simply that the offending had occurred.

But Mr Jones's barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, pushed back, telling the court she had prepared and argued a case based on alleged offences happening in 2004.

"What is the Crown's case?" she said.

"We were not asked to prepare a case in relation to those events at Fitzroy Falls happening in 2005 and 2006."

She said the Crown had known about the inconsistencies in its witnesses' evidence and chose to raise them part-way through the trial, instead of at the beginning.

Mr Jones denies all charges. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

But Judge Glenn Walsh said he did not believe the time of alleged offences mattered much in this trial.

"The defendant's case is that it doesn't matter when it is said these things occurred, they never occurred," he said.

"I cannot see that this application wields any unfairness."

He said it was common in summary hearings in his experience, that witnesses differed in their evidence about the timing of alleged events.

The court had previously heard Complainant J initially told police in a statement that Mr Jones gave him a mobile phone as a schoolboy.

Under cross-examination, and after being shown Telstra phone records, he accepted he must have been given the phone after he had left school, and that he was recalling historical events to the best of his memory.

World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes that have had a glow-up
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes that have had a glow-up Shona Hendley August 12, 2026 — 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether it’s updating with modern technology, installing new flooring, appliances or fixtures, or landscaping the garden, a renovation, big or small, can have a serious impact on a property, from property value to greater comfort, flexibility and style. Here are our five luxury homes that have had a glow-up. 185 Palmer Street, Darlinghurst, NSW Rebuilt by Golek and architecturally designed by CO-AP, this tri-level home with a basement garage also features a separate, self-contained one-bedroom apartment.



The home features a contemporary light-filled design with skyline views. There is a playful use of colour, curved lines and unique finishes, including a vivid green Artedomus Esmeralda Quartzite island breakfast bar in the kitchen. The exterior is just as impressive, with landscaping by Secret Gardens, including a rooftop garden and a centrepiece courtyard accessible via floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors. 4 Grosvenor Court, Toorak, VIC On the market for only the second time since its original 1930s construction, this Toorak home has been extensively renovated while preserving many of its period features, such as the striking brick facade, Juliet balcony and grand staircase.



Set over two levels, the home includes a north-facing family living area and indoor-outdoor entertaining space. Other highlights include timber floors laid in a herringbone pattern, zoned ducted heating and air-conditioning, natural stone finishes, wainscotting, landscaped gardens with high fencing, and a plunge pool. 30 Woonona Road, Northbridge, NSW Retaining some of its period features, including its facade, high ceilings and decorative cornices, this double-storey California bungalow in Northbridge has been updated with a modern extension.



There is light-filled open-plan living and dining, and a designer kitchen with an induction cooktop, all connected by sliding doors to the outdoor entertaining terrace. Towards the rear of the property, there’s also a separate studio suite with its own bathroom. Located in a quiet no-through street, the property is a short walk to local schools, bushwalking trails and the Northbridge Golf Course. 1/21 Albany Road, Toorak, VIC



This ground-floor apartment in Toorak has undergone a contemporary and luxurious makeover. Located in the corner position with plenty of northern light, the residence features open-plan living and dining that open to an expansive wrap-around terrace and a lush garden. There is a brand-new stone kitchen appointed with premium Miele appliances, and three elegantly redesigned bathrooms with bespoke new wardrobes. One of only two apartments in the complex with a private lift, the property also features polished timber flooring and is close to Toorak Village. 31 Gladstone Street, Indooroopilly, QLD



Architecturally renovated by Trebilcock Architects, this Queenslander sits on a treeline street with views of Mount Coot-tha. With five bedrooms and a separate study that may be used as a sixth, a flexible layout across its two levels, and a recently added extension, the home caters to families, including multigenerational families, with its private lift that serves all levels. With high coffered ceilings, new wool carpets, sheer curtains, block-out blinds, and a kitchen with imported marble, bespoke cabinetry, a Liebherr fridge, and dual ovens, the home’s fittings, fixtures, and materials are high quality and stylish. Outside, enjoy the magnesium pool, landscaped gardens with feature lighting, a citrus grove and a city-style kitchen garden for growing fresh herbs and vegetables.
