World.title: Liberals’ ‘broad church’ has lost its way
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s all very well for John Howard to tell his present Liberal cohort that they should “be the best demonstration of themselves” (“Howard’s advice to Liberals to win back voters flocking to Pauline Hanson”, August 12). It’s probably sound advice, but the problem is they don’t have any idea of who they are or what they represent. Howard knew how difficult it was to wrangle this group of self-interested, patriarchal old men when he used the term “broad church” to describe his fractious party room. His broad church has been reduced to an irrelevant rump and I would argue that rather than being the doyen of the Liberal Party, he was the beginning of the end of it when he declared himself the most conservative leader the party had ever had. It was when it abandoned any semblance of liberalism and embraced conservatism that its eventual demise was assured. Chris McKimm, Karangi Former PM John Howard opposes the idea of a Liberal alliance with Pauline Hanson. Like reader Craig Jory, I applaud John Howard’s views on gambling reform (Letters, August 12). And also his advice to Angus Taylor on how to combat Pauline Hanson. But when he dismisses the current government as “this miserable, rotten mob” and offers support to those in his party who claim Anthony Albanese is the worst-ever PM, he loses the last shred of his credibility. He can criticise Albo all he wants, like the rest of us, but when he indulges in such personal and absurd abuse he abandons all hope of positioning himself as the elder statesman he aspires to be. Richard Walsh, Woollahra Decrease a collective gain If there was any doubt regarding Angus Taylor’s loyalties, his remarks in parliament this week about house prices clarify everything. After years of most people wanting house prices to stop rising, we finally get a small decrease. Yet Taylor asserts this is destroying the market. Destroying it for whom? For investors. As RBA head Michele Bullock suggested, if the market dropped 20 per cent we might see 5 per cent of the population in negative equity, which would only be a problem for someone who wanted to sell in a hurry. Clearly, Taylor is no friend of the aspiring young homeowner. Bruce Johnson, Lakewood US’s cautionary tale Sussan Ley told Sarah Ferguson on ABC’s 7.30 that she travelled by Greyhound bus through the US, listening to punk music and observing the disconnected, the lost, the lonely and the poor. Hopefully she also noticed the political failure of right-wing ideology, the widening income gap through trickle-down economics and the lack of government support through underfunded Medicaid and pension payments. Denise Young, Thirroul



Losing faith The question of “religion” on the census form was vexing for many of us who for years were fully immersed in Christian communities but are now deconstructing a faith that was ultimately coercive. Self-surveillance, control of sexuality and rigid gender prescriptions were masqueraded as freedom. Like your correspondent Andrew Cohen (Letters, August 12), I wonder if “no religion” can ever describe the search for the numinous and mysterious that ended in my disillusionment and disengagement from evangelical churches. I settled on “ex-evangelical” which, while inadequate, summarises the journey of searching then rejecting the straitjacket on offer. Josie McSkimming, Coogee The census has raised the issue of faith. Tanya Macheda Perhaps it is not surprising your correspondent was unable to find a religion in mainstream Christian churches. In his book What’s Wrong with the World, G.K. Chesterton has a chapter called “The Unfinished Temple”. In this chapter he wrote: “The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult and left untried.” Mark Porter, New Lambton Despite being a “person of faith”, Andrew Cohen wound up being classified as an atheist in the census because he declared he had no religion. The word atheist has become problematic and needs reinterpreting because it comes from an era when “theism” was the only option. “Atheism” was therefore “wicked” and “of the devil” – pejorative attitudes which persist to this day. Even though I have the equivalent of a theology degree, I find “mainstream” Christians hostile to me, not because I am “without belief” but they are “without knowledge” and know not what they do. Time for a new definition. Suggestions? John MacKay, Asquith Hot topic Brussels’ newly unveiled city square is being pilloried as “Europe’s largest frying pan”. Is Sydney hoping to snare the world title (“First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square”, August 11)? Yes, the Town Hall square will have some trees and a fountain, but who in their right mind would sit on those concrete steps on a hot summer day in Sydney? Global heating is real, it’s happening now, and it will only get worse. Is it too much to ask for designers to take it seriously? Tom McGinness, Randwick



What is this obsession with destroying Sydney and spending millions on an unnecessary “town square”? Sydney already has enough public spaces. What we desperately need is affordable social housing. The buildings that council has acquired should be repurposed into safe, affordable housing for people who actually need it – right in the heart of Sydney, close to jobs, transport, schools and essential services. And before council dreams up another grand public space, perhaps it should focus on maintaining the one it already has. Wentworth Park on Wattle Street would be a far better meeting place for the people of Sydney, looking toward the new fish market and Sydney skyline, especially once the dog track is finally demolished. That is real, usable space that could serve the community far better than another expensive civic experiment. Christopher Vidler, Willoughby As a former arborist, trust me when I say that lilly-pillies and blueberry ash are inappropriate species for a large square in the CBD (Letters, August 12). Not only do they drop copious amounts of potentially slippery fruit and seeds, their high domes aren’t very shadeworthy, and they’re a small tree at maturity. What is needed are trees complimentary to the scale of surrounding buildings that are a mix of deciduous and evergreen, that can thrive in heavily engineered growing medium and will tolerate heat reflection from hard surfaces while coping with city wind tunnels, and are reliant on rainwater through mostly impermeable pavement surfaces. Not too much to ask of trees. Clare Raffan, Campsie Bernie Bourke, after you’ve taken Pauline Hanson for a walk through Gosford Hospital (Letters, August 12), please take her through an aged care facility. From my observations these places are largely staffed by highly competent and compassionate people from South Asia and South-East Asia who diligently care for our most vulnerable citizens. I can think of no better place for Ms Hanson to start her Australia-wide listening tour. Rhonda Seymour, Castle Hill Photo: Cathy Wilcox Bulk-billing dilemma Bulk-billing gives easier access to medical care but sadly may not reflect quality care (Letters, August 12). I dare any bulk-billing doctor to prove they spend sufficient time to truly hear complex patients. Like all of my obese and anorexic patients who insist they are on a perfect diet, bulk-billing doctors will no doubt rebel at my implication. But there are enough anecdotes to corroborate my claim, which of course, can never be proven given the confidentiality of consultations. There is no doubt that with current Medicare rebates, bulk-billing centres need a high throughput. Dr Ashley Berry, Wollongong



Storm in a teacup Columnist Kate Halfpenny believes the coverage of Anthony Albanese’s schoolboy responses about the Japan’s PM Sanae Takaichi and singer Kylie Minogue has been overblown (“I’m hyper-alert to misogyny and sexism, but even this from the PM had me cackling”, August 12). The fact is, if Albanese had not been so eager to appeal to the people who might find this titillating it would have received no coverage at all. Harmless or not, what irritates many people is the campaign led by numerous female Labor MPs (whom I suspect are privately fuming) and others, to downplay the issue. These same supporters would be howling from the rooftops if a member of the right had made the same comments. I suppose the one benefit arising out of it all is that Albanese will be better prepared for the inevitable appearance on Kyle Sandilands’ podcast. Mike Kenneally, Manly I wonder if other readers, like me, are fed up with the Coalition’s obsession with what the prime minister might or might have not meant on a popular podcast months ago. To try and confect a diplomatic gaffe out of it is pathetic (“Coalition wants probe into leaked Japan note”, August 12). Australians are interested in what politicians can do to improve their lives and this behaviour will only confirm the Coalition’s irrelevance. At present, their policies seem to comprise the reinstatement of financial arrangements that clearly helped the better off, and a race to the bottom with One Nation on immigration. The Japanese are not bothered. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi strikes me as a very knowledgeable and focused politician. She has her own issues to deal with, both domestically and globally. I’m sure she will rightly dismiss the Coalition’s behaviour as mere fluff. John Jones, Armidale Albanese deserves a rap over the knuckles for his recent faux pas. Intentional or not, he would have known that his comment contained a double entendre. It wasn’t a cardinal sin but showed poor judgment. Language is a powerful tool in politics and should always be above reproach. The PM’s comment may have been disrespectful, but it pales in comparison to the misogynistic language of some Liberal Party members at times. Angus Taylor’s belated attempt to use Albo’s error for political gain is typical and hypocritical. Graham Lum, North Rocks No wonder the Liberal Party is in such a mess. They are presently concentrating on attacking our PM for his light-hearted comments in a podcast about Japanese melons. Really, of all the important issues facing the country they focus on this. This behaviour reeks of desperation from a party not fit to govern. David Boyd, Bondi Beach Dear Mr Albanese, please stay away from social media and podcasts. It is not your forte. Stick to what you do best – which is the art of negotiations and running the country. Ruth Pojer, Double Bay



ABC crisis control Jenna Price asks us to “give this kid a break” (“What apology over Rinehart skit tells us about Hugh Marks’ ABC. It’s not good,” August 12). This would have to be the first time I have heard a 29-year-old postgraduate described as a kid. Has adulthood reached a new starting point of 30? Or has Price engaged in a bit of overreach in her attempt to defend the video by Kate McGuinness on Race around the World? She admits that the comments made by McGuinness about Gina Rinehart were not funny, but defends them as attempt at humour. I would argue that the comments were out of context with the rest of the video, which makes no reference to Rinehart, and were nothing more than an unnecessary, nasty dig that had no place in the show. ABC boss Hugh Marks did the only thing he could do – apologise to Rinehart and edit the piece out. It speaks more to the producers for allowing the video into the show and thus throwing Kate McGuiness to the wolves of social media. Brendon Flynn, Tasmania ABC boss Hugh Marks issued an apology to Gina Rinehart. Fair play In another life as an English head teacher, I dealt with the problem of compromised take-home tasks by introducing three changes (“AI can be taking the escalator when you need to use the stairs”, August 10). First, the task was prepared at home but written at school; second, students were given two possible questions for which to prepare, with only one being the question on the day; third, we supplied the paper on which the response was written. In this way, the objective of take-home tasks – private research, deeper thinking and reasoning – was preserved and the writing of the response within a set time period enabled students to practise an important HSC skill. Wayne Duncombe, Lilyfield Migrants’ vital contribution We should never lose sight of the great contribution migrants have made to this country, as indicated by your correspondent Tony Simons (Letters, August 11). Without that contribution, the workforce, particularly in the areas of healthcare, agriculture and construction, would have been found seriously wanting. Those who have come from overseas countries to care for our sick and aged, harvest our primary produce and build our infrastructure have played a big role in adding to our prosperity and simply making our lives easier. Migration has taken up the slack of our ageing population and helped pay the taxes to keep health and welfare commitments afloat. The narrow-minded scaremongering of people like Pauline Hanson should never lead us to forget the debt we owe to migrants, who are now unfairly being blamed for the current housing shortage. Hanson’s incoherent babbling should not blind us to the part migrants have played in our country’s progress. Derrick Mason, Boorowa

World.title: Gold Coast looking at Pendlebury for Hodge-like role
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Gold Coast looking at Pendlebury for Hodge-like role Jake Niall August 12, 2026 — 6:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gold Coast have expressed interest in recruiting Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury for a Luke Hodge-style role on the field next year. Essendon also have inquired about whether Pendlebury would be interested in playing with and mentoring their young list next year, as the AFL’s games record holder weighs up his next move, industry sources familiar with Pendlebury’s discussions have confirmed. The Suns, who have slumped from a 7-3 start this season to be 8-13 and out of finals contention, are primarily interested in Pendlebury as a player next year, rather than as an assistant coach, though he harbours coaching ambitions and could easily move from playing to (assistant) coaching if he chooses to leave the Magpies. Collingwood veteran Scott Pendlebury. AFL Photos via Getty Images Collingwood are yet to put an offer to Pendlebury for 2027, as they continue the difficult transition of a playing list that they aim to regenerate with a mix of youth and seasoned recruits over post-season. Steele Sidebottom, as this masthead reported, is expected to finish up at Collingwood after this year, while defender and team leader Jeremy Howe has a contract offer on the table.



Pendlebury’s future is being handled sensitively by Collingwood who wish to avoid a Brent Harvey like scenario when the then AFL games record holder was a reluctant retiree a decade ago. Pendlebury’s appeal to the Suns is obviously for his leadership capacity and renowned ability to direct teammates and act as a de facto on-field coach. The Suns have arguably lacked leadership support for their skipper Noah Anderson and have not performed well in the centre bounces - including defensively - this season, despite the arrival of superstar Christian Petracca from Melbourne. Matt Rowell, hurt in the pre-season with a foot injury, has not reached the stellar heights of his 2025 Brownlow Medal season. Collingwood are the favourites to land Brisbane Lions dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale, who has met with the Magpies on multiple occasions and has a sizeable three-year contract offer on the table from them, having saved significant salary cap space with the exit of Bobby Hill, who was reportedly contracted at close to $750,000 for the next four seasons.



While Pendlebury will have the option at playing on in 2027 at other clubs and adding further to the games record he broke in round 11 against West Coast, the champion has indicated that the decision on his future with the Magpies would be one that was in the best interests of the club. “Me and Sidey (Sidebottom) will sit down at the end of the season with the footy club and work out what’s best for everyone,” Pendlebury told Seven’s The Front Bar last week. “I’ve heard comments like it’s up to Sidey, or it’s up to me. I think we’re mature enough, you know, to know that it’s a club decision, and we’ll make what’s best for the footy club.” Hodge’s move to the Lions followed his retirement from the Hawks in 2017, and was prompted by the four-time premiership hero and dual Norm Smith medallist’s wish to continue playing and Brisbane’s then need for on-field direction and guidance for a younger list. It has become a template for experienced players who move to younger or developing teams.

World.title: Premier to prune taxpayer splurge on office plants after $1.6 million contract revealed
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCBD Premier to prune taxpayer splurge on office plants after $1.6 million contract revealed Fiona Byrne and John Buckley August 12, 2026 — 6:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Since taking over as premier a little over two weeks ago, Ben Carroll has been busy scraping barnacles from the Jacinta Allan era from his government. The proposed work-from-home law has been delayed, he has committed to a royal commission into allegations of corruption in the construction industry, announced his intention to limit court suppression orders, and he has downsized his ministry. Ben Carroll conceded the pot plant contracts were “not a good use of taxpayer money”. Jason South And now he has vowed to stamp out bloated taxpayer spending on office pot plants less than 90 minutes after Opposition Leader Jess Wilson called out eye-raising examples of government contracts for indoor shrubbery – including a $1.6 million spend. In question time on Wednesday, Wilson asked Treasurer Colin Brooks, aka “the real Colin from Accounts”: “Why has Rail Projects Victoria spent almost $1.6 million hiring and maintaining pot plants for its offices?” and followed it up with, “How many police could be put on the beat in Sunshine for $1.6 million?”



Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Nicole Werner appeared in a social media video with a “money tree” to illustrate their claims that the Labor government acts like money grows on trees. Instagram/@JessWilsonMP Making the point, Liberal members Nicole Werner and Brad Battin produced pot plant props and promptly got booted out of the chamber. Wilson’s figures related to a $1.6 million contract to hire and maintain plants for Rail Project Victoria’s (now part of the Victoria Infrastructure Delivery Authority) offices in the CBD and Sunshine for four years from August 2022 to July 2026 and a $200,000 contract for indoor-plant hire and maintenance for the Suburban Rail Loop Authority which expires in August 2027. “Labor has no respect for taxpayer money or the people that earn it. Under Labor, Victoria’s corrupted Big Build still doesn’t have a royal commission, but it does have millions of dollars of rented office pot plants,” Wilson later said. Not wanting to be flagellated by the foliage folly, Carroll moved surprisingly quickly for a pollie and pulled that weed.



“This is not a good use of taxpayer money. I’ve asked my department to end this,” Carroll countered, before adding the usual line about spending taxpayer dollars responsibly. His move came as the Liberals unleashed another snappy social media reel, this time with Wilson, Werner, Battin and their colleagues holding a plastic tree covered in notes and lambasting Labor for acting like money grows on trees. Game on. Things are heating up over at Spring Street. Walden clocks up double figures in new gig There must be something in the air. Hot on the heels of Melbourne foodie Iain Hewitson launching his 10th book, comes former newsreader Mal Walden with his latest literary offering – which just happens to also take him into double figures as an author.



Mal Walden is already writing book number 11. Eddie Jim Walden, who was a fixture for decades behind the news desk on channels 7 and 10, is gearing up for the release of his 10th book, Power of the Voice: Words that shaped Australia, later this month. “When I was in the media, we were told that 12 words was six words too many and on that basis, you can’t write a book,” Walden told CBD on Wednesday. “So, in 2013, my last year at Channel 10, I did an online, non-fiction writing course for six months and learnt long-form writing, then I wrote my memoir, The Newsman, which was published in 2016. “My publisher asked me if I had another book in me and I told him, ‘it’s taken me 54 years to write this one – on that basis, neither of us is going to be around for the next one’.”



Turns out Walden got his skates on and a decade along now has 10 titles to his name. “It’s like my career in media has not stopped, it’s just taken a different direction,” he said. “Most of the books have a common theme, and it’s about unique Australians.” In a case of “can’t stop, won’t stop”, there is more to come. He is already deep into writing number 11. Sussan Ley’s former spinner revives dormant press chat



Former opposition leader Sussan Ley’s ex spinner Liam Jones went on to start his own consulting shop after the former opposition leader left politics earlier this year. But he’s clearly been missing the game – and relevance that came with his old gig. On Tuesday night, Jones revived the old background briefing WhatsApp group which had been dormant since Ley was opposition leader to let reporters know she would be on the ABC’s 7.30 to talk about the US road trip she wrote about for The Australian Financial Review. Sussan Ley starts her post-politics road trip at Minot, North Dakota, on the Canadian border. After Ley left politics, Jones went on to set up Deep Roads Strategy, and has been doing some lobbying work for the Movember men’s health charity. Jones was also recently in the US, where we hear he was the least notable attendee of the Australian American Leadership Dialogue in Washington DC.



The Australian contingent for that talkfest included former prime minister Scott Morrison and former UN ambassador Mitch Fifield, along with Speaker Milton Dick, Labor senator Raff Ciccone, and Liberal senators James Paterson and Jonno Duniam. If Tuesday evening was anything to go by, we doubt Jones needed any invitation to talk up his list of clients.

World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes that have had a glow-up
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes that have had a glow-up Shona Hendley August 12, 2026 — 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether it’s updating with modern technology, installing new flooring, appliances or fixtures, or landscaping the garden, a renovation, big or small, can have a serious impact on a property, from property value to greater comfort, flexibility and style. Here are our five luxury homes that have had a glow-up. 185 Palmer Street, Darlinghurst, NSW Rebuilt by Golek and architecturally designed by CO-AP, this tri-level home with a basement garage also features a separate, self-contained one-bedroom apartment.



The home features a contemporary light-filled design with skyline views. There is a playful use of colour, curved lines and unique finishes, including a vivid green Artedomus Esmeralda Quartzite island breakfast bar in the kitchen. The exterior is just as impressive, with landscaping by Secret Gardens, including a rooftop garden and a centrepiece courtyard accessible via floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors. 4 Grosvenor Court, Toorak, VIC On the market for only the second time since its original 1930s construction, this Toorak home has been extensively renovated while preserving many of its period features, such as the striking brick facade, Juliet balcony and grand staircase.



Set over two levels, the home includes a north-facing family living area and indoor-outdoor entertaining space. Other highlights include timber floors laid in a herringbone pattern, zoned ducted heating and air-conditioning, natural stone finishes, wainscotting, landscaped gardens with high fencing, and a plunge pool. 30 Woonona Road, Northbridge, NSW Retaining some of its period features, including its facade, high ceilings and decorative cornices, this double-storey California bungalow in Northbridge has been updated with a modern extension.



There is light-filled open-plan living and dining, and a designer kitchen with an induction cooktop, all connected by sliding doors to the outdoor entertaining terrace. Towards the rear of the property, there’s also a separate studio suite with its own bathroom. Located in a quiet no-through street, the property is a short walk to local schools, bushwalking trails and the Northbridge Golf Course. 1/21 Albany Road, Toorak, VIC



This ground-floor apartment in Toorak has undergone a contemporary and luxurious makeover. Located in the corner position with plenty of northern light, the residence features open-plan living and dining that open to an expansive wrap-around terrace and a lush garden. There is a brand-new stone kitchen appointed with premium Miele appliances, and three elegantly redesigned bathrooms with bespoke new wardrobes. One of only two apartments in the complex with a private lift, the property also features polished timber flooring and is close to Toorak Village. 31 Gladstone Street, Indooroopilly, QLD



Architecturally renovated by Trebilcock Architects, this Queenslander sits on a treeline street with views of Mount Coot-tha. With five bedrooms and a separate study that may be used as a sixth, a flexible layout across its two levels, and a recently added extension, the home caters to families, including multigenerational families, with its private lift that serves all levels. With high coffered ceilings, new wool carpets, sheer curtains, block-out blinds, and a kitchen with imported marble, bespoke cabinetry, a Liebherr fridge, and dual ovens, the home’s fittings, fixtures, and materials are high quality and stylish. Outside, enjoy the magnesium pool, landscaped gardens with feature lighting, a citrus grove and a city-style kitchen garden for growing fresh herbs and vegetables.

World.title: Chris Penk says he will not seek re-election after losing ministerial portfolios
World.content:
Chris Penk has decided not to seek re-election in November, hours after the prime minister stripped him of his portfolios for his role in a leadership challenge.

On Wednesday, following an emergency caucus meeting, Christopher Luxon confirmed the party had undertaken a confidence vote, and he remained prime minister and leader of the National Party.

A few hours later, Luxon removed Penk's ministerial portfolios.

"Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said.

On Wednesday evening, Penk said he had reflected on his political future with his family, and decided not to seek re-election as an MP.

"I am a proud member of the National Party, and I fully back National and Christopher Luxon to lead the government after the election and take New Zealand forward," he said.

"It has been a privilege to serve my community of Kaipara ki Mahurangi for the last nine years, and I am proud of the progress I have contributed to as a minister this term. However, I have decided it is the time for me to seek other opportunities to serve New Zealand."

Penk's statement did not address the allegations he had launched a leadership challenge.

Paul Goldsmith will pick up the Defence, Veterans, Space, GCSB, and NZSIS portfolios.

Simon Watts will become Minister for Building and Construction.

The Prime Minister's Office told RNZ its position was that Penk was challenging for himself, not on behalf of someone else.

Earlier on Wednesday afternoon, Luxon held a press conference where he announced he had survived the second attempt to oust him this year.

In an abrupt statement to media, he said he had the full confidence of the National Party caucus before leaving without answering questions.

"Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he said.

"Our focus is on National's positive plan to fix the basics and to build the future, so that we realise the incredible potential that sits in this country, and that we set it up for our kids and our grandkids."

He was flanked by senior MPs, including Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell and Chris Bishop.

Standing just behind them was Erica Stanford, who was rumoured to be gunning for the top job.

Chris Penk at Parliament on Wednesday. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Later on Wednesday evening, Bishop said rumours Penk was doing the numbers for him were "utterly incorrect," and people did not launch leadership challenges on behalf of anybody else.

"He was not doing the numbers for me. Chris Penk, as the prime minister said, launched a challenge. It didn't succeed, obviously, and any suggestion that he was involved in doing numbers for me is completely wrong.

Bishop said there was "no suggestion" Penk was doing the numbers for Stanford either.

He said it would be "tough" for Penk, saying he was talented and the two had worked closely together, but he understood why the prime minister had made the decision.

"He'll be a loss to the government, but that's what happens."

Penk, who was ranked 14th on National's list published at the weekend, had earlier denied any involvement in a leadership challenge, after Politik and the New Zealand Herald reported he was doing the numbers for an Erica Stanford bid.

Upon arriving in Wellington on Tuesday night, Penk had said he had confidence in Luxon, and would support him in any vote.

"I've always expressed confidence in the leader. Now is no different."

He would not say if anyone had called him about the leadership, saying he would not disclose private conversations, but said reports of his involvement as an instigator were "wrong".

He stuck to that position on Wednesday morning, again saying he had confidence in Luxon, and suggested people might be making up stories about him making calls for Stanford.

"I think everyone else needs to get their story straight because I'm hearing multiple different versions. None of them are true, and as I said, I'm not prepared to disclose private conversations, except only to say I have confidence in Christopher Luxon."

Penk had only been promoted to the Cabinet in April, following the retirement of Judith Collins.

He has been an MP since 2017, first in the Helensville seat, then in the redrawn Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate.

ACT Party leader David Seymour said for Luxon to remain leader after several challenges showed he was well-positioned to stop the destabilisation in the party.

World.title: Wellington's after-hours clinic doesn't have staff to extend hours
World.content:
Wellington's after-hours medical service (WAMC) says it doesn't have the staff to extend opening hours to help it cope with a winter surge of patients.

Wellington Hopsital's emergency department had one of its busiest days in almost a year on Monday, seeing 258 patients,

Health NZ said the GP-run urgent care clinic would be extending its hours in an effort to cope with the influx. It was aiming to do this within six months of signing a contract.

But the clinic said it was still in negotiations with the agency and hadn't yet reached an agreement.

It said a new workforce model would have to be agreed before the hours could be extended and the change could take up to 15 months.

World.title: Rotorua seeks four-week extension after Head Start proposal falls apart
World.content:
Rotorua Lakes Council has asked the government for a four-week extension to enter its Head Start local government reform process.

Mayor Tania Tapsell said she had asked Local Government Minister Simon Watts for more time to resolve councillors' concerns and formally submit the proposal.

Introduced in May, Head Start gave councils three months to propose voluntary reforms, with those not progressing facing a compulsory backstop, in which the government will design the future structure for them after the 2028 elections.

The request follows the collapse of a co-ordinated plan to create three unitary authorities: Tauranga-Western Bay, Rotorua, and an Eastern Bay authority covering Whakatāne, Kawerau and Ōpōtiki.

Each would develop its own structure while the councils presented a unified regional approach through a shared cover letter.

However, the plan unravelled before the 9 August deadline.

On Thursday, Western Bay voted against Head Start, by one vote, and the Eastern Bay councils submitted their own proposal, leaving Rotorua with Tauranga as its only potential partner.

Rotorua chief executive Andrew Moraes said the council had been advised by the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) that it needed at least one other council to qualify for Head Start.

Rotorua Lakes Council chief executive Andrew Moraes. Andrew Warner / LDR

A Tauranga-Rotorua proposal covering a Baywide approach, minus the Eastern Bay, would have required including Western Bay despite its opposition, dividing Rotorua councillors. A proposal including only Tauranga and Rotorua would not qualify.

The council voted 6-5 against the Tauranga-Western Bay alternative and the backstop option, leaving Rotorua without an approved proposal or an obvious route into Head Start.

Tapsell said Rotorua had previously resolved to pursue a Head Start proposal, but the rejection at the final meeting on Friday left it without an "approved" final proposal.

The minister now has Rotorua's draft proposal, Tapsell said, and the council is waiting to see whether the extension will be granted.

Whakatāne Mayor Nandor Tanczos, Kawerau Mayor Faylene Tunui and Ōpōtiki Mayor David Moore present East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick (second from left) with their council's outline proposal for an Eastern Bay unitary council on the Beehive steps in Wellington. NZME

Whakatāne Mayor Nándor Tánczos said the Eastern Bay councils had always intended to submit their own proposal, supported by the cover letter demonstrating a co-ordinated regional approach.

"We were all committed to signing it," he said.

The Eastern Bay councils waited for Western Bay's decision before submitting, but Tánczos said there was too little time to change tack and develop a new arrangement with Rotorua.

"It's Thursday night we're talking about," he said.

The intention had been for the three sub-regions to move together, even if their proposals were submitted separately.

"We wanted it to be seen that the Bay of Plenty was coming up with a solution for the whole Bay together," Tánczos said.

He said that principle had not changed despite the collapse of the co-ordinated process.

"If there is a possibility that there's still this idea of an across-the-Bay three sub-regional authorities' approach, we'd still support that," he said.

"It still seems the best idea for the Bay of Plenty."

Tapsell said she "understood and supported" the Eastern Bay councils proceeding independently, saying it was "ultimately the best decision" for them to "determine and be part of their own future".

She said the three-authority concept reflected what the region's mayors believed was the most realistic option.

"We understood and agreed that we have three very clear and distinct sub-regions," she said.

Tapsell said she still believed the three-authority model was the best solution for the region and remained viable.

She said Tauranga and Western Bay were the most logical parts of the region to merge because of their geography and infrastructure, but Rotorua councillors had been reluctant to support a model that would effectively force Western Bay into an arrangement it had rejected.

She said the "short time frames" had contributed to the impasse.

Tánczos also questioned whether councils had been given enough time to make decisions of such magnitude, saying the process had placed enormous pressure on councils and strained relationships.

"Everyone's been put in this extremely difficult position with really impossible time frames," he said.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Watts rejected the suggestion that the government's process had failed in Rotorua.

"Head Start is a voluntary process for councils that are ready and able to work together to simplify local government," he said.

Councils without a Head Start proposal proceeding to detailed design would enter the Backstop, he said, with its design to be determined by the government in 2027.

Watts declined to comment specifically on Rotorua's position but said the detailed design phase would allow successful proposals to be expanded, communities consulted, and legislation developed before the 2028 elections.

He said the government had received 18 proposals covering 48 councils by the 9 August deadline, including proposals from the Eastern Bay councils and one from Tauranga City Council, without a willing partner.

Moraes said Rotorua's options beyond Head Start remained unclear, with the government yet to set out what the Backstop process would look like.

"The Head Start process is closed," he said. "Anything that happens outside of that process will depend on future government policy announcements."

For Tapsell, that is why the extension matters.

"Head Start was the only option available to determine our own future," she said.

"I'm genuinely gutted that we're on the edge of losing this opportunity."

World.title: Kiwi dairy industry rides the Wegovy wave as  whey protein booms
World.content:
New Zealand dairy companies are cashing in on a surge in global demand for bioactive proteins found in cow's milk, like whey, off the back of the surge in weightloss drugs.

Boosting immune health or developing muscles for elderly or appetite suppressant patients were believed to be driving a recent upsurge in demand for dairy-based proteins.

Fresh cow's milk consisted mostly of water, with small fractions of lactose, fat and protein.

After dairy processors removed fat and separated the casein protein, the leftover liquid was whey, a protein-rich by-product valued for amino acids and minerals that supported human health.

This year, prices for whey powder in key market the United States were soaring.

The rural news with Gianina Schwanecke Rural News Download MP3 3m

Rabobank said in a recent agribusiness report, whey powder prices were up 76 percent in June, compared to the same time last year, with spot prices up 60 percent from the start of 2026.

The bank's senior analyst in animal proteins, Jen Corkran said high-protein yoghurt and dairy drinks containing whey were now in high demand globally.

"We've got these Gen-Zs and even your millennials in the gym, but also just everyday prioritizing protein," she said.

Do you consume whey protein, and why? Let us know monique.steele@rnz.co.nz

"We've seen this really big protein demand, and milk protein in particular benefits from this," said Corkran.

"We're seeing a lot of protein labelling, your yogurts, protein powders, and this is really adding to that demand story."

Wegovy wave

South Island dairy company Westland Milk was expanding its lactoferrin production facility in Hokitika to meet demand, advertising a number of jobs online at the West Coast facility.

Its owner, Yili Oceania's chief executive, Alex Turnbull said body builders drove early bioactive protein demand, but it was now much more mainstream, especially with the rise of GLP-1 medication use.

"Particularly with these aging populations in Western and Eastern culture," Turnbull said.

The Westland Milk Products Hokitika plant is the largest industrial coal user on the West Coast following extensive development of the site in the past decade. Greymouth Star/Brendon McMahon/

"And then, what's happened is with this crazy trend in the world for these weight loss drugs known as GLP-1, which is an appetite suppressant.

"Whatever you eat needs to be very, very nutritiously dense, because you lose a lot of muscle mass when you lose weight so quickly. And those are the casein proteins and the whey proteins."

In the United States, the use of appetite-suppressant GLP-1 medications for diabetes and weight loss had become much more widespread in recent years, with the development of brands Ozempic or Wegovy.

Turnbull said there was good demand for whey in the US, Europe and Asia.

He said people better understood the important role of proteins in the body thesedays.

"You're seeing customers putting protein into anything.

"And that's been the second catalyst to drive such enormous demand for dairy proteins, indeed throughout the world, but particularly the epicentre being in the United States of America."

Westland Milk was bought by China's Yili Group in 2019.

The whey to boost immune health

Selling the health benefits of a whey protein complex was the name of the game for Quantec, a small but longstanding company in Waikato.

It sourced milk from companies in one of the country's key dairy regions, then contract manufacturers extracted a natural mix of bioactive proteins including lactoferrin to create an ingredient that promoted immune health.

Chief executive, John Dawson said half the team were scientists who had spent years testing and working to prove the product's health benefits, like reducing the frequency of colds in children.

"We are focused on a very, very small subset of the bioactive proteins in milk. This really has carved out a unique niche for us in the dairy space," he said.

"We've been able to create a branded ingredient we call IDP, immune defense proteins, and that branded ingredient is used as an active ingredient in dietary supplements, health supplements, mainly in China, but also in other parts of the world."

Dawson said China was its top export market, that Taiwan and Japan were going well, and it was sending a little bit into Europe, with hopes to grow the US market.

123RF

"That's where the value is for us, is in building that brand supported by the science and the clinical studies. So that's a pretty narrow focus, but that's going to keep us busy for the foreseeable future."

Dawson said a focus on immune health was huge during the Covid-19 years, but had since dropped off a bit.

In addition to immune defence, he said it was exploring whey's other functional traits like anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial, as well as benefits for pets, riding on the back of the trend of owners humanising their pets.

World.title: Three arrested 45 minutes after sleeping man attacked, van and phone stolen
World.content:
Three people - including a youth - were arrested 45 minutes after a man was attacked in his van while he slept.

The attack, which left the victim with a bloody nose, happened around 2am near Lake Puketirini, Huntly, on Wednesday.

Police said the victim called from a service station, saying four people wearing balaclavas had attacked him, then stolen his van and phone.

"Responding officers located the van on Harris Street shortly after 2:30am, and set up road spikes around Tainui Bridge Road," Senior Sergeant Mary Van Dongen said.

The van was stopped on Great South Road and three occupants arrested at about 2:45am, she said, with help from a police dog unit.

"It's pleasing to have been able to locate and arrest people for this so quickly in order to hold them to account."

Two of the alleged attackers, aged 20 and 18, were due in Hamilton District Court on aggravated robbery charges, and the third in Hamilton Youth Court on an aggravated robbery charge.

World.title: New Zealand bus drivers ‘duped’ into Sydney jobs, unable to return home
World.content:
Union says Kiwis misled over Sydney bus driver jobs Nine To Noon Download MP3 18m

After being promised a Sydney beach lifestyle, a group of Kiwi bus drivers were left living in sub-standard housing and unable to return home unless they stumped up thousands of dollars.

The New South Wales transport union (RTBU) said bus company Keolis advertised jobs for New Zealand drivers promising flights, a live-by-the beach lifestyle, and attractive pay.

But a $10,000 bonding payment - holding them to the job - was sprung on workers shortly before their contracts started.

With many already having resigned from their jobs in New Zealand and sold their belongings, it was hard to turn back.

The union's secretary Toby Warnes told Nine to Noon they are aware of at least three drivers who have indicated they want to go home.

"We understand there's about 17 of them at the moment and the whole scheme allows for about 30 to be brought over."

He said the union currently had a court proceeding against Keolis, alleging the company had "duped a bunch of people to get on planes to come and work for them with this bonding arrangement in place".

Warnes indicated this arrangement could, under the Australian criminal code, amount to human trafficking and are hoping to prove the bond is not legally binding.

"Under our law over here, if you are induced to get on a plane to leave the country and come into Australia on the promise of something and that something isn't delivered, then that can carry really serious consequences."

The bus company Keolis has rejected the claims, saying the company was upfront with all contractual terms before people signed up.

Warnes said bus contracts in Sydney were funded by the taxpayer and run by private companies like Keolis.

"We, in particular, do not want to see taxpayers' money going into the pockets of private companies that are using these sort of, potentially modern slavery-like conditions on drivers that have been brought from overseas."

Warnes said bus contracts in Sydney were funded by the taxpayer. 123rf

He said the union had spoken to the transport minister about the issue, and it appeared that Keolis had not run the arrangement by the transport department.

"Which is concerning in and of itself that we could have a sort of wildcat cowboy company imposing these sorts of arrangements using taxpayer money."

Warnes said the company has also been promising an "idyllic, relaxed, laid-back lifestyle on the beach in Sydney ".

It was a lifestyle that was not reality due to the long hours, "bumper-to-bumper traffic" and the general low pay for Sydney bus drivers.

"That's why Keolis feels like it needs to try and bond these drivers to the job because they know that it's not what was promised and they know that if they don't have this kind of arrangement, these drivers are just going to get up and leave."

While the bond does scale down the longer that a driver has worked with the company, Warnes said most drivers know they want to leave within the first two weeks.

Warnes said some had brought their families with them and had been cramped into one-bedroom apartments.

Drivers were only given accommodation for their first six weeks and then had to find their own home.

"The Northern beaches of Sydney is one of the most expensive areas... on a bus driver's wage, you just simply cannot afford to live there."

Warnes said he understood the company was currently continuing with the scheme but is hoping it will come to an end with the court proceedings with the potential for government intervention.

"We think that this is the most grave of breaches of public trust... the very least the government could do is shut down this particular practice and then look at how the company responds to that and make decisions accordingly."

In a statement to Nine to Noon Keolis said employees who get relocation assistance sign an agreement detailing the support available and any repayment obligations that may apply.

"These terms are provided and agreed to before employment and relocation begin.

World.title: NZ Warriors coach Andrew Webster backs former All Blacks coach Scott Robertson for shock code switch
World.content:
NZ Warriors coach Andrew Webster has some advice for former All Blacks coach Scott Robertson, if he is to cross codes to guide a proposed South Island NRL side in the near future.

Robertson's name was surprisingly floated this week to steer Southern Orcas, a Christchurch-based bid to become the Aussie competition's 20th franchise.

Orcas president Sir Graham Lowe claimed the organisation had offered the former Crusaders maestro a four-year contract, if it was successful in winning the licence.

Robertson won seven Super Rugby crowns with the Crusaders, making him a popular choice as All Blacks coach, but his reputation took a hit, when he became the first All Blacks coach fired mid-term, after compiling a 20-win, seven-loss record over two years.

Nevertheless, Webster was impressed during his one meeting with Razor.

"I had a coffee with him, Stacey Jones and Darryl Halligan in Christchurch, when we had a trial there a couple of years ago," he recalled. "I think he had just been named All Blacks coach.

"Terrific guy, I learnt a lot off him in two hours. You could see how passionate he is about coaching and about the game."

Robertson has never coached in rugby league, but Webster didn't necessarily think that was a handicap. History is littered with examples of coaches who had switched from rugby to league or vice versa.

Australian Alan Jones coached the Wallabies from 1984-87, before linking with the Balmain Tigers for four seasons, achieving a 36 percent winning record.

Current Ireland and British & Irish Lions rugby coach Andy Farrell played rugby league most of his career, helping Wigan to seven championship crowns, before jumping codes. Webster was Farrell's guest at training last month, when the Irish faced the All Blacks at Eden Park.

Former NZ Kiwis coach David Kidwell was an NRL assistant with South Sydney Rabbitohs, Melbourne Storm, Wests Tigers and Parramatta Eels, before becoming a defensive coach with the Argentina Pumas and Japan, under former Wallabies coach Michael Cheika.

Wigan league legend Andy Farrell has made a successful coaching switch from league to rugby. PHOTOSPORT

Cheika has also flitted backwards and forward across the divide, coaching Lebanon at the Rugby League World Cup and acting as assistant coach with Sydney Roosters.

"I find, if people want to cross codes, they've got to be good man managers and I've heard that he is - he's obviously had a lot of success - and they've got to be willing to make sure they hire people who are absolute experts in their areas of the game," Webster said of Robertson.

"I'm sure Razor, if he got that opportunity - and by the way, he might not want it - I'm sure he's smart enough to realise that and get the right people. I'll leave that up to Razor, but he's a terrific guy."

The Warriors have mixed feelings about the prospect of conceding their monopoly on support on this side of the Tasman.

In June, they hosted North Queensland Cowboys at the new Te Kaha indoor stadium, attracting 25, 365 fans.

Afterwards, Webster was loathe to relinquish grip on a notoriously parochial fanbase that had taken so long to crack.

"I just struggle personally, because I really enjoy the fact that the top of the [country] to the bottom of the [country] are Warriors fans and they love their team," he said afterwards.

"We never used to have that, but we've got the whole country behind us now, not just the region.

"Will it have that same feeling if we add a team? I'm not sure."

The attempt to engage Robertson feels more like a publicity stunt in a part of the country that still fondly remembers his break-dancing victory celebrations.

Another Warrior to cross paths with him early in his career was former St Bede's College product Tanner Stowers-Smith, now an integral member of the Warriors interchange bench.

"I did a bit under Razor with the Junior Crusaders, when I was at school," he said. "Success is success and, with the amount of success he has had, I'm sure he could do something special with a league team.

"Obviously, it's a new code, but there's always room for learning and I wouldn't put it past him to excel there too, with the mindset that he's brought through the Crusaders and the amount of championships they've had under him.

World.title: The Opportunity Party could decide next government, new poll shows
World.content:
The Opportunity Party has the numbers to enter Parliament - and act as kingmaker - according to the latest 1News Verian poll.

The poll, which was taken in the days leading up to the prime minister's confidence vote, has Labour in the lead, and National riding steady.

It suggests a left bloc that includes Opportunity could form a government, after Christopher Luxon ruled out working with the party.

The results of the poll:

Labour: 30 percent, down 2 (38 seats)

National: 29 percent, no change (36 seats)

Green Party: 12 percent, down 1 (15 seats)

ACT: 9 percent, up 3 (11 seats)

New Zealand First: 8 percent, down 3 (10 seats)

Opportunity: 9 percent, up 3 (9 seats)

Te Pāti Māori: 1 percent, down 1 point (6 seats)

11 percent of people said they did not know, or refused to answer.

The 1News Verian poll assumes the current Māori electorate incumbents hold their seats, meaning the poll has a 125-seat Parliament.

It means neither current bloc would have enough seats to form a majority, with Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori on 59, and National, ACT and New Zealand First on 57.

With Opportunity, the left bloc would have 68 seats - enough to govern. If Luxon changed his mind about working with Opportunity, the right bloc would have 66 seats.

Luxon ruled out working with Opportunity near the end of July, while Chris Hipkins officially ruled out New Zealand First earlier this week - earning a rebuke from Winston Peters.

The new poll comes after a bruising day for Christopher Luxon's premiership. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

The poll was conducted from August 8 to 11, with a sample size of 847.

Earlier on Wednesday, the poll revealed a further 1 point drop for Luxon in the preferred prime minister ratings, putting him on 17 percent.

That was still ahead of Chris Hipkins, who was on 15 percent, also down one point.

Rounding out the top three, Winston Peters was on 7 percent, down 3 points.

Chlöe Swarbrick was steady on 6 percent, David Seymour was up 1 point to 5 percent, Erica Stanford was up 1 point to 2 percent, and Kieran McAnulty was also up 1 point to 2 percent.

Another difficult day for Luxon

The new poll comes just hours after Christopher Luxon survived the second attempt to oust him in the past few months.

Luxon held an abrupt press conference on Wednesday afternoon, where he confirmed he had survived that confidence vote.

He said he had the "full support" of the National Party caucus, and was focused on the election.

Later on Wednesday, Luxon confirmed he had removed MP Chris Penk's ministerial portfolios.

"Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said earlier on Wednesday.

Paul Goldsmith is taking up the Defence, Veterans, Space, GCSB, and NZSIS portfolios.

World.title: Legendary boot-studder hangs up his own after 58 years with Port Adelaide
World.content:
He's outlasted big names and seen many more games without the limelight but after nearly six decades looking after boots for Port Adelaide Football Club, Alfie Trebilcock is hanging up his own.

A young butcher from Broken Hill who came to the club during 1968, the boot-studder enjoyed 11 SANFL premierships, one AFL premiership, and watched footwear evolve from ankle-high boots with wooden knock-in sprigs, to light-weight multi-coloured fashion statements.

"I came down here [to Adelaide] in 1961. My grandparents followed Port Adelaide so I started following them and used to go to their games and all that type of thing," Trebilcock told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I got friendly with the runner, Harry Vincent, got talking one day and said I'd like to get into the club and he said, 'I'll keep an eye out for you'."

A position opened up in the boot department and Trebilcock was told to have a "talk to the sprigger" who was also a bootmaker.

"He said, 'Are you prepared to learn?', and I said, 'Oh yeah', so I did a seven-year apprenticeship with him," Trebilcock said.

"After those seven years he got leukaemia and said, 'You're going to have to take over', and I said, 'Gee whiz, I'm a butcher'.

" But I was pretty lucky because moulded soles were coming in then and so I took it on and I've been there ever since and enjoyed every single minute of it. "

But from the day Trebilcock started looking after the players' footwear in 1968 and up to 1976, the Port Adelaide Magpies played without winning a SANFL premiership.

"I was beginning to think I was jinx," Trebilcock said.

But the club won a flag in 1977 and another 10 during Trebilcock's time, as well as a 2004 AFL premiership with its AFL side, The Power.

"The 2004 AFL premiership was mighty.

"I always pictured standing on the MCG on Grand Final day, celebrating a flag. That dream came true in 2004. I'll never, ever forget that day."

Bobby to say farewell as well

Also retiring is fellow volunteer Bob "Bobby" O'Malley after 18 years at the club mixing water barrels and player rehydration bottles, and helping set up for training sessions.

Former Port Adelaide Power player and captain Travis Boak with Bob O'Malley during a game against Carlton. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

"I just loved being involved in this football club," he said.

"Port Adelaide was always a family club, and all my family barracked for Port Adelaide."

He will have his final home game with Port Adelaide against Melbourne on Saturday night.

Trebilcock will be saying goodbye after 58 years with the club.

He said he became "real friends" during this time with the late and great Russel Ebert OAM, who started with the Magpies the same year as him.

An Australian Football Hall of Fame member since 1996, Ebert played 392 games for the Magpies and remains the only SANFL player to win four Magarey Medals.

"He was a people's person," Trebilcock said.

"He was a player that never played a game of football in moulded sole boots. To the day he retired he still had knock-in sprigs.

"Every now and then you'd have to re-sprig his boots.

"As he got older his sprigging would change … then he got his Achilles problems and we made a [raised] heel for him."

The late Russell Ebert shares a laugh with Alfie Trebilcock at Port Adelaide Football Club. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

Ebert once said of Trebilcock that he loved the players and the club, and the players loved him.

"He can talk to any player at any time and would have the complete respect of the entire playing and coaching group … we couldn't have had the success we had without him," Ebert said.

The AFL awarded Trebilcock the Jack Titus Award for conspicuous service to the game in 2013.

He was awarded Life Membership at PAFC in 2013 and was inducted into its Hall of Fame in 2025.

PAFC chairman David Koch said the club was what it was today because of people like O'Malley and Trebilcock.

"Nearly 60 years of turning up, asking for nothing and giving everything to the club he loves," he said.

"On behalf of every player, coach and supporter we say thank you, Alfie, and thank you, Bobby. We are the club we are today because of people like you."

World.title: 'Nowhere to hide' for Australia's under-fire batters against Bangladesh
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan says some of Australia's batters are under pressure to make significant scores as the summer of cricket begins against Bangladesh in the Top End this week.

"If you're in the Australian Test team, and not performing regularly, there is just nowhere to hide," Cowan said on the ABC Cricket Podcast.

"And unfortunately, sometimes you get these weaker teams, and the expectation actually goes up. Cricket is hard enough, let alone with the weight of the world on your shoulders."

The Australian team is about to enter a 12-month period with potentially 21 Tests scheduled, including key away fixtures in India, South Africa and England.

Between June 2025 and the start of this cycle tomorrow, they played eight Tests, five of which were in Australia.

Australia played five of their eight Tests over the last 12 months at home, including the Ashes against England. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"That's two careers, 21 Test matches. You could have two careers in that time. That's a lot of Test cricket," Cowan said.

That cycle begins in Darwin when they take on Bangladesh, a nation ranked ninth in the ICC Test rankings.

At the conclusion of the recent successful Ashes series against England, the average age of the Australian team was just under 34. This is a team that has played together and had great success for a long time.

The Test between Australia and Bangladesh starts on Thursday August 13 in Darwin, and you can hear every ball live on ABC Listen.

Cowan does not believe that playing lower-ranked opposition necessarily provides younger players with a chance to gain experience.

"I think you are trying to pick your best available team and there's always an opportunity to work through your portfolio of players, and they've done this in recent years, usually away from home and it's less opposition dependent and more condition dependent," he said.

The bowling attack has been well established for some time with the likes of Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon proving a recipe for success.

Where the questions creep in is around the batting line-up.

Jake Weatherald was given an opportunity to open the batting in the recent Ashes series but is yet to score an international century, with a top score of 72.

Jake Weatherald will be looking to impress in front of his home crowd in Darwin against Bangladesh (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cowan expects the Northern Territory product to open in the first game, but says he remains under pressure.

"If Jake Weatherald doesn't get 100 in the next five Test matches, more than likely we'll find someone who will get an opportunity to open the batting. And so there's going to be some natural attrition over the coming months," he said.

He is not the only player who will be searching for form in this two-match series against Bangladesh. Marnus Labuschagne has averaged 26.61 with the bat in his last 20 tests and has taken time away from playing to focus on a training block in Queensland.

"After eight weeks of being able to just go back to my fundamentals and working on my game, spending hours and hours on the simple things, just my shots, working on my shapes and my technique as a whole, is something that I definitely needed," Labuschagne told reporters in Brisbane last week.

Loading Instagram content

It has been over 1,100 days since he last reached triple figures in a Test match back in 2023. Cowan believes these Tests could be a step in the right direction for Labuschagne.

"The greatest thing that you can have as a Test batsman is confidence. And confidence is only bred through performance," he said.

The youngest member of Australia's most recent Test team is Cameron Green. When the West Australian debuted in 2020, aged 21, he was touted as one of the best young talents in the country, but his recent form has some questioning his future in the side.

The now 27-year-old has played 37 Tests and has a batting average of 32.75 and a bowling average of 38.94, but Australian coach Andrew McDonald is resolute that Green remains a vital member of his side.

"We believe Cam Green is a very, very skilled player, and we believe, sometimes, his performances have been taken a little bit out of context," McDonald told SEN Radio.

"He's been contributing to this team, as have a lot of that top seven, in conditions that haven't been favourable to batters."

Cowan believes these two Tests present an opportunity for those out of form to find some form at a time when there is less pressure coming from other domestic players.

The last time Australia played a Test against Bangladesh was 2017, where Australia won the series 2-1. (Getty Images: /SOPA Images/LightRocket/Md Manik)

"They get first crack at it. And when there's no other cricket going on, there was a CA XI game that we'll come to, but there's no Shield cricket, there's no Aussie A tours, no-one's putting pressure on anyone," he said.

"It's a bit of a free swing. And in many respects, that should free the batters up to just go and play."

World.title: High school American footballer rattled by snake in helmet
World.content:
A high school American football player in the United States had every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.

A team was going through its paces at Maumelle High school in Central Arkansas when a student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warm-ups and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection.

A slithering 2-foot (61cm) cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.

The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag.

Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.

Cottonmouths are the second-most-venomous snakes found in Arkansas.

Snake caught in bike chain bites woman The woman, in her 60s, was riding on a northern NSW rail trail when she ran over a two-metre snake that became trapped then bit her.

Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he was not bitten.

"It was unreal," Davis said. "You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real."

The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice.

But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, to check for insects or anything larger and more dangerous.

AP

World.title: 'Right to privacy': Scott speaks as Geelong concussion saga continues
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists there has been no negativity around the playing group since Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of the Cats' concussion crisis.

Kolodjashnij, who is out of contract at season's end, faces an uncertain future after being ruled out of playing at any level this weekend.

The 31-year-old has played 11 AFL games this season, but was managed out of the team in round 19 and has since made one appearance in the VFL.

Geelong sits atop the VFL ladder and should make a deep run in the finals, potentially giving Kolodjashnij more opportunities to press his case for an unlikely new contract.

Chris Scott would not be drawn on the details of what's going on behind closed doors at Kardinia Park. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

The mental toll of the saga is unknown, with Scott simply saying Kolodjashnij had been supported by teammates and the club.

The dual premiership coach also refused to go into the exact reasons why Kolodjashnij had been ruled out for the club's matches against North Melbourne this weekend.

Kolodjashnij decided to name himself last Friday, a day after news broke of Geelong's controversial waiver for a previously unidentified player.

"I think any player deserves the right to privacy," Scott said.

"I understand that we are in a public game, and there's a quite savage desire to know certain things.

"I suspect the players are saying, 'Hey mate, if there is anything we can do …'

"In terms of the impact on our broader group, I haven't seen any negativity at all.

Jake Kolodjashnij (right) with brother Kade. Kade was forced into early retirement due to concussion issues. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"I thought our players, as they have done for a long period of time, they just get on with the job.

"Difficult to compartmentalise sometimes, maybe this is a little more challenging than other times, but I'm still pretty confident we can do it.

"Because the situation is the status quo, I haven't felt the need to get an update [on Kolodjashnij].''

Geelong are facing a nervous wait after being issued with a belated "please explain'' for their handling of the secret concussion deal with Kolodjashnij.

The AFL has hired independent legal counsel to help decide on the case.

It was expected the league would wrap up its investigation yesterday, but the findings will likely not be released until early next week.

Kolodjashnij unavailable amid concussion saga Geelong confirms Jake Kolodjashnij will not be available for selection at VFL or AFL level this weekend as the spotlight continues to shine on the club over the controversial secret concussion waiver in his contract.

Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and former Cats president (now AFL Commission boss) Craig Drummond have been under fire since news broke of the controversial waiver.

"There's a part of me that would like to give an impassioned defence of certain people within our club, but I just don't think it would help at the moment," Scott said.

"Even if it is to our detriment, our responsibility, and especially my responsibility, is to respect his [Kolodjashnij's] privacy."

Kolodjashnij dealt with concussions in the 2024 season, but ultimately signed a two-year deal until the end of 2026.

Instead of receiving a definitive answer when forced to face the AFL concussion panel in 2024, Kolodjashnij was left in limbo about playing on or retiring.

His twin brother Kade, who played for the Gold Coast and Melbourne, prematurely retired in 2020 due to concussion.

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, and former number-one pick Paddy McCartin, have also been forced into retirement because of repeated concussions.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
